name: Ade (Yoruba Beaded Crown)
description: The ade is the beaded crown of the Yoruba oba, the king, a cone- or basket-shaped headdress whose cascading fringe of glass beads veils the wearer's face, leaving only the mouth visible as he speaks. The patterns worked in the beads are a language of their own: birds, the Ogboni eye, the royal face, and motifs recalling Oduduwa, the founding ancestor from whom the kingship descends, whose divine gaze the veil is said to shield his subjects from. The crown is worn only at the most solemn moments, enthronement, annual festivals, the great ceremonies of the palace, and when a king dies his ade is buried or retired with him, for the crown is not the ruler's property but the office's. Coronation is unthinkable without it, and the beadwork, done by the royal artisans, may take months for a single crown. In the diaspora the ade has become the emblem of Yoruba monarchy and of the dignity of the ancestral religion.

name: Adinkra Cloth
description: Adinkra is the stamped cloth of the Akan, dyed in dark tones and printed with the symbolic motifs that bear the same name, each one carrying a proverb and a moral lesson: the sankofa bird that looks back to learn, gye nyame, 'except God,' and dozens more that together form a written language in cloth. The dye is made from the bark of the badie tree, boiled down to a deep black, and the blocks are carved from calabash, pressed into the fabric to stamp the patterns row by row. The cloth was traditionally worn at funerals and by the bereaved, its dark ground expressing mourning while the symbols spoke of the virtues of the dead, and it is still made at the great adinkra center of Ntonso in Ghana. Today the symbols have spread far beyond the cloth, appearing in architecture, jewelry and design, but the textile remains the root of the tradition. Adinkra cloth is wisdom made wearable.

name: Aegis
description: The storm-bearing shield of Zeus, lent to Athena and sometimes Apollo, an aegis of goatskin fringed with gold tassels; in Homer it scatters armies with terror and houses the gorgoneion, the severed head of Medusa. Hephaestus forged its golden version for Zeus, and the aegis became Athena's emblem in art, worn over her breast or carried on her arm. It marks divine protection and terror in Greek epic, and the name later passed into ordinary speech for any protecting force or shield of authority. The gorgoneion set on its face remained a common apotropaic image on shields and buildings through antiquity.

name: Aegis
description: The aegis, the storm-shield of Zeus, is the awesome goatskin or bronze buckler with which the god of the Iliad terrifies armies and shakes the field of battle, and which his daughter Athena also wears in the fight; its name, from the Greek for 'goat', points to its origin as a ritual skin, though Homer treats it as a wrought shield forged by Hephaestus. Its surface bears the severed head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turns all who meet it to stone, so that the shield is as much a weapon of terror as a defence. Zeus lends the aegis to his champions and shakes it as a sign of wrath, and in Athena's hands it accompanies the goddess of war and wisdom into battle. In art the aegis appears as a scaly breastplate fringed with serpents, with the gorgoneion at its centre. The word has passed into English for any protective backing or patronage.

name: Agadez Cross Pendant
description: The Agadez cross, or tanaghilt, is the best-known of the Tuareg silver pendants of Niger, a cruciform amulet with four or more arms radiating from a central square, traditionally cast by the smiths (inadan) of Agadez. Agadez and the wider Air region have their own named cross designs, and the form is sometimes said to be a stylised map, a key, or the four directions that guard the wearer on the paths of life. The pendant is given at the passages of life, at a birth, a naming, an initiation, or a marriage, and it is worn by both men and women as a protective amulet, especially in the desert, where silver is believed to bring safety and luck. Older pieces are worked in silver and niello, while modern crosses are also cast in gold for the jewellery trade. Beyond Niger, the Agadez cross has become an emblem of Tuareg culture worldwide, appearing on flags and in the tourist crafts of the Sahara even as the full meaning of the form remains a matter of oral tradition.

name: Ajrak
description: The ajrak is the block-printed shawl of Sindh, stamped in deep indigo and madder red with concentric borders of geometric stars, flowers and trellis patterns, worn over the shoulder and used to cover sacred objects. The name is linked to the Arabic word for blue, and archaeologists point to indigo-dyed and resist-printed cotton found at the Indus valley site of Mohenjo-daro as evidence that such cloth was made in the region thousands of years ago. A single ajrak may pass through some twenty-one stages of washing, printing and dyeing, using wooden blocks carved by hereditary craftsmen and mordants of iron and alum, so the finished shawl carries the redness of the earth and the blue of the river. It is a strong marker of Sindhi identity, draped at weddings, offered to guests and honoured guests, and presented as a mark of respect on formal occasions.

name: Akan Goldweight (Abrammuo)
description: The Akan goldweight, the abrammuo, is a small cast-brass piece used from the fifteenth century onward to weigh gold dust in the trade of present-day Ghana, one of the great mercantile tools of the Atlantic world. The weights were cast by the lost-wax method, and the figurative ones depict animals, people, proverbs, objects and scenes of daily life in miniature, each one with a story to tell. The art of the weights lay in the proverb: a man could hand his companion a weight of a crocodile with a bird, and the pair would 'speak' the proverb it illustrated, making the weights a language in the marketplace. They were kept in carved boxes or purses with brass spoons and balances, and their quality was judged by law, with penalties for false weights. Collectors prize them as sculpture, but they began as everyday instruments of commerce. The goldweight joins trade, law and orature into a single small object.

name: Aladdin's Lamp
description: The lamp of the tale of Aladdin, added to the Thousand and One Nights by Antoine Galland from the oral telling of the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab and first printed around 1709. Rubbing it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes, while its twin, the old magician's lamp, drove the plot's theft and recovery, exchanged by the sorcerer for new lamps. No medieval Arabic original of the tale survives, so the lamp is a literary invention of the folk tradition, set, like the story, in China while speaking a Syrian idiom. The image of the rubbed lamp and its wish-granting servant became one of the most widely known of all magical objects, carried into every later retelling and adaptation from pantomime to film, and its shape still means 'genie' in world popular culture.

name: Alms Bowl Relic
description: The alms-bowl relic is the bowl that the Buddha is said to have used for his daily begging round, which became a sacred object after his death together with his tooth, his staff and other personal belongings. According to a well-known legend recorded in Gandharan art and later Buddhist texts, after the enlightenment four guardian kings, the lokapalas, each offered the Buddha a stone bowl, and the Buddha miraculously fused the four into one, so that he had a single vessel of modest size for his food. Monks of the Theravada tradition still beg with an alms bowl, holding it in both hands while householders place food in it, and the bowl is for a monk one of his few possessions, a reminder of simplicity and of the gift of the laity. In various Buddhist countries the alms bowl of the Buddha was claimed as a relic by rival pilgrim sites, and the Chinese tradition asserts that the original bowl was carried to China, where it was long venerated. For the believer the bowl embodies the Buddha's poverty and his dependence on the generous, and its veneration is part of the cult of the relics.

name: Altai Komus (Jew's Harp)
description: Jew's harp of the Altai people, usually of metal or wood with a flexible tongue, played by strumming the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The komus is widely used for personal music and to accompany songs; its voice imitates natural sounds. It belongs to the same family of Siberian mouth harps as the Yakut khomus and the Buryat khuur. The player shapes the note with the mouth and breath, producing a low drone with ringing overtones that can mimic the wind, a running stream, or the calls of birds. In Altai tradition the komus was played by young men courting, by shepherds in the mountain pastures, and by singers practising the khoomei throat styles, and it is sometimes said that the sound of the komus carries the voice of the taiga itself. The instrument is small enough to be carried in the pocket, and its repertoire is largely improvised. Today the komus is performed at festivals, taught in music schools, and prized in the pan-Siberian revival of the mouth harp.

name: Amauti
description: The amauti is the woman's parka of the Inuit, cut from caribou skin with a large hood and a deep pouch across the back, the amaut, in which a baby rides warm against its mother's body. The pouch lets the child nurse and sleep without being lifted into the cold, while the hood shields mother and child together from the wind, and the whole garment is sewn with the legendary precision of Inuit women, who cut and stitch by eye so that the seams shed weather. A well-made amauti is a work of both craft and love, the fit of the pouch, the length of the tails, the fur trim at the hood's edge are all judged by the women who wear them. The garment is so central to Arctic motherhood that its making was a skill passed from mother to daughter over generations. Today the amauti is still worn in the North, and contemporary Inuit designers have carried its shape into modern fashion as a proud mark of identity.

name: Amber Jewelry
description: Necklaces, pendants, and beads of Baltic amber, the fossil resin thrown up on Danish shores, worn as adornment and as protection since the Stone Age. Danish Bronze Age graves hold hundreds of amber beads, and amber amulets were believed to guard against the evil eye and sickness, while small amber figures of animals and tools were made for magic and trade. In the Baltic legend the sea-goddess Jurate's palace of amber broke apart, and the pieces scattered across the waves became the amber that still washes up on the beaches. The stone's warmth and light have given it a lasting place in charms for health and luck.

name: Ancient Egyptian Kohl Tube
description: The kohl tube is a small cylindrical vessel used in ancient Egypt to hold kohl, the black and green eye paint worn by men and women from the Old Kingdom onward. Eye paint was prepared by grinding minerals on a slate palette and mixing the powder with fat, then applying it around the eyes with a stick; green paint from malachite was mainly cosmetic, while black paint from galena protected the eyes from the glare of the sun and, because of its lead content, repelled flies and bacteria that could cause eye disease. Kohl was so valued that the ancient Egyptians ranked it second only to water as a preventive of disease, and tubes were made from wood, faience and glass, often with a small applicator stick and a pin at the base. Some New Kingdom tubes, especially from the Ramesside period of the 13th to 11th centuries BCE, were decorated with the figure of the dwarf god Bes, whose fearsome image was invoked to drive away the supernatural forces believed to cause eye infections. The word kohl itself, of Arabic origin, later spread across the Islamic world for the same dark cosmetic used to line the eyes.

name: Ancile
description: The ancile was the sacred shield of Mars that fell from heaven in the reign of Numa Pompilius, Rome's second king, and was kept as a pledge that the city would rule the world as long as the shield was preserved. Fearing theft, Numa had the smith Mamurius Veturius make eleven identical copies, so that the twelve shields carried in procession by the Salian priests could not be told apart, and the legend adds that Mamurius asked as his only reward that his name be sung in the Salian hymn. Plutarch, Ovid in the Fasti, and Servius all tell the story, and the Salii struck the bronze ancilia with staffs as they danced through the city each March at the opening of the campaigning season. The shield thus joined the palladium and the fire of Vesta among the pignora imperii, the tokens of Rome's eternity. Its name passed into later usage as a word for any safeguard of the state.

name: Andvaranaut
description: Andvaranaut is the ring at the heart of the cursed gold of the dwarf Andvari, taken from him by Loki at the waterfall Gnitaheiðr after the god caught the dwarf in the shape of a pike. When Andvari was forced to give up his treasure hoard, he kept a single ring, and when Loki wrenched that away too, the dwarf laid a curse on the gold: it would destroy every possessor who came after him. The treasure passed to the chieftain Hreiðmarr as wergild for his murdered son Otr, then to the dragon Fáfnir, and finally to the hero Sigurðr, and ruin followed each owner. The story is told in the Völsunga saga and echoed in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied, and Andvaranaut is widely seen as the direct ancestor of the Ring of the Nibelung in Richard Wagner's opera cycle. Its name, 'Andvari's gift', has become shorthand for a treasure that brings only doom.

name: Ankh
description: The ankh, the looped cross that is the Egyptian hieroglyph for 'life', is the most recognisable of Egyptian symbols, appearing on temple walls, tomb paintings, and amulets for more than three thousand years. Shaped as a cross with a looped handle, it was carried by gods and goddesses, who hold it to the nostrils of kings and of the dead to breathe life into them, and pharaohs are shown with the ankh as the sign of the eternal life that kingship conferred. It is at once a writing sign, a sacred object, and a talisman: placed on the lips and eyes of mummies, worn as jewellery, and offered to the deceased in the scenes of the Book of the Dead. Through the Coptic Church, whose cross owes its form to the ankh, the sign became the crux ansata of Christian Egypt. It has been adopted in modern culture as a symbol of life and of the African heritage. Its meaning, simply and permanently, is life itself.

name: Ardagh Chalice
description: The Ardagh Chalice is a two-handled silver cup made in Ireland in the eighth century AD and found in 1868, together with a hoard of other church metalwork and a bronze pin, inside a ring-fort at Ardagh in County Limerick. The vessel is built of silver with a bronze core, and its decoration of gold filigree, glass studs and enamel panels, executed in the interlacing animal style of Insular art, ranks it among the greatest treasures of early medieval Europe. It was probably made for use at Mass in a wealthy monastery, and it shares its technical brilliance with the contemporary Derrynaflan Chalice and the illuminated gospel manuscripts of the same age. The hoard in which it was found had been concealed in a stone-lined hollow beneath the fort, apparently during a time of danger. The chalice is displayed in the National Museum of Ireland in Dublin, where it is a centrepiece of the medieval collection and a national icon.

name: Arrows of Cupid
description: The arrows of Cupid in Ovid's Metamorphoses are of two kinds: the golden-headed shaft that kindles love and the blunt leaden one that drives love away, and the pair together explain the passions of gods and mortals alike. When Apollo taunts Cupid about his bow, the boy shoots the golden arrow into Apollo and the leaden into the nymph Daphne, so that the god burns with desire while she flees him in terror, and the chase ends only when Daphne is changed into the laurel tree. The two arrows turn love and rejection into a kind of physics of the heart, a divine mechanism behind human obsession and coldness alike. The imagery was taken up endlessly in Renaissance and Baroque art, where a gold-tipped and a lead-tipped shaft dangle from Cupid's quiver. The motif survives in the everyday phrase 'arrows of love' and in Cupid's double quiver as the emblem of love's cruelty and arbitrariness.

name: Arthur's Mantle
description: Arthur's mantle, Llen Arthur, is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain in medieval Welsh tradition. Whoever wore the cloak became invisible, yet could still see everything about him, a power that made it a garment of spies and guardians. The treasure list, which survives in several Welsh manuscripts from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, records the object among the possessions of the old heroes of British legend, and one version places the mantle 'in Cornwall'. The cloak belongs to the Welsh Arthur of marvel and quest, distinct from the later continental king of Malory and the French romances. Its power of selective invisibility, hiding the wearer while leaving his sight intact, is echoed in later folklore and fantasy. Unlike Arthur's sword and ship, the mantle appears nowhere outside the Welsh treasure catalogue, and it remains one of the more mysterious items in the list.

name: Asson
description: The asson is the sacred rattle of Haitian Vodou, a gourd fitted with a handle and wrapped in a beaded net threaded with snake vertebrae, held only by the houngan or the mambo, the priest and priestess who lead the congregation. Its sound opens the ceremony: as the rattle is shaken before the peristyle, the lwa, the spirits, are called into the space, and its rhythm marks the moment they descend to possess the faithful. The beads are strung in the colors of the spirits, white for Damballah, the great serpent, black and red for Legba, yellow for Kouzen Zaka, and the gourd is kept consecrated, rubbed with red palm oil and cinnamon so that it grows dark and glossy with use. The asson is given to the priest only at the end of a long initiation, and handling another's asson is a grave offense; a related instrument, the chacha, serves the Petro rites. The rattle is thus the credential and the voice of the priest, the object that rings the spirits into the world of the living.

name: Atlatl
description: The atlatl is the carved wooden spear-thrower that hurls darts with far greater force than an unaided arm, used across Mesoamerica from the Olmec era through the Aztec empire and beyond. Spanish accounts and Aztec codices show warriors and hunters gripping the notched end of the thrower while the dart rests in its socket, and its power is credited with punching through the cotton armour and even the mail of the Spanish at short range. The atlatl was also a ritual object: the great Aztec festivals included darts thrown in honour of the gods, and the weapon appears in the hand of deities such as Huitzilopochtli in the codices. The thrower was made of hard wood, sometimes decorated with shell and turquoise, and the socket that fits the dart's butt allowed the lever to add speed and reach. The atlatl survived in the New World long after it fell out of use elsewhere, and it is the ancestor of the spear-throwing devices of the Americas.

name: Azerbaijani Carpet
description: The Azerbaijani carpet is the hand-knotted pile rug of Azerbaijan, woven on vertical looms in distinct regional schools - Karabakh, Shirvan, Tabriz, Baku, Gazakh and Ganja among them - each with its own palette, knot and field layout. The traditional repertoire of motifs includes the buta, the dragon, the medallion, the stylised garden and the khoncha offering tray, and the carpets combine rich reds, blues and ivories dyed from madder, indigo and walnut husk. Weaving was and is a women's craft, learned in the family, with the design passing from mother to daughter and the loom set up for dowry carpets that would serve the household for generations. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving on the Representative List, and the carpet remains Azerbaijan's best-known craft, displayed in national museums and in the carpet museum of Baku.

name: Aztec Death Whistle
description: The Aztec death whistle, sometimes called ehecachichtli or skull whistle, is a small clay whistle about three to five centimetres long, modelled as a human skull, whose internal chambers produce a shrill, wind-like and unsettling tone. The most famous examples were excavated in the late 1990s at Tlatelolco, clasped in the hands of a sacrificed man buried before a temple of the wind god Ehecatl, and they have been linked to both Ehecatl and the death god Mictlantecuhtli. Scholars such as Arnd Adje Both argue the original instruments mimicked the howling winds that Aztec souls met in the underworld rather than a human scream; the terrifying shriek heard in popular recordings comes from larger modern replicas. Whether they were blown in battle to frighten enemies is sometimes said but remains unproven, since none have been found on battlefields or in warrior graves. The whistle's grim fame has nonetheless made it a museum and internet sensation, with replicas sold worldwide.

name: Baba Yaga's Mortar and Pestle
description: Iron mortar and pestle ridden by Baba Yaga, the witch of Russian fairy tales, who flies over the forest in her mortar, sweeping away her trail with a broom and driving the mortar onward with the pestle. In Afanasyev's tales she is called 'Baba Yaga the Bone Leg' and travels in this way; the mortar, pestle and broom are among the most iconic props of Russian folk narrative. Folklorists note that the mortar echoes the work of grain-pounding and the boundary between the farmstead and the wild, fitting the witch who lives at the edge of the forest. She is sometimes said to fly at great speed, using the pestle as her engine and the broom to erase her traces so that pursuers cannot follow. The trio of mortar, pestle and broom has passed into art, film and illustration wherever Baba Yaga appears, and remains instantly recognisable even outside Slavic tradition.

name: Baganda Barkcloth (Olubugo)
description: Olubugo is the barkcloth of the Baganda of Uganda, made by stripping the inner bark of the mutuba fig tree and beating it with wooden mallets until it becomes a soft, pliable, chestnut-brown textile. The craft is usually practised by men, who peel the bark in the wet season and beat it on a log, folding and turning the sheet until it reaches the desired fineness, and a single tree can be harvested again and again. In the Buganda kingdom, barkcloth was the dress of kings and chiefs, worn in layers that grew thicker with rank, and it was also used in burial, wrapping the dead and lining the royal tombs of Kasubi. Because it belonged to the court and the ancestors, the cloth carries sacred associations, and it is still worn and laid out at funerals and important rituals. UNESCO inscribed Baganda barkcloth-making on the list of intangible cultural heritage in 2005, and makers in the Kampala region produce cloth for ceremony and for the contemporary art and fashion markets alike.

name: Bagua Mirror
description: The bagua mirror is a circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy, sha qi, and to return an attacker's evil gaze. In domestic use it is placed above the main door or facing a threatening structure such as a road, a corner, or a neighbour's roof-ridge, so that the mirror deflects or reflects the influence back to its source. The mirror also appears in Daoist talismanic practice, paired with written spells against hauntings and possession, and the convex form is said to disperse harm while the concave form gathers or focuses it. Because of its power to reflect, the bagua mirror is one of the few feng shui remedies that practitioners advise using with care, lest the mirrored effect fall on an innocent. The object joins the practical science of geomancy to the older Chinese belief in mirrors as revealers of spirits, a connection that goes back to the bronze mirrors of the Han period.

name: Balalaika (Russian Triangular Lute)
description: Three-stringed Russian lute with a characteristic triangular body, plucked or strummed to accompany folk songs and dances. The balalaika became a symbol of Russian folk music in the 19th century, when Vasily Andreyev standardised its sizes into a whole family of instruments; it is played solo and in orchestras, and its bright, percussive tone carries well in open-air music-making. The body is usually of spruce or maple, with three strings historically of gut and now of nylon or metal, and the left hand often uses a single downward stroke that produces the crisp, rhythmic drive of dance tunes. Andreyev's balalaika orchestra, founded in 1888, gave the instrument respectability and set off a craze for balalaika ensembles across Europe. It remains the best-known Russian folk instrument abroad, appearing in concert halls, films and comedy routines alike, and its solo repertoire is still taught in Russian music schools.

name: Bamileke Elephant Mask
description: Beaded elephant masks of the Cameroon Grassfields are worn by men's societies of the Bamileke and related peoples, who dance them at the funerals of notables, the installation of chiefs, and the festivals of the kwifo, the regulatory society that enforces chiefly authority. The mask takes the shape of an elephant head, with broad flat ears and a central trunk, and is built over carved wood or a cloth and raffia frame before being covered in glass beads in the royal colours of the chiefdom. The elephant, like the leopard, belongs to the forest powers that underwrite Grassfields kingship, and the mask links the wearer, the fon, and the world of the bush spirits. Only society members and people of rank may wear or even touch such masks, which are kept hidden and given offerings in the chiefdom's storehouses. Collections in European and American museums have carried the form worldwide, and Grassfields bead artists continue the tradition today.

name: Bamum Beaded Throne (Mandu Yenu)
description: The Mandu Yenu is the royal throne of the Bamum kingdom of the Cameroon Grassfields, a carved wooden stool and footstool completely encased in glass beads, cowrie shells, and brass studs. Mandu Yenu means 'rich in beads', and the most famous example, made for the Bamum court in the nineteenth century, was given by King Njoya to the German Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1908 and now rests in Berlin; a near-identical copy he commissioned remains in the palace at Foumban. The carving carries royal symbols such as the two-headed snake and the spider of wisdom, while two large figures, the protective twins Mandu and Yenu, stand behind the seat, and smaller rifle-bearing figures on the footrest speak of military might. The beads from Europe and cowries from the Indian Ocean were costly imports, so the encrusted surface itself proclaimed the king's reach. In Bamum belief the throne was bound to the authority of the fon, and the Berlin throne remains central to debates over colonial-era restitution.

name: Banarasi Sari
description: The Banarasi sari is the handwoven silk sari of Varanasi (Banaras) in Uttar Pradesh, famous for its rich brocade, its gold and silver zari, and its intricate pictorial motifs, among them the jangla (vine), bel (creeper), kalga and jal patterns. The weaving tradition grew under the patronage of the Mughal court, which encouraged Persian-inspired floral and arabesque designs in silk and metal thread, and the craft produced the heavy, opulent fabric called kinkhab, woven with real gold thread. A Banarasi sari is woven on a manually operated pit loom, and a single elaborate piece can take weeks or months of work by a karigar, the brocade being built up in fine threads on the wrong side of the cloth. The sari is the classic bridal costume of the region, worn as a symbol of marriage and prosperity, and its silk is still produced in the workshops of the old city, though zari is now often of silver or imitation. In 2009 the Banarasi sari received a Geographical Indication tag, protecting the name for genuine Varanasi work.

name: Bandura (Ukrainian Zither-Lute)
description: Plucked string instrument of Ukraine combining a lute's neck with a zither-like soundboard holding up to several dozen strings, played by folk singers called bandurysts and kobzars. The kobzar tradition of singing epic dumy to the bandura is among Ukraine's most distinctive musical heritage; the instrument descends from the older kobza and spread across Ukraine from at least the 18th century. In performance the player fingers the melody on the neck while sweeping across the accompaniment strings on the soundboard, producing a resonant, harp-like texture. The blind kobzars who wandered the villages singing historical ballads were famed for long improvisations, and the term 'kobzar' became a byword for the wandering epic singer. The instrument survived the suppression of the kobzar guilds in the Soviet era and is now taught in conservatories, performed in ensembles, and honoured at festivals of Ukrainian music.

name: Bangmangi
description: The bangmangi is the magic club of the dokkaebi, the mischievous goblin of Korean folklore, which grants whatever a person wishes when it is struck. In the folktales the dokkaebi owns the club and uses it to summon food, gold, and servants, and clever humans trick the gullible goblin into surrendering it: a thief or a poor man persuades the dokkaebi that a beating with the club will bring a blessing, then runs off with the prize. In other variants the club is swapped, or its possessor uses it to draw endless rice and healing, and the object is so tied to its owner that the dokkaebi and its bangmangi are nearly interchangeable in stories. The club appears in the collected Korean tales of Im Bang and Yi Ryuk and in the oral tradition of the pansori storytellers, and it remains a beloved fixture of Korean children's literature and animation. The bangmangi embodies the dokkaebi's double nature as both threat and source of luck.

name: Batá Drum
description: The batá is the consecrated drum of Cuban Santería, an hourglass-shaped instrument with two heads of different sizes, played in a set of three, the small okónkolo, the middle itótele and the great iyá, the mother drum that speaks the lead voices. The drums descend from the Yoruba bata of West Africa, carried to Cuba by enslaved people and kept alive behind the Catholic saints, and their rhythms are said to speak the language of the orishas during ceremonies, each rhythm belonging to a particular spirit. A consecrated batá has the orisha Añá installed within it, and only initiated male drummers, omo Añá, may play it; the drums are never allowed to touch the ground and are fed and dressed when not in use. Changó, the thunder deity, is held to be the drums' spiritual owner. The iyá leads and the smaller drums answer, and together they call the orishas down into the gathering; beyond the temple, batá rhythms entered Cuban music and from there the world, but the sacred instrument remains the heart of the religion it serves.

name: Baule Goli Mask
description: The goli is a round-faced, painted mask of the Baule people of the Ivory Coast, worn with a full costume during village celebrations, funerals, and the dances of the goli society. The word names a whole sequence of masks that appear in a fixed order, from the round kpan faces through animal forms to the large, frightening figured masks, a progression that retraces the Baule cosmos and the order of communal life. Male and female variants dance in pairs, and the female face, with its calm forehead and scarified temples, is regarded as the model of Baule beauty. The dance is closely tied to the goli spirit powers believed to enter the masked dancers, and the performances draw the entire village together at moments of joy and mourning. In Baule belief the mask is not decoration but a doorway for those powers, which is why its storage and handling follow strict tradition.

name: Benin Bronze Plaque
description: The Benin bronzes are the cast-brass plaques that once covered the pillars of the Oba's palace in the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, depicting the king, his warriors, chiefs and courtiers in high relief against openwork backgrounds. They were made by the guild of the Igun quarter using lost-wax casting, a craft reserved for the palace, and they record royal history, court protocol, the regalia of office and even the Portuguese visitors who came to the coast in the sixteenth century. In 1897 a British punitive expedition took the city, looted the palace and carried thousands of objects to Europe, where they entered museums from London to Berlin; the word bronze is traditional, but most of the plaques are brass, an alloy of copper and zinc. The plaques have since become the center of one of the world's great restitution debates, as Nigeria and the museums negotiate their return. They remain masterpieces of African cast metalwork and a record of a kingdom that Europeans both traded with and destroyed.

name: Betel and Areca Tray
description: The betel and areca tray is the lacquered brass container that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the essential offering of Vietnamese hospitality, courtship, and marriage ritual. In the founding legend two twin brothers, Cao and Lang, loved the same woman; when the woman married Cao, Lang wandered away and died by a stream, and Cao, grieving, drowned himself; the woman then died too. The gods transformed the brothers into the areca tree and the betel vine that climbs it, and the woman into the limestone that binds their flavour, so that the chewing of betel and areca joins the three together in eternal kinship. The tray is presented at weddings as a symbol of this bond, offered to guests as a mark of respect, and placed before ancestors during rites. In village custom the exchange of betel seals a promise, and the phrase 'to invite betel' still means to ask for a daughter's hand. The tray is among the most symbolic household objects of Vietnamese culture.

name: Bhutanese Festival Mask
description: The Bhutanese festival mask is a carved and painted wooden face worn by dancers in the cham dances of Bhutanese monasteries, taking the forms of fierce deities, animals, black-hatted dancers and the skeleton guardians of the faith. The tradition of cham is said to have been brought to the Himalayan world by the teacher Padmasambhava, and the dances are performed in the courtyards of the dzongs during the yearly tsechu festivals, when onlookers gather to see the masked dancers turn in slow circles to drum and cymbal. Each mask follows strict iconographic rules, and the identities of the dancers are kept within the monasteries, while the lay people watch and are held to receive blessing and protection from the performance. The festival masks are made by Bhutanese carvers, painted with mineral colours, and are among the most recognisable art forms of the kingdom.

name: Bilum (Loop String Bag)
description: Loop-woven string bag made and worn by women across Papua New Guinea, worked in a continuous spiral of knotless looping that varies in gauge and pattern from region to region. Carried on the head, over the shoulder or around the neck, it holds garden produce, firewood and bush tucker, and in the Highlands it cradles infants, who travel in a woman's bilum until they can walk. Made originally from bush vines and bark fibre and today often from brightly coloured synthetic yarn, a single bilum can take weeks of work and carries meaning in every stitch. Bilums are given as prestigious gifts at marriage, childbirth, feasts and mourning rites, and their designs and colours can mark the wearer's clan and homeland.

name: Birchbark Canoe
description: The birchbark canoe, wiigwaasi-jiimaan in Ojibwe, is the light, silent and remarkably strong craft built of sheets of birchbark sewn over a cedar frame with spruce root and sealed with spruce gum, the great carrier of the Anishinaabe and other northern peoples. Light enough for one person to carry across a portage, a full canoe could still move families, furs and goods across hundreds of miles of lakes and rivers, which is why French traders and the voyageurs adopted it wholesale. Master builders selected a smooth-barked birch, stripped the bark in the right season, and shaped the craft with the same materials and joinery used for centuries. The canoe also runs through the region's stories, from the flying canoe of the Passamaquoddy to the journeys of culture heroes. Today a handful of carvers still build bark canoes, and museums preserve the finest examples of this northern engineering triumph.

name: Bjargástafur
description: Bjargástafur, the 'rescue stave' or 'saving stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn so that the bearer could escape or survive any danger. Its name derives from the verb bjarga, 'to save', and the grimoire tradition promises that no misfortune could hold a person who bore it, whether on land, at sea, or in a dispute. It is one of the general talismans of protection in Icelandic folk magic, carried on paper, carved on wood, or worn on the person in times of peril. Like all the galdrastafir, its earliest known source is a 19th-century manuscript that gathered older material, and it is now widely reproduced in books and on jewellery. The rescue stave remains popular today as a general symbol of safety and deliverance.

name: Bogolanfini Mud Cloth
description: Bogolanfini, the mud cloth of the Bamana of Mali, is a cotton textile painted by women with a dye of fermented river mud, worked over a yellow ground to leave dark geometric patterns that record proverbs, clan histories and the teachings of initiation. The cloth is made in a slow sequence: the cotton is washed and dyed with a yellow infusion of leaves, then the designs are drawn in mud, which reacts with the yellow to leave a deep brown-black as the background is rinsed away. The cloths were worn at initiations, by hunters, and by women at the turning points of life, and the patterns are held to protect the wearer and to carry the memory of the family. Since the 1980s bogolan has left the village for the fashion world, worn by Malian musicians and designers and celebrated as a national art. Each bolt of bogolanfini is a document of the society that made it, written in earth.

name: Bogrács
description: The bogrács is the black cast-iron cauldron of Hungarian outdoor cooking, a three-legged pot suspended from a chain over an open fire, in which gulyás, pörkölt and fish stew are boiled and stirred with a long wooden spoon. The vessel dates from the world of the herdsmen of the Hungarian Plain, who cooked their one-pot meals over campfires, and the same pot is still the centrepiece of bográcsgulyás gatherings at weekends, feasts and village festivals. Its size and weight vary from small two-litre pots to great cauldrons for hundreds of eaters, and the cast iron is seasoned by use, giving the stew its characteristic smoky savour. Cooking in the bogrács is a slow, sociable ritual - the meat is seared, onion and paprika added, and the pot tended for hours - and for many Hungarians the cauldron over flame is the very image of hospitality and good eating.

name: Bolas
description: The bolas, or boleadoras, are throwing weights of the South American plains: two or three stone or iron balls, often covered in hide, joined by braided cords of leather. The hunter or gaucho swings them overhead and releases them to wrap around the legs of fleeing cattle, horses or rheas, tangling the animal in an instant fall. The weapon was developed by the Indigenous peoples of the Pampas and Patagonia and adopted wholesale by the colonial herders, and chroniclers recorded its use among the Mapuche and Tehuelche; a heavier solid type, the bolas perdidas, was hurled at enemies in war. The gaucho made the bolas his own, and the tool became so identified with him that it appears throughout the gauchesque literature, most famously in José Hernández's epic poem Martín Fierro. Today it survives in the cattle country of Argentina and Uruguay, used by the last horse-riding vaqueanos and kept alive as a symbol of the pampas.

name: Boomerang
description: The boomerang is the curved throwing stick of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, carved from hardwood and used for hunting, fighting, digging and ceremony. Returning boomerangs are shaped with a twist across the wings so that they curve in flight and come back to the thrower, while heavier non-returning forms are hurled flat and low to strike game or an enemy, and the same shapes were used as clapsticks, digging tools and fire-sticks. The weapons are sometimes engraved or painted with the designs of the maker's clan. The returning boomerang is one of the oldest known engineered tools and was taken up worldwide as a sport object, while in Australia the boomerang remains an emblem of Aboriginal skill and appears in Dreaming stories and modern cultural display.

name: Borgund Stave Church
description: The best-preserved of Norway's stave churches, built around 1180 at Borgund in Sogn and never drastically altered since. Its stacked tiers of steep gabled roofs, four carved dragon-head finials, and decorated west portal are the classic image of the stave church, and the interior keeps medieval furnishings, runic graffiti cut by medieval visitors, and one of the oldest surviving altars in Norway. The building stands today much as its builders left it, its timber frame and tarred shingles intact, and it has served as the model for church designs and for the stave-church revival of the 19th century. It is owned by the Society for the Preservation of Norwegian Ancient Monuments.

name: Bow of Odysseus
description: The great bow of Odysseus, which no other man could string and which he alone could drive an arrow through all twelve axe heads, stands at the centre of the final test of the Odyssey. Penelope sets the contest of the bow for her suitors at Ithaca, and when the strongest of them fail even to bend it, the disguised Odysseus takes the weapon, strings it effortlessly, shoots through the axes, and then turns it on the suitors, slaughtering them with the help of his son and his faithful servants. The poem relates that the bow was a gift from Iphitus, a token of their friendship given in youth, and it had been left at home in Ithaca when Odysseus sailed for Troy, so that it keeps its place as the symbol of the household and its absent master. Its unyielding curve measures the hero's identity: only the true master of the house can draw it. The bow remains the emblem of Odysseus' patient cunning and of the return that restores order to Ithaca.

name: Brass Urli
description: The urli is the wide, shallow brass vessel of South India, most often associated with the kitchens and courtyards of Kerala and Tamil Nadu, where it holds water, flowers and floating candles for decoration or worship. Traditional urulis are hammered or spun from brass and bell metal with a flared rim, and in a Malayali home one may stand on the floor of the entrance hall piled with fresh flowers, or be pressed into service as a cooking and storing pot for rice and water. In temples and festivals the urli has a ceremonial role, holding oil for the brass lamps that are floated in it or receiving offerings of fruit and garlands, and the wide bowl is also used as a base into which a tall traditional oil lamp is set. Because brass is durable and easily polished, old urulis are passed down as household treasures, and the vessel appears in Malayali folk memory as a wedding gift, an heirloom and a standard prop of the naturalistic home garden.

name: Briar Rose's Spinning Wheel
description: The spinning wheel in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Briar Rose' (Dornröschen, KHM 50) is the instrument of the sleeping curse: the princess pricks her finger on its spindle, and the whole castle falls asleep for a hundred years. The king had ordered every spindle in the land burned to cheat the witch's prophecy, but an old woman in a forgotten tower still spins, and curiosity leads the princess to the fatal prick. When the prince at last cuts through the hedge of thorns and wakes the princess with a kiss, the spindle's curse is undone and the castle stirs back to life. The tale is the German form of the widespread Sleeping Beauty story, and the spinning wheel is its local signature, replacing the flax and distaff of older versions. Spinning in folklore is linked with fate, age and magic, so the wheel carries symbolic weight beyond the plot. The story was popularised in the Grimms' collection and in Perrault's and later cinematic retellings.

name: Bridal Crown
description: The bridal crown (brudkrona), a crown of gilt silver or brass that Swedish churches owned and lent to brides for the wedding ceremony. The custom, recorded from the Middle Ages, made the bride a 'crowned bride' and the crown a symbol of honour and virginity. Rules sometimes required a fee, and the crown was kept locked in the church between weddings. The crown became common in Sweden only after the Reformation, when it spread from the nobility and the towns to country parishes in the seventeenth century; it was usually owned by the parish itself, lent out for the wedding and locked away again afterwards. Made of gilt silver with red and green glass set in imitation of gems, it recalled the crown of the Virgin Mary, and a bride who had once worn it was said to keep that honour for life. The fee charged for the lending supported the church, and the rules could be strict: the crown was returned the same day, and its use bound the bride to a good name.

name: Bridle of Bellerophon
description: The golden bridle Athena gave the Corinthian hero Bellerophon to tame the winged horse Pegasus, the instrument that let him ride the stallion and, mounted, destroy the fire-breathing Chimera of Lycia. Apollodorus records the dream in which Athena brought the bridle to Bellerophon as he slept at her altar, and the hero woke with the gift in his hand; later tellings place the meeting at the spring of Peirene on Corinth's acropolis. The bridle is an emblem of god-given mastery over a divine beast, and Pegasus, once bridled, served the hero through the trials laid on him by King Iobates, including the slaying of the Chimera. Pausanias reports that the bridle was preserved and dedicated in a temple of Athena Chalinitis, 'the Bridler', at Corinth, a relic claiming to be the very object of the legend. Its story shows how a seemingly small tool, a horse's bit, becomes the pivot of a hero's fate.

name: Brísingamen
description: Brísingamen, the necklace of the goddess Freyja, is one of the great treasures of the Norse gods, forged by the dwarves. The Prose Edda lists it among the wealth of the gods, and in the poem Lokasenna Loki taunts Freyja that she had to sleep with each of the four dwarves who made it to obtain it — a story expanded in the later Sörla þáttr, where Freyja is described as bartering her favours for the jewel. The necklace is also central to the legend of the hero Þórólfr and to the tale of the god Heimdallr and Loki, who fought over it in the shape of seals at Singasteinn; Heimdallr recovered it for Freyja. The name is sometimes taken to mean 'bright' or 'gleaming' necklace, and the jewel later became a model for Freyja's shining golden hair of amber. Brísingamen remains a standard example of the dwarven treasure hoard in retellings of Norse myth.

name: Buganda Royal Drum (Mujaguzo)
description: The mujaguzo are the royal drums of the Buganda kingdom of Uganda, a set of tuned drums kept in a sacred drum house and regarded as the spiritual king of the kingdom. Ganda tradition holds that Buganda has two rulers, the human kabaka and the drums, which never die, and the drums are sounded to announce the birth of a prince, the death of a kabaka, the call to war, and the great ceremonies of state. The principal drum, Kawulugumu, is the 'king among drums', and at a coronation the new kabaka must first visit the drum house, tighten its hide, and strike it to take up his rule; its companion Namanyonyi is spoken of as its wife. The drums are kept suspended above the ground and are smeared with ghee and beer in ritual care, guarded by custodians of the Butiko clan. When the kingdom was abolished in 1966 the drums were hidden away and survived, and they were brought out again for the coronation of 1993. The royal drum tradition remains a living institution of the kabaka's court.

name: Bukkehorn
description: A natural folk horn cut from a hollowed goat or cow horn and sounded through a mouthpiece pierced in the side. Herders used it on the summer seter pastures and at festive gatherings, carrying loud calls and dance tunes across mountain valleys. The horns range from small finger-hole instruments to long curved signal horns, and survived into the 20th century in Norwegian oral folk music. The bukkehorn's voice was part of the pastoral soundscape of the high pastures, heard alongside the kulokk and the shepherd's whistle, and each herder had his own way of making it carry. In the 20th century the instrument was revived in folk-music ensembles and is played again on the seter and in concerts, keeping the old mountain calls alive.

name: Bullroarer
description: The bullroarer is an oval wooden slat whirled on the end of a cord to produce a low, roaring hum, used by the Aboriginal peoples of Australia in initiation and ceremony. As the slat spins, it cuts the air and the pitch rises and falls with the speed of the whirling, and the sound can carry across a surprising distance. In south-eastern Australia the voice of the bullroarer is sometimes said to be the voice of the ancestor Daramulum, and in many traditions the instrument is kept for the men's law, so that women and children are not shown it. The bullroarer is found in many parts of the world, but in Australia it is bound to the initiation grounds, where its humming warns of the sacred ceremonies taking place and draws the attention of the ancestors to the land.

name: Bunad
description: The festive national costume of Norway, sewn from wool in patterns that vary by district, with embroidery, silver brooches, and distinct headwear. Modern bunads grew out of the folk dress of the 18th and 19th centuries and were revived and standardized in the 20th as a symbol of national identity. Hundreds of regional variants are worn at holidays, weddings, and Constitution Day. Each bunad is made to a pattern from a particular valley or town, with the cut of the skirt, the colour of the cloth, and the shape of the headdress marking the wearer's district, and the silver brooches and buckles, often inherited, carry the family's history. The revival was led by folk-costume societies and the Husflid movement, which researched old garments and codified the modern forms. The bunad is worn with pride across Norway and is a living record of regional dress made national.

name: Burnous Cloak
description: The burnous is the hooded, floor-length cloak of the Maghreb, worn by Amazigh (Berber) and Arab men across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya. It is woven in one seamless piece from pure sheep's wool, often left in the natural cream or brown colour of the fleece or dyed, and it is fitted with a single pointed hood that can be drawn over the head in sun, wind or rain. In pre-modern times the burnous served as overcoat, blanket and sleeping bag for travellers and shepherds on the steppe, while a white burnous became the ceremonial dress of chiefs, religious leaders and notables, handed down as an honour and worn at weddings, feasts and festivals. The garment is also remembered in legend, since tribal saints and warriors are described in oral tradition as being wrapped in or given a burnous as a mark of protection and blessing. Today the burnous is worn mainly on formal occasions, but it remains a defining element of Maghrebi identity and appears in the national dress of several North African countries.

name: Buryat Shaman's Drum (Hese)
description: Oval single-headed frame drum of the Buryat shaman (bo), fitted with a cross-shaped handle and a rawhide head often painted with images of animals and the world tree. Struck to summon spirits and to carry the shaman between the worlds, the drum (hese) is the central instrument of Buryat ritual practice; obtaining one marked the shaman's consecration. The frame is bent from a single strip of wood, the head is stretched over it, and the inside carries an iron cross that the shaman grips with the thumb and fingers. The drum is beaten with a padded mallet, and its rhythm varies with the rite: slow strokes for the long journeys to the upper world, quick ones for warding off hostile spirits. A new drum was consecrated at the shaman's initiation, and the first sound it made was sometimes said to reveal which ancestors' spirits would assist him. Ethnographic collections hold drums painted with the sun and moon, the tree of life and the shaman's animal helpers, each image tied to the songs he sang.

name: Buryat Shaman's Horse-Staff
description: Ritual staff of the Buryat shaman, carved from birch wood and topped with a horse's head; senior shamans who had passed the fifth consecration carried iron-tipped versions. In Buryat belief the horse-staff served as the shaman's mount to ride through the spirit world, and it remains a recognised emblem of Buryat shamanic practice alongside the drum. The staff is held upright in the ritual tent, its butt struck on the ground to punctuate the songs, and its carved horse-head top is draped with ribbons and small bells. The iron-tipped staff was a privilege of the senior shaman, and a shaman's degree was read in part from the staff he carried and the number of drums he owned. When a shaman died, his staff and drums were sometimes left in the forest at the place of his last ritual. The custom links Buryat practice to a wide Inner Asian pattern, in which the shaman rides a staff or drum as a steed into the spirit realm.

name: Butterfly Jigha
description: The butterfly jigha is a jewel-set turban ornament of Mughal court fashion, shaped as a butterfly with wings that tremble on a spring as the wearer moves, pinned to the front of the turban by princes, nobles and high officials. Such ornaments are shown in Mughal miniature painting and in later court portraiture of the Deccan and the regions that became Pakistan, where the jigha, sarpesh and other turban jewels marked rank and the favour of the ruler. Surviving examples worked in gold and enamel with rubies, emeralds and pearls sometimes include a socket for a heron or egret plume that rose above the turban, a feature historically restricted to the royal family and those granted the privilege. The butterfly form with its quivering spring is one of the most recognisable types in museum collections, prized for the delicate chasing and stone-setting of the court jewellers.

name: Bychakh (Yakut Knife)
description: Traditional knife of the Yakut (Sakha) people, with an asymmetric blade bearing a fuller on one side and a convex edge on the other, a birch-burl handle and a leather sheath. Forged by Yakut blacksmiths from local iron since pre-Russian times, it is used for carving wood, dressing hides and preparing fish and meat, an everyday tool with a remarkably constant design. The blade is set into a short, rounded handle of birch burl, and the whole knife, worn at the belt in a wooden-lined leather sheath, fits the hand so well that it can be used for hours without fatigue. Yakut smithing was famed in Siberia: local marsh iron was smelted and worked into knives, and the blacksmith's trade was held in such honour that it was treated as almost sacred. The bychakh is carried by men for nearly every task of taiga and farm life, and examples found in old burials show the same form as knives made today. It is sometimes said that a good Yakut knife is judged by its balance and by the feel of the birch-burl handle.

name: Caduceus
description: Hermes' herald's staff, first described as a rod wrapped with fillets or ribbons and only later twined with serpents; it charmed mortals and spirits and led the souls of the dead to the underworld. In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the god trades it for his newly invented lyre, and in later art it appears winged and entwined with two snakes. Through the Romans it became the sign of peace, commerce, and the herald's craft, and it survives today as a symbol of commerce and of the medical profession, though the rod of Asclepius is the older emblem of healing.

name: Caduceus
description: The caduceus, the kērykeion, is the staff of the herald carried by Hermes, the messenger god, and in Greek literature it is the token of his office, the rod with which he conducts souls to the underworld, lulls the watchful, and opens the way before him; in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the staff is given to the young god by Apollo together with the golden wand and the arts of prophecy. Its familiar form, a staff entwined by two serpents and topped with a pair of wings, is the later iconography that became standard in Roman art and was revived in the Renaissance, and through it the caduceus came to stand for commerce, negotiation, and safe passage. The same image, easily confused with the single-serpent rod of the physician Asclepius, is now widely used as a medical symbol, though the two are distinct in origin. As the badge of the eloquent envoy, the caduceus remains the emblem of diplomacy itself.

name: Caladbolg
description: Caladbolg, the great sword of Irish legend, is carried in the Ulster Cycle by Fergus mac Róich, the strong-armed former king of Ulster, and in some traditions it is also the blade of Cú Chulainn, who is said to have wielded it in the great single combat against his foster-brother Ferdiad in the Táin Bó Cúailnge. Its name, often translated 'hard lightning' or 'hard cleft', describes a sword of fearsome cutting power. The word is the Irish cognate of the British Caledfwlch, the sword of Arthur better known as Excalibur, which makes Caladbolg the Irish link in the family of the great legendary blades of the Celtic world. In the tale of the Feast of Bricriu the sword is counted among the marvels tested by the heroes. No historical sword bearing the name survives, so its power is entirely in the literature, and it stands for the violent, glamorous world of the sagas.

name: Calumet (Peace Pipe)
description: The calumet, or chanunpa in Lakota, is the sacred pipe of Plains peoples, a stone bowl joined to a wooden stem, smoked in ceremonies of prayer, treaty and peace. In Lakota tradition the chanunpa was given to the people by White Buffalo Calf Woman, who taught its songs and the meaning of its smoke as a bridge between humans and the sacred. The word 'calumet' came from French traders by way of a Norman term for a reed pipe, reflecting how early Europeans witnessed its power to seal alliances. Catlinite, the red pipestone of southwestern Minnesota, was traded widely for the finest bowls. A pipe was a living sacred object: its keeper followed strict rules, and to smoke together bound the parties to truth, as the famous peace-pipe ceremonies with colonial powers recorded. The pipe remains central to Lakota ceremony and has become a lasting symbol of Indigenous diplomacy.

name: Canopic Jar
description: Canopic jars are the four vessels in which ancient Egyptian embalmers placed the organs removed from the body during mummification, the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines being preserved separately so that the deceased could use them again in the afterlife. The jars, made of alabaster, limestone, wood or pottery, stood in the tomb chest beside the coffin, and by late times each lid was carved as the head of one of the Four Sons of Horus, the protective genii Imsety, Hapy, Duamutef and Qebehsenuef. Spell 151 of the Book of the Dead invokes these guardians, and the whole procedure was overseen by Anubis, the jackal-headed god of embalming who is said to have invented mummification when he treated the body of Osiris. The practice of preserving the viscera is attested from the Old Kingdom onward and illustrates the Egyptians' conviction that the body must remain intact for the next life. Excavated canopic sets, with their carved lids and painted texts, are among the most recognizable objects of the Egyptian burial assemblage.

name: Cauldron of Rebirth
description: Pair Dadeni, the Cauldron of Rebirth, appears in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, the story of Branwen daughter of Llŷr, where it is given to Bran the Blessed by a giant couple, Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and his wife, who have carried it out of Ireland. Warriors slain in battle and cast into the cauldron are restored to life, though the revived come back unable to speak. When Bran invades Ireland to avenge the insult to Branwen, the cauldron is used to raise the enemy dead again and again, until Efnysien, the family's half-brother, destroys it by throwing himself into it and bursting it apart. The cauldron thus carries both the power of rebirth and the need for its own sacrifice. Scholars connect it with the Irish cauldrons of plenty and with the later Grail legends. Its story remains among the strangest and most discussed episodes of the Mabinogion.

name: Cauldron of the Dagda
description: Coire an Dagda, the cauldron of the Dagda, is one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland and described in the Lebor Gabála Érenn. The cauldron of plenty is said to be so generous that no company ever left it unsatisfied, feeding any number of people from its unfailing depths. It is named beside the spear of Lugh, the sword of Nuada and the stone of Fal as one of the great wonder-gifts of the Old Gods, and the four treasures together symbolise the powers of kingship, war and plenty that the Tuatha Dé Danann brought to the island. In the later tradition of the Cath Maige Tuired the Dagda himself is a god of fertility and abundance, and his cauldron matches his appetite and generosity. The cauldron is sometimes linked to the Irish motif of the endless vessel that feeds all comers, a theme found across Celtic folklore. It remains the archetype of the cauldron of abundance in Irish myth.

name: Cauldron of the Underjordiske
description: In Danish legend the underjordiske, the folk who live inside burial mounds and under the fields, are said to borrow pots, kettles, and spoons from farmhouses, as when a mound-man calls, lend me kettle and spoon, while I cook lamb soup under the hill. They always return what they borrow, and those who refused their request brought misfortune on the household. The motif is recorded in Evald Tang Kristensen's great collections of Jutland legends. The borrowed cauldron is a reminder that the hidden folk and the farmers shared a domestic world of borrowed pots and bargains kept.

name: Cedar Bark Basket
description: Northwest Coast weavers, above all Haida, Tlingit and Tsimshian women, weave baskets and hats from shredded cedar bark and split cedar root, some so tightly that they hold water and can be used for cooking by dropping hot stones into the liquid. The twined technique, in which wefts are twisted around warp strands, produces the fine diagonal patterns that distinguish each nation's basketry, from simple checkerwork to complex animal and mountain designs. Cedar itself is honoured as a giver: in Haida tradition the cedar tree appears as Ts'uu Jaas, the Cedar Woman, a supernatural being whose generosity gave people the bark, wood and root for their tools and homes. Weavers harvest the inner bark in spring with prayers and care, taking only what the tree can spare. The art continues, and master weavers' baskets are now sought after by museums and collectors.

name: Ceridwen's Cauldron
description: Ceridwen's cauldron belongs to the medieval Ystoria Taliesin, the Tale of Taliesin, in which the enchantress Ceridwen, a figure of wisdom and magic, brews a potion of inspiration and knowledge in a great cauldron for her son Afagddu. The brew must simmer for a year and a day, and the three drops of its divine inspiration, the Awen, fall instead on the boy Gwion, who guards the pot and swallows them, gaining all its wisdom at a stroke. Ceridwen pursues Gwion through a series of transformations, each side changing shape until she swallows him as a grain of wheat, and in time bears the child who becomes the poet Taliesin. The cauldron thus stands at the origin of the Welsh bardic tradition, the source of the Awen that inspires poets and seers. It is sometimes linked by scholars to the cauldrons of rebirth and plenty in Celtic myth. The object is wholly legendary, known only from the medieval tale and its retellings.

name: Chac Mool
description: A chac mool is a reclining stone figure with its head turned to one side, knees drawn up and a flat basin held on its stomach, set at the entrances of temples across Mesoamerica from Toltec Tula to Aztec Tenochtitlan and Maya Chichen Itza. The basin served as a receptacle for offerings, and in Aztec contexts the figure is especially linked to the rain god Tlaloc and to the hearts and blood of sacrifice. The name was coined in 1875 by the explorer Augustus Le Plongeon, who found one at Chichen Itza and dubbed it 'chac mool' from Maya terms, so it is a modern label for figures whose original name is unknown. Famous examples include the Temple of the Warriors chac mool and several recovered from the Templo Mayor of Mexico City. The form appears to have spread with the Toltec-influenced art of the Early Postclassic, and modern replicas have made the reclining figure one of the most familiar images of ancient Mexico.

name: Chaoui Aures Kilim
description: The Chaoui kilim is a flat-woven woollen rug made by the Chaoui Amazigh women of the Aures mountains in eastern Algeria. Because the Aures is a cold, high country of oak forests and steppe, the weavers use the fleece of the local sheep to create blankets, saddle cloths, tent curtains and floor rugs, working on a horizontal ground loom that can be set up and dismantled as families move between seasonal pastures. The weaving is warp-faced, so that the geometric design is visible on both faces, and the patterns of diamonds, ladders, zigzags and small protective 'eye' motifs are handed down within each family rather than copied from books. Dyes traditionally came from madder roots, walnut husks, indigo and other plants gathered in the mountains, giving a palette of warm reds, browns and indigo against undyed cream wool. Like other Amazigh textiles, the Aures kilim carried apotropaic meaning, with border motifs believed to turn aside the evil eye, and today these rugs are also valued by collectors as documents of Chaoui identity.

name: Cheonbuin
description: The cheonbuin, the heavenly seal, is the seal that the Samguk Yusa says Hwanung, son of the sky god Hwanin, carried when he descended to Mount Taebaek with three seals to govern the world. In the Dangun foundation myth Hwanung established a sacred city at the summit, legislated for the people, and accepted the prayers of a bear and a tiger who wished to become human; the bear that endured the ordeal of a hundred days in a cave became the woman Ungnyeo, whose son Dangun founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon. The seal is given to the king's descendants as the mark of royal mandate, anchoring Korean sovereignty in the descent of the royal line from heaven. The story is recorded in the Samguk Yusa and the Jewang Ungi, and it is the foundational myth of Korean identity, celebrated in the founding day festival of Gaecheonjeol. The cheonbuin is often paired in royal regalia with the sword of office, and the image of Hwanung descending with the seal is a fixed scene in Korean national symbolism.

name: Chest of El Cid
description: The chest of El Cid is the wooden coffer, bound with iron, that the exiled hero in the Cantar de Mio Cid fills with sand and pawns to the moneylenders Raquel and Vidas as a supposed hoard of gold, to raise the funds his banishment has denied him. The poem has El Cid swear the chest is full of pure gold, and the lenders accept it on his word, never daring to open it, and the ruse lets the hero mock the greed of the Jews while financing his campaign; the joke is that the treasure is worthless sand and the bargain is never meant to be redeemed. The episode, told with wry comedy, is one of the most famous of the epic, showing the hero's resourcefulness and his contempt for those who trust appearances. It is a literary invention with no historical basis, and no such chest is known to have existed. The chest remains a stock image of the confidence trick that passes off worthlessness as wealth.

name: Chipendani Mouth Bow
description: The chipendani is a mouth bow of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a curved wooden stave with a single fibre or wire string, held against the open mouth and plucked so that the mouth shapes the tone. Because the cavity of the mouth acts as a resonator, the player can vary pitch and timbre while the string keeps up a light, rhythmic pattern. It is above all an instrument of herders and young men, who play it alone in the fields to pass the hours, to court, and to accompany themselves while singing. The chipendani is small and portable, carried in the hand or tucked in the belt, and its soft sound suits the quiet company of cattle rather than the crowd. Related mouth bows appear across southern Africa under different names. Although the mbira overshadowed it in the modern Shona music revival, the chipendani is still heard in the countryside and is taught in some schools and cultural programmes.

name: Chiwara Headdress
description: The chiwara is the antelope headdress of the Bamana of Mali, a carved figure with a long neck, elegant horns and an openwork body, danced in pairs at the agricultural festivals in honor of the mythic being who, the Bamana say, taught humanity to farm. The dance re-enacts the teaching: the headdresses are tied to a cap on the heads of two dancers who leap and crouch like antelopes feeding, while the rest of the village raises the hoe to the rhythm. The long horns curve toward the sun, and the zigzag crest on the back of the older style recalls the sun's rays falling on the fields; two forms are recognized, the vertical style of the north and the horizontal style of the south. The chiwara is not worshiped but honored, it is the remembered teacher of agriculture, and the dance gives thanks for the gift. Today the headdress is among the best-known of African sculptures, though it is still danced at sowing time in the Bamana villages.

name: Chokha (Georgian Men's Coat)
description: The chokha is the traditional men's coat of the Caucasus, a long woollen garment with a fitted waist, a flared skirt and, most distinctively, rows of small cartridge cases - the gazyr - sewn diagonally across the chest. The gazyr began as real ammunition holders, with silver, wood or bone caps, and survived as ornament long after firearms made them obsolete, so the decorated chest became the emblem of Caucasian dress. In Georgia the chokha has been worn since at least the seventeenth century, with regional cuts: the Khevsur highland variant is richly embroidered in wool, while the plain dark chokha of the lowlands is the classic civic and military coat. After generations of everyday use the chokha is today reserved for festivals, folk dance, weddings and ceremonial occasions, and it remains the strongest single emblem of Georgian national dress.

name: Chokwe Chief's Throne
description: The carved wooden thrones of the Chokwe chiefs of Angola are low seats supported by figural groups, ancestors, rulers, hunters, and scenes of everyday life, that turn each throne into a small chronicle of the chiefdom. The seat and backrest are often studded with brass tacks and worked with openwork motifs, while the supporting figures served as personal emblems of the soba and his lineage. Thrones were made by the chief's carvers and passed down the chiefly line, and a new ruler might commission a throne that linked him to the ancestors shown beneath the seat. In Chokwe court culture the throne was a public statement of the dignity of the soba and the continuity of power, used at audiences and ceremonies. The same woodcarvers made the masks, drums, and staffs of office that completed chiefly regalia. Museum examples from the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries have made the Chokwe throne a celebrated form of Central African royal art.

name: Chokwe Pwo Mask
description: The pwo is the carved female mask of the Chokwe of Angola and neighbouring lands, with a finely finished face, gently closed eyes, and filed or scarified markings on the forehead and cheeks. Danced at the mukanda initiations that turn boys into men and at celebrations of the community, the mask embodies the idealised ancestress, Mwana Pwo, the Young Woman, whose beauty and calm set the standard of Chokwe womanhood. The dancer who wears it takes on the gentle, swaying movements of a woman, while a headdress of fibre and feathers completes the costume. Pwo masks come in pairs with the male cihongo mask of the chief, and both are danced with wit and prestige. Carvers claim to receive guidance in dreams, and each mask is finished with a dark patina meant to evoke the oiled skin of a beautiful woman. Chokwe carving, of which the pwo is the best-known face, has been admired since the first pieces reached Europe.

name: Chonguri (Georgian Four-String Lute)
description: The chonguri is the four-string fretless lute of western Georgia, carved from a single block of walnut or maple into a shallow bowl, with a flat spruce soundboard and a short drone string called the zili that buzzes beneath the melody strings. It is the instrument of Guria and Samegrelo, where it traditionally accompanied women's songs and the nadi, the evening working gatherings at which women spun, wove and sang, and where the chonguri's quiet, flexible tone fitted a female voice. Unlike the fretted panduri of the east, the chonguri is played with a light, flowing touch, and its three melody strings are named after the three voices of Georgian polyphony. Still made and taught today, the chonguri belongs to the living polyphonic tradition that UNESCO inscribed in 2008.

name: Choron (Yakut Kumys Vessel)
description: Carved wooden drinking vessel of the Yakut (Sakha) people, made from a single piece of birch or spruce burl, with a conical or rounded body and short legs. The choron is the principal ritual vessel of the ysyakh summer festival, filled with kumys and offered in honour of the aiyy deities, then shared among the celebrants; its elegant form is held to resemble a bird. The body swells gently from a small mouth and stands on three or four short carved legs, and the outer surface is often engraved with bands of geometric ornament. At the festival the first choron of kumys is raised to the sky and poured to the four directions, and the celebrants then drink in turn, some vessels holding several litres. The carving follows the grain of the burl, and the best chorons are so carefully balanced that they stand firm on uneven ground. Old examples in Sakha museums show the same proportions as those made today, the form passed down unchanged for centuries.

name: Chukchi Walrus-Ivory Carving
description: Carved objects of the Chukchi and Siberian Yupik of the Chukotka coast, worked from walrus tusks into harpoon heads, amulets, figurines and engraved scenes of sea-hunting and animal life. Walrus ivory carving is a hallmark of Chukchi art, celebrated by the Uelen bone-carving workshop and collected by the Russian Museum of Ethnography. The tusk is cut and sawn, then shaped with knives and polished with the hide of the walrus itself, and engravers trace outlines of hunters, walruses, whales and spirits in fine, firm lines. In the past ivory was also the material of daily life: harpoon points, toggles and needle cases were carved for use at sea, and small figurines were carried as charms. The workshop at Uelen, founded in the 1930s on the Bering coast, gathered carvers of the Chukchi and Yupik villages and gave the craft a lasting home. Ivory is sometimes said to hold the luck of the hunt, and a well-carved tusk remains a family treasure on the Chukotka coast.

name: Chuniri (Svan Bowed Fiddle)
description: The chuniri is the bowed fiddle of the Georgian mountain province of Svaneti, a round or tubular wooden body with a skin soundboard, three gut or horsehair strings and a heavy bow, held against the shoulder like a small violin. Because a bowed string can sustain a note, the chuniri is said to sing in place of a human voice, standing in for a singer in Svan hunting songs, work songs and choral polyphony; its two-string cousin, the chianuri, serves the same role in other highland regions such as Racha and Adjara. The instrument was the personal companion of Svan shepherds and hunters, who played it at home, at vigils and in the towers of the mountain villages. It remains one of the two bowed instruments of Georgia, heard at festivals and in the polyphonic ensembles that carry Svan tradition.

name: Cifraszűr
description: The cifraszűr is the decorated shepherd's cloak of the Hungarian Great Plain, a knee-length mantle of white felt cut from a single piece, split down the middle so the wearer can slip it over the shoulders and pin it under the chin. Its name pairs szűr, the plain cloak of Hungarian herdsmen, with cifra, 'ornamented', and indeed the best cifraszűr covers the felt with black, red and green wool applique arranged in rosettes, tulips, fringes and braided borders. Herdsmen wore the szűr against sun and rain and slept in it on the puszta, and a richly worked cloak was a sign of skill, wealth and pride, passed down in the family or given as a groom's gift. By the twentieth century the cifraszűr had moved from pasture to festival dress and museum collections, remaining a striking emblem of Hungarian shepherd culture.

name: Cimbalom (Hungarian Hammered Dulcimer)
description: Large hammered dulcimer of Hungary, a trapezoid box with rows of metal strings struck by small wooden hammers; the concert cimbalom developed in Budapest in the 1870s. It appears in Romani music and in the works of composers such as Kodály and Bartók, while its village relatives are played across Eastern Europe; the Hungarian word cimbalom names the whole family of hammered dulcimers. The instrument has two registers of strings crossing the soundboard, a damping pedal to stop the ringing, and a boxy, resonant tone that carries clearly in a hall. Virtuoso players command a solo repertoire, and the cimbalom is also used in gypsy bands, where it once set the tempo and the harmony. Since the 19th century it has travelled to the Americas with emigrants, and it remains a fixture of Hungarian folk and folk-influenced classical music.

name: Cinderella's Glass Slipper
