description: The glass slipper of Cinderella is the shoe lost as the heroine flees the prince's ball, the object that lets the prince find his bride because it fits no other foot in the kingdom. In the Grimms' version, Aschenputtel, the lost shoes are of gold, and the slipper motif belongs to the older tale-type in which the hero proves identity by an object that fits only the true owner. It was Charles Perrault's 1697 version, with its shoe of glass, that fixed the slipper in popular imagination, and the fragility of glass made it a perfect emblem of the tale's magic and brevity. Folklorists note that shoe-matching scenes occur in versions of the tale from China, where the heroine loses a shoe, to Europe, making it one of the oldest plot devices in storytelling. The glass slipper appears in no surviving material object, and no such slipper exists. It remains, with the pumpkin coach, the defining image of the Cinderella story.

name: Ciupaga (Podhale Axe-Staff)
description: Small axe with a long wooden haft carried by the highlanders (górale) of the Polish Tatra mountains as a walking staff, herding tool and dance prop. The ciupaga's haft is often carved, and highlanders strike it on the floor in the energetic zbójnicki dance; it accompanies the shepherd's life of the Podhale region and is a recognised emblem of Tatra highland culture. Its head resembles an ice-axe, with a short blade on one side and a rounded butt on the other, and it serves as a climbing stick, a lever, and a defence against wolves and bears. The wooden haft, up to a metre long, is a canvas for ornament: stars, suns and geometric bands are burned or incised into the ash or beech wood. The zbójnicki, the dance of the historic brigands who sheltered in the mountains, is performed with the ciupaga raised and struck, and the object remains a proud mark of highland identity worn on formal dress.

name: Claddagh Ring
description: The Claddagh ring, a gold or silver finger-ring shaped as two hands clasping a crowned heart, has been made in Galway since the seventeenth century and is named after the old fishing village of Claddagh beside the city. The design descends from the medieval 'fede' ring, whose clasped hands stood for faith and betrothal, with the heart and crown added locally. The best-known origin story tells of Richard Joyce, a Galway goldsmith who was captured by Algerian pirates in the late seventeenth century and sold into slavery in North Africa, where he supposedly made the ring before returning home; the tale is recorded in James Hardiman's 1820 History of Galway, though its details cannot be fully verified. The oldest surviving Claddagh ring, dated to about 1700 and stamped with Joyce's mark, is held by Galway City Museum. The ring is still a living custom, passed down from mother to daughter and worn in different positions to show whether the wearer is single or betrothed.

name: Clapsticks
description: The clapsticks are the paired hardwood percussion sticks of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, struck together by singers and dancers to mark the rhythm of ceremony and song. In Arnhem Land they are known as bilma, and they are often painted or engraved with the designs of the clan, with the length and tone of each pair chosen by the songman. The sticks accompany the didgeridoo and the singing in corroboree and ceremony, and each song owns a particular beat that encodes the Dreaming story it carries, so the rhythm is part of the knowledge held by the singers. Clapsticks are simple in form but exact in use, and they are also played by hand-clapping groups where no wood is at hand, in the musical traditions of the north and the centre of Australia.

name: Claíomh Mór
description: Claíomh Mór, 'the great sword' of Irish tradition, is one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried with them when they came to Ireland, and later lore links it to Nuada Airgetlám, king of the Tuatha Dé Danann. In the Lebor Gabála Érenn the sword of Nuada is said to be irresistible once drawn from its sheath, and it is listed beside the spear of Lugh, the cauldron of the Dagda and the stone of Fal. The name is close to, and often confused with, Claíomh Solais, the sword of light, a term that later folklore attached to the magic weapons of heroes and even to a buried golden sword that would rise against the invader. Some regional retellings describe the blade as drawing light from the Otherworld so that it blazed like a torch in battle. The sword remains a staple of Irish storytelling and has been invoked in poetry, ballad and political symbolism.

name: Co Loa Crossbow
description: The magic crossbow of Co Loa is the weapon of An Duong Vuong, the legendary king of the Au Lac kingdom, whose trigger was forged from the golden claw of Kim Qui, the golden turtle god, and which could kill thousands of men with a single shot. The king built the spiral citadel of Co Loa with the turtle's help, but his defence was undone by his own daughter: My Chau, newly married to the spy Trong Thuy of the northern enemy, showed him the secret of the trigger, and the enemy stole it, the citadel fell, and An Duong Vuong fled with his daughter. Learning of the betrayal, the king beheaded My Chau, and her blood is said to have turned into pearls. The story is told in the Lĩnh Nam chích quái and the Dai Viet su ky toan thu, and it is one of the foundational legends of Vietnamese national memory, the site at Co Loa near Hanoi being among the oldest archaeological monuments of the country.

name: Codex Argenteus
description: The Silver Bible, a sixth-century manuscript of Wulfila's Gothic Bible translation written in silver and gold ink on purple-dyed vellum, probably copied in northern Italy for the Ostrogothic court. Rediscovered at the monastery of Werden, it came to Sweden during the Thirty Years' War and is now kept at Uppsala University Library. It is the most substantial surviving text in the Gothic language. The manuscript is written in silver uncial script on leaves stained with purple dye, a colour reserved for imperial books, and only the gospel canon tables and a few headings are picked out in gold. Of its original two hundred or so leaves about 188 survive, making it the longest witness to the Gothic tongue, which was spoken by the East Germanic peoples into the Middle Ages. The codex has been studied, repaired, and reproduced again and again since its arrival in Sweden, and it remains a treasure of European cultural history.

name: Comal
description: The comal is a flat, round clay griddle set on three hearth stones and used to toast tortillas, roast seeds and warm tamales across Mexico and Guatemala. The word comes from Nahuatl comalli, and clay comales appear in Mesoamerican archaeological sites from the Classic period onward, showing the griddle's deep roots in the region's cooking. Colonial accounts describe the round hearth as the fixed centre of the household kitchen, the comal standing always over the fire beside the metate where maize was ground. Potters still shape comales by hand, and the clay version is prized because it gives tortillas a particular toasted flavour, though metal comales have become common. In the mythology of everyday Mesoamerican life the comal completes the arc from maize harvest to tortilla, and it remains a standard tool of the Mexican and Central American kitchen.

name: Cook Islands Adze (Toki)
description: Stone-bladed adze of the Cook Islands, ground from fine-grained basalt and lashed to a wooden handle with sennit, used to fell and shape the timber for canoes, houses, war clubs and carvings. The toki was the essential tool of the master craftsman, and the quarries that supplied the prized basalt — above all the great quarry on Mangaia — were controlled by chiefly families and treated as resources of mana. Fine adzes were treasured heirlooms, their lashing and finish a mark of the carver's standing, and the same tool type, its design carried by voyagers across the Pacific, appears in the founding histories of many island traditions.

name: Coolamon
description: The coolamon is the carved wooden carrying dish of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, shaped from the root growth of eucalyptus trees or cut from bark, and used to hold water, food, seeds, fire and babies. A single piece of wood is gouged and shaped so that the dish has a curved bottom, and it is carried on the head, in the hand or under the arm, with smaller coolamons made as cradles for infants and larger ones used for grinding seeds and winnowing grain. The dish is a working tool of daily life, used especially by women in food gathering, and it can be painted with the clan designs of the maker. In the desert and riverine regions the coolamon remains a practical and ceremonial vessel, and examples are held in museum collections of Aboriginal material culture.

name: Cormac's Cup
description: The cup of Cormac mac Airt appears in Echtra Cormaic, the Adventure of Cormac, a medieval Irish tale in which a warrior who is really Manannán mac Lir gives the high king a golden cup in exchange for his wife and daughter. The cup is a cup of truth: if three lies are spoken over it, it breaks into pieces, and if three truths are told it is made whole again, so that Cormac uses it to test the words of his court. In the end Cormac learns that his wife and daughter have been carried to the Otherworld, and the cup is restored to him along with the lesson that no man can hold the truth's secrets without giving up what he loves. The tale, recorded in the Book of Ballymote and related manuscripts, belongs to the tradition of moral test-objects in Irish wonder literature. The cup is sometimes called the cup of truth, and its shattering and mending remain its best-known feature.

name: Corona Civica
description: The corona civica, the civic crown of oak leaves, was Rome's highest honour for a citizen soldier, awarded to the man who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground where he did it; Pliny the Elder in the Natural History and Aulus Gellius in the Attic Nights describe its rules. Woven from holm, esculent, or common oak, it was granted by the rescued man himself, who was bound to honour his saviour as a parent, and the crown carried with it the right to wear it for life, to sit with the senators at the games, and to be free of many burdens; its inscription 'ob cives servatos', 'for saving citizens', became the slogan of imperial beneficence. Pliny records that it was counted second only to the grass crown, the corona obsidionalis, in the scale of Roman decorations, and Julius Caesar and later emperors displayed it with pride. The oak crown remained a political symbol of protection down to the end of the empire.

name: Coup Stick
description: The coup stick, or counting-coup staff, is a decorated staff or lance carried by Plains warriors such as the Lakota, Cheyenne and Crow for the act of 'counting coup', touching an enemy in battle without killing him. Among the Plains peoples touching a living enemy was ranked the bravest feat of war, above killing, and each time a warrior counted coup he added an honour, often marked on the staff with an eagle feather. The four grades of war honour were carefully ranked, and a man could also count coup on enemies' horses or possessions. Such sticks were wrapped with cloth and fur, hung with feathers, and treated with the respect due a record of personal bravery. Ethnographers recorded how these honours were proclaimed at dances, and the staff became the physical tally of a warrior's reputation.

name: Croatian Nosnja
description: The nosnja, the traditional folk costume of the Croatian regions, is worn on feast days, at weddings, and at folklore festivals, and each district had its own cut, fabric, embroidery, and colour code that told the wearer's village, age, marital state, and even family at a glance. The dress is built from linen, hemp, and wool, spun, woven, and embroidered at home, and on it appear the characteristic Croatian embroideries, from the gold-worked caps of Posavina to the red-and-black geometric designs of the Dalmatian hinterland and the ornate festive dress of Slavonia. The nosnja belongs to the wider Balkan tradition of festive clothing, but its regional variety made it, in the 19th century, a badge of national identity during the Croatian national revival. It is still made by hand and worn with pride, and the rich costumes of the folk ensembles are among the most recognisable images of Croatian folklore. It is a garment of identity rather than a single mythic object.

name: Crown of Ariadne
description: The golden crown Ariadne wore when she helped Theseus escape the labyrinth of Crete after he slew the Minotaur, and the circlet Dionysus later set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis. In Catullus' Carmen 64 the crown is the gift that marks Ariadne's fate after Theseus abandons her on Naxos, where Dionysus finds her and raises her crown to heaven in her honour; Apollodorus also preserves the tradition of the celestial setting. Different sources make Hephaestus or Dionysus its maker, and its gems were said to shine with a brightness of their own in the night sky. The seven bright stars of Corona Borealis still carry her name, and the crown is a standing emblem of the abandoned bride turned into a celestial monument. In Renaissance and later art the corona of Ariadne appears again and again, marrying astronomy and myth in a single golden ring of stars.

name: Crown of Saint Stephen
description: The Holy Crown of Hungary, identified with the crown of the first king Saint Stephen I (ruled 1000-1038), is a circlet of gold hung with enamelled plaques, pearls and gemstones, with a distinctive cross set at an angle on top. Scholars date the surviving bands and figures to the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and the crown as it exists today was almost certainly assembled from older parts for later coronations, so its precise age and original form are still debated. It was used to crown Hungarian kings from the Middle Ages down to Charles IV in 1916, the last Hungarian coronation, and legend held that no ruler who wore it could ever be overthrown. Hidden in chests, walled into castles and smuggled abroad over the centuries, the crown returned to Hungary from the United States in 1978 and has been displayed in the Hungarian Parliament building since 2000 as the supreme symbol of Hungarian statehood.

name: Crown of Saint Wenceslas
description: The Crown of Saint Wenceslas, the Svatováclavská koruna, was made in 1347 for the coronation of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, and was named after the tenth-century Bohemian duke and martyr Saint Wenceslas. It is set with large rubies, sapphires, emeralds, spinels and pearls, and together with the orb, sceptre and coronation robes it forms the Bohemian crown jewels, now kept in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague. The crown carries a famous curse: legend holds that a usurper who sets it on his head will die within a year, a fate sometimes connected with the Nazi governor Reinhard Heydrich, though the story is modern and unverifiable. Because of the legend the crown is shown rarely, displayed only on high feast days and under strict conditions, with seven keys held by separate officials. The medieval form, with its pointed arches and jewel-encrusted circlet, makes it one of the most striking royal insignia in Europe.

name: Cuauhxicalli
description: A cuauhxicalli (Nahuatl 'eagle gourd bowl', from cuauhtli 'eagle' and xicalli 'gourd vessel') is a stone bowl that held the hearts of sacrificial victims in Aztec Tenochtitlan, placed before temple platforms where priests raised the still-beating heart to the sun before casting it into the vessel. Carvers shaped many examples as crouching eagles or jaguars with the bowl hollowed from the back; a celebrated andesite eagle cuauhxicalli found in the Templo Mayor precinct in 1985 measures some 139 centimetres. Others carry a sun disk carved inside and the earth goddess Tlaltecuhtli on the base, leading scholars such as Karl Taube to read the vessel as the earth's blood-filled womb receiving the sacrifice that renews the sun. The relief-covered Stone of Tizoc is sometimes identified as such a vessel, while the term also covers the reclining chacmool form that catches offerings on its belly. Spanish chroniclers and the colonial codices confirm the vessels' place at the centre of Mexica public ceremony.

name: Czech Glass Christmas Ornaments
description: Czech glass Christmas ornaments are hand-blown and hand-painted baubles made in the glass towns of northern Bohemia, above all around Jablonec nad Nisou and the Krkonoše foothills, where the craft grew out of the region's bead and glass-button industry in the mid-nineteenth century. Workers blew thin globes from molten glass, silvered them from inside with a solution that gave the characteristic metallic glimmer, and then painted them by hand with snow, berries, flowers or fairy-tale figures before hanging them from the family fir tree. The delicate ornaments became a celebrated export, so prized that Bohemian and Moravian glassmakers supplied Christmas trees across Europe and America for more than a century. A few family workshops still fire the baubles by mouth today, and the region's museums display both the finished ornaments and the wooden and metal tools of the old glasshuts.

name: Dacian Gold Bracelets
description: The Dacian gold bracelets are heavy spiral arm rings of the ancient kingdom of Dacia, hammered from Transylvanian alluvial gold in the mid-first century BC and worn as ornaments and marks of rank, possibly also deposited as votive offerings. The surviving pieces, each forged from a single ingot into five to seven coils that end in serpent or animal heads, weigh between roughly 680 grams and nearly 1.2 kilograms, a concentration of royal wealth unmatched in the Balkans. Around two dozen were looted from ritual pits near the sacred precinct of Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian capital in the Orăștie Mountains, between 1999 and 2001 and smuggled abroad; an international police operation has since recovered at least thirteen, and others remain missing. The recovered bracelets are displayed in the Historical Treasury of the National History Museum of Romania in Bucharest as masterpieces of Dacian goldwork.

name: Dahomey Applique Cloth
description: Dahomey applique is the court textile of the Fon, a rectangular cloth of cotton on which cut-out cloth figures are sewn to record royal history and proverb: kings, warriors, the kingdom's celebrated women soldiers, animals and scenes of triumph, each figure placed in a tableau that tells a story at a glance. The cloths were commissioned for the royal court of Abomey and were carried as banners and hung as umbrella covers in the great processions, where the king's deeds marched before him in fabric. The leading artisans were the kings' own embroiderers, and the tradition was passed down in workshops that still practice it in Abomey today, now serving collectors and museums as well as the court. Every figure is a word: the king appears as a buffalo or a lion, enemies as the animals that were felled, so the cloth is read like a text. Dahomey applique carries the memory of a kingdom in colored cloth.

name: Dala Horse
description: The Dala horse (Dalahäst), the carved wooden horse of Dalarna, painted in red, white, blue, and green with a floral saddle. The craft grew from toys carved during long winter evenings in the 17th century into a famous local industry around Mora, where the horses are still hand-carved and painted. The Dala horse has become the best-known symbol of Swedish craft. The carvers of the villages around Lake Siljan — above all Bergkarlås, Risa, Vattnäs, and Nusnäs — made the horses from pine left over from furniture and clock-making, and by the early seventeenth century the toys were already being sold, the oldest written mention dating to 1623. The figure is hollowed out of two carved halves and glued, then painted in the kurbits folk style with a saddle of flowers and leaves. What began as a child's toy became, in the twentieth century, a national emblem, and the Nusnäs workshops still ship the red horse to buyers the world over.

name: Dan Mask
description: The dan mask is a carved wooden face mask of the Dan people of western Ivory Coast, admired for its smooth, polished surface, narrow eye slits, and the fine balance of its features. Each mask is inhabited by a spirit called gle, and the wearer becomes that spirit during the dance, so the mask is handled with ritual care: it is oiled, fed, and hidden from profane eyes when not in use. Masks take many characters, from the playful entertainment mask to the warrior mask and the judge that fines wrongdoers in village disputes, and the same basic form was adopted by the neighbouring We and Guro peoples. Some masks belong to whole communities or age sets, while others pass through family lines, and their guardianship is a position of real responsibility. European and American collectors prized dan masks in the twentieth century for their serene, 'classical' faces, and the form had a marked influence on modernist sculpture.

name: Daruma Doll
description: The daruma is a rounded paper-mache doll modelled on Bodhidharma, the semi-legendary founder of Zen Buddhism, whose hollow weighted body always rocks back upright when tipped. The likeness plays on a famous story in which Bodhidharma sat facing a wall in meditation for nine years, until his legs withered and were lost; the doll keeps his determined, round form and his fierce brow. Bought as a talisman of perseverance, the daruma is customarily sold with blank white eyes, and the owner inks in one eye when a wish or goal is set and the second when it is achieved, the rite turning the doll into a kind of visual contract with oneself. At the end of the year the accumulated daruma are taken to temples such as Dairyoji in Gunma, the dolls' birthplace, and burned in the daruma-kuyo ceremony, releasing the accumulated wishes. Originally a charm against smallpox in the Edo period, the doll has become a national symbol of resilience, famously adopted by political candidates, and its self-righting property gives the Japanese phrase 'falling seven times, rising eight' a concrete image.

name: Dejbjerg Wagon
description: The frame of a Celtic-style ceremonial wagon found in the Dejbjerg bog in West Jutland, Denmark, in 1881. Its richly ornamented bronze fittings, with scrolls and masks in a Mediterranean-influenced style, were long thought to be imports, and the wagon was probably the property of a chieftain, used in procession and then taken apart and sacrificed in the bog. Recent study suggests the fittings may be local Norse work following Celtic models. The wagon is exhibited in the National Museum of Denmark and is among the finest Iron Age vehicles found in Scandinavia.

name: Dhakai Jamdani
description: The dhakai jamdani is the handwoven muslin of the Dhaka region, patterned with fine floral, geometric and figural motifs that are worked into the cloth itself on the loom, rather than printed or embroidered after weaving. The weaver picks out each motif with extra weft threads, often of silver or gold, using a technique of supplementary weft float work, so that the pattern appears woven through the sheer, fine-count cotton. The craft was patronised by the Mughal courts and has been practised for centuries along the banks of the rivers around Dhaka and Narayanganj, and it was inscribed by UNESCO on the list of intangible cultural heritage in 2013. Jamdani saris remain prized ceremonial dress for weddings and festivals across Bengal and beyond.

name: Didgeridoo
description: The didgeridoo is the long wooden trumpet of the Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, made from a eucalyptus limb whose core has been hollowed by termites, cut, cleaned and fitted with a beeswax mouthpiece. The player vibrates the lips to produce a deep, continuous drone, often with circular breathing so the note never stops, and skilled players add vocal calls and rhythmic syllables over the drone. It accompanies ceremony, song and dance, and in the traditions of northern Australia its sound is connected to the great ancestral beings, including the Rainbow Serpent of the creation stories, who is said to have given the music of the Dreaming. The word didgeridoo is a European coinage from the early twentieth century, while the instrument's own names include yidaki and magaru, and it has spread far beyond Australia as a musical instrument in the decades since.

name: Diya Oil Lamp
description: The diya is the small clay oil lamp of the Indian subcontinent, a shallow bowl of baked earth filled with ghee or oil and fitted with a cotton wick, lit during worship and festivals. Its name comes from the Sanskrit deepa, meaning lamp, and the rows of little lamps called deepavali gave Diwali its name, the 'row of lights' that greets the goddess Lakshmi at the new moon and celebrates the victory of light over darkness. A diya is lit at the evening arti in Hindu homes, placed at the feet of the deities, on doorsteps and on the thresholds of shops, and floated on rivers during the festivals of the goddesses. Although the classic diya is a simple wheel-thrown cup, the same form is made in bronze, brass and silver for permanent use, and temples keep brass lamps with multiple wicks for the daily ceremony. The flame of the diya carries a fixed set of meanings, purity, warmth and the presence of the divine, and to keep a lamp burning through the night is a common vow and act of devotion.

name: Dogon Kanaga Mask
description: The kanaga is the wooden headdress of the Dogon of Mali, a crest of crossed bars rising from a vertical plank, danced by the men of the masked society at the dama, the great funeral rites that lead the souls of the dead to their ancestors. The mask is worn on the top of the head, the dancer looking out through the costume as the double cross revolves, and its form is read as the structure of the world, the arms of the cross as the sky and the earth, or as the hand of the creator god Amma shaping the cosmos. Every sixty years the Sigui, the great regeneration ceremony, renews the tradition, and the masks mediate between the living and the dead, banishing the souls gently from the village. The Dogon are famous for the depth of their cosmology, studied by ethnographers since the 1930s, and the kanaga has become the emblem of that tradition in African art. In dance the mask sets the universe spinning.

name: Dombra (Kazakh Two-String Lute)
description: Pear-shaped, long-necked two-stringed plucked lute of the Kazakh steppe, the country's signature instrument. Solo instrumental pieces (kuy) performed on dombra are central to Kazakh identity and the tradition of Dombra Kuy is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List. Legendary kuishi like Qurmangazy composed famous kuys on it, and epic singers accompanied their tales with the instrument. The two gut or nylon strings are tuned a fourth apart, and the player fingers the melody with one hand while striking both strings with the other, giving the kuy its driving rhythm and its dialogue between high and low voices. The dombra is sometimes said to have been created by Korkyt Ata, the legendary sage who, fleeing death, hung a string over the waters and let its note speak for him. Dombra-playing is taught in schools, and the instrument appears in the emblem of the National Philharmonic and in the hands of every Kazakh ensemble.

name: Dorje
description: The dorje is the ritual thunderbolt of Bhutanese and Tibetan Buddhism, a bronze or gilt sceptre with a central grip and prongs that curve inward at each end, held in monastic hand rituals and placed on altars. The word is the Tibetan translation of the Sanskrit vajra, and it means lord of stones, hard as diamond and indestructible as the thunderbolt; the five prongs of the common form stand for the five Dhyani Buddhas and their wisdoms. In the older Hindu and Buddhist myth the vajra was the thunder-weapon of the god Indra, and in Himalayan ritual the dorje is paired with the hand bell, held in the right hand while the bell sounds in the left. Monks raise the dorje through ceremonies and empowerments, where it represents the unbreakable method of enlightenment that the practitioner cultivates.

name: Doshpuluur (Tuvan Three-String Lute)
description: Long-necked, three-stringed plucked lute of the Tuvans, with a small wooden body often carved in a canoe shape and gut or nylon strings. The doshpuluur forms a key part of Tuvan music, accompanying songs and dance and often played in duet with the igil; it is a close relative of the Altai topshur and the Mongolian tovshuur. The player plucks the strings with one hand while fretting the melody with the other, and its dry, percussive sound supports the rhythmic side of Tuvan song. It is used in folk ensembles and by throat-singers to keep the beat, and in the kargyraa style its notes double the low drone. The instrument's simple construction, from a single carved body and a hide or wooden soundboard, keeps it light enough to travel with the herder's household. In modern Tuva it is played in conservatories and by groups such as the Alash ensemble, which carry the doshpuluur's sound to concert halls abroad.

name: Draumstafir
description: Draumstafir, the 'dream staves', is an Icelandic magical stave recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn so that the sleeper receives good or revealing dreams. It belongs to the family of galdrastafir, the sigils of the Icelandic grimoire tradition that developed between the 16th and 19th centuries, and it was drawn on paper or carved on wood and placed with the sleeper or worn about the person. The drawing instructions vary between manuscripts, and the sign is one of the many staves collected by 19th-century antiquaries from a folk-magic tradition that was already fading. In modern times draumstafir is widely reproduced in books, jewellery, and tattoos, and the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík presents such staves as living expressions of Icelandic folk belief. Its simple promise — sound sleep and meaningful dreams — keeps it among the more popular of the recorded staves.

name: Draupnir
description: Draupnir, 'the dripper', is the golden ring of Odin, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri in the same wager that produced Mjölnir. Every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from it, making it an endless source of gold and a symbol of abundance. When Baldr was laid on his funeral ship Hringhorni, Odin placed Draupnir on the pyre; the ring was later fetched back from Hel by Baldr's brother Hermóðr, who rode the eight-legged horse Sleipnir to the underworld at Frigg's bidding. In that story Hermóðr returns to the gods bearing Draupnir and the gifts that the dead send back to the living — Nanna's linen robe for Frigg and a ring for the goddess Fulla. The ring's self-replicating nature has made it one of the most studied of the dwarven treasures, and its name is sometimes used in modern writing as a shorthand for limitless wealth.

name: Dreamcatcher
description: The dreamcatcher is a small hoop of willow or other wood bound with a web of netting and hung above a cradle, believed in Ojibwe tradition to catch bad dreams in its mesh while good dreams slip through the central hole to the sleeper below. The web form is tied to stories of the spider grandmother, a protective figure of Anishinaabe tradition, and early twentieth-century ethnographic accounts record such charms made for infants. Since the 1960s the dreamcatcher has been adopted across North America as a pan-Indian emblem and mass-produced as a souvenir, a development many elders and scholars caution has drifted far from its original use. The central opening matters: a web tied shut is sometimes said to hold bad dreams, while an open web lets them drain away. Modern Ojibwe and other Indigenous artists continue to make dreamcatchers in the traditional spirit, restoring its function as a guardian of children's sleep.

name: Drilbu Bell
description: The drilbu is the ritual hand bell of Himalayan Buddhism, cast in a bell-metal alloy so that it rings a long, clear note, and struck or rung during ceremonies as the companion of the dorje sceptre. The bell is held in the left hand while the dorje is held in the right, and the two together are used in most monastic rituals of the Tibetan schools. The handle of the drilbu is cast as the face of a deity, most often the goddess Prajnaparamita, the embodiment of wisdom, whose head forms the knob above a vajra finial. The sound of the bell is used to summon the attention of the practitioner and the deities, to mark the turning points of a rite, and to fill the space of the ritual, and its tone is said to carry the compassion and clarity that the ceremony invokes.

name: Drotárstvo (Wire Craft)
description: Drotarstvo is the Slovak craft of working iron wire, born in the eighteenth century when travelling drotári from the hills of northern Slovakia walked across Europe mending cracked pottery, glass and pipes with fine wire bindings. What began as tinkering became an art: journeymen and masters built up latticework jugs, birdcages, vases and small household utensils entirely from wire, and the reinforced pots with their neat braided seams were admired as folk masterpieces. The craft was carried by emigrant drotári as far as Russia, the Balkans and America, and the region around Považie in particular produced dynasties of wiremen. In 2019 UNESCO inscribed drotarstvo on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and museums in Bratislava and Považská Bystrica preserve both the tools and the elaborate wirework that survives from the trade's heyday.

name: Drómi and Leyding
description: Leyding and Drómi are the first two fetters with which the gods tried to bind the wolf Fenrir, before the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir finally held him. The gods first had a great chain called Leyding forged, but the wolf snapped it as easily as a cord. They then made a second, much stronger fetter called Drómi, but when Fenrir braced his feet against the ground and braced his back against a rock, he burst the chain apart, sending fragments flying across the countryside. The two failed fetters set up the famous scene in which the suspicious wolf agreed to be bound by the 'silken ribbon' Gleipnir only if a god placed his hand in the beast's mouth as a pledge — the pledge that cost Týr his hand. Leyding and Drómi thus frame the myth of the binding of Fenrir, and the story of the chain that was too strong for its maker remains one of the best-known episodes of the Eddas.

name: Duduk (Armenian Double-Reed Flute)
description: The duduk is the double-reed woodwind of Armenia, carved from apricot wood into a short cylindrical tube fitted with a wide, flat reed, and played with circular breathing so the sound never stops. The technique of breathing in through the nose while squeezing air from the cheeks gives the duduk its characteristic long, breathy, singing notes, and the instrument is called the voice of Armenia for its warm, mournful tone. It accompanies folk songs, dances and round dances, but above all the lament, and it pairs with songs of mourning and love at weddings, funerals and the great feast days. In 2008 UNESCO inscribed duduk music on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and the instrument has also found a wider audience in world music and film scores.

name: Duho
description: The duho is the carved wooden seat of the Taíno, a low ceremonial stool of guaiacum or mahogany on which caciques and behiques sat in ritual, carved in the shape of an animal, a crouching figure or a reclining zemi with upturned chin and closed eyes. Spanish chroniclers recorded chiefs receiving Columbus and his men seated on duhos, and surviving museum pieces dated to around AD 600 span the islands from Cuba to the Bahamas, showing the form was ancient and widespread. The stool lifted its sitter above the ground and toward the spirits, and it was used in the cohoba ceremony, when the behique inhaled the sacred powder and entered a visionary state; some duhos are carved with a flat surface that could support a tray or zemi during those rites. The finest are praised for the grace of their carving, with four legs and a curved back shaped from a single piece of wood. The duho is one of the most distinctive objects of Taíno art and a proud emblem of Caribbean Indigenous heritage.

name: Durendal
description: Durendal, Roland's sword in the eleventh-century Chanson de Roland, is the greatest blade of the Frankish epic, carried by the hero and given to him, according to the poem, by the emperor Charlemagne. Its gilded pommel holds holy relics, a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil and hair of Saint Denis, making the sword a reliquary as much as a weapon. Wounded and dying after the rearguard's defeat at Roncevaux, Roland refuses to let the Saracens take the blade and tries to shatter it against a marble rock; the sword survives and the rock splits open. The same motif appears in the later Old French epic tradition, and a weapon reputed to be Durendal was long displayed at the church of Rocamadour in France. In Italian romance the blade passes to other heroes, including Ruggiero, showing how the object travelled across medieval literary cultures. Durendal stands beside Excalibur and Joyeuse as one of the archetypal Christian hero-swords of the Middle Ages.

name: Dvojanka
description: The dvojanka is a double flute of North Macedonia, carved from a single piece of wood, sometimes elder or ash, as two parallel pipes joined at the mouth, with fingerholes on one pipe only. The second, unholed pipe serves as a drone, sounding a steady note beneath the melody and giving the instrument its haunting, reedy character; regional names include dvojnica, and similar double flutes are known across the Balkans. Shepherds played the dvojanka in the mountains, and it accompanied the slow, ornamented tunes of Macedonian pastoral music, the whistle of the drone carrying over pasture and dance ground alike. A small community of folk musicians and instrument makers keeps the dvojanka alive today, and it is heard at ethnographic concerts and village festivals alongside the kaval and the gaida.

name: Dyrnwyn
description: Dyrnwyn, meaning 'white-hilt', is the sword of Rhydderch Hael, the Generous, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain listed in medieval Welsh texts. If anyone but Rhydderch himself drew the blade from its scabbard it burst into flame from its cross-guard to its point, burning the unworthy bearer until it was sheathed again. Rhydderch, famed as one of the Three Generous Men of Britain, refused no one who asked to borrow the sword, but every borrower quickly handed it back once its fiery property was revealed. The treasure list survives in a group of Welsh manuscripts, and the earliest versions record only the names of the treasures without explanation. The sword is sometimes said to have been drawn by a noble warrior who alone could wield it without harm, though the tradition records nothing more of its fate. Dyrnwyn belongs to the same family of test-weapons as many Celtic blades, punishing the unfit and rewarding the worthy.

name: Edan Ogboni Staff
description: The edan are paired staffs of brass or iron belonging to the Ogboni, or Osugbo, the elders' society of the Yoruba, each staff topped by a seated human figure, one male and one female, joined by a short length of chain. The pair stands for the moral unity of the earth, and the edan is kept on the society's altar, where oaths are sworn over it; to swear falsely while the edan rested before the assembly was to call down the earth's judgment. The society, whose name means 'elders,' served as the council of justice and the keeper of the land's authority, and its emblem carried that weight. Members wear small edan hung about the neck as badges of office, while the great pair on the altar is used in the society's rites. The figures are cast by the brassworkers and kept polished, and the edan remains one of the most distinctive objects of Yoruba governance. It joins the sacred and the legal in a single staff of iron.

name: Eglė's Dress
description: In the Lithuanian tale 'Eglė the Queen of Serpents', the garment Eglė wore when she bathed at the lake: a coiled grass snake slipped into her sleeve and would return her clothing only if she promised to marry its king. That pledged dress drives the whole tale — the serpent bridegroom, nine years lived beneath the sea, three impossible tasks set for her children — and at the end Eglė, refusing to follow her transformed husband's cruelty, is changed into a spruce tree, while her children become the oak, ash and birch of the Lithuanian forest. The dress is the object that binds the human and the serpent world in one of the best-loved tales of the Baltic.

name: Ehecailacacozcatl
description: The ehecailacacozcatl, the 'wind jewel,' is the spiral shell breast ornament of the wind god Quetzalcoatl in his aspect of Ehecatl, worn at the throat and tied to the whirlwind that sweeps the road before the rain god Tlaloc and scatters the seeds of the world. Aztec images of Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl show the cut conch worn as a pectoral and the spiral shell among his emblems, and the Florentine Codex connects the wind god's journeys to the clearing of the rain's path. The shell is the conch of the wind, its spiral echoing the whirlwind and its sound carrying the breath of the god, and the ornament is sometimes paired with the crown of feathers of the wind god's dancing form. The ehecailacacozcatl belongs to the larger Mesoamerican symbolism of the conch as music, rain, and fertility. It is one of the defining attributes of Ehecatl in Aztec and earlier Teotihuacan art, and it remains a standard emblem of the wind deity in studies of Mesoamerican religion.

name: Ektara
description: The ektara is the one-stringed lute of rural Bengal, made from a gourd or a bamboo tube with a skin face and a single steel string that is plucked and struck to produce a thin, continuous drone. It is the instrument of the wandering Baul singers of Bengal, who carry the ektara with their other small instruments and sing songs of the divine within the human body, of love and of the inner search, in an oral tradition that is not written down. The Bauls move from village to village, and the drone of the ektara sets the rhythm and pitch for the song, sometimes with a gopichand drum in the other hand. The instrument is simple to make and to carry, and its name means one string, so that the whole music of the sect is often summed up in the single note it produces.

name: Eleke
description: The eleke is the beaded necklace of Cuban Santería, strung in the colors of a particular orisha and given in ceremony to place the wearer under that spirit's protection. White for Obatalá, red and white for Changó, blue and white for Yemayá, yellow for Oshun, the pattern of the beads names the orisha to anyone who knows the tradition, and the necklaces are worn close to the skin as a constant guard. The eleke descends from the beaded collars of Yoruba religion, brought to Cuba with the people who were enslaved and transformed into the religion's regalia; each necklace is consecrated before it is given, and the ceremony of receiving one marks a step into the religion's life. Removing the necklace, or letting it break, is treated with concern, and the beads are handled respectfully and kept clean. The eleke is thus at once ornament, devotion and a visible map of the sacred.

name: Elixir of Immortality
description: The elixir of immortality is the drug of eternal life that the Queen Mother of the West, Xiwangmu, is said to have kept in her paradise of Kunlun, and it is the pivot of one of the most famous tales in Chinese mythology. The archer Hou Yi obtained the elixir as a reward for shooting down the nine suns, but his wife Chang'e swallowed it to keep it from a thief, and was lifted to the moon where she lives forever in the cold lunar palace. The tale, recorded in Han-era sources such as Huainanzi, gave the moon its goddess, and the jade rabbit that pounds herbs in a mortar is her companion on the lunar surface. In later Daoist tradition the elixir became the goal of alchemy, both as a physical drug of cinnabar and gold and as an inner refinement of the body's energies. The story anchors the Mid-Autumn Festival, when offerings of mooncakes recall Chang'e's flight, and the elixir remains the standard image of the Daoist quest for transcendence.

name: Estonian Kannel
description: Estonia's plucked box zither, a small winged or trapezoid instrument carved from a single piece of wood and strung with wire or gut strings, played to accompany regilaul, the ancient runic-song tradition shared with Finland's kantele and Lithuania's kanklės. Folk songs and folk archaeology place the kannel in Baltic-Finnic music for well over a thousand years, and the instrument was long the companion of song and dance in the village. It survives and flourishes in the folk revival, where ensembles play both the small historical kannel and enlarged chromatic versions, keeping the oldest instrument of Estonian music on the concert stage.

name: Ethiopian Ketab Protective Scroll
description: Ketab are protective prayer scrolls of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, strips of parchment inscribed with prayers, sacred names, and devotional images, then rolled and worn or hung as amulets. They are written by debtera, the church's trained scholars, and by diviners, who combine liturgical texts with protective formulae in Ge'ez. The scrolls guard the wearer against evil spirits, illness, the evil eye, and the harm that is believed to come from buda, the people accused of possessing the evil eye. A scroll's shape follows its purpose: some are narrow strips folded into a leather case for wearing round the neck, while others are long, illustrated rolls made for the sick to keep at home. The images, crosses, eyes, saints, and the Archangel Michael on his horse, echo church painting in miniature. Ketab are still commissioned today, keeping alive a manuscript tradition that reaches back centuries.

name: Ethiopian Processional Cross
description: Ethiopian processional crosses are tall brass, silver, or bronze crosses carried on staffs before the clergy during the liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Each cross is unique, built from a dense tracery of openwork that varies with the workshop and the region; the arms are set in a frame that may be square, round, or diamond-shaped, and the patterns are filled with small figurative and geometric motifs. The cross is both instrument and image: it is held over the congregation as a blessing, kissed by the faithful, and its openwork is understood to evoke the Tree of Life and the victory of Christ. Processional crosses accompany the tabot at outdoor festivals such as the Meskel finding of the True Cross, when the square cross itself stands at the centre of the bonfire ceremony. Silver crosses were made for the great monasteries of Lalibela and Axum, while brass crosses were the common liturgical object of every church. Related hand crosses, carried by every priest, share the same design language.

name: Evenki Shaman's Costume
description: Ceremonial cloak of the Evenki shaman, sewn from reindeer hide and hung with iron pendants shaped as birds, fish, deer, snakes and human figures that represent the shaman's spirit-helpers, with a fringed apron and iron rattles. The costume is preserved in the collections of the Russian Museum of Ethnography and Siberian regional museums. Each pendant is forged to correspond to a spirit that the shaman called upon, and their number and variety grew with the shaman's rank and experience. The cloak is worn over the ordinary clothes with an apron and a headdress, and the iron objects ring together in motion, so that the shaman's very movements sound the spirits' presence. A new costume was made at consecration, sometimes according to the vision of an ancestor shaman, and it was kept apart from daily garments and handed down or destroyed at the shaman's death. The costume is the physical map of the Evenki spirit world, and ethnographers have used its pendants to reconstruct the lists of helpers in Evenki belief.

name: Excalibur
description: The great sword of King Arthur, given to him by the Lady of the Lake after he broke his first blade, and returned to her waters by Sir Bedivere when Arthur died at Camlann. In Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485) the scabbard, not the blade, is the true treasure, since it protects the wearer from wounding in battle. The name, from the Latin Caliburnus and the Welsh Caledfwlch, also attaches in later romance to the sword Arthur drew from the stone, though the oldest sources keep the two blades separate. The weapon already appears in Welsh tradition in Culhwch ac Olwen, where Arthur's sword Caledfwlch is named among his possessions. Its giving and return make it a gift of the Otherworld that cannot be kept by mortal hands, a pattern echoed across Celtic legend. Excalibur has become the archetypal magic sword of modern fantasy, carried into films, games and retellings of the Arthurian cycle.

name: Eye of Horus
description: The Eye of Horus, the wedjat, is the ancient Egyptian amulet of the eye that the god Thoth healed after the falcon god Horus lost it in his contest with Set for the throne of Egypt. The healed eye became a sign of wholeness, healing and protection, and wedjat amulets in gold, lapis lazuli, faience and stone were worn by the living and placed on mummies from the Old Kingdom into the Graeco-Roman period. In the myth of the contendings of Horus and Set, recorded in the Chester Beatty papyrus, the eye is torn out and later restored, and the restoration made the sign a symbol of renewal. The hieroglyphic form of the eye also served in Egyptian mathematics: its parts represented the fractions used for measuring hekat volumes of grain. The eye was painted on coffins, boats and tomb walls to guard the dead, and it was often combined with a cobra or sun disk. It remains today one of the most widely recognised of all Egyptian symbols, worn as jewellery across the world.

name: False Face Mask
description: The False Face masks of the Haudenosaunee are distorted human faces carved from living basswood, painted red and black, and used by the False Face Society in curing ceremonies that drive sickness from the sick. The twisted features recall the forest beings of tradition, above all the Great Face who is said to have broken his own face in a contest with the sun and gained power over disease, appearing in the story of the Flying Head. Traditionally the masks are carved from the living tree without metal tools, so the bark and spirit of the tree remain part of the carving, and they are kept by society members where tobacco can be offered to them. Historically the masks were never sold; their acquisition by museums and collectors in the late twentieth century became a major controversy, and some collections have since returned them. Worn by dancers who blow warm ashes over the patient, the masks embody the being that both causes and cures sickness.

name: Fijian Masi (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of Fiji, beaten by women from the inner bark of the paper mulberry into broad sheets, which are felted together on a wooden anvil and painted with geometric designs in black, brown and red. Masi is made in working parties for gifts, dress and ceremony: it wraps the body at weddings and funerals, lines the walls of the chiefly house, and the finest decorated pieces are given on occasions of state. The patterns are handed down within clans, whose history the cloth records, and the same barkcloth family is known across the Pacific — masi in Fiji, siapo in Samoa, ngatu in Tonga, kapa in Hawai'i — with each island giving the craft its own style.

name: Fijian War Club
description: Carved club of the Fijian islands, made from the dense wood of the vesi (ironwood) or Pacific casuarina and shaped in a wide range of named forms: the long-bladed ulato, the throwing club, the bulbous totokia with its blunt striking head, and ceremonial clubs inlaid with shell or whalebone. War clubs were the emblem of the Fijian warrior and badges of rank, carried by chiefs as symbols of office and passed down as named trophies and treasures whose owners' histories were remembered. Some were also laid with chiefs in burial, and clubs and whale teeth together formed the ceremonial wealth used to seal alliances and settle the fiercest disputes.

name: Firebird's Feather
description: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. In Afanasyev's tale the feather, and later the bird itself, is sought as a task set by the tsar; the radiant Firebird became a favourite motif of Russian decorative art. The feather is usually the first test: the hero who takes it must then capture the living bird, often with a golden cage, and afterwards the horse with the golden mane and the fair princess Vasilisa. Because the bird is otherworldly, its feather is sometimes said to burn whatever it touches and to heal the sick if kept near. The motif later inspired Stravinsky's 1910 ballet 'The Firebird', which made the glowing feather a worldwide image of Russian fairy-tale art.

name: Flaming Pearl
description: The flaming pearl, huozhu, is a luminous orb wreathed in curling flame that Chinese art shows two dragons chasing or guarding, and it is one of the most common motifs of East Asian decoration. The image appears on temple roofs, ceramic dishes, paintings, and lanterns, and its meaning draws on several layers: in Buddhist iconography the pearl is the cintamani, the wish-granting jewel that fulfils every desire, while in Daoist cosmology it can stand for the moon, the sun, or the inner pearl of spiritual refinement. The dragon that guards the pearl is usually the celestial dragon of rain and water, and the chase motif is sometimes read as the play of yin and yang or of the sun and moon across the heavens. In folk belief the pearl is also linked to the treasure of the dragon's undersea palace, and stories tell of heroes who descend to the sea king's court for the jewel. Whatever the reading, the flaming pearl carries a consistent charge of wisdom, wealth, and transformation, and it remains the standard companion of the dragon in pan-Asian art.

name: Fon Asen Altar Staff
description: The asen is the commemorative altar staff of the Fon of Benin, a forged iron pole topped with a figurative scene, an ancestor at work, an animal, a scene of daily life, set in a base of clay or iron and placed beside the ancestor altar of the compound. When a family member dies, an asen is raised for the dead, and through it the ancestor receives offerings during the rites of remembrance and is fed and spoken with as if still present. The iron is worked by smiths, who are themselves set apart in Fon society, and the figures are made to be read: a hunter with his gun, a woman at the mortar, the emblems of the life the dead one lived. The asen is central to the Vodun practice of ancestor veneration, and older pieces, their iron darkened with age and offerings, are valued in museums as records of Dahomey's families. In the compound, the row of asen is the visible genealogy of the household.

name: Franks Casket
description: The Franks Casket, also called the Auzon Casket, is an eighth-century Anglo-Saxon chest carved from whalebone, about 23 centimetres long, with panels bearing scenes from Germanic legend, the Bible and classical history, framed by inscriptions in runes and Latin. Its front panel shows the smith Weland being released by the maiden Beadohild after his imprisonment by King Nithhad, while the right panel shows the Adoration of the Magi, a pairing of pagan and Christian imagery typical of the period. The runic inscriptions, including a cryptic challenge in Old English verse, make the casket one of the most studied objects in early English archaeology. It was bought in the nineteenth century by the antiquarian Augustus Franks after being found at Auzon in France, and is now in the British Museum, with one panel in the Bargello in Florence. The casket's mixture of whalebone, runes and interwoven legends marks it as a key witness to Anglo-Saxon storytelling.

name: Frau Holle's Feather Bed
description: Frau Holle's feather bed is the great bedding that the old woman shakes out in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Frau Holle' (KHM 24), causing its feathers to fall to earth as snow. The industrious heroine, after her fall into the well and a period of service shaking the bed each morning, is rewarded with a shower of gold, while the lazy sister earns only pitch. The tale explains the seasons through household labour, the winter snow being nothing more than Frau Holle's feathers flying. Frau Holle herself, a fair, long-toothed old woman who rewards diligence and punishes idleness, is sometimes identified by scholars with the Germanic goddess Holda of folklore, who was said to shake her feather pillows to make snow. The episode is among the most famous comic explanations in the Grimms' collection. The feather bed is the story's hinge, turning domestic work into the natural world's weather.

name: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
description: Freyja's falcon cloak, also called the feather cloak or fjaðrhamr, is a garment of feathers that lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon. In the Prose Edda the cloak is kept by the goddess Freyja and lent out when the gods need swift flight: Loki borrows it to search for the goddess Iðunn after the giant Þjazi carries her off, and later uses it to pursue Þjazi, who had taken the shape of an eagle, back to the walls of Asgard where the gods kill him. In the poem Þrymskviða, Freyja's cloak is likewise the means by which Loki flies out to steal back the hammer Mjölnir. Shape-shifting feather-cloaks appear elsewhere in Norse legend, most famously in the story of the smith Völund and his swan-maiden bride. Freyja's falcon cloak is the standard example of the feathered flying garment of Norse myth.

name: Freyr's Sword
description: Freyr's sword is the magic blade of the god Freyr that fights by itself, without a hand to wield it. In Skírnismál, Freyr gives the sword to his servant Skírnir as payment for wooing the giantess Gerðr on his behalf — a gift of the self-fighting sword in exchange for love. The loss is fatal at Ragnarök: the Prose Edda recounts that Freyr, lacking his good sword, fights the fire giant Surtr and falls, having given away his only weapon. The sword is thus remembered in the Eddas as the price of love and the cause of a god's death, and it is often read as a parable of how love and war can demand the same sacrifice. It remains a standard example in discussions of the self-acting weapons of myth, and the tale of the sword given away for Gerðr is retold in most modern versions of the Eddas.

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a very long overtone flute of the Slovak shepherds, the central instrument of the Podpoľanie region, made from elder, maple or ash wood and reaching 160 to 200 centimetres in length, with a short side tube that carries the wind to the main bore. It has only three finger holes, yet a skilled player produces a low, humming bass and high, crying overtones by overblowing, and the traditional repertoire imitates the gurgle of springs, the wind and long pastoral calls. Shepherds played the fujara while tending flocks on the slopes of Poľana, and each maker decorated the instrument individually with burnt or carved ornament, so no two fujaras are alike. UNESCO proclaimed the fujara and its music a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008, and it is now heard both at folk festivals in Detva and in concert music.

name: Gaida
description: The gaida is the Bulgarian bagpipe, an instrument built from a whole tanned goatskin that serves as the air bag, with a chanter pipe for the melody and a single long drone pipe that sounds a constant bass note. Its bright, cutting tone comes from a single beating reed in the chanter, and a skilled player holds the bag under the arm, fingers the chanter's holes and taps out rhythms as he squeezes. The gaida is the leading instrument of Bulgarian folk music, accompanying the horo line dances at weddings, village feasts and festivals, and in the Rodopi mountains it is traditionally played for the slow, meandering dance tunes of the region. Because shepherds were the first players, the gaida is bound up with the pastoral life, and it remains the national instrument of Bulgaria, heard from folk ensembles to wedding bands.

name: Galdrastafir
description: Galdrastafir, the collective name for the magical staves of Icelandic folk tradition, drawn from the 17th century onward in grimoires such as the Huld manuscript. Each stave mixes rune-like strokes into a sigil for a single aim — protection, luck, healing, or harm. They form the best-documented stave-magic corpus in Europe, though many survive without clear instructions for use. The signs descend from medieval rune practice, but they were amplified into dense, staff-like figures that could be carved on wood, cut into horn or bone, or drawn on paper and skin. Manuscripts like the Huld collection of 1860 preserve dozens of them, from the famous Vegvísir and Ægishjálmr to obscure personal signs, and their modern revival has made them symbols of Icelandic heritage as much as instruments of folk magic.

name: Gallehus Golden Horns
description: The Gallehus golden horns are two magnificent drinking and ritual horns of the 5th century AD, found in a field at Gallehus in southern Jutland in 1639 and 1734 and among the most famous objects of Nordic antiquity. The shorter horn bore a Proto-Norse runic inscription along the rim, 'ek hlewagastiR holtijaR horna tawido' — 'I, Hlewagastir (also read as LagestheR) of Holt, made the horn' — one of the earliest complete sentences written in the Elder Futhark. Both horns were built up from rings of sheet gold covered with stamped and soldered figures of men, beasts, and symbols, whose meaning scholars still debate. In 1802 they were stolen from the Royal Kunstkammer and melted down by the goldsmith Niels Heidenreich, an act that made the horns a national tragedy in Denmark; reconstructions made from the surviving 18th-century drawings are displayed at the National Museum in Copenhagen, and the horns inspired Oehlenschläger's poem 'Guldhornene'.

name: Ganesh Idol
description: The Ganesha idol is the murti or sacred image of Ganesha, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, who as the remover of obstacles is invoked at the beginning of every undertaking, from weddings and housewarmings to examinations and journeys. According to the most widely repeated story, Parvati created the boy from the paste with which she bathed and set him to guard her door; when Shiva tried to enter, the boy barred the way, and Shiva struck off his head with his trident. At Parvati's grief the god promised to restore the boy, taking the head of the first living creature he found, an elephant, and this origin is retold in ganesha-story and in the tale of the origin of Ganesha's elephant head. Ganesha idols range from tiny brass household figures to the huge clay and plaster images commissioned for Ganesh Chaturthi in Maharashtra and elsewhere, which are worshipped and then immersed in water at the close of the festival. The idol carries his attributes, including the broken tusk, the modaka sweet and the mouse vehicle, each of which is glossed in sermons and picture books.

name: Garamantian Rock-Art Chariot
description: The Garamantian chariot is the two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle represented in the rock art of the Libyan Sahara, above all in the massif of the Tadrart Acacus, which was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1985. The engravings, often showing the horse at a stylized 'flying gallop', belong to the Horse Period of Saharan rock art and are attributed to the Garamantes, the desert people whose kingdom in the Fezzan and capital at Garama are confirmed by archaeology and by the classical writers. Herodotus describes the Garamantes driving four-horse chariots into the desert to hunt the 'Troglodyte Ethiopians', and hundreds of similar chariot drawings are scattered across the Sahara from Libya to the Atlantic, along the ancient routes of the trans-Saharan trade. These images record the arrival of the horse as a prestige and military animal in the region around the first millennium BCE, even if long-distance chariot travel in the deep desert is now doubted by scholars. The chariot pictures of the Acacus survive as the clearest visual testimony of the Garamantian world, the same world that built an underground network of foggaras to irrigate the desert farms.

name: Gata Bera Drum
description: The gata bera is the large cylindrical drum of Sri Lanka, slung from the hip and beaten with sticks or open hands at Buddhist perahera processions, temple rites, village festivals and healing ceremonies. Its name comes from the Sinhala word for a pot, and the barrel is traditionally carved from jak or asala wood with heads of cowhide braced by rope and leather thongs, tuned so the deep beat carries over crowds. It is the lead drum of the Kandyan dance tradition, where drummers and dancers train together from boyhood, and it also drives the masked exorcism dances that the Sinhalese perform to pacify the sanni and riri yaksha, the disease demons of the folk tradition. A Sinhalese story holds that the drum's rhythms were first given by a god, and the instrument remains the sound of celebration and of healing alike in the island's ritual life.

name: Gelede Mask
description: The Gelede mask is a carved wooden headdress of the Yoruba, worn tilted on the top of the head by a dancer who gazes out through the costume's veil while the crest rises above him, bearing figures of animals, people, market scenes or the faces of those being honored. The performance honors the great mothers, awon iya wa, 'our mothers,' the powerful women, both living and of the night, whose spiritual force underlies the community, and the dance at once celebrates them and gently mocks the follies of the town, using laughter to restore harmony. Gelede belongs especially to the Yoruba of southwestern Nigeria and spreads across the border into Benin and Togo, and in 2008 UNESCO inscribed it on the list of intangible cultural heritage. The Efe, the night performance that precedes the daytime Gelede, carries the weight of the ritual, with its songs of praise and warning. The masks, painted in bright colors, are the festive and formidable face of that whole tradition.

name: Geobukseon
description: The geobukseon, the turtle ship, is the armoured warship that Admiral Yi Sun-sin built for the Korean fleet in the 1590s to repel the Japanese invasions of the Imjin War, and it is the most celebrated naval vessel in Korean history. The ship was roofed with an iron-studded shell that shed fire arrows and repelled boarding parties, and it was fitted with cannon that could be fired from the sides while the deck stayed protected. Although the turtle ship was a real and effective warship, it passed quickly into folklore as an invincible protector of the coast, celebrated in songs, tales, and the war memoirs of Admiral Yi himself. Modern scholarship notes that the historical vessels were smaller and less dramatic than later depictions, but the legend endures, and the turtle ship is a national symbol of defence and ingenuity. Reconstructions are displayed and sailed at memorials such as the Hyeonchungsa shrine and the war museum in Seoul, and the turtle ship remains the emblem of Korean naval power.

name: Ghot Pot
description: The ghot is the pot placed before the bride and groom in the ashirbad blessing of Bengali Hindu weddings, a brass or clay vessel filled with paddy, durba grass and other auspicious items, with a red-and-white thread tied around its mouth. The word ghot covers the pot itself and its role in the blessing, and the pot is kept in the wedding space while the elders speak their good wishes over the couple. The paddy stands for grain and fertility, the durba grass for growth and prosperity, and the ghats are prepared by the women of the two families as part of the wedding's household ritual. The pot is a small, everyday object carrying a large ceremonial meaning, and the same kind of vessel appears in other Hindu rites of the region as a seat for the divine presence.

name: Ginfaxi
description: Ginfaxi is an Icelandic magical stave recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn to ensure victory over a rival in a contest or argument. In the tradition it is used together with the stave Gapaldur: Gapaldur is kept under the heel of the right foot and Ginfaxi under the toes of the left foot, so that the wearer wins bouts of Icelandic wrestling, glíma, and other competitions. The name echoes the horse-names of Norse myth such as Skinfaxi and Hrímfaxi, and a horse called Ginfaxi is attested in the sagas, though the stave itself is a folk-magic sign rather than a mythic beast. It belongs to the combative family of galdrastafir, used when the prize was a bout, a trade, or a court case. The stave is still reproduced in modern collections of Icelandic magical signs.

name: Gjallarhorn
description: Gjallarhorn is the great horn of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods who guards the rainbow bridge Bifröst, and its sound carries across all the worlds. At Ragnarök Heimdallr raises the horn to his lips and its blast summons gods and men to the final battle on the field of Vígríðr, a call that is among the great set-pieces of Norse eschatology. Snorri also says that Heimdallr drinks from the horn at the well of Mímir, suggesting that it doubled as a drinking vessel in some accounts. The name 'resounding horn' or 'shrill horn' fits its role as the signal of the end times. Gjallarhorn has passed into modern culture as the archetype of a world-ending call, and it appears in fantasy fiction, music, and art whenever the Ragnarök myth is retold.

name: Gjellestad Ship
description: A Viking-age ship burial discovered at Gjellestad in Ostfold, Norway, first detected with ground-penetrating radar in 2018 and excavated from 2020 to 2021. The oak keel and strakes of the roughly twenty-meter ship survived as a dark imprint in the clay, along with iron rivets, beads, and a soapstone vessel, though the wooden hull itself had largely rotted away. The site sits beside the Jellhaug burial mound and an older cult or settlement area, suggesting a high-status burial landscape of the late Viking age. It was the first ship excavation in Norway in more than a century, and the finds are intended for the future Museum of the Viking Age in Oslo.

name: Gjermundbu Helmet
description: The only reasonably complete Viking-age helmet found in Scandinavia, recovered from a wealthy chieftain's burial mound at Gjermundbu in Ringerike, Norway, in 1943. The iron helmet has a rounded cap, a spectacle-like eye guard, and a mail curtain for the neck, and was buried with a mail coat, swords, and gaming pieces. It now stands in the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo. The helmet's deep brow and eye guard give it the fierce face that popular images of the Viking age draw, and its iron cap was built of several plates riveted together under a brow band, with the mail aventail protecting the neck and throat. Because so few pieces of Viking-age armour survive, the Gjermundbu helmet is the single most important witness to what a Norse warrior actually wore into battle.

name: Gleipnir
description: Gleipnir is the third and final fetter with which the gods bound the wolf Fenrir, after the great chains Leyding and Drómi both snapped. It was made by the dwarves from six impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, and a bird's spittle — which is why, the Edda explains, none of these things now exist in the world. Gleipnir is as thin as a silken ribbon, yet nothing could break it. To persuade the suspicious wolf to let himself be bound, the god Týr placed his hand in Fenrir's mouth as a pledge, and lost it when the wolf found himself unable to escape. The binding holds until Ragnarök, when the wolf breaks free in the final battle. Gleipnir is the classic example of the 'impossible object' in Old Norse mythology.

name: Gogok
description: The gogok is the comma-shaped jade ornament threaded onto the gold crowns, belts, and necklaces of the ancient Silla kingdom, excavated in large numbers from the tombs of Gyeongju, and it is the most distinctive form of Korean prehistoric jade. Carved from hard nephrite and often pale green or white, the beads may derive from the shamanic curved beads of the north and are linked by scholars to fertility symbolism and to the bear-woman Ungnyeo's offering in the Dangun foundation myth. In the tombs of Silla's elite the gogok hangs from the crowns and diadems in cascading rows, and the form persisted into the Gaya and Baekje kingdoms. Modern Korean scholarship sees in the curved bead an image of a claw or a moon-crescent, and the gogok appears on the national emblem of the modern Gyeongju region. It remains the emblem of ancient Korean royal regalia and one of the most recognizable objects of the country's archaeological heritage.

name: Gokstad Ship
description: A seaworthy Viking-age longship found in a burial mound at Gokstad in Sandefjord, Norway, in 1880. Around 23 meters long with sixteen pairs of oars, it was built for open-sea sailing and held the remains of a chieftain. A full-scale copy, the Viking, crossed the Atlantic to Chicago in 1893, proving its sailing qualities. The original is displayed in the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo. The Gokstad ship's clean, clinker-built lines, deep keel, and tall mast made it the working sea-boat of the Viking age, able to carry a crew across the open ocean and up narrow rivers alike. The burial in its mound included shields along the rail and a full set of gear for the dead chieftain, and the successful Atlantic crossing of the replica demonstrated that the old ships were no mere coastal craft.

name: Golden Bough
description: The golden bough is the branch Aeneas must pluck before he may enter the underworld, the passport of his descent in the sixth book of the Aeneid. The Sibyl of Cumae tells him the bough grows in a dark wood, is of gold like mistletoe in midwinter, and can only be plucked if Fate allows: no human strength can break it, but if the Fates consent it yields at the touch, and it is the gift that Proserpina, queen of the dead, demands before any living man may pass the gate of Dis. Aeneas finds the bough on the tree, plucks it, and carries it down through the underworld, leaving it at last on the threshold of Proserpina's palace. The bough has been read since antiquity as an image of initiation, secrecy, and the crossing of death's threshold. Frazer made it the title and organizing symbol of his great study of myth and ritual, and it remains one of the most suggestive objects in classical poetry.

name: Golden Fleece
description: The golden fleece of the winged ram that carried Phrixus and Helle to Colchis, where Phrixus sacrificed the ram and hung its fleece in the grove of Ares under a sleepless dragon's guard. Jason and the Argonauts sailed the Argo to retrieve it, and the quest, with its trials set by King Aeetes, is the central adventure of the Argonaut cycle. The fleece stands for the distant prize that turns a voyage into a legend, and the dragon that guarded it became one of the best-known monsters of Greek myth.

name: Gourgui Water Jar
description: The gourgui is a large earthenware water jar of Tunisia, made of porous red terracotta and fitted with a narrow neck and a pouring spout, traditionally used to store and cool drinking water. Because water slowly seeps through the unglazed clay and evaporates from the surface, the contents of the gourgui stay noticeably cooler than the air in the hot Tunisian summer. The jar was kept in the skifa, the entrance hall of traditional houses, mounted on a wooden stand formed of three crossed branches and a crescent-shaped tray, where it greeted family and guests alike, and similar jars still stand in the courtyards of mosques and in front of shops for passers-by and travellers. Before piped water, the gourgui supplied both daily drinking water and water for the ritual ablutions of Islam, and it was produced in three sizes, large, medium and small, in the pottery-making towns of the country. Though plastic and refrigerators have replaced it in most homes, the gourgui is still remembered as a symbol of hospitality and of Tunisian craft.

name: Govi
description: The govi is the earthenware jar of Haitian Vodou that holds the presence of the dead, a red clay vessel or bottle kept in the temple where it contains a spirit or the reclaimed spirit of an ancestor. The most solemn use of the govi belongs to the rite of reclamation, when, a year and a day after a death, the priest retrieves the gwobonanj, the 'big guardian angel,' from the waters of Ginen, the abyssal homeland of the spirits, and the wete mò nan dlo ceremony settles it into the jar. The vessel is then fed with offerings, manje mò, food for the dead, and becomes the place where the ancestor may be consulted, giving advice and protection to the living. If the rite fails or the govi is neglected, misfortune is said to follow the family. The plain clay jar is made extraordinary by the ritual that fills it, and its handling is governed by the strictest respect. Through the govi, the family of the living and the world beneath remain one household.

name: Gram
description: Gram is the great sword of the Völsung heroes, first owned by Sigmund and later reforged for his son Sigurðr, the slayer of the dragon Fáfnir. The sword enters the story when Odin, disguised as a wanderer, thrusts it into the great tree Branstock in the hall of King Völsung, declaring that the one who draws it shall have it as a gift; only Sigmund could pull the blade free. When the sword broke in battle, the shards were kept and re-forged by the smith Regin, and Sigurðr proved the new blade by laying it on the anvil and cleaving it in two before using it to kill Fáfnir. In the German tradition the same sword is called Nothung in the Nibelungenlied and Balmung in other versions, and it lives on in Wagner's Ring cycle as Siegfried's reforged sword. Gram is therefore one of the most famous swords in all of Germanic legend.

name: Great Torc of Snettisham
description: The Great Torc of Snettisham is a large neck-ring of two interlocking gold-alloy tubes with ornate buffer terminals, made in eastern England around 75 BC and worn by a high-status Iron Age Briton. It was found in 1950 in the famous Snettisham hoard excavations in Norfolk, where ploughing repeatedly revealed pits packed with torcs, bracelets and coins.
