The torc was cast by a lost-wax process in a gold-silver-copper alloy that gives it a pale, silvery gleam, and its twisted bodies and polished terminals are masterpieces of Celtic metalwork. Torcs signalled rank and wealth across the Celtic world, worn by warriors, chieftains and sometimes gods, and classical writers record that the Gauls wore gold neck-rings in battle. The Great Torc is dated by the coins found with it and is usually displayed with the slightly larger Snettisham Great Torc of the same hoard. It forms the centrepiece of the British Museum's Iron Age Celtic collection.

name: Green Knight's Holly Branch
description: The holly branch carried by the Green Knight in the opening scenes of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight marks him as a figure of the winter season when he rides into Arthur's hall on New Year's Eve. The poem says the knight carried no shield or spear, only a holly bough in one hand and the great axe in the other, the evergreen symbol of the old year's endurance. He holds the branch in the same hand that grips the axe as he delivers his challenge, so that the two objects together present him as a green man of the turning year. Some readers see the holly as a sign of peace, since it was the emblem used in medieval Christmas observances, while others read it as the badge of a wild, pre-Christian power that intrudes on the court. In the poem's seasonal frame the branch connects the challenge to the cycle of death and renewal. It remains one of the most discussed details of the medieval masterpiece.

name: Gris-Gris Bag
description: The gris-gris bag is a small flannel pouch, often red, filled with herbs, roots, coins, stones or personal items and made by Louisiana root doctors and hoodoo practitioners to carry a 'work' for love, luck, money, protection or success. The name gris-gris is used in New Orleans, while the same charm is known as a mojo bag or hand elsewhere, and the tradition blends West African spiritual practice with colonial folk belief. A bag must often be 'fed' with oils, powders or an offering to keep its power, and it is carried on the body, usually in a pocket or at the waist, and kept secret. Roots such as High John the Conqueror are among the classic ingredients, and the making of a bag follows precise instructions about days, colours and prayers. Gris-gris remains part of New Orleans culture and the Voodoo-hoodoo exchange, a portable connection to the conjure tradition.

name: Grotte Mill
description: The great hand-mill owned by King Fróði, which ground out gold, peace, and abundance. In the Eddic poem Grottasöngr the giantesses Fenja and Menja were forced to turn it until they raised an army; carried aboard a ship, the mill then ground salt until it sank, and so the sea became salt. The same wonder-mill lies at the heart of the Swedish folktale 'Why the Sea Is Salt'. The mill was named Grotti, and it had been quarried from a mountain together with two giant-women who alone had the strength to turn it; King Fróði kept them at the work night and day, and in their grinding song they at last ground out a war-host against him. Bought from a poor man and set to grind salt, the mill went on past the owner's command until the ship was overloaded and went down in the sea. Wonder-mills of the same kind appear again in Swedish tales, where a small hand-mill grinds out flour and salt for its lucky owner until it is stolen and lost to greed.

name: Gríðarvölr
description: Gríðarvölr is the staff of the giantess Gríðr, mother of Víðarr, which she lent to Thor along with iron gloves and a belt of might when he set out against the giant Geirröðr. In the tale told in Skáldskaparmál, Thor uses the staff to fend off the giantess Gjálp and her kin and to brace himself when Geirröðr's sons try to crush him in a chair, and he finally breaks the giant's back with the aid of the borrowed gear. The loan is a rare act of kindness by a giantess toward the thunder god, and Gríðr is remembered as the wisest and most generous of the giantesses for it. The story shows that even Thor needed the help of the giants' own world to defeat the greatest of their kind. Gríðarvölr appears in most modern retellings of the tale of Thor's visit to Geirröðr.

name: Guan Dao
description: The guan dao is the heavy curved-blade polearm historically associated with Guan Yu, the great general of the Three Kingdoms period who was deified as the god of war and of righteousness, and its most famous example is the Green Dragon Crescent Blade. In Romance of the Three Kingdoms Guan Yu carries the enormous weapon, and in legend the blade was so heavy that only he could wield it; temples honouring him display a ceremonial guan dao in his image, and the weapon became a standard of the military temples and of martial artists. The actual historical guan dao developed later than the general's lifetime, and the famous blade is a literary creation, but the association made the weapon a fixture of Chinese and East Asian iconography. In the folk tradition a guan dao kept in a home or temple is thought to carry Guan Yu's protective presence, and it is still carried in lion-dance performances and temple processions. The blade's name has passed into popular culture across the world as the emblem of the bearded warrior-saint.

name: Guksi
description: The Sami cup carved from a single piece of birch burl, with a shallow bowl and a flat handle, worn at the belt for coffee, broth, or water. Because each guksi is shaped from a burl, every piece has a unique grain, and the cup is seasoned by use until it holds the taste of coffee and smoke. Carving is part of the Sami duodji handcraft tradition, still practiced in Norway, Sweden, and Finland, and the finest cups are made of burl that has grown slowly in the cold. Traditionally it was a personal possession, and a well-worn guksi became a valued companion on the reindeer-herding path. In modern use the guksi has also become popular in outdoor life far beyond Sapmi.

name: Gule Wamkulu Mask
description: The gule wamkulu masks of the Chewa of Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique are carved wooden face masks worn by the dancers of the Nyau society, whose great dance of the same name is performed at initiations, funerals, and the memorials of the dead. Nyau means 'the big dance' or 'the dance of the spirits', and the masked dancers embody the ancestors, the animals of the bush, and the forces of the forest, revealing their meanings only to initiates. Each mask has a name and a character, the gentle, the comic, the terrible, and the dancer becomes the spirit while he wears it, speaking in its voice. The Nyau society, open only to initiated men, holds the history and the law of the Chewa, and the masks are stored in hidden groves away from women and strangers. UNESCO inscribed the gule wamkulu on the intangible heritage list in 2005. The tradition is still danced with force in the villages of the Chewa heartland.

name: Gullinbursti
description: Gullinbursti, the 'golden-bristled boar', is the boar of the god Freyr, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri in the same wager that produced the hammer Mjölnir. Its bristles are of gold and shine so brightly that they light the darkest night, and the boar can run through air and water faster than any horse, drawing Freyr's chariot in place of a steed. Snorri records that Odin judged Gullinbursti the best of all the dwarves' gifts, naming the boar along with its second name Slíðrugtanni, and that Freyr rode it to Baldr's funeral. The boar is also the ancestor of the golden boar of Swedish royal imagery and of the Christmas ham that crowns the Swedish table, traditions that carry the myth quietly into modern life. Gullinbursti is one of the most beloved minor treasures of Norse mythology.

name: Gundestrup Cauldron
description: A richly decorated silver cauldron found dismantled in a peat bog at Gundestrup in Himmerland, Jutland, in 1891. Its silver plates show gods, warriors, a horned figure holding a torc, and a great cauldron into which a figure is being lowered, imagery with strong links to Celtic and Thracian art. It was probably made in the southeast of Europe and carried north, then taken apart and offered to the bog as a sacrificial gift. The cauldron is kept in the National Museum of Denmark and is among the most famous objects of Iron Age Europe.

name: Gungnir
description: Gungnir, 'the swaying one', is the spear of Odin, the All-Father, forged by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi in the same contest of treasures that gave the gods their greatest gifts. In the Prose Edda the spear is listed as one of the three marvels the sons of Ivaldi made — the others being Skíðblaðnir and Sif's golden hair. The All-Father opened the war between the Æsir and the Vanir by hurling Gungnir over the enemy host, and that gesture of casting a spear at the start of a battle became the archetype for the practice in Old Norse and later Germanic warfare. Oaths sworn on Gungnir, often called the 'spear-oath', were held to be unbreakable, and the name was used in skaldic kennings as a kenning for 'spear' or 'weapon'. At Ragnarök Odin rides against the wolf Fenrir armed with the spear, though the weapon cannot save him. Gungnir remains a byword for Odin's authority and appears constantly in art and fiction that draws on Norse myth.

name: Gusle
description: The gusle is a single-stringed bowed instrument of the southern Balkans, a round or pear-shaped bowl of maple or other wood covered with a skin, with a single horse-hair string played with a horse-hair bow, used to accompany the chanted epic poetry of the South Slavs. The singer, the guslar, plucks or bows the one string as he recites long heroic songs of battles, outlaws, and ancestral heroes, and among Croats, Serbs, Bosnians, and Montenegrins the instrument is inseparable from the living tradition of oral epic that Milman Parry and Albert Lord made famous with their studies of formulaic composition in the 1930s. In the Croatian lands the gusle was long carried by singers of the Dinaric highlands and the coast, and it has served both as a patriotic symbol and, at times, as an instrument of political song. The one-stringed fiddle is among the simplest instruments of European folk music, yet it carries an oral tradition of exceptional depth.

name: Gusli (Russian Psaltery)
description: Ancient Russian plucked zither, a shallow trapezoid or helmet-shaped board with gut or metal strings, played by the epic singers who performed the byliny. The legendary Novgorod merchant Sadko of the byliny plays the gusli so well that the Sea Tsar summons him to the underwater palace; the instrument is attested in chronicles, miniatures and archaeological finds from Novgorod. Excavated Novgorod gusli date from the 11th to the 14th centuries and were carved from a single block of wood, often with a decorated sound hole. In the bylina Sadko's playing so delights the Sea Tsar that the hero is offered a bride among the sea maidens, and when the gusli breaks the music stops and the underwater court falls silent. The instrument also accompanied ritual song and dance, and it survived among folk musicians into the 19th century, when it was revived for concert and ethnographic performance.

name: Gáe Assail
description: Gáe Assail, the great spear of Lugh, is one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann brought to Ireland, and Lugh carried it into battle at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired against the Fomorians. The Lebor Gabála Érenn and Cath Maige Tuired describe it as a weapon of such force that no warrior could withstand it, and Lugh, who arrives at the battle as champion of the Tuatha Dé Danann, uses it in the rout of the Fomorian host. Its name, sometimes written Gáe Assal, links it to the Otherworld gift-bearers of Irish tradition, and later manuscripts count it among the possessions the god brought from across the sea. In some retellings the spear is said to thirst so strongly for battle that it had to be kept in a vessel of soporific herbs to calm it, a detail that echoes the restless weapons of Celtic legend. It survives today as a symbol of Lugh's kingship and of the ancient Irish world of craft and war.

name: Gákti
description: The traditional dress of the Sámi, a tunic worn with a decorated collar, belt, and headgear, trimmed with bands of red, blue, and yellow and pewter-thread embroidery. Each region of Sápmi has its own cut, colors, and embroidery, so the dress tells the wearer's origin and family. The gákti is still worn for ceremonies and festivals and carries strong cultural identity among Sámi in Norway. The dress is made of wool for the cold, and its bands and borders follow the wearer's home district, with the colours and the shape of the collar, the buttons, and the silver so specific that a knowing eye can read the wearer's valley at a glance. The belt and its ornamented pouch hold the personal tools of the wearer, and the pewter-thread embroidery catches the light in the long winter dark. The gákti has been worn unbroken through the centuries and today is both everyday dress and festive costume.

name: Hagoromo
description: Hagoromo, the feather mantle, is the robe that lets a heavenly maiden, the tennyo, fly between the mortal world and the sky, and it is the central object of one of the most famous Noh plays, Hagoromo, set at Mio Bay. In the play a fisherman named Hakuryo finds a robe of feathers hanging from a pine and refuses to return it until the angel who owns it teaches him the dance of the moon palace, the promise of the robe's return drawing the divine world briefly into the human. The story belongs to the wider family of swan-maiden tales told across Eurasia, in which a supernatural woman loses her flying garment, marries a mortal, and departs when the garment is restored. In Japanese folklore the robe is woven from a thousand feathers and cannot be lifted by any ordinary hand, and a man who hides it may win the maiden's love but loses her when it is found. The play's theme of the boundary between human and divine, and the price of crossing it, has made the hagoromo a staple of Japanese literature and a name given to shrines and dance traditions honouring the heavenly maidens.

name: Haint Blue Paint
description: Haint blue is the pale blue-green paint used on porch ceilings, doors and window frames of Gullah homes in the Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia, said to keep haints, the restless spirits of the dead, from entering the house. Water is traditionally the veil between the living and the dead, and the blue is read as the colour of water that haints cannot cross; the eerie 'boo hag' who slips in through keyholes is among the beings the colour is meant to repel. Some writers also trace the hue to practical roots, noting that the lime-based blue paint helped repel insects and resist damp, and that indigo dye was a staple of Lowcountry plantations. The custom has spread far beyond the Sea Islands into a popular Southern decorative style, with paint companies selling shades called haint blue. For the Gullah, the paint remains a visible sign of a protective, deeply held worldview.

name: Hannya Mask
description: The hannya is a Noh theatre mask sculpted as the face of a woman transfigured by jealousy, resentment, or obsessive love into a horned, serpent-eyed demon with a gaping, fang-filled mouth and trailing metallic teeth. It is worn in plays such as Dojoji, where a spurned woman becomes a serpent that pursues the monk Anchin into a temple bell, and Aoi no Ue, where the living Rokujo no Miyasudokoro torments her rival through spirit-doctoring. The mask is carved in ascending grades of intensity, from a slightly raised mouth to a fully open jaw with gilded fangs, so a single hannya can move on stage from grief to pure fury. In the folk tradition the finished mask is treated with care because it is thought to retain the dangerous emotional charge it depicts, and carvers historically disposed of flawed examples ritually rather than letting them circulate. The hannya name is also used for the demon itself in the wider yokai lore that grew up around the Noh stage.

name: Harpoon
description: The harpoon of the Inuit is the throwing weapon perfected for the open sea, a wooden shaft fitted with a detachable head of bone or ivory that buries itself in the seal's hide and toggles, turning beneath the skin so the animal cannot tear free as the line plays out. The hunter cast from the kayak, holding the line so that the wounded seal could be hauled in as it tired, and the same principle was scaled up with heavier heads and floats for walrus and whales. The design is one of the great achievements of Arctic engineering, refined over millennia of open-water hunting, and it was among the tools that European whalers and explorers adopted and copied. In the belief of the Inuit, the success of the hunt was bound to the goodwill of the sea mother Sedna, who released the animals to a hunter who honored her; a harpoon cast without that favor was said to come back empty. The toggle-head harpoon remains a symbol of the Arctic hunter's skill and restraint.

name: Hawaiian Feather Cloak (ʻAhuʻula)
description: Royal cloak of the Hawaiian chiefs, built on a netted base of olonā fibre and covered with hundreds of thousands of small feathers tied in bundles by a technique called kahekahe. Yellow feathers were taken from the ʻōʻō and mamo — birds whose feathers were pulled by the tens of thousands, contributing to their extinction — and red from the ʻiʻiwi and ʻapapane; Kamehameha I's great cloak is said to contain some 450,000 yellow mamo feathers. The ʻahuʻula was the mark of the highest aliʻi, worn in war and ceremony as a living symbol of chiefly mana and passed down as the supreme heirloom of the kingdom, and surviving examples are counted among the treasures of world museums.

name: Hawaiian Kapa (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of the Hawaiian islands, beaten by women from the inner bark of the wauke, the paper mulberry, on a stone anvil with grooved wooden beaters, and joined and felted into wide sheets. The cloth was printed by stamping with carved bamboo tubes and blocks and with leaves and water-stamped patterns, in colours drawn from earth, charcoal and plants, and the designs were named and passed down within families. Kapa served as clothing, bedding, bandages and swaddling, and in ritual it wrapped the dead and clothed the altars, so that the finest pieces carried the mana of the maker and the household.

name: Hawaiian Pahu (Drum)
description: Standing drum of the Hawaiian islands, carved from a single log of coconut or breadfruit wood and headed with sharkskin or stingray skin stretched and braced with cords. Two kinds are known: the pahu hula, struck with the hands to accompany the hula and chant, and the larger pahu heiau, the sacred temple drum beaten in the heiau to summon the gods and mark the rites of the priests. The drum stands upright and is played with open palms or heel and fingertips, and in the temple it was considered so sacred that only certain priests might sound it, its rhythms regarded as a channel of divine mana.

name: Hei Tiki
description: The hei tiki is the carved greenstone pendant worn at the neck by the Maori, representing a human figure with the head tilted to one side, often with the tongue pointing from the mouth. It is made from pounamu, the nephrite jade of the South Island, and carved with stone drills and abrasive cords in the time before metal tools. The hei tiki is a taonga passed down within families, worn by men and women, and the older a pendant is, the more it is valued, for each one is believed to carry the presence and mana of the ancestors who wore it before. New pendants are given as gifts to mark births, weddings and farewells, and the form appears in Maori tradition in the story of the origin of the tiki, which tells how the first human figure was shaped.

name: Heian Court Fan
description: The Heian court fan, the hiōgi, is the folding fan of the Japanese court of the 9th to 12th centuries, made of slender strips of cypress wood joined at the base and spread in a fan of pale wood, often painted with seasonal flowers and scenes or inscribed with poems; the folding fan itself is a Japanese invention, and these court fans were among the earliest fans to reach China and Korea. Courtiers of the Heian aristocracy used the fan to conceal the face, to gesture in the dance, to signal discreetly at court, and, in the elaborate etiquette of the age, to express shades of meaning the spoken word could not carry; in the paintings of the Tale of Genji the fan is as much a badge of rank as an accessory. Fans were also carried in the rituals of the court, held before the face in ceremony and in the kagura dance, and a painted fan was a gift that carried the giver's taste and standing. The hiōgi survives in the formal fans of Shinto ritual and in the court dance traditions of Kyoto.

name: Herati Carpet
description: The herati carpet is a hand-knotted wool carpet of the Herat region of western Afghanistan, woven with repeating medallion, star and floral patterns that have been exported from the city for centuries. The trade flourished under the Timurid court, when Herat was a centre of craft and patronage, and the rug's patterns are still carried by weaving families who pass the designs from one generation to the next. The name herati is also attached in the rug trade to a pattern with a central diamond, hooked leaves and corner motifs, and the same terms cause lasting confusion with the rugs of Heriz in north-west Iran, which are distinct carpets from a different region. Afghan herati rugs are made of wool on cotton warps, often with the reds and blues of madder and indigo dyes, and are laid as household and prayer carpets.

name: Hermes’ Sandals
description: The talaria, the winged sandals of Hermes, the messenger of the gods in Greek myth, carry the wearer swift as the wind across land and sea and between the realms of mortals and gods; Homer already knows them, and in the Iliad Hermes ties on his 'ambrosial, golden' sandals before his errands. In later art the sandals are always shown with small wings at the ankles, and together with the winged cap and the caduceus they make up the messenger god's badge. They are worn not only by Hermes but by heroes and deities on his errands, and in some accounts give their speed to Perseus in his flight from the Gorgons. The talaria passed into Roman tradition as the attribute of Mercury and were revived in the Renaissance as a symbol of swiftness and eloquence. The winged shoe, with the winged hat, has become the universal shorthand for the courier of the gods.

name: Hex Sign
description: Hex signs are the painted circles and eight-point stars fixed to Pennsylvania Dutch barns from the 18th century onward, their bright patterns of tulips, hearts, distelfinks and stars drawn from the folk art and fraktur of German-speaking settlers. The word 'hex' comes from the German Hexe, 'witch', and many outsiders came to believe the signs were charms to ward off witchcraft, bad luck and fire; in local Pennsylvania German, 'hex' can also mean 'spell'. Scholars argue that the protective meanings were largely a popular invention layered over decoration, though some symbols such as stars clearly carried good-luck associations. Painted by barn artists on the large gable-end 'banks' of Swiss-German barns, the signs became a regional icon of southeastern Pennsylvania. Today hex signs are a celebrated folk art, reproduced on houses, businesses and souvenirs across Berks County.

name: Hjortspring Boat
description: A slender light war canoe of linden wood, about 18 meters long, dug from a bog on the island of Als, Denmark, in 1921 along with the shields, swords, and spears of a defeated army. Built around 350 BCE, it held perhaps twenty paddlers and was offered up after a battle, likely as a sacrifice of the enemy's arms. Its sewn and lashed plank construction shows a northern boat-building tradition far older than the Viking ships. It is the oldest and finest of the Nordic war boats and rests in the National Museum of Denmark.

name: Hliðskjálf
description: Hliðskjálf is the high seat of Odin in Valhöll, from which the All-Father can see across all the worlds and watch everything that happens among gods, men, and giants. The Prose Edda describes it as a throne of far-seeing power, and both Odin and, at times, his wife Frigg use it to scan the cosmos. Sitting in it unbidden was dangerous: the god Freyr once took the seat, was struck by a sight of the giantess Gerðr in the distance, and fell so hopelessly in love that he sent his servant Skírnir to woo her, giving away his own magic sword as payment — the sword whose loss later costs Freyr his life at Ragnarök. The name appears in Skírnismál and throughout the Eddas, and the throne has become the standard image of Odin's all-seeing kingship over the nine worlds.

name: Hou Yi's Bow
description: The red bow of Hou Yi is the weapon of the legendary archer of Chinese myth who shot down nine of the ten suns that once scorched the earth, leaving a single sun to light the day. Each of the ten suns was the child of the goddess Xihe, and when all ten rose together the world began to burn; Hou Yi, a peerless bowman, felled nine of them with arrows tipped against the sun-birds that drew the solar chariot. In the same cycle of tales his skill earned him the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, but his wife Chang'e swallowed it and drifted to the moon, and the archer was left behind. The bow therefore stands for the archetypal marksman and for the human cost of divine power, and Hou Yi is invoked across Chinese literature whenever perfect archery is described. The tale, recorded in Han-era sources and echoed in the poem 'Tianwen', gives the bow a permanent place among the weapons of Chinese mythology.

name: Hringhorni
description: Hringhorni is the greatest of all ships, the vessel on which the gods laid the body of Baldr the Beautiful after his death by the mistletoe dart. When the gods tried to launch Hringhorni for the funeral, the ship was so heavy that no god or giant could move it, until the giantess Hyrrokkin came riding on a wolf and sent the vessel sliding into the sea with a single shove, the earth shaking with the force. The funeral of Baldr, with the pyre lit on the ship, the ring Draupnir laid upon it, and the dwarf Litr cast into the flames, is one of the most famous scenes in the Prose Edda. The name is sometimes taken to mean 'ring-prowed' or 'ship with a ring-shaped stern'. Hringhorni appears in skaldic references and remains a fixed image in retellings of Baldr's death.

name: Huipil
description: The huipil is the loose cotton blouse woven and embroidered by Maya women of highland Guatemala, each town preserving its own colours, patterns and motifs that encode lineage, landscape and the sacred order. It is made on the backstrap loom, a pre-Columbian technology in which the weaver controls the tension with her own body, and the knowledge of patterns passes from mother to daughter. Motifs such as mountains, quetzal birds, suns and ancestors link the garment to Maya cosmology, and Ix Chel, the goddess of the moon and of weaving, is said to have taught the craft. Spanish colonial authorities taxed the garment and at times tried to suppress it, yet it survived and became a powerful emblem of Maya identity. Today huipiles are worn daily and at festivals across the highlands, and their woven patterns are studied by anthropologists as a living textile code.

name: Hymir's Cauldron
description: The great cauldron of the giant Hymir, fetched by Thor and Týr so that the gods could brew ale enough for a feast. Hymiskviða says it was a mile deep; when Hymir refused to give it up, Thor took the kettle and carried it away. The same visit produced the god's famous fishing for the Midgard serpent Jörmungandr. The poem is one of the most comic of the Eddic tales: Thor eats a pair of oxen at the giant's table, breaks Hymir's cups by shattering them against a stone pillar, and finally lifts the great kettle from its post and walks off with it. In Snorri's retelling the story explains why Thor is expected to supply a cauldron for the gods' feasts, and the mile-deep kettle became a byword for the impossible scale of the giants' household goods.

name: Hāngi (Māori Earth Oven)
description: Traditional earth oven of the Māori, in which stones that can withstand great heat — usually river and greywacke stones rather than beach rocks, which can shatter — are heated in a shallow pit until white-hot. Food is laid on the stones in woven baskets, covered with leaves and cloth, and sealed with earth so that the meal steams slowly over several hours. The hāngi has cooked for hui (gatherings), tangihanga (funerals), Waitangi Day and Christmas for generations, and while modern cooks often heat the stones with gas, the principle and the shared meal remain the heart of Māori hospitality.

name: Hǫfuð
description: Hǫfuð, meaning 'head', is the sword of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in the Prose Edda. Snorri lists the blade beside Heimdallr's duties as guardian of the gods, and later tradition links the sword to the final battle, in which Heimdallr and Loki are said to slay one another at Ragnarök. Very little else is recorded about the weapon, and no detailed story of its forging or use survives, which makes it one of the more mysterious named swords of the Eddas. The name 'head' is sometimes explained as a kenning-like epithet for a sword, or as a reference to the head that Heimdallr and Loki were said to have fought over. Hǫfuð is nevertheless a fixture in catalogues of Norse mythic weapons, even though its owner's story is told almost entirely through other objects.

name: Igil (Tuvan Horsehead Fiddle)
description: Two-stringed bowed fiddle of the Tuvans, its hollow wooden body covered with hide and its neck crowned with a carved horse's head. The igil accompanies khoomei throat singing and Tuvan epic song, evoking the gait and voice of a steppe horse; it is prized across Central Asia and appears in the collection of the Russian Museum of Ethnography. The two strings, traditionally of horsehair, are tuned a fifth apart and played with a bow, the instrument held upright on the knee; the sound is soft and nasal, and players imitate the walk, trot and gallop of the horse with the bow. In Tuva, 2009 was declared the Year of the Igil, and the master player Bady-Dorzhu Ondar was celebrated for carrying the instrument onto the world stage. The fiddle accompanies the long epic recitals, its repeated ostinato supporting the singer's phrases, and it is sometimes said to carry the voice of the horse that bore the hero. Today the igil is taught in Tuvan music schools and performed in ensembles around the world.

name: Ikenga Shrine Figure
description: The ikenga is the carved wooden shrine figure of Igbo men, a seated human form with curving horns, a sword and a carved knife held in its hands, standing on the family altar as the image of its owner's achievement and strength. The figure represents the owner's chi, his personal spirit of accomplishment, and the horned head recalls the ram and the aggressive power of the ancestor-hero; when a man prospered, his ikenga was washed, oiled and given offerings, and when he failed or fell, the figure might be cast away. The right hand, in Igbo thought the hand of action, is honored in the ikenga's upraised arm, and the figure is bound up with the owner's own commitment to strive, the word itself carrying the sense of personal strength. Ikenga are carved in many sizes, from small household figures to great ritual sculptures, and they are among the most recognizable of Igbo arts. They remain in use in the shrine houses of Igboland today.

name: Inukshuk
description: The inuksuk, often spelled inukshuk, is a figure of stacked stones built by the Inuit and other Arctic peoples as a landmark in landscapes where trees offer no bearings; the Inuktitut name means 'something that acts in the capacity of a human'. Inuksuit marked travel routes, safe crossings, good hunting and fishing places, food caches and camps, and their shapes could carry messages, from the direction to point to a warning of danger. In northern Alaska the Inupiat built lines of them to herd caribou toward hunters. The human-shaped form is properly an inunnguaq, but the simpler inuksuk on the flag of Nunavut has made the stone figure an emblem of the Arctic and of Canada as a whole. Inuit still build them today, and the pattern appears on the Vancouver Olympics emblem, in art and in jewellery.

name: Ivory Statue of Galatea
description: The ivory statue carved by Pygmalion of Cyprus, which the sculptor loved as a living woman until Aphrodite, moved by his prayer, brought it to life as Galatea, who became his wife; Ovid's Metamorphoses tells the story as the classic fable of art animated by desire. Pygmalion, disgusted by the mortal women around him, carves a maiden of such beauty that he adorns, dresses, and kisses his own work, and at the festival of Venus prays for a wife like the image; the goddess answers by warming the ivory, and the statue, turned to flesh and blood, steps into his arms. The tale is set on Cyprus, the island of Aphrodite, and later writers gave the bride her name, Galatea. It has been retold endlessly in literature and art, most famously in Shaw's Pygmalion and its musical descendant My Fair Lady, as the image of the artist remaking the beloved. The living statue remains the supreme emblem of creation and love in Western culture.

name: Iðunn's Golden Apples
description: The golden apples of Iðunn, which the gods must eat to keep from growing old. When the giant Þjazi tricked Loki into luring Iðunn out of Asgard, the gods aged and greyed, until Loki stole her back in falcon shape, carrying her and her apples from the giant's stronghold. The apples are a life-giving treasure whose loss threatens the whole pantheon. Snorri records the tale in Skáldskaparmál: Iðunn kept the apples in a casket, and without them the gods began to wither, so that the ageing assembly pressed Loki to restore her. Returning in falcon form, Loki snatched the goddess up and flew for Asgard, and the eagle-shaped Þjazi pursued until the gods kindled a fire that burned his wings. The story ties Iðunn's name to eternal youth and explains why the gods were so jealous of her keeping.

name: Jack-o'-Lantern
description: The jack-o'-lantern is a hollowed pumpkin carved with a face and lit from within, set out at Halloween as the American descendant of the Irish carved-turnip lantern of 'Stingy Jack'. In the legend Jack tricked the Devil and was barred from both heaven and hell, left to walk the dark with only a burning coal inside a hollowed turnip, and the bog-lights of swamps were long called jack-o'-lanterns after him. Irish and Scottish immigrants carried the tale to North America in the 19th century, where the larger, easier-to-carve native pumpkin replaced the turnip. The practice absorbed older Celtic traditions of lighting Samhain fires, and by the early 1900s pumpkin carving was a fixture of American Halloween. The jack-o'-lantern has since become a global symbol of the season, carved each October with faces ranging from folk-mask grins to elaborate art.

name: Jade Bead Necklace
description: Classic Maya rulers and nobles wore necklaces and collars of drilled jadeite beads, the green stone valued above all others in the Maya world and linked with rain, water, maize, the world centre and the breath of life. Royal portraits on stelae show long bead necklaces draped over the chest, often layered with earflare assemblies and bracelets of the same material. The richest evidence comes from tombs: the burial of K'inich Janaab' Pakal at Palenque held hundreds of beads and jade plaques, and the burial of the Red Queen of Palenque was accompanied by masses of jade beadwork. Jadeite itself was traded over great distances from highland sources in the Motagua River valley of Guatemala and elsewhere, and craftsmen drilled and polished it into tubes, spheres and carved pendants. The jade bead collar was thus both wealth and talisman, binding its wearer to the fertile green forces that sustained Maya life.

name: Jade Dragon
description: The jade dragon of the Han dynasty is a small, coiled dragon pendant carved from nephrite jade, found in the tombs of the Chinese aristocracy of the 2nd century BC to the 2nd century AD, where it was laid among the burial goods as a symbol of the celestial forces that governed the dead and of the soul's journey through the heavens. The dragon, the long, was the creature of the east, of rain, and of imperial power, and jade, the most precious stone of the Chinese world, was believed to preserve the body and to concentrate life-force, so that the pairing made the pendant a powerful talisman of protection and rank. The Han dragons, with their sinuous, leaping forms and spiralled bodies, are masterpieces of the lapidary's art, worked with thread-cutting saws and drills into openwork curls. The motif continued for centuries, and the jade dragon remains a symbol of Chinese imperial authority and good fortune. These pendants are among the most prized objects of Chinese art in the world's collections.

name: Jade Funerary Mask of Pakal
description: The funerary mask of K'inich Janaab' Pakal, the great seventh-century ruler of Palenque, is a mosaic of more than 340 pieces of green jadeite fitted over his face in the stone sarcophagus of the Temple of the Inscriptions. Discovered in 1952 by the Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier, the mask has eyes of shell and mother-of-pearl with pupils of black obsidian and stands about 25 centimetres tall. Jade carried deep meaning for the Classic Maya: the green stone evoked water, maize, the world centre and the breath of life, and the portrait is interpreted as showing the dead king reborn with the attributes of the maize god. Pakal's burial outfit contained around a thousand jade ornaments in all, including necklaces, bracelets, rings and a headband, marking jade as the supreme royal material. The mask and its companions now rest in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City, where they are regarded as masterpieces of Mesoamerican art.

name: Jade Rabbit's Mortar
description: The mortar and pestle with which the Jade Rabbit pounds the elixir of immortality is a fixed image in the Chinese moon, the rabbit standing beside the cassia tree on the lunar surface as the companion of the goddess Chang'e. In the Moon Rabbit folklore, the rabbit first earned its place when it offered itself as food to a disguised deity, who spared it and set it on the moon to grind the herbs of immortality, and the same moon-rabbit motif recurs across East Asian lore. In Korea the rabbit is said to pound the ingredients of the rice cake tteok, while in Japan it pounds mochi, and in Vietnam it is the companion of the moon goddess Hang Nga. The mortar is depicted in Mid-Autumn Festival imagery on lanterns, mooncakes, and shadow-puppets, and the figure of the rabbit at work is one of the most recognizable of the moon's markings. Across all these traditions the mortar turns the mundane labour of grinding grain into the cosmic work of producing the elixir of life.

name: Jebena Coffee Pot
description: The jebena is the round, clay coffee pot of Ethiopia, with a narrow neck, a round belly, and a small spout, fired without glaze and used in the country's coffee ceremony (bunna). In the ceremony, green beans are roasted in a pan over coals, ground, and boiled three times in the jebena, and the pot sits on a bed of fresh grass while incense burns beside it. The first brew, abol, is the strongest and most honoured; the second and third rounds, tona and baraka, follow as the gathering lingers. Pouring from the high-necked pot without spilling is a skill, and the tiny cups are filled from a single unbroken stream. The jebena is central to hospitality: hosting the ceremony is a daily ritual of friendship and community, and the coffee is shared with anyone who arrives. Modern jebena are also made in metal and glazed ceramic, but the hand-built clay pot remains the heart of the tradition.

name: Jiu Ding
description: The jiu ding are the nine bronze tripods that the culture hero Yu the Great is said to have cast from tribute metal gathered across the Nine Provinces after he tamed the great flood, inscribing each region's creatures and things on the sides so that the people could recognize them. Passed down through the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties as the physical warrant of the Mandate of Heaven, they became the archetype of legitimate rule in Chinese historiography, and losing them was read as the fall of a dynasty. No actual ding survive, and their very existence is a matter of debate, but the story carried enormous political weight: Confucius, Mencius, and the historian Sima Qian all allude to the tripods as the vessels of sovereignty. In the Warring States tale of the King of Chu who 'asked about the tripods' at the Zhou court, the sheer idea of the ding became a test of ambition. The jiu ding remain the standard Chinese symbol of rightful imperial power and of the unity of the realm.

name: Járngreipr
description: Járngreipr, the 'iron grippers', are the iron gloves of the thunder god Thor, named in the Prose Edda as one of his three great treasures beside Mjölnir and the belt Megingjörð. Their purpose is practical as much as martial: the shaft of Mjölnir is said to grow white-hot in flight, and only the iron gloves let Thor catch and hurl the hammer without burning his hands. In the tale of Thor's visit to the giant Geirröðr, gloves of the same kind are what allow the god to catch the red-hot lump of molten iron that the giant throws at him, which Thor hurls back to kill Geirröðr. The gloves are sometimes said to have been forged by the dwarves, though the Edda does not name their maker. Járngreipr appears in most modern retellings of Norse myth as the practical complement to the great hammer.

name: Jāņi Wreath
description: The midsummer wreath of Jāņi: for women and girls, plaited from flowers, grasses, herbs and leaves, a braid of twenty-seven plants being held to ward off disasters, disease and enemies, while men and boys wore rings of oak leaves as tokens of strength. Worn through Līgo night on 23 June with singing, cheese, beer and bonfire jumping, the wreath is kept afterwards — hung in the house, given to the cattle or laid under the pillow — for protection and healing through the year. The customs, described since the seventeenth century, make the wreath the visible emblem of the great festival of the Latvian summer solstice.

name: K'awiil Scepter
description: The K'awiil scepter, often called the manikin scepter, is a short staff topped by a small figure of the Maya lightning god K'awiil, a deity shown with a mirror set in his forehead, an elongated snout and a serpent leg. Classic Maya rulers carried it as proof of divine kingship, and royal portraits at Copan, Tikal, Piedras Negras and Palenque show it held at accession and in dance rituals, its snake leg trailing to the ground. The forehead mirror links the scepter to the lightning that K'awiil sent forth, and the god himself belonged to the Palenque Triad of patron deities. Stelae record how the scepter was handed to a new king as part of the regalia that made him a living link between his people and the gods. Carved in stone or wood, its surviving depictions let scholars trace how the symbol of royal lightning passed across the Maya world over centuries.

name: Kabyle Earthenware
description: Kabyle earthenware is the red-clay pottery of the Great Kabylia mountains of northern Algeria, a craft kept almost exclusively in the hands of women. The pots are built by hand from coils of local clay, without a wheel, then burnished with a pebble while still damp and painted before firing with geometric patterns in black, beige and red. The repertoire includes water jars, storage pots, and wide platters used to serve couscous at weddings and other feasts, and the interior of each piece is divided into circles, checkerboards, crosses and triangles that radiate from the centre. These motifs are named and read by the women who make them, and they are believed to carry meanings of supernatural protection and fertility, some of which are shared with the diamond patterns of Amazigh weaving, jewellery and facial tattoos. Because the recipes for clay, paints and firing are handed down from mother to daughter, each pot carries the imprint of a lineage, though the regional styles differ from village to village across the massif.

name: Kachina Doll
description: Kachina dolls, or katsina tihu in Hopi, are small figures carved from cottonwood root and painted with the attributes of the katsinam, the spirit beings who visit Hopi villages from the winter solstice until July. Given to children, especially girls, by katsina dancers, they are teaching objects rather than idols: each doll helps a child learn the identity, dress and power of a particular spirit. More than three hundred katsinam are known, from the gentle and humorous to the fierce ogre katsinam who discipline children. Since the late 1800s Hopi carvers have developed the craft into an internationally collected art, moving from small flat tihu to fully carved figures, yet the ceremonial gift remains the core of the tradition. To the Hopi the katsinam are ancestors and forces of the natural world, and the doll carries their blessing into the home.

name: Kada Bangle
description: The kada, also spelled kara, is the unadorned steel or iron bangle worn by Sikhs on the right wrist, one of the five Ks prescribed at the founding of the Khalsa in 1699. Because it is a closed circle without beginning or end, the bangle is understood as a reminder that God is eternal and without form, and its touch on the wrist constantly recalls the wearer to righteous conduct and restraint. The plain steel of the traditional kada contrasts with the gold ornaments worn by many Hindus and Muslims, signalling that a Sikh should live simply and without attachment to display. In the Punjab the broad steel kada is also worn by non-Sikhs as an item of dress, and in combat the heavy circular bangle could be used as a guard and a blunt knuckle-weapon. The kada is one of the most visible articles of Sikh identity, worn in the workplace, in court and at the gurdwara.

name: Kalfak (Tatar Women's Embroidered Cap)
description: Velvet cap worn by Tatar women, richly embroidered with gold thread, pearls and gilt coins, with a long embroidered tail or tassel hanging down the back. Part of a woman's dowry, the kalfak was the most original piece of Tatar women's festive headwear and demanded great skill in gold embroidery; unlike the man's tubeteika it marked marital status and rank. The cap is sewn in a crescent or beaked shape that sits toward the back of the head, its velvet embroidered in gold thread laid in tight couched stitches, with a pendant band falling to the shoulder. In the 19th century married and unmarried women wore different forms, and the kalfak was trimmed with pearls, sequins and small gilt coins that rattled softly as the wearer moved. Embroidering a kalfak could take weeks of exacting work, and girls prepared them as gifts within the trousseau. Kazan museums display 19th-century examples, and the kalfak is now revived in festive dress and on the stage.

name: Kalinga Royal Drum
description: The Kalinga was the most sacred drum of the Rwandan court, the principal of the four royal drums that together stood for the kingship of the mwami. Kept in a sacred house where a fire burned day and night, the drum was never allowed to touch the ground and was rubbed with bull's blood and herbs to renew its power. According to oral tradition the Kalinga reached the court with the seventeenth-century king Ruganzu II Ndori, and it travelled with the king on campaign, acquiring personal names as if it were a living ruler. The Kalinga stood for the male principle and the king, its companion drum for the queen mother, and Rwandans said 'he is king who has the drums': beating it at coronations, harvests, and victories affirmed the dynasty's authority. After the monarchy was abolished in the early 1960s the royal drums vanished from public sight, and no trace of the originals has been found, though the drums live on in the country's drumming tradition and in the re-created court dances of the Intore.

name: Kamancha (Azerbaijani Spike Fiddle)
description: The kamancha is the bowed spike fiddle of Azerbaijan, built with a spherical or bowl-shaped wooden body covered with fish- or lambskin, a long neck that pierces the body, and four steel strings, played upright with the bow resting on the knee. Its bright, precise tone carries well indoors, which is why the kamancha sits beside the tar in the mugham trio and in the ensembles of Azerbaijani folk music, doubling and answering the melodic line. The instrument has a long history across the Caucasus, Persia and Central Asia under the name kamancheh, and Azerbaijani craftsmen and players developed their own distinguished school. In 2017 UNESCO inscribed the art of crafting and playing the kamancha on the Representative List, and the instrument remains central both to classical mugham and to the folk music of weddings and festivals.

name: Kamcha (Kazakh Whip)
description: Braided leather whip of the Kazakhs, carried by horsemen and elders as a riding tool and badge of authority. In Kazakh folklore the kamcha carried protective power: the whip of a respected man was hung near a woman in childbirth, and its crack was said to drive off evil spirits. Skilled craftsmen braid the lash from several plaited leather cords. The handle is carved of wood or bone, often ornamented with silver, and the lash tapers from the handle to a thin tip that cracks sharply in the air when snapped. In the steppe the kamcha was as much a tool of the herd as of the saddle, used to guide horses and cattle at a distance, and an elder carried it as a mark of rank and command. Kazakh custom holds that the whip is never pointed at a person, and a man leaving on a journey might hang his kamcha over the threshold as protection for the house.

name: Kandyan Crown
description: The Kandyan crown is the royal crown of the Kandyan kingdom of Sri Lanka, the last independent Sinhalese state, which fell to the British in 1815. The crown, of gold richly set with rubies, sapphires and other gems, was worn by the kings of Kandy at great coronation ceremonies and processions, and it carried the whole sovereignty of the kingdom, so that possession of the crown was taken to mean possession of the realm. When the Kandyan chiefs signed the Kandyan Convention of 1815, the regalia, including the crown and the throne, was handed to the British and sent to England, and tradition records memorials of the crown at Windsor Castle, where the regalia long remained. In Sri Lankan memory the loss of the crown is bound up with legend: omens, the fall of a star and other portents are said to have accompanied its removal, and the crown is still popularly spoken of as the sign of a sovereignty that was not handed back. Today the Kandyan crown is remembered through replicas and regalia kept in museums, and the original remains the subject of scholarly dispute between the United Kingdom and Sri Lanka.

name: Kanklės
description: Archaic Lithuanian plucked box zither, a trapezoid of solid wood — maple, linden or ash — hollowed from a single piece and strung with parallel strings, of the same Baltic psaltery family as the Latvian kokle and the Estonian kannel. Old belief held that the bards, the vaidilos, sang heroic songs and served the gods to its music, and that the best instrument wood was cut between a person's death and funeral, for a mourned tree lent the kanklės a sorrowful, spirit-voiced tone. The instrument accompanied wedding songs and dances, its players, the kanklininkai, being honoured guests, and it was revived in the twentieth-century folk revival as a national instrument.

name: Kantsi (Georgian Drinking Horn)
description: The kantsi is the drinking horn of the Georgian highlands, cut from the curved horn of an ox, aurochs or mountain goat, polished, and often mounted at the rim in chased silver, sometimes with a small stand or a chain to hang it by. It is the fixed vessel of the supra, the Georgian feast, where the tamada raises the horn for each toast and custom requires it to be drained to the bottom in one draught before it is passed on; to drink from the kantsi is to honour the wine, the host and the speaker. The largest horns, holding a litre or more, are prized heirlooms of Svaneti and Khevsureti, and the same vessels appear in medieval Georgian manuscripts and in modern feast painting. Because the horn cannot be set down with wine in it, every toast must be finished, which is why the kantsi is remembered as the instrument of Georgian generosity.

name: Karagoz
description: Karagöz, the shadow puppet of Ottoman Turkish theatre, gives its name to the traditional play performed behind a lit cotton screen with flat, articulated figures of dyed translucent camel hide worked on sticks, which cast coloured shadows as the single puppeteer, the hayali, moves them. The hero Karagöz, a bald, rough-spoken everyman, bickers endlessly with his polite, wordy friend Hacivat, and their exchanges of puns and misunderstandings drive the comedy, framed by music, song, and a stock cast drawn from the Ottoman city. Popular legend, recorded from the 17th century onward, is sometimes said to trace the form to two workers, an ironworker called Karagöz and a bricklayer or timber seller called Hacivat, whose banter halted the building of a mosque, so that the sultan had them executed and a puppeteer conjured their shadows back onto a screen. The genre was performed in Ramadan and before the sultans. It remains a living oral-dramatic tradition of Turkey, inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage.

name: Karahi
description: The karahi is the deep rounded pan of Pakistan, forged from cast iron or pressed steel, with two handles and steep sides, set over an open flame to cook the spiced stew that shares its name. The name of the vessel has passed to the dish itself, and a karahi of lamb, chicken or vegetables cooked with tomato, green chilli and ginger is one of the most familiar foods of Pakistani homes, roadside dhabas and bazaars, served hot straight from the pan with fresh naan. Because the karahi sits directly on the fire, the oil and spices fry hard before liquid is added, giving the gravy its characteristic rich colour and edge. It is the daily cooking vessel of many households and the centre of festive and communal meals, and iron karahis are prized for seasoning with use, so that old pans are handed down within families.

name: Kastane Sword
description: The kastane is the traditional ceremonial sword of the Kandyan kingdom of Sri Lanka, worn at court as a mark of office and carried in procession, and it is one of the most characteristic creations of Sinhalese metalwork. Its signature feature is the hilt, whose pommel is carved as the head of a lion, the symbol of the Sinhalese people, often in ivory, horn or silver, with the guard and quillons finished with makara heads and scrollwork; the blade itself was frequently a European hanger or cuttoe blade imported by the Dutch and riveted into the local hilt. The kastane was not primarily a battlefield weapon but a dress sword, the attribute of chiefs, princes and royal officials, and it also entered the world of Sinhalese ritual, being used in the masked devil dances and exorcism rites in which the sanni demons and Gara Yakka are invoked. In those rituals the flashing blade is used to dominate the demons and sweep away the evil they represent, linking the courtly sword to the folk religion of the low country. Museums classify the kastane among the finest of Sri Lankan arms, and modern reproductions still accompany Kandyan dancers and drummers.

name: Katar
description: The katar is the Indian punch dagger, a straight, usually double-edged blade set between two parallel side bars that form an H-shaped grip, the whole weapon being pushed forward with the fist like a punch. Because the palm push concentrates the whole force of the arm behind a single point, the katar could pierce mail and helmets in close combat, and it became the characteristic weapon of Rajput and Maratha warriors from about the 16th century onward. In addition to the plain fighting blade there were katar with wavy edges, double blades and side blades, and the wealthiest owners carried gold-damascened pieces with jewelled hilts that were as much jewellery as arms. The katar was also a ceremonial object, presented as a token of loyalty or reward and displayed in processions, and a small katar could be carried concealed in the waistband. Because it is unique to South Asia, the katar is one of the most discussed Indian weapons in the history of arms and armour.

name: Katsina Owl Doll
description: The owl katsina doll, or mongwau tihu in Hopi, is a carved and painted cottonwood figure of the owl spirit of the Hopi katsinam, given to children so they may learn the owl's identity and power. The owl is a night hunter whose eyes and voice mark it as a being of wisdom and, in some traditions, a messenger connected to the spirit world. Like all katsina tihu the doll is carved from the soft root of the cottonwood, a wood the Hopi link to water and moisture, and painted with the colours and markings of the particular spirit. The owl katsina appears among the hundreds of katsinam who visit the villages in season, and its doll carries the teaching of that visit into the home. Collectors prize such carvings, but to the Hopi the doll's first purpose remains the instruction of children in the ways of the spirits.

name: Kaupaloki
description: Kaupaloki, the 'trade-luck stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn for success in buying and selling. Merchants and farmers drew or carved the stave so that bargains would turn in their favour, a piece of practical magic in a seafaring and trading society where a fair deal was a matter of survival. It belongs to the group of luck-giving galdrastafir, distinct from the protective and aggressive staves of the same grimoires, and it was carried on paper, wood, or metal when goods went to market. Like most of the staves, its earliest known source is a 19th-century collection of older material, and it is now reproduced in books and on jewellery as an emblem of Icelandic folk magic. The Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík keeps the trade staves among its displays of the everyday uses of magic.

name: Kayak
description: The kayak is the one-man hunting boat of the Inuit, Yupik and Inupiat, a frame of wood or bone stretched tight with sealskin, so light and watertight that a single hunter could carry it, launch it alone, and paddle it silently across the open sea after seals, walrus and whales. The hunter sat in its small cockpit, wearing a skin parka lashed to the rim so that the boat sealed around him, and with his harpoon and lance he could hunt from the surface and even right the kayak in the Eskimo roll, turning it over and back with a twist of the paddle. The design was perfected over millennia and was one of the Arctic inventions that explorers and missionaries carried back to the world, giving the English word kayak from the Inuktitut qajaq. In legend the boat carries its own weight too: in the tale of Sedna, the sea mother, her father rows her out over the water in his kayak before she becomes the ruler of the sea beasts. The kayak remains a living Arctic boat, rebuilt in traditional materials for festivals and races.

name: Kelaghayi (Azerbaijani Silk Headscarf)
description: The kelaghayi is the square silk headscarf of Azerbaijani women, woven on narrow silk looms in the town of Sheki and the village of Basgal, then dyed and printed with woodblocks so that a patterned border frames a plainer field. The classic ornament is the buta, the curved teardrop or flame motif that runs along the edge, and the colours carry meaning: white and light shades for older women and mourning, red and bright colours for brides and young women. The scarf is folded and tied in many ways - under the chin, at the back, or draped over the shoulders - and it belongs to daily wear, weddings, funerals and religious observance alike, its symbolism bound up with the woman's age and occasion. In 2014 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art and symbolism of the kelaghayi on the Representative List, and silk masters in Basgal still print the scarves by hand.

name: Kente Cloth
description: Kente is the strip-woven cloth of the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana, built up from narrow bands of silk and cotton woven on narrow looms and sewn edge to edge into bold geometric patterns, each of which has a name and a proverb meaning. Weaving was traditionally a male craft tied to the royal court, and particular patterns were reserved for the king; the colors carry their own language, with gold for royalty, green for growth, red for passion or danger, and the cloth is worn for the great occasions of Akan life. The Asante origin tradition credits the spider Anansi with teaching the first weavers, and the name kente comes from the Akan word for the open basket that the patterns recall. Kwame Nkrumah wore kente at Ghana's independence, and the cloth has become a worldwide emblem of African identity, worn by leaders and diaspora communities alike. Every strip of kente is woven memory, pattern by pattern.

name: Kero
description: The kero is the paired ceremonial drinking cup of the Andes, a flared goblet most often carved from wood, drunk from in twos at rituals of alliance, hospitality and the great festivals of the Inca calendar. The paired cups were passed so that each party drank the other's offering, sealing friendship and reciprocal obligation, and the drink was usually chicha, the maize beer central to Andean ceremony. Inca nobles and officials received keros as marks of office, and the cups appear in colonial accounts as indispensable to the toasts that accompanied every treaty and celebration. After the Spanish conquest, colonial-era keros were painted with elaborate scenes of Inca life, rulers, animals and ceremony, creating a crucial record of how the empire remembered itself. The kero tradition survives among Andean communities, where the paired cup still seals the bonds of ayllu and fiesta.

name: Kete (Māori Basket)
description: The kete is the woven basket of the Maori, plaited from the strips of the harakeke flax plant and used to carry food, tools, feathers and other goods in daily life. Plain kete are made quickly for carrying, while the patterned kete whakairo is woven with a coloured design and given as a mark of respect. In Maori tradition the three kete of knowledge were brought down from the heavens by the god Tane, who returned with the basket of ritual knowledge, the basket of ancestral knowledge and the basket of practical knowledge, and so established learning among humankind. The kete is therefore both an everyday object and a powerful image of knowledge itself, and the phrase to hand over a kete of knowledge means to teach. Kete are still woven today in the traditional materials and patterns.

name: Khachkar (Armenian Cross-Stone)
description: The khachkar is the Armenian cross-stone, a freestanding stele carved from a single slab of local stone, most often the volcanic tuff of the Armenian plateau, its face dominated by an ornamented cross set over a rosette or a wheel of eternity. Around the cross the carver fills the stone with interlace, vine scrolls, leaves, pomegranates and birds, and the whole composition is framed in a decorated border; the earliest dated example bears the year 879, and the art reached its richest period from the thirteenth century. Khachkars were raised as tombstones, memorials for the dead, church dedications and thanksgivings, linking the everyday and the divine, the village and the monastery. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the symbolism and craftsmanship of khachkars on the Representative List, and carved examples stand at Armenian churches from Julfa to Jerusalem.

name: Khaen
description: The khaen is the free-reed mouth organ of Laos, built from rows of bamboo tubes bound around a wooden wind-chest, whose drone-and-melody sound is the soul of the Lao folk song called lam. The player breathes in and out through a single mouth-hole while covering the finger-holes of the tubes, producing the interlocking melody and drone that lam singers improvise against, and the instrument accompanies courtship, festivals, and ritual across Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao tradition says that the khaen shaped the speech and poetry of the people, and the instrument is central to the great courtship tradition of the khap and lam. In the origin legend the khaen was first made by a man who wanted to imitate the sound of the wind in the bamboo, and its seven-note scale is regarded as the seed of Lao musical thought. UNESCO has inscribed the khaen playing of the Lao people as intangible cultural heritage, and the instrument remains the emblem of Lao national music.

name: Khanda
description: The khanda is the broad, straight, double-edged sword of the Indian subcontinent, heavier and stiffer than the curved tulwar, and it is principally associated with the Sikhs of the Punjab and with the Marathas of western India. In Sikh tradition the khanda is the emblem of the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, and the central motif of the Nishan Sahib, the tall flag of a gurdwara, which shows a double-edged khanda with a chakkar (discus) and two kirpans arranged around it. The sword was carried as a weapon of war in the 17th and 18th centuries and remains a ceremonial and ritual object, used at the initiation ceremony of Amrit, where the sacred syrup is stirred with a khanda, and kept in reverence in Sikh homes and temples. Because the double edge and straight blade allowed a powerful, chopping stroke, the khanda was well suited to the tested cavalry work of the Sikh and Maratha armies. The same term is used in Sanskrit and Hindi for any large sword, so the object carries a long martial lineage beyond the Sikh faith.

name: Khomus (Yakut Jew's Harp)
description: Metal Jew's harp of the Yakut (Sakha) people, an elongated iron frame with a flexible steel tongue, played by plucking the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The khomus imitates bird calls and natural sounds, accompanied songs and held shamanic associations. Yakutsk's Khomus Museum, the republic's Khomus Day and an international festival honour it as a symbol of Sakha culture. The player holds the frame against the teeth and strikes the tongue with a finger, shaping the note with the mouth and breath, so that a single harp produces a shifting range of overtones. The khomus is among the oldest of instruments, with wooden and bone examples and a metal specimen dated around the 3rd to 1st centuries BC attributed to the Xiongnu. The Yakut khomus is sometimes said to have been made first from the wood or bone of a tree struck by lightning, and later from iron, in the shape of the horseshoe that frames the tongue. Its repertoire includes pieces for healing, for the dance, and for imitating the sounds of the taiga.

name: Khukuri
description: The khukuri is the curved blade of the Nepali Gurkha tradition, broad and heavy near the tip, tapering to the hilt, and used for cutting wood, clearing brush, daily chores and ceremonial display. The name is spelled kukri in British usage, and the blade is forged by Nepali kamis, the metal-working caste, who shape it at a charcoal forge and temper the cutting edge while leaving the spine soft enough to absorb shock. It is carried in a leather scabbard together with two smaller knives, the karda for fine work and the chakmak for sharpening, and the distinctive notch at the blade's base is a mark of the traditional shape. A well-known folk saying holds that once the khukuri is drawn it must taste blood before being sheathed again, a custom linked to its history as a weapon of war and to the rituals of the Gurkha regiments.

name: Khyber Knife
description: The khyber knife is the long, straight-backed belt knife of the frontier regions of Afghanistan and the border country of the Khyber Pass, with a wide spine, a single cutting edge and a simple handle of horn, bone or wood. It is worn at the belt and used for cutting, skinning and defence, and the name comes from the pass that links the Afghan highlands with the plains, a corridor of trade and conflict for centuries. Frontier bladesmiths forged the knives for daily work and for display, and the handles of older examples are often incised or decorated, showing the owner's pride in the weapon. The khyber knife appears in the material culture of the borderlands and in ethnographic collections of frontier weaponry, a practical tool that also served as a mark of the bearer.

name: Kihnu Woolen Skirt
description: The striped woolen skirt and knitted garments of Kihnu Island's women: bright red, green and blue striped cloth woven on home looms from local wool, worn with embroidered blouses, sashes, mittens and stockings whose colours and patterns recall old legends. With the island's men long at sea, Kihnu's women carried the culture of the island, and the making of these garments — together with the songs, dances and handicraft skills of the Kihnu cultural space inscribed by UNESCO in 2003 — became an emblem of Estonian island identity. The striped skirt, folded and held by a woven belt, is still worn daily by older women and with pride at festivals.

name: Kirivöö Belt
description: The kirivöö, the Estonian pick-up patterned belt: a narrow woven band of wool over a linen or wool ground, carrying rows of small crosses, rhombuses, triangles and diagonal figures worked by the pick-up technique. Each parish knew its own edge patterns, so that the belt could tell where a woman came from, and the belts were worn wrapped at the waist with folk dress, and given as gifts, love-pledges and protective charms. The Estonian National Museum holds belts from across the country, and studies of the small patterns at the belt edges continue to map the regional styles and their meanings.

name: Kirkebåt (Church Boat)
description: A long rowing boat shared by a whole parish to carry people to Sunday service, built clinker of pine or oak and owned jointly by several farms. Church boats rowed people across fjords and lakes until the early 1900s, carrying fifty or more parishioners at a time; surviving examples like the Rols from Stryn are kept and rowed again. Racing between parishes on the way home was part of the tradition. The kirkebåt was a true communal vessel, each farm holding a share and supplying rowers, and the boat itself served as the village's gathering place on the water as the crew sang and traded news on the long pull to church. When roads reached the fjord settlements the great boats were laid up, but many were preserved, and the old race-rowing has been revived as a summer sport along the Norwegian coast.

name: Kirpan
description: The kirpan is the curved sword or dagger that an initiated Sikh wears as one of the five Ks, the panj kakkar, along with unshorn hair (kesh), a comb (kanga), a steel bangle (kara) and the cotton undergarment (kachera). Introduced at the founding of the Khalsa in 1699 by Guru Gobind Singh, the kirpan embodies the Sikh duty to defend the weak and to stand against injustice, and it is worn constantly as a reminder of that responsibility. The size and form of the kirpan vary with the community and the wearer's circumstances, from a small symbolically worn blade in parts of the diaspora to the long ceremonial kirpan of Amritdhari Sikhs, and it is treated not as an offensive weapon but as a sacred article of faith. In Sikh scripture and hagiography the kirpan is praised as the protector of the oppressed, and the five Ks together mark the body of a Sikh as the visible form of the faith. Legal accommodations for the kirpan exist in several countries, and the practice remains an active case study in religious freedom law.

name: Kitsune's Crescent Comb
description: The crescent-shaped comb of Japanese legend is the small hair ornament that a shapeshifting kitsune is said to drop when its disguise is betrayed, and finding it is supposed to bring a strange fortune or a lasting bond with the fox. The comb appears again and again in tales of fox wives, in which a man marries a beautiful woman who turns out to be a fox in human form; at the crucial moment the tail is seen, or the comb is left behind when the wife vanishes, and the discovery ends the marriage. In some variants the man who keeps the comb may command the fox's service or its gratitude, while in others the comb proves the spirit nature of the householder and drives the fox away for good. Because the fox in Japanese belief is both a trickster and a messenger of the rice god Inari, the comb carries an ambiguous charge: it is a clue, a keepsake, and a token of a crossing between the animal and human worlds. The motif is old enough to appear in the earliest collections of Japanese fox tales, and it still shapes modern retellings in which a comb on a shrine step promises a fox encounter.

name: Knotted Rope Charm
description: A rope or cord with three knots, tied by a 'wise' seller and sold to sailors as a wind charm. Untying the first knot raised a gentle wind, the second a stronger breeze, and the third a storm, so prudent captains kept the third knot tied. The three-knotted wind cord is documented in Nordic and Sami maritime folklore and was often credited to Lapp (Sami) sorcery. Olaus Magnus drew and described the custom in 1555: a seaman from the north sold a cord of three knots to sea captains, warning that the third must never be loosed unless the ship stood in danger. The poet Petter Dass and later collectors repeated the account, and the 'wind knot' appears in accounts of Finnish and Sami magic, where the seller was sometimes said to have learned the skill from the Sami themselves. Frazer gathered the custom as the classic example of sympathetic wind magic, in which loosening a knot looses the wind the knot had bound.

name: Kokle
description: The Latvian plucked box zither: a trapezoid soundbox with parallel strings over a flat board, carved from maple, ash or lime, played by strumming and plucking. A chronicle entry of 1225, when Henricus de Lettis wrote of a kokle played by Livonian youths, makes it the oldest documented psaltery in Europe, and Latvian folk songs call its strings 'silver war' and 'golden war'. The kokle accompanied the dainas, the great corpus of Latvian folksong, and in the twentieth century a larger concert kokle was developed; in 2008 the kokle and the art of koklēšana were placed in the Latvian Cultural Canon as the national instrument.

name: Kokoshnik (Russian Women's Headdress)
description: Crest-shaped ceremonial headdress of Russian women, a stiff crown of brocade, velvet or silk embroidered with pearls, gold thread and beads. Worn over the braids from the 17th century, the kokoshnik varied by region, from horned and high-crested to flat-topped forms, and marked the married woman; after Peter the Great's court reforms it survived as festive wear in the provinces. The word derives from 'kokosh', the old Russian name for a hen or cockerel, from the crest-like shape, and the headdress was worn at weddings and church festivals together with the best dress. Regional types carry distinct names, such as the one-horned kika of Tula and the morshen of the north, each built on a stiffened cardboard or birch-bark base covered in rich fabric. Museums hold examples sewn with river pearls, and the form has been revived on the stage, in film and in neo-Russian fashion, making it one of the most recognisable images of Russian national costume.

name: Koschei's Needle
description: Needle in which the Russian fairy-tale villain Koschei the Deathless hides his soul, so that he cannot be killed while it remains intact. In Afanasyev's collected tales the needle lies inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a hare, and the hare inside a chest locked on an island oak; the hero must open each container in turn and break the needle to destroy Koschei. The motif recurs across Slavic and wider folklore, and variants replace the needle with a flower, a spider or a bird's egg. Folklorists class it among the 'external soul' tales, in which a being stores its life force outside its body for safety; the moment the chain of containers is broken, the villain collapses and dies. The needle is therefore the hinge of the whole story, and the hero's task becomes one of patience and sequence rather than of strength.

name: Kraków Szopka
description: The Kraków szopka is a Nativity crib built as a glittering model of the city itself, cramming Wawel Cathedral, St Mary's Basilica, castle towers, spires and arcades into a many-storeyed facade of cardboard, tin foil and painted paper around the central stable. The tradition took shape in the nineteenth century, when Kraków bricklayers and building workers made portable cribs to earn money at Christmas, and it gained its civic form after 1937, when the first official contest was held; makers known as krakowianie still compete every first Thursday of December on the Main Market Square beside the Adam Mickiewicz monument. The best szopki show great technical ambition, with moving figures, hidden candle-lit interiors and window scenes re-enacting nativity and patriotic tableaux. In 2018 UNESCO inscribed the szopka tradition on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and collections such as the one in the Historical Museum of the City of Kraków preserve competition winners going back decades.

name: Kryždirbystė Cross
description: Carved oak wayside crosses of the Lithuanian cross-crafting tradition, one to five metres tall, with small roofs, carved figures and flower and geometric ornament, standing at village entrances, crossroads, cemeteries and shrines. Once consecrated by a priest, a cross is sacred and draws offerings — food, rosaries, scarves and aprons — seeking fertility, healing or protection, and the craft's masters, the kryždirbiai, shape stogastulpiai, koplytstulpiai and full crosses in styles that vary from region to region. Under Russian imperial rule and again under the Soviet occupation the wayside cross became a symbol of national identity, and in 2001 the tradition was proclaimed by UNESCO a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

name: Kuba Beaded Cup
description: The beaded drinking cups of the Kuba kingdom of the Democratic Republic of the Congo are carved from wood and densely covered with cowrie shells, brass tacks, and patterns of imported glass beads in geometric bands. Owned by kings, titled nobles, and wealthy men, the cups were used in the court ceremonies where palm wine was shared, and they were kept among the treasured possessions of the palace or the lineage house.
