Some cups take the form of a human head or a pair of feet, while others are plain beakers, and the intricate beadwork set the craftsmen of the royal workshops apart from ordinary potters. In Kuba court culture, drinking vessels were markers of rank, and the most elaborate pieces announced the generosity and wealth of the man who poured from them. The cups entered museum collections during the colonial period, and beaded Kuba cups are now recognised as a high point of African decorative art.

name: Kuba Ndop Royal Figure
description: The ndop is a carved wooden portrait figure of a Kuba king of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, showing the ruler seated cross-legged on a small platform. Each ndop was made for a reigning or remembered king and bears his personal emblem (ibol), a drum, a weapon, or a game board carved beside the seat, while the pattern of scarification on the torso identifies the individual monarch. The figures were kept in the sacred houses of the palace, guarded by the king's titleholders, and were brought out in ceremonies where they stood for the continuity of the throne. Despite the name, the ndop is not a naturalistic likeness but an idealised image of royal authority, and scholars disagree over whether some figures were carved after the king's death as memorials. The oldest surviving examples date to the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and a group of them was carried from the capital during the colonial expeditions before entering the British Museum and other collections. They remain the most celebrated images of Kuba kingship.

name: Kubbestol
description: A Norwegian chair hollowed from a single upright log, with seat, back, and arms carved from the same piece of wood, often decorated with chip-carving and floral patterns. Kubbestol chairs stood in farmhouses as the seat of honor and were even used as the bridal chair at weddings. They show the woodcarver's art also seen in stave church portals and seter crafts. The chair is made from the trunk of a thick pine or birch, the heart cut out to form the seat while the bark and the shape of the log keep the outer form, and the arms grow out of the same block so that the whole chair is one piece of wood. The carving, with its roses, leaves, and interlaced bands, made each chair a signed work of its maker, and a well-carved kubbestol was handed down in the family for generations. It is the most famous piece of Norwegian folk furniture and a showpiece of the old carving tradition.

name: Kuchi Jewelry
description: The kuchi jewelry is the heavy silver ornament of the Kuchi, the nomadic herding people of Afghanistan, who carry their wealth on their persons in the form of large necklaces, headpieces, earrings, bracelets and belt buckles. The pieces are made of silver, often with added amber, carnelian, turquoise and glass beads, and the forms echo ancient styles of Central Asia, with coin-rimmed discs, stamped patterns and chains that jingle as the wearer moves. For a nomadic family, jewelry is a portable bank, and for a bride the dowry ornaments show the status and resources of the two families. Kuchi jewelry is made by silversmiths who work for the nomad trade, and older pieces are collected and reused, so the ornaments carry the history of generations of wandering life across the Afghan plains.

name: Kukeri
description: The kukeri are the masked dancers of the Bulgarian winter, men dressed from head to foot in sheepskin and goat-hide, crowned with tall carved wooden masks and hung about the waist with heavy bronze and copper bells, who process through villages around New Year and before Lent. Their dance - a hopping, swaying, bell-shaking performance - is meant to drive out evil spirits, ill luck and sickness and to bring health, fertility and a good harvest in the season to come. Masks differ from region to region: Pernik favours towering feathered and horned figures, while the Rhodope makers carve flatter, beast-like faces, and each costume can weigh tens of kilograms. Since 1966 the International Festival of Masquerade Games Surva in Pernik has gathered hundreds of groups every January, and in 2015 UNESCO inscribed the Surova folk feast of the Pernik region on the Representative List.

name: Kultrún
description: The kultrún is the sacred drum of the Mapuche of Chile and Argentina, a shallow wooden bowl covered with a hide head and beaten with a single stick or by hand, played almost exclusively by the machi, the ritual specialist and healer. Its head is painted with a quartered design, a cross and the four directions, which orients the ceremony and maps the structure of the Mapuche universe, and around it the ngillatun ceremony of prayer and thanks is built. The machi sounds the kultrún to summon the spirits, to guide healing rites called machitun, and to call the community into a single rhythm; the drum is so closely tied to the office that a machi's calling is said to announce itself partly through the drum. The instrument is treated with the respect owed a sacred object, carried into the center of the ceremonial circle and held close by its keeper. In the twenty-first century the kultrún remains central to Mapuche religious life and has also become a symbol of Indigenous identity and resistance in Chile.

name: Kumgan (Tatar Copper Ewer)
description: Narrow-necked copper or brass ewer with a spout and handle used by the Tatars for water and for the ritual ablution before Muslim prayer. Made by Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), the kumgan was a symbol of the Tatar home, kept with a towelled basin and used at festivals and religious observances. Kazan and the villages of Zakazanye produced the finest examples. The ewer's long spout and slender neck pour a controlled stream, and the body is often engraved with floral or geometric ornament; some examples carry a lid and a pierced foot. The kumgan is used in the washing that precedes prayer, and its shape reflects centuries of contact between Volga Tatar craftsmen and the metalwork of Central Asia and the Middle East. In the 18th and 19th centuries the coppersmiths of Kazan and its surrounding villages supplied ewers, basins and kettles far beyond the Volga, and their work was praised at the great fairs. Museum collections preserve kumgans from the 16th to the 19th century, showing the craft's long and steady development.

name: Kundu Drum
description: Hourglass hand drum of Papua New Guinea, carved from a single block of light hardwood with a membrane of lizard or snake skin stretched over the open head and held with wax and resin studs, which also tune the drum. It is played with the palm and fingers, its patterns of beats belonging to the village and its ancestors; in the Sepik region the Iatmul associate the drum with the crocodile-creator, and the instrument is used in initiation rites, spirit cults, mourning and the sing-sing gatherings that draw communities together. The kundu is so emblematic that it appears on the national coat of arms, and a fine carved example is a valued heirloom handed down through families.

name: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
description: The legendary grass-cutting sword drawn from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by the storm god Susanoo, who then offered it to his sister Amaterasu; it is the sword of the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia, with the mirror and the jewel. Its name, 'grass-cutter', recalls the later story of the hero Yamato Takeru, who escaped a burning field by using the blade to mow the grass and turn the fire back on his enemies. The sword is said to be kept at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, where it is guarded and almost never shown, and no one outside the shrine has verified its state. Alongside the mirror and the jewel it stands for the martial virtue of the imperial line and for the divine descent of the throne, as told in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki.

name: Kākahu (Māori Cloak)
description: The kakahu is the woven cloak of the Maori, made from the muka fibre of the flax plant and covered with the down, feathers and tags of native birds, and worn as a cloak of rank and prestige. The weaver prepares the flax fibre, spins and dyes it, and weaves the body of the cloak on a small loom, then decorates it with feathers of kiwi, kaka, huia and other birds, or with tags of dog skin and fibre. The finest cloaks, such as the kahu kiwi, were made over months and were worn by chiefs on great occasions, and each cloak carries its own name and history. The black-feathered korowai with hanging tags is among the best-known forms, and kakahu are still woven today and worn at hui and ceremonies, treasured as taonga of the iwi that own them.

name: Lahij Copperware
description: Lahij copperware is the hammered copper and brass craft of the mountain village of Lahij in Azerbaijan's Ismayilli district, where smiths have worked for centuries in a tight warren of craftsmen's streets. A vessel such as an ewer, basin, cauldron or tray is raised from a single sheet of metal by hammering, never cast or soldered, then engraved with geometric rosettes, floral scrolls and inscriptions, and finally coated with a silvery tin alloy that protects the copper. The craft flourished in the nineteenth century, when Lahij's copper goods travelled the Silk Road and were sold in Baku, Tbilisi and Persian cities, and the village's self-governing craft guilds kept the techniques alive. In 2015 UNESCO inscribed the copper craftsmanship of Lahij on the Representative List, and master coppersmiths still work in the old street, training apprentices in hammer, chisel and furnace.

name: Laima's Distaff
description: The distaff of fate in Latvian and Lithuanian belief: a carved spindle-holder on which the goddess Laima, or the forest fairy Lauma, spins and measures the thread of a human life, fixing its length and its luck. Folk accounts describe laumas borrowing distaffs and spindles from village women and spinning linen by night, and the spindle's turning thread stands in countless spinning dainas for fate being spun out for a newborn child. The distaff itself was a treasured, often carved and painted object passed from mother to daughter, so that the homely tool of flax-spinning carried a double meaning: the thread of cloth and the thread of destiny.

name: Lajkonik
description: The Lajkonik is the hobby-horse rider of Kraków, a bearded figure in pointed Tatar dress and Mongol robes who parades the Old Town each year on the first Thursday after Corpus Christi, playfully striking onlookers with his gilded wooden mace to bring them good luck. Legend traces the custom to 1287, when Vistula raftsmen of the Zwierzyniec district, called włóczkowie, are said to have surprised and overwhelmed a sleeping Tatar raiding party camped by the river, then ridden into the city dressed in the captives' robes to celebrate their victory. The earliest written notices of the procession date from the 1730s and 1750s, and the mayor still greets the Lajkonik at the Main Market Square with a ceremonial ransom of money and a toast drunk from a chalice. The key elements of its costume, from the cream-crested head to the golden mace, were designed in 1909 by Stanisław Wyspiański, and the figure remains one of the unofficial symbols of Kraków, reproduced on trams, shop signs and festival posters.

name: Lasabrjótur
description: Lasabrjótur, the lock-breaker of the Huld manuscript, a stave said to open locks, fetters, and bonds. Its name literally means 'breaker of latches'. It was the kind of sign that made the Icelandic staves feared as well as respected, promising a power over iron and bindings that no ordinary key could match. In the collection of Geir Vigfússon, compiled at Akureyri in 1860, the stave is recorded with the simple instruction that it serves 'to open a lock without a key' — a task that in folk practice extended to releasing fetters, opening chests, and loosening binding magic laid on people or property. Users were cautioned to draw the sign with care, since a stave aimed at another's lock was itself a threat.

name: Latvian Josta (Woven Belt)
description: Ornamental belt woven by Latvian women on a small rigid loom, patterned with geometric symbols of the sun, moon and stars and the zigzag josta motif, worn by men to hold shirt and breeches. A full-length josta measures several metres and is wound twice around the waist; its weaving is a living craft, and the Latvian National Centre for Culture keeps a register of master weavers. The belt is part of the national costume worn at song festivals, and its symbols are read as protective signs: the sun for light, the grass snake for the household, and the endless repeating band for continuity. Traditionally the josta was a woman's gift, woven for her husband or son, and a richly patterned belt showed both the weaver's skill and the family's standing. Museum examples from the 19th century show the standard red, white and green palette with the black zigzag that gives the belt its name.

name: Lavvu
description: The conical tent of the Sámi people, raised on a tripod of poles and covered with reindeer hide or, in modern times, canvas. The lavvu is light enough to carry on a sledge or a reindeer and quick to pitch on the open tundra, with the hearth at the center and smoke escaping through the crown. It has been the seasonal home of reindeer-herding families for centuries and is still raised at festivals. The layout of the lavvu follows a strict order, with the back of the tent and the space opposite the door kept sacred and reserved, and the family's places arranged around the fire by rank and custom. In winter the hide cover and the inner snow-wall turned the tent into a warm shelter against the Arctic cold, and in summer the lighter canvas version followed the herds. The lavvu remains the pattern for modern Sámi life, at once a practical tent and a symbol of the herding culture.

name: Lechuguilla Mask
description: The lechuguilla is the masked costume of the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes in Hatillo, Puerto Rico, held every December 28, when costumed runners race through the streets of the town in painted wire-mesh masks and gowns covered in ruffled fabric curls. The celebration descends from a custom brought by the Canary Island settlers who founded Hatillo in 1823, and it re-enacts the biblical Massacre of the Innocents: the masked runners, called corredores, take the part of King Herod's soldiers, hunting the Christ child, while the crowd flees and turns the hunt into a chase of laughter. The masks, made of cedazo wire covered in papier-mâché and painted in bright colors, are the work of local artisans, and the whole costume is often finished with a crown of fabric flowers or ribbons. Though the name lechuguilla is only partly explained, in Puerto Rico the same word names an aquatic plant, the festival itself is one of the island's most beloved traditions, a December carnival that has run for two centuries.

name: Lei Niho Palaoa (Whale-Tooth Pendant)
description: Pendant of the Hawaiian chiefs made from a carved sperm whale tooth suspended on a braid of human hair, worn by men and women of high rank. The hair cord was itself a gift of honour, braided from hair offered by relatives and friends of the wearer, and the whole ornament was kapu — forbidden to anyone beneath the chiefly class. The lei niho palaoa signalled genealogical status and royal favour, and after the arrival of whalers and traders whale teeth and later ivory from walrus tusks were carved in its place, so that the oldest examples, in the richest carving and finest hair-work, are the most treasured heirlooms of Hawaiian families.

name: Lia Fáil
description: Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny, stands on the hill of Tara and is one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish tradition. In the Lebor Gabála Érenn it is counted among the treasures carried into Ireland, and later tales say the stone cried out beneath the rightful king when he stood or stepped on it, so that the whole assembly heard its voice. The best-known account is in Baile in Scáil, where the stone roars under the high king Conn of the Hundred Battles and reveals the line of kings who will follow him. Medieval writers and antiquaries long claimed that the Irish stone was the same as the Stone of Scone used in the coronation of the kings of Scotland, a belief still attached to the Lia Fáil by visitors to Tara. The present standing stone on the hill is a weathered monolith, and its identification with the legendary stone is itself a matter of debate. It remains the most potent symbol of Irish kingship.

name: Lielvārde Belt
description: The Lielvārde belt: a wide woven wool sash of red-and-white geometric patterns, with small figures worked into the bands, worn with Latvian folk costume and woven in the Lielvārde region of central Latvia. Folklore remembers it as a protective band that warded off evil, and since the 1970s the repeating patterns have been read by some as a hidden code of the universe — even of human DNA — a theory championed in popular writing though not by all scholars. The folklorist Janīna Kursīte traces its red-white symbolism to ancient protective clothing and incantations, and the belt was admitted to the Latvian Cultural Canon in 2008 as a national symbol.

name: Lietuviška Juosta
description: Hand-woven sash of linen and wool, rich with geometric patterns in several colours, worn by Lithuanian men and women wrapped at the waist over festive dress and given as gifts at weddings, christenings and funerals. The juosta was woven on narrow looms or by tablet weaving, and every region knew its own ornament — rhombuses, zigzags, crosses and small stars — so that a sash could name the wearer's parish. In folk belief the sash was protective: it binds, fastens and marks a sacred boundary, and a woven band given away could carry goodwill or serve as an offering, mediating between people and the spirits of field and forest.

name: Lituus of Romulus
description: The lituus of Romulus was the curved augur's staff with which, in Roman tradition, Rome's founder marked out the regions of the sky when he took the auspices that sanctioned the building of the city. The relic was kept among the sacred gear of the Salian priests in the Curia Saliorum on the Palatine, and Cicero, Plutarch, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus record how it was found unharmed after the building burned, a survival read as a portent that the augural science, and with it Rome's favour with the gods, would endure. The lituus, a crook-like staff, was the professional badge of the augur, used to trace the templum, the sacred area of the sky, before any public act, and its shape became the pattern of the augur's staff in all later Roman state ritual. The Romulus relic belongs with the ancile and the fire of Vesta among the talismanic objects on which Rome's continuance was thought to hang. No such staff survives; the legends are our only record of it.

name: Liver of Piacenza
description: The Piacenza liver, a life-sized bronze model of a sheep's liver found in 1877 near Gossolengo in the countryside of Piacenza and dated to the late 2nd or early 1st century BC, is the most important surviving document of Etruscan divination. Its convex upper surface is divided into sixteen inscribed zones, each naming a deity or region of the sky, and its outer edge is marked out in sectors, mapping the heavenly templum onto the organ of sacrifice. Etruscan haruspices read the future from the form, markings, and lobes of a sacrificial animal's liver, and the model, with its ritual vocabulary of gods and boundaries, served both as a teaching instrument and as a working reference for the practice. It now stands in the Museo Civico di Palazzo Farnese in Piacenza, and parallels from Mesopotamia show the antiquity of the tradition. The liver is the concrete remains of a priestly science that Rome borrowed and then let die.

name: Lozi Royal Barge
description: The Lozi royal barge, the nalikwanda, is the great wooden vessel that carries the Litunga, the king of the Lozi people of western Zambia, at the Kuomboka ceremony. When the annual floods rise on the Zambezi, the king leaves the lowland palace and is paddled in procession to higher ground, the barge covered with an immense shroud of black-and-white cloth and surrounded by dozens of escort boats. The crossing is the climax of Kuomboka, a pageant that renews the bond between the king and the waters that shape Lozi life, and the barge's heavy, deliberate movement through the flood is timed to the songs of its rowers. The nalikwanda is built of timber by Lozi boatbuilders, and a new barge is commissioned when the old one fails. Kuomboka, whose name means 'to get out of the water', draws thousands of spectators each year. The barge is the central object of the most famous river festival in southern Africa.

name: Lukasa Memory Board
description: The lukasa is a wooden memory board of the Luba peoples of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, its surface covered with beads, shells, and metal pins arranged in clusters that encode historical and ritual knowledge. A member of the Mbudye association, the court's body of historians, reads the board by touch, tracing the beads as a mnemonic that calls forth genealogies, royal protocol, migration legends, and the esoteric teachings of the kingdom. Because each board belonged to a particular specialist and was arranged to fit his memory, no two lukasa are identical, and the objects were kept secret from the uninitiated. The tradition is bound to the founding legends of the Luba state, and the boards are still referenced in the stories of the culture heroes Kalala Ilunga and Mbidi Kiluwe. Scholars such as Mary Nooter Roberts have studied the lukasa as a case of embodied, non-written memory, and the boards are among the best-known objects of Central African court art. Luba historians and diviners continue to use them in their work today.

name: Lukkustafir
description: Lukkustafir, the luck staves of the Huld manuscript, a set of ten separate signs each drawn for good fortune in a different undertaking. The grimoire gives them as a family of practical charms for games, trade, travel, and daily life, so that the luck seeker could choose the sign that matched the task. They remain among the most reproduced of the Icelandic staves, second only to Vegvísir and Ægishjálmr in modern popularity. Unlike the aggressive defensive staves, the luck signs were turned to peaceful aims — winning at play, closing a bargain, finding a safe road — and were usually drawn on paper or wood and carried about the person. Because each of the ten signs answered a separate need, the family survives as a record of the everyday concerns that Icelandic folk magic was asked to serve.

name: Lund Minster
description: Lund Cathedral (Lund domkyrka), the great Romanesque church of the Swedish Middle Ages, begun in the late eleventh century when Lund was the seat of the archbishopric of the Nordic lands and consecrated in 1145. In legend the giant Finn built the cathedral in exchange for the sun and the moon, and was tricked out of his wages; in some versions he was turned to stone, and a carved giant figure still guards the crypt, stroking his beard while a column he was shaping bends above him. The crypt with its thick pillars and the twin towers over the high altar are among the finest Romanesque works in Scandinavia. The cathedral crowns the story 'Finn the Giant and the Minster of Lund', and the carved stone giant remains one of Lund's best-known sights.

name: Luzzu
description: The luzzu, the brightly painted wooden fishing boat of the Maltese islands, carries on its prow a pair of apotropaic eyes painted on either side of the bow, an inheritance many trace to the Eye of Osiris or of Horus of the ancient Mediterranean, meant to ward off the evil eye, protect the crew, and guide the boat home to a good catch. The boats, broad-beamed and high-prowed, are built and repaired by family yards at Marsaxlokk and on Gozo, painted in reds, blues, yellows, and greens, with the eyes and often a patron saint's image or a religious motto on the bows. Though the modern luzzu form dates only from the early 20th century, the eye motif is ancient and links the boats to a seafaring world older than Malta's recorded history. The working fleet of Marsaxlokk harbour, still bright with the painted gaze, is one of the most photographed sights of the island. The luzzu stands for the persistence of a Mediterranean folk belief on the decks of modern boats.

name: Lyre of Orpheus
description: The lyre of Orpheus, a gift from Apollo or Hermes with the power to charm beasts, trees, and stones and to move the dead; its music soothed Cerberus and won Hades' consent to let Eurydice return, a bargain lost when Orpheus looked back on the way out of the underworld. Ancient poetry names it a gift of Apollo or Hermes, and its seven strings were said to mirror the seven planets. After his death the lyre was set among the stars as the constellation Lyra. It is the emblem of music's power over nature and death in Greek myth, and its sound has been painted and sung for three thousand years.

name: Lævateinn
description: Lævateinn, the 'wounding wand', is the blade of the poem Fjölsvinnsmál, the only weapon said to be able to slay the rooster Viðófnir that perches at the top of the world tree. The wand lies in a chest beside the giantess Sinmara, bound by nine locks that can be opened only by a feather plucked from Viðófnir's own tail, a riddle-like condition that keeps the weapon out of reach. Scholars debate whether the name means 'wounding-wand' and whether the blade is to be identified with Loki's sword, since the name in the manuscripts may be a late emendation of 'Hævateinn', the 'high-wand'. The weapon's place in the late, riddling poem Fjölsvinnsmál sets it apart from the better-known Eddic swords. Lævateinn is nonetheless a favourite of catalogue-writers and of modern fantasy that draws on Old Norse weaponry.

name: Maasai Nborr Collar
description: The nborr is the flat beaded collar worn by Maasai women and, on ceremonial occasions, by young men (moran) of Kenya and Tanzania. Built on a base of hide or wire and covered with dense rows of tiny glass beads, the collar forms a broad crescent that lies across the chest and shoulders. The colour combinations are not arbitrary: red stands for the cattle that are the heart of Maasai life, white for milk and peace, and the patterns signal the age-set, clan, and status of the wearer. Beaded ornaments are made by women, who learn the craft from their mothers, and whose beadwork circulates in the exchanges that build family alliances. The nborr is worn at dances, initiations, and the celebrations that mark the passage of the age-sets. Maasai beadwork has also become an economic mainstay, with women's cooperatives selling collars and jewellery to the wider market.

name: Maasai Rungu Club
description: The rungu is a short throwing club of the Maasai, a knobbed head on a tapering wooden shaft that herders and warriors carry as they move with their cattle. In the past the rungu was a practical weapon for defending livestock against predators and for settling disputes, thrown with a spin that drove the heavy knob home with force. Today it is still carried, but its main work is ceremonial and social: elders raise the rungu to command attention at meetings, and the club is a badge of authority for spokesmen and age-set leaders. Decorated rungu, carved with rings and bands and sometimes tipped with metal, are made for chiefs and for the tourist market. The word has passed into the region's popular culture, and the rungu remains the most recognisable symbol of Maasai leadership.

name: Maasai Shuka Cloth
description: The shuka is the checked cloth, usually in shades of red, that Maasai wrap around the body as a toga-like garment, a dress so distinctive it has become the visual signature of the Maasai in Kenya and Tanzania. Red is the colour of cattle blood and of the warrior ideal, and the bold plaid stands out in the savannah where the herds graze. The shuka replaced the older dress of hides and skins during the twentieth century, when imported cotton cloth spread through the region, and its adoption shows how a modern commodity was absorbed into Maasai identity. Different communities favour different colour families, and the way the cloth is folded and worn, over one shoulder, around the waist, or across the mouth of a herder sheltering from dust, varies with occasion and age-set. Factories in the region now print shuka cloth in bulk, and the checked patterns are also worn far beyond the Maasai as a mark of East African style.

name: Macuahuitl
description: The macuahuitl is the flat wooden sword edged with rows of razor-sharp obsidian blades that was the signature weapon of Aztec and Mesoamerican warriors at the time of the Spanish conquest. Chroniclers including Bernal Diaz describe its edge as sharp enough to behead a horse with a single stroke, and the codices and tribute lists record it as both a weapon of war and a mark of rank, with captured enemies often carrying the most ornate examples. The weapon was made of a wooden paddle, in some examples the paddle slotted and the blades set in, and obsidian edges were renewed as they dulled. The macuahuitl belonged to the wider Mesoamerican tradition of the maquahuitl and the atlatl, and it was used by elite warriors such as the jaguar and eagle knights. After the conquest the weapon passed quickly into legend, and no complete original survives, but it remains the most iconic weapon of the Aztec empire.

name: Mahafaly Aloalo Funerary Post
description: The aloalo are the carved funerary posts of the Mahafaly people of southwestern Madagascar, tall wooden stelae that stand on the stone tombs of chiefs and wealthy families. The name comes from alo, 'intermediary' or 'messenger', and the posts are believed to help the dead cross into the community of the ancestors. A classic aloalo rises through a column of openwork geometric shapes, crescents and circles often read as the phases of the moon, to a finial carved as a human figure, a zebu, or a bird such as the cattle egret, while the horns of zebu sacrificed at the funeral are arranged at the tomb's base. The zebu, the measure of wealth in the region, is carved again and again, and recent aloalo add motifs such as bicycles, aeroplanes, and scenes from the deceased's life. Only commissioned carvers make aloalo, which were once the right of royalty alone. The posts have become an emblem of Madagascar, and the Mahafaly tomb country is a candidate for the World Heritage list.

name: Makonde Lipiko Mask
description: The lipiko is the carved wooden mask of the Makonde people of northern Mozambique, worn by male dancers in the mapiko, a masked dance that forms part of the likumbi initiation rite marking the passage from puberty to adulthood. The mapiko performance, which UNESCO inscribed on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in 2023 under the name Ingoma ya Mapiko, takes place in an open enclosure, often beneath mango trees, with dancers, drummers and a choir of men and women facing each other. The dancer's whole body is covered by the costume, and the mask, carved from a single block of wood and sometimes from scrap metal such as old cooking pots, shows a stylized face with pronounced lips and painted details, and is kept hidden from the uninitiated. Within the rite the masked dancer is held to embody the spirit of a dead ancestor, and the dance both solemnly stages the world of the dead and entertains the living, since it may also be danced at funerals of group members and for general celebration. Young Makonde men learn the making and wearing of masks and the steps of the dance during the secret initiation camp, with the knowledge passed down from elder carvers to the initiates.

name: Makonde Shetani Figure
description: The shetani carvings of the Makonde are dark hardwood figures of contorted, expressive spirits, carved from the ebony-like mpingo of the Tanzanian and Mozambican coast. Beginning in the 1950s, carvers turned from ancestor figures to the shetani, capricious bush and ancestral spirits, twisting human and animal forms into elongated, agonised, or playful shapes that seem to catch a spirit mid-transformation. Each carving is original, the forms said to be revealed to the carver in dreams, and the pieces are exhibited as art as much as ritual objects. The word shetani, from the Arabic for 'evil spirit', entered Swahili through Islam, but the figures draw on older Makonde beliefs about the dark forest and its inhabitants. Shetani carving has become one of the most recognisable genres of contemporary African art, sold from Dar es Salaam to international galleries. The tradition also carries the older meaning of the spirits themselves, who are remembered as crowding the Makonde homeland on both sides of the border.

name: Malitsa (Nenets Reindeer-Fur Coat)
description: Men's winter coat of the Nenets reindeer herders, sewn from reindeer skins with the fur turned inward, a hood attached inside, and worn with a belt (sok) and fur mittens. Decorated with white or red fur tufting and fur mosaic, the malitsa is made from autumn- and winter-killed reindeer and is the herders' everyday Arctic dress. Because the fur faces inward, the garment traps warm air against the body while the smooth outer hide sheds wind and snow, and the sewn-in hood protects the head without an added collar. The malitsa reaches to the knees, its hem edged with the dark leg fur of the reindeer, and the belt holds the coat closed at the waist and carries the hunter's knife and pouch. Nenets women sew the coats with sinew thread, using the tough winter hide for the body and the soft fur of young deer for trimming. In the polar cold the malitsa is sometimes said to be warm enough to sleep in, and herders keep it on even indoors.

name: Mama Cocha Effigy
description: Mama Cocha, the mother of the sea, was counted among the great Inca divinities, the wife and sister of the creator god Viracocha and the mother of Inti the sun and Mama Killa the moon. Fisherfolk along the Pacific coast made offerings of shells and small carved images, and poured maize beer into the waves, and colonial chroniclers record that the goddess was honored among the household and regional deities of the empire, receiving her share at the great festivals. Her image in miniature, worn as an amulet or set at the shore, carried her protection onto the boats that worked her waters, calming storms and guiding the catch. Though the Inca state collapsed, the cult of the sea mother survived in coastal communities, where she is sometimes said to ride the currents still and to reward the faithful with a full net. The effigies are the tangible trace of that devotion, small objects that held an ocean in the mind of an empire.

name: Mangal Kalasha
description: The mangal-kalasha, also called purna-kalasha, is a metal or clay pot filled with water and topped with fresh mango leaves and a coconut, an indispensable emblem of auspiciousness in Hindu ritual. It stands at the door of homes during weddings and housewarmings, is established at the beginning of pujas, and is brought to receive honoured guests, because the overflowing pot signifies abundance, fertility and the fullness of the home. In practice the leaves and coconut are taken to invite natural and divine energies, and the water in the pot may be treated as the presence of a deity: during rituals a thread is often tied around the neck of the kalasha and mantra recited over it. The kalasha also appears in the story of the churning of the ocean, in which the pot of amrita, the nectar of immortality, was stolen by the demon Rahu, and the pot is a standard motif over temple doors in South India. Because of this layered meaning, the kalasha is one of the most photographed objects of Hindu domestic life, at once a water jar, a greeting and an invocation.

name: Mangalsutra
description: The mangalsutra is the necklace that marks a Hindu woman as married, tied around her neck by the groom during the wedding ceremony and then worn for life, though widows set it aside. The name means 'auspicious thread', and the simple gold and black-bead ornament of the north differs from the heavier gold pendant called thali worn in the south, where the tying ceremony is called mangalyam and is the most solemn moment of the wedding. The black beads are traditionally believed to protect the wearer and her husband's family from the evil eye, while the gold signals prosperity, and the number of knots parallels the vows exchanged during the rites. Because the mangalsutra is the visible sign of the married state, its presence or absence is read at once by the whole community, and it is never worn casually. In modern India the ornament has also become a fashion item, with contemporary designs keeping the two beads in silver or diamond settings.

name: Mani Wall
description: The mani wall is a long, low wall of carved stone raised beside mountain paths, passes and villages across the Himalayan world, its blocks inscribed with the six-syllable mantra Om Mani Padme Hum and set in rows under a capping course of stones. The name comes from the first syllable of the mantra, which is the prayer of the bodhisattva of compassion Avalokiteshvara, and the walls are treated as sacred, so that travellers keep them on their right and walk past them clockwise, the direction of ritual circumambulation. Passing pilgrims and travellers add their own stones, carved or plain, so the wall grows as a living offering along the route, and the carved stones are believed to carry blessing to everyone who walks by, whether or not they can read the letters. Long chains of mani walls line the pilgrim roads of Nepal, Ladakh and the approaches to Mount Kailash.

name: Mantle of Tegau Eurfron
description: Tegau Eurfron's mantle, the Mantle of Tegau Gold-Breast, is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain listed in medieval Welsh tradition. The garment would fit only a woman who had been faithful to her husband; a wife who had broken her vows could not wear it, and it would not cover her, revealing the truth of her conduct to the court. Tegau herself, the wife of Caradog, is praised in the Welsh triads as one of the three faithful wives of Britain, and the mantle is the token of her chastity. The object belongs to a family of chastity-testing garments found across medieval Europe, from the Arthurian mantel mal taillé to the test-mantles of later romance. Like the other treasures, the mantle is described in the later manuscript lists with explanatory notes. The Welsh tale survives as a parable of marriage, honesty and the public testing of private virtue.

name: Marquesan War Club (Uʻu)
description: Polished war club of the Marquesas Islands, carved from toa, the dense ironwood, with a long shaft and a flattened, slightly flared head incised with the stylized face of a tiki and other relief designs. The uʻu was the principal weapon of the Marquesan warrior, swung in hand-to-hand combat, but it was equally a work of sculptural art and a badge of rank, kept and treasured as a personal trophy and handed down within families. Some clubs were inlaid with whale tooth or, it is said, with the bone of a fallen enemy, marking the uʻu as both weapon and memorial of its owner.

name: Marshall Islands Stick Chart
description: Navigation chart of the Marshall Islands built from pandanus ribs and coconut fibre, with small cowrie shells marking the islands and curved sticks recording the swell and wave patterns of the ocean. Charts come in three kinds: the mattang, which teaches the principles of wave reflection without naming real islands; the meddo, covering a particular group of reefs; and the rebbelib, a large chart of the whole archipelago. Read and memorised by trained navigators before a voyage and then left ashore, the charts encode wave and current knowledge passed down within navigators' families, and the same skill is remembered in the legend of the first navigator who learned to read the sea.

name: Martenitsa
description: The martenitsa is the Bulgarian talisman of March, a twisted length of red and white yarn, often finished with beads or a small tassel, exchanged on 1 March to wish health, strength and good fortune for the new year. The red stands for life and the blood, the white for purity and spring light, and the name honours Baba Marta, the capricious old woman of folk belief whose moods are said to govern the early-spring weather. The martenitsa is worn on the wrist, lapel or neck until the wearer sees a stork, a swallow or the first blossoming tree, then it is tied to a fruit tree so the tree will bear, or slipped under a stone for luck. The custom, shared across Bulgaria and its neighbours, was inscribed in 2017 on the UNESCO Representative List through a joint file on 1 March cultural practices, and whole streets of Bulgaria are strung with martenitsi every spring.

name: Mate Gourd
description: The mate gourd is the dried calabash cup from which yerba mate, the leafy infusion of the Guaraní, is drunk through a metal straw called a bombilla, passed hand to hand around a circle of friends. The Guaraní of Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina prepared a drink of the herb before the Spanish arrived, and colonial accounts already describe it being shared; the Spanish word mate itself comes from the Quechua mati, for the gourd that holds it. Etiquette is precise: the cebador pours, drinks the first, often bitter, sip and refills, and the gourd circles clockwise, never returning to the cebador for a second serving until it has passed everyone. To drink from another's gourd is an act of trust and closeness, which is why the sharing of mate is still the everyday gesture of friendship in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Modern gourds are carved and sometimes rimmed with metal, but the meaning is unchanged: one gourd, many hands, a shared breath.

name: Matyó Embroidery
description: Matyó embroidery is the flamboyant floral needlework of the Hungarian town of Mezőkövesd and its surrounding villages, where from about the 1860s women stitched huge roses, tulips and pansies in red, blue and green silk thread on white linen. The style covered festive women's costume, shirts, aprons, pillowcases, tablecloths and wall hangings, and the bold single blooms grew ever larger as the local Matyó identity took shape at the turn of the twentieth century. Unlike the fine satin stitch of other Hungarian regions, Matyó work used long, loose stitches that give the flowers a sculpted, three-dimensional look. The craft, passed from mother to daughter, was inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2012, and embroiderers, fashion designers and textile artists in Mezőkövesd continue to develop it.

name: Mbira Dzavadzimu
description: The mbira dzavadzimu is the lamellophone of the Shona people of Zimbabwe, a wooden soundboard fitted with rows of metal keys and placed over a gourd resonator that buzzes with shells, bottle caps, or other rattling matter. Its name means 'mbira of the ancestor spirits', and it is played at the bira ceremonies where the spirits of the departed are called to advise the living. The interlocking patterns of the mbira weave around the singing and clapping of the assembly, and the buzzing, layered sound is thought to attract the spirits so that they can speak through a medium. The instrument is learned by hand within Shona families, and certain mbira pieces are held by specific lineages as inherited property. After independence the mbira became a national emblem of Zimbabwe, and its sound now opens radio broadcasts and accompanies church hymns. The instrument's deep, hypnotic cycles have also carried it into world music through Zimbabwean players and teachers.

name: Medicine Bag
description: The medicine bag is a small hide pouch carried or kept privately by many Plains and Woodlands people, holding the herbs, feathers, stones, roots or small objects revealed to its owner in a vision or dream. Unlike the communal sacred bundles kept by whole clans or societies, such as the Lakota pipe bundle, the medicine bag is personal: its contents are chosen by the spirits for one individual and are usually kept secret. Its power, elders say, depends on how faithfully the owner follows the instructions that came with the vision, and careless handling is believed to drain or endanger that power. Ethnographic accounts record that the bag is never opened lightly, is not shown to others without reason, and is often buried with its owner or passed on with ceremony. The bundle tradition underlies much of the healing and 'medicine' concept that travellers, traders and missionaries encountered across the continent.

name: Medicine Wheel
description: The medicine wheel is a circle of stones laid out on high plains ground with lines of stones radiating from the centre like spokes, read by Plains peoples as a sacred map of the cosmos, the four directions, the seasons and the circle of life. The most celebrated example, the Bighorn Medicine Wheel in Wyoming, measures some 23 metres across and has 28 spokes, and studies have suggested its outer cairns may align with the summer solstice and stars, though the precise purpose of the old sites remains debated. Similar wheels at Moose Mountain in Saskatchewan and elsewhere show the form was widespread. Modern Plains nations still use stone circles as places of prayer and ceremony, and the wheel's four directions have become a teaching symbol for balance and guidance. Whatever its original astronomy, the medicine wheel endures as a model of harmony between people and the land.

name: Megingjörð
description: Megingjörð, the 'might-girdle', is the belt of the thunder god Thor, and the Prose Edda names it as one of his three great treasures together with the hammer Mjölnir and the iron gloves Járngreipr. When Thor girds the belt about his waist his already godlike strength is doubled, so that no giant can stand against him in the wrestling-matches and battle-tales of the Eddas. In the tale of Thor's journey to the giant Geirröðr, the giantess Gríðr lends the god a similar belt of might along with her staff, showing that such power-girdles were a fixed part of the mythic image of the thunder god. The belt is sometimes said to be made of leather with a heavy buckle, though the sources give no detailed description of its form. Megingjörð survives in modern retellings as the standard third element of Thor's arsenal, and its name is a stock kenning-adjacent byword for supernatural strength.

name: Mehter Davul
description: The mehter davul is the great two-headed drum of the mehter, the Ottoman military band, struck with a heavy beater to drive the slow, thundering rhythm of the janissary march, the pulse of an army on the move. The davul, a large double-skin cylinder slung at the waist or on a strap, is played with a curved stick and a thin switch, producing the deep boom and sharp crack that set the soldiers' gait; together with the shrill zurna, the kettle-drums, and the cymbals it made the band that European observers from the 16th century described as terrifying in battle and overwhelming in its din. The mehter's music was meant both to inspire the Ottoman troops and to daunt the enemy, and it marched before the army in campaigns from the Balkans to Persia. The band was abolished in 1826 together with the Janissary corps it served, but the davul lives on in successor ensembles and in the marches still played at Turkish ceremonial occasions. It remains the emblem of Ottoman martial music.

name: Mere Pounamu
description: The mere pounamu is the short, broad-bladed club of the Maori, carved from pounamu, the greenstone of New Zealand, and regarded as a chiefly weapon and a great heirloom. The blade is leaf-shaped and polished, straight-edged and thicker along its length, and the rounded grip is pierced for a wrist cord, so that the club swings with a stroke of the forearm. Named meres were handed down through the generations, and the mana of the weapon passed from hand to hand, with the saying that a chief was lifted by receiving such a weapon. Because pounamu comes from the rivers and mountains of the South Island, the meres of the northern tribes were carried along the trade routes, and the blades were so greatly valued that they were not allowed to touch the ground.

name: Message Stick
description: The message stick is a carved piece of wood sent between Aboriginal groups to carry news and to prove the authority of the messenger who carries it. The marks cut and painted on the surface record something of the message, the sender's clan and the places or groups concerned, and the stick is accepted as a sign that the bearer speaks with the consent of the people who sent them. The marks are not writing in the modern sense, but they carry meaning within the system of the sender and receiver, and the practice of carrying such sticks is recorded from many parts of Australia. The messenger is greeted with formal welcome when the stick is presented, and the stick itself is often destroyed or returned once the message has been delivered and answered.

name: Metate
description: The metate is the slightly concave stone grinding slab at the heart of Mesoamerican cooking, used with a hand-held stone (mano) to grind nixtamalised maize into masa for tortillas, tamales and atole. Basalt and other volcanic stone were preferred, and the craft of shaping the slab, often on carved supports or a tripod base, goes back to the Preclassic era and continues in rural households today. The grinding of maize was never mere kitchen work: Mesoamerican myth held that the gods made people from maize dough, as the Popol Vuh recounts, so the metate transformed the sacred staple into human food. Codices show women kneeling at the metate, and elaborately carved examples from later periods suggest the tool could also carry prestige. Modern lava-stone metates are still sold in markets across Mexico and Guatemala, prized for the flavour they give tortillas.

name: Midsummer Maypole
description: The midsummer pole (midsommarstång or majstång), a tall pole decorated with greenery, flowers, and rings, raised on Midsummer Eve and danced around in Swedish tradition. Songs, ring-dances, and games circle the pole, and the custom is recorded in Sweden from the 17th century. The pole is central to the Midsummer celebration and its bonfire-night rites. The pole is decked with leaves and flowers and hung with two crossed rings, and the village raises it in the open place of the farm or village before dancing the ring-dances that circle it. The custom was already described in the seventeenth century, when the pole was sometimes called a 'majstång' even in midsummer, and scholars have read it as a survival of the old fertility rites of the turning year. Around the pole the shortest night is kept with music, flowers, and the bonfires that guard the livestock, and the maypole remains the fixed centre of every Swedish Midsummer.

name: Mjölnir
description: Mjölnir, 'the grinder', is the war-hammer of the thunder god Thor, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri as the prize of a wager Loki placed on his own head. Because Loki, in the shape of a fly, bit the smith's hand while he worked the bellows, the hammer's handle came out too short — which is why Thor wields it with one hand. The Prose Edda counts it among the god's three great treasures, beside the belt Megingjörð and the iron gloves Járngreipr; its head is sometimes said to be iron and the shaft wooden, and the hammer returns to the thrower's hand like a boomerang after striking. Beyond battle it hallows marriages, births, funerals, ships, and fields, and it will be the weapon with which Thor fells Jörmungandr at Ragnarök. Small iron and silver hammer pendants of the Viking Age, such as the figure from Eyrarland, are widely read as images of Mjölnir worn for protection. It remains the most recognised symbol of Norse paganism and is still used as a badge of identity in modern heathen communities.

name: Morin Khuur
description: The morin khuur, the horse-head fiddle, is the two-stringed instrument of Mongolia whose scroll is carved as a horse's head, whose strings and bow are of horsehair, and whose sound is held to imitate the breath and song of the horse. The classic origin legend tells of a herdsman whose beloved horse was killed by a treacherous lord; from the horse's skull, skin, mane, and tail the man made the first fiddle, so that the animal's spirit would sing on. The instrument carries a deep spiritual charge: it is played in homes, at ceremonies, and at the Naadam festival, and traditional players observed taboos in its presence, regarding it as a living being. In the twentieth century the morin khuur was adopted as the national instrument of Mongolia and inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Its two strings are often described as the two poles of Mongol identity, and the instrument is taught, collected, and displayed as the emblem of Mongolian national culture.

name: Mukut Crown
description: The mukut is the jewel-set crown of the royal traditions of Nepal, worn by the Malla kings of the Kathmandu valley and later the Shah kings at state and religious ceremonies, and linked by tradition to the goddess Taleju, protector of the ruling dynasties. The crowns are worked in gold and silver with gemstones, pearls and brocade by the Newar goldsmiths of Kathmandu, and the king's crown was held to draw its right to rule from the favour of Taleju, whose temples stood beside the royal palaces. The living goddess tradition also places a crown on the young Kumari during festivals, echoing the belief that divine favour descends on the wearer. Royal regalia of this kind survives in the museums of Kathmandu and in the courts' surviving records, and the mukut remains a powerful image of Nepali kingship.

name: Mărțișor
description: Mărțișorul is the Romanian March talisman, a red-and-white twisted silk thread finished with a small charm, coin or bead, given on 1 March as a wish of health, love and good luck for the coming year. The name and the month both come from martie, March, and folk memory links the custom to the return of spring and to the capricious weather-woman Baba Dochia, whose shepherding stories echo the alternating mild and cold spells of early spring. Worn on the wrist or pinned to the chest for the whole month, the mărțișor is taken off at the end of March and tied to the branch of a fruit tree, believed to bring the tree good luck and fertility. The tradition is shared with the neighbouring lands that joined the joint UNESCO file of 2017, and Romanian jewellers now cast the charms in gold and silver alongside the older coins and shells.

name: Naglfar
description: Naglfar, the 'nail-ship', is the great ship of the dead in Norse mythology, built from the untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead. The Prose Edda warns that the ship is always under construction, and that the dead should therefore be buried with clipped nails — every unclipped nail added to the awful ship. At Ragnarök Naglfar sails from the east carrying the forces of chaos across the waters: in the poem Völuspá the giant Hrym steers it, while Snorri places Loki at the helm, and the ship bears the host of frost giants toward the battlefield of Vígríðr. The galleon of the dead is one of the most striking images of the end of the world in Old Norse literature, and the practical folk-custom of trimming nails for the sake of delaying the ship's completion kept the myth alive in daily life. Naglfar remains a standard image in retellings of Ragnarök and in art inspired by Norse mythology.

name: Nakshi Kantha
description: The nakshi kantha is the embroidered quilt of Bengal, sewn by village women from stacked layers of old saris and dhotis and covered with running stitch in patterns of flowers, birds, animals, boats and scenes of daily life. The name comes from the fine nakshi stitching, and the needlework is built up by hand so that the whole surface becomes a picture, with borders, corner motifs and a central lotus or mandala medallion. A kantha made for a bride is a gift of love and skill, and the making of kanthas is passed between mothers, daughters and granddaughters, each woman adding motifs from memory and imagination. The craft is practised across Bangladesh and West Bengal, and finished quilts are used as bedding, wraps and covers, treasured as much for the maker's hand as for their warmth.

name: Nan Madol (Basalt City)
description: Ruined city of the island of Pohnpei, built on about ninety artificial islets separated by canals, with walls, tombs and terraces raised from great prismatic basalt columns ferried and set into place. It was the ceremonial and political centre of the Saudeleur dynasty, and legend holds that the massive stones were flown and set in place by magic, and that the city fell to the warrior Isokelekel, who came from the east and overthrew the last Saudeleur. Today the site is a World Heritage monument of Micronesia, its canals and basalt ramparts still bearing the names and stories of the chiefs, gods and sorcerers of Pohnpei.

name: Nanteos Cup
description: The Nanteos Cup is a small, badly damaged wooden bowl, a late medieval mazer of wych elm, held for many years at Nanteos mansion near Aberystwyth in Ceredigion and kept today by the descendants of the Powell family. From at least the late nineteenth century it was treated as a healing cup: sick people borrowed it, leaving a valuable pledge, and drank from it in the hope of a cure, and its jagged edge was blamed on pilgrims who bit or scraped off pieces as relics. Some traditions said the bowl was made from a piece of the True Cross, and after 1905, when a visitor published Sought and Found, it was proclaimed one of at least two hundred European candidates for the Holy Grail. Folklorists have shown that there is no credible reference to the cup before about 1836, and no connection with the Grail before 1905, with one legend holding that monks carried it from Glastonbury to Strata Florida during the Dissolution of the Monasteries. The cup is now preserved at the National Library of Wales, a living relic of Welsh folklore.

name: Naqqara Drum
description: The naqqara is a pair of kettledrums, usually of copper with goatskin heads, beaten with two sticks and carried before rulers or sounded from gate towers to announce arrivals, processions and festival days. The instrument came into South Asia with the Indo-Islamic courts, where paired kettledrums were part of royal ceremonial music, and it remains in use at shrines and at processions across Pakistan and the wider Muslim world. In the Punjab and Sindh the deep paired notes of the naqqara mark the high moments of a gathering, and the drum is still played at the doors of shrines and at the head of festival processions, where its sound is said to carry the blessing of the occasion through the crowd. Naqqara bands of several drums of different sizes are also a feature of military and civic celebration in the region.

name: Nau Catrineta
description: The Nau Catrineta is the legendary ship of the great Portuguese romance 'A Nau Catrineta', which is lost at sea for years until the starving crew cast lots to decide who must be sacrificed to save the rest, and the lot falls on the captain-general. The devil, in the shape of the lookout or of a strange ship's boy, appears to claim his soul, but the captain, praying to the Virgin, is rescued by an angel, the demon is driven off, and the ship sails safely into port. The ballad, collected by Almeida Garrett in his Romanceiro and known in many oral versions across Portugal, Brazil, and the Portuguese islands, blends the old motif of the doomed captain with Christian redemption, and some versions soften the ending or let the captain bargain his way free. The song remains among the best-loved of the Portuguese oral tradition. The ship itself has passed into speech as a name for an ill-fated vessel, and the legend mirrors the sea's deep hold on the Portuguese imagination.

name: Nazar Boncugu
description: The nazar boncuğu, the blue-and-white glass bead of Turkey, is the country's most widespread protective amulet, worn as jewellery and hung in homes, cars, and workplaces, and fixed to new buildings, to ward off the evil eye. The bead, usually of blue glass with concentric white, dark blue, and black circles suggesting an eye, is made by glass blowers of the Aegean region, long centred on villages such as Görece near Izmir. The Turkish tradition treats the amulet itself as expendable: a nazar that has absorbed the envious glance is said to crack or fall, and a broken one is simply replaced with a fresh bead. The belief in the evil eye, the nazar, is ancient and Mediterranean-wide, and blue eye-amulets are documented across Anatolia for centuries. Similar amulets appear throughout the region, from the Greek mati to the Arab ayin, but the Turkish nazar boncuğu, with its distinctive glassy eye, has become a global souvenir of protection.

name: Neverlur
description: A long natural trumpet of birch wood, split in two, hollowed out, and bound together with birch-root lashing or bark to form a flared conical tube. Herders in the Norwegian mountain pastures blew the neverlur to call the flocks and to signal across valleys, and its deep, carrying note could be heard for miles; shorter versions with finger holes could play melodies. The instrument fell out of common use with the decline of the old seter dairying life but was revived in the 20th century by folk musicians and folk-music scholars. It is related to the similar bark-wound horns of Scandinavia, such as the Finnish liru and the Swedish birch trumpet.

name: Ngoma Drum (Swahili Coast)
description: The ngoma is the wooden drum of the Swahili coast of Tanzania and Kenya, built as a barrel or goblet with a hide head and played in the ensembles that accompany weddings, dances, and life-cycle rites. In Swahili the word ngoma covers drum, dance, and festivity together, and the drumming groups of the coast keep a repertory of named rhythms passed down through families. Ngoma also reaches into the spirit world: in the ceremonies of the pepo, the capricious spirits of the coast, drumming summons the spirits so that they may be spoken to and soothed, and drummers are chosen for their knowledge of the right rhythm for each spirit. Coastal ensembles combine drums of several sizes and pitches, and the master drummer leads with improvised phrases while the group holds the pattern. The tradition is alive today in the taarab and dansi scenes as well as in the village ceremonies where the drums still call the community together.

name: Nisse's Porridge Bowl
description: The bowl of Christmas porridge set out on the farm each Christmas Eve to thank the nisse for his care of the household, cattle, and barn. In the best-known story the nisse hides in the rafters while the porridge is eaten, and his anger when he finds the butter scraped from the bottom teaches the lesson of gratitude; the tale of the nisse and the Christmas porridge tells the same custom from the nisse's side. The custom of julegrot is kept across Norway today, now also in city homes, and a bowl is often left on the doorstep or in the barn for the nisse of the house.

name: Nisselue
description: The pointed red wool cap worn by the nisse, the small household spirit of Norwegian farms and barns. The red cap became the nisse's signature in 19th-century folklore and illustration and is worn today as a Christmas hat. In Danish and Norwegian legend the underground folk are likewise described in red caps, as when an underjordisk man wearing a red nissehue runs after a farmer with a message. The nisselue is knitted in the round with a point, and museum collections, such as those of the Norsk Folkemuseum, hold folk caps of just this shape from the 19th century that give the spirit's headgear a real counterpart. The cap made the invisible household helper visible in art and fancy dress, and it remains the readiest sign of the Christmas nisse in the Nordic countries.

name: Nivkh Shaman's Drum
description: Oval frame drum of the Nivkh people of Sakhalin and the Amur region, with a wooden handle, used by the shaman to accompany spirit journeys and healing rituals. Its sound marks the shaman's passage between the worlds, as recorded by ethnographers including Emiko Ohnuki-Tierney in her study of Nivkh shamanism. The drum is made with a bent wooden rim and a hide head, tightened while wet and dried over the frame, with a carved handle or cross-bar on the underside. It is beaten with a soft mallet, and the shaman uses both the strokes and the pauses to summon and question the spirits. In the bear festival, the greatest Nivkh ceremony, the drum accompanied the songs honouring the bear and the masters of the forest and sea. The Nivkh shaman served the community as healer and guide, and his drum, like his helpers, was passed on within the family line. Museum examples come mainly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the Amur peoples were collected most intensively.

name: Nkisi Nkondi Power Figure
description: The nkisi nkondi is a power figure of the Kongo people of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a carved wooden human or animal figure studded with nails, blades, and other iron objects. A ritual specialist (nganga) activated the figure to hunt down wrongdoers, witness and seal oaths, settle disputes, and protect homes and villages, and each blade or nail driven into the body recorded one act sworn before it. The figure's aggressive posture, with a raised arm, staring eyes, and a mirror set in the belly, proclaimed its readiness to act, and the nganga called on its spirit to pursue thieves and sorcerers. The most celebrated form is the anthropomorphic 'mangaaka' of the coastal Kongo, commissioned by chiefs for justice-making. When colonial courts suppressed the use of the figures, many were collected by Europeans, and they are now celebrated in museums as masterpieces of Kongo art even as their ritual role faded. The word nkisi itself points to the wider Kongo class of spirit-charged objects.

name: Nkul Slit Gong
description: The nkul is a wooden slit gong of the Beti and related peoples of southern Cameroon, made from a hollowed log with a long longitudinal slit that is beaten with sticks to produce two distinct tones. In forest villages where sound carries poorly, the nkul served as a talking instrument: different rhythms announced deaths, births, hunting results, danger, and the summons to ritual, and a skilled beater could be understood over several kilometres of valley. It also marked the rhythm of communal life, accompanying dances, initiations, and the sessions of the secret societies, and the largest gongs were communal property hung in the meeting house. Slit gongs of the same type are found across Central and West Africa under many names, showing how widespread this early signalling technology became. The nkul remains in use in rural Cameroon, although radio and telephones have taken over most of its message-carrying role.

name: Nyckelharpa
description: The keyed fiddle (nyckelharpa), a bowed string instrument with keys that stop the strings, played in Swedish folk music since the 16th century and especially associated with Uppland. Its buzzing drone strings and chromatic key rows give it its characteristic sound. It was revived in the early 20th century and remains a national instrument, played at dance and fest. The instrument's keys press tangents against the strings to change their pitch, while one or more drone strings ring beneath the melody, giving the nyckelharpa its humming, hurdy-gurdy-like timbre. Surviving church paintings and written sources place it in Sweden by the sixteenth century, and by the eighteenth the great three-row instruments of Uppland were played at village dances and weddings. When the tradition waned, the revival of the 1920s, led by makers and players such as Eric Sahlström, rebuilt the instrument for a new audience; today the nyckelharpa is taught in Swedish folk-music schools and played around the world.

name: Nydam Boat
description: A clinker-built oak rowing boat, about 23 meters long, dug from the Nydam bog in southern Jutland in 1863 together with swords, spears, and shields offered after a battle. Built around 320 CE for a war fleet, it shows mature northern plank construction a thousand years before the Viking ships, with iron rivets and overlapping strakes. The boat was sacrificed in the bog together with weapons, a practice documented across the great bog finds of the region. It is the oldest clinker-built boat preserved in Scandinavia and is displayed at Gottorf Castle in Schleswig.

name: Nábrók
description: Nábrók, the 'corpse breeches' or necropants, is a garment of Icelandic folk magic made from the skin of a dead man's lower body. According to the tradition recorded by Jón Árnason and still told today, the wearer first made a pact with a living friend that if either died, the survivor might flay the dead man's skin from the waist down; the intact skin was then worn like trousers, becoming one with the wearer's own body. To activate the charm, a coin had to be stolen from a poor widow on a great festival day and placed in the scrotum of the pants, which would then constantly draw money from the living so that the purse never ran empty. The pants had to be passed on before the wearer's death, leg by leg to a new owner, or the corpse would be swarmed with lice. A famous reproduction hangs in the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík.

name: Obsidian Smoking Mirror
description: Aztec priests and rulers used disks of highly polished obsidian as divination mirrors, gazing into the glossy black face for visions of what was hidden or to come. The name is inseparable from Tezcatlipoca, the 'Smoking Mirror', whose emblem was just such an obsidian mirror (tezcatl); his power to see everything was said to come through it. Fray Bernardino de Sahagun's Florentine Codex records seers and sorcerers working with mirrors, and carved examples survive with drilled holes for suspension, worn as pectorals or set in wooden frames with resin. Such mirrors were not only for seeing: because polished obsidian gathers the sun's heat, it could also be used in fire-making ritual. The black glass itself was sacred, a product of volcanic earth that the Mexica prized for knives, the eyes of effigies and the dark windows of prophecy. The smoking mirror remains a symbol of Tezcatlipoca's all-seeing, unpredictable power.

name: Ohrid Pearl
description: Ohrid pearls are handmade jewellery pearls of North Macedonia, built up from a ground shell core coated with layer after layer of a milky emulsion made from the scales of the plasica, a small silvery fish endemic to Lake Ohrid. Because the recipe and the painstaking process are guarded as family secrets, only two families - the Talevs, who bought the formula in 1924, and the Filevs, who learned it in 1928 - have made authentic Ohrid pearls, passing the craft from father to son and hand-coating each grain up to ten times. Local tradition credits the secret to Jovan Subanović, a Russian emigrant said to have brought the technique to Ohrid after the 1917 revolution, and the name 'Ohrid Pearl' was fixed by 1935. Their soft lustre and durability made them famous beyond the Balkans; Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana are said to have worn them, and a handmade necklace remains a proud family heirloom.

name: Oni no Kanabo
description: The kanabo is the iron-studded club that Japanese legend and art place in the grip of the oni, the ogre of the folk imagination, and it has become the oni's stock attribute to the point that the two are nearly inseparable in picture scrolls and festival prints. Tales from the Heian-era exploits of the demon queller Minamoto no Yorimitsu, above all his campaign against the bandit-ogre Shuten-doji, show the oni swinging the heavy mace with crushing force against heroes and their retainers; the same weapon appears in the folk tale of Momotaro, whose companions win against the ogres' island through wit. The club is conventionally imagined as a wooden shaft bound with iron hoops and studded with iron knobs, heavier than a man could lift, and it is treated as a mythological attribute rather than a documented artifact, since no original example survives. It carries real cultural weight, standing for brute strength that must be overcome by cleverness, and it remains the default prop of oni in the Setsubun bean-throwing rite and in modern manga and games.

name: Opanak
description: The opanak is the traditional leather shoe of the Serbian countryside, a soft moccasin cut from a single piece of cured pig or calf hide, stitched at the heel and gathered over the foot with thongs that cross above the ankle. Its most striking feature is the turned-up toe, the špic, which lifted the foot clear of dew, grass and stones and, in the most famous regional pattern, curls back into a small horn over the instep. Opanci were worn with woollen footcloths called obojci and tied with long straps, and they served peasants, herdsmen and even soldiers for centuries before factory footwear displaced them. Because almost every village had its own cut - the wide Šumadija form, the sharp Bosnian toe, the flat Montenegrin sole - the opanak became a strong marker of Serbian folk dress and is still worn at festivals, by folk dancers and on ceremonial occasions.

name: Opon Ifa Divination Board
description: The opon ifa is the round wooden tray on which the Yoruba babalawo, the priest of divination, reads the will of the orisha Orunmila: dusted with wood powder, the tray receives the patterns traced as the diviner casts the palm nuts or swings the divination chain and interprets the emerging odu. The rim of the tray is carved with the face of Eshu, the messenger who carries the signs, and with figures of proverb scenes, and the flat face is kept smooth so the powder can be drawn and redrawn again and again through the reading. The tray is treated as sacred: it is never set directly on the ground, only the initiated handle it, and after each consultation the powder is gathered and the board cleaned with ceremony. The opon ifa is the visible center of Ifa divination, the system that has guided Yoruba families for centuries and has since spread with the diaspora to the Americas. In its carvings and its signs it holds the memory of a people.

name: Oseberg Ship
description: The richly carved oak vessel of a Viking-age ship burial uncovered at the Oseberg farm near Tønsberg, Norway, in 1904. About 21.8 meters long, the ship carried two women and rich grave goods, including the carved Oseberg wagon and sledges. Its animal-head prow and decorated frames show the craft of early 9th-century Norse shipbuilding, and it is exhibited in the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo. The ship was built of oak felled in the early 800s and was rowed and sailed on the coast before it was drawn ashore and buried under a great mound, where it lay until the excavation. The grave goods, from textiles and a tapestry to wooden buckets and the famous wagon, make the burial one of the richest ever found in Scandinavia, and the ship's shallow hull marks it as a ceremonial craft of the highest rank.

name: Oshe Shango Dance Wand
description: The oshe is the carved wooden dance wand of the Yoruba Shango cult, its upper end shaped into a double-bladed axe, the emblem of Shango, the god of thunder and lightning. Dancers of the cult swing paired oshe during worship, and the axe is said to carry the deity's power: the flash of the blade is his lightning, the heft of the wood his strength, and the double edge his two faces of destruction and renewal. Older examples are carved with a face of the deity or of a priestess, and the wand is kept on the shrine and treated with respect, often touched to the ground before the dance begins. The oshe is danced at festivals, at the great ceremonies of the Shango priests, and wherever the thunder god is honored, and the carving tradition is among the best known of Yoruba art. The wand thus speaks without words, holding in a single object the whole theology of the storm.

name: Pachamanca
description: The pachamanca is an Andean feast cooked in the earth: stones are heated in a dug pit, and layers of meat, potatoes, maize, beans and fragrant herbs are set over them, covered with leaves and earth, and steamed until done. The name comes from Quechua and means 'earth pot,' and the method is shared across the Peruvian and Bolivian highlands, where it is served at weddings, patronal fiestas, harvests and the raising of a new house. Before anyone eats, the first portion is set aside and offered to Pachamama, the earth mother, often with a splash of chicha or a libation poured on the ground, a gesture of return for what the land gave. Regional variants distinguish the cooking of the sierra from the coastal pachamanca a la olla, and the dish has become a badge of Andean identity even as families adapt it to modern stoves. The offering that opens the feast keeps alive the old understanding that eating from the earth demands giving back to it first.

name: Palau Storyboard
description: Carved wooden panel of Palau recording the myths, histories and village legends of the islands in low-relief figures. The form descends from the painted facade boards of the bai, the great men's meeting house, whose gables carried scenes of the ancestors and of village life, and from the 1930s carvers began to translate those painted narratives into portable low-relief wood. Storyboards show culture heroes, voyages, sea creatures and village quarrels, and they are carved as commemorative gifts, as teaching pieces for the young, and for the market, keeping the island's oral tradition alive in carved form.

name: Pandora's Jar
description: The great jar or pithos that Pandora opened, releasing sorrows and evils upon humankind and keeping hope alone trapped inside, in Hesiod's Works and Days; the familiar 'box' is a later Latin mistranslation of pithos. Given to Epimetheus as Zeus' gift, together with Pandora herself, the jar explains the origin of toil, sickness, and death in Greek myth. Whether hope remaining in the jar is a comfort or another evil has been argued over for two and a half thousand years. The jar is thus a founding image of the human condition in Greek thought.

name: Panduri (Georgian Three-String Lute)
description: The panduri is the three-string fretted lute of eastern Georgia, a shallow wooden instrument carved from a single block of mulberry, walnut or other fruitwood, with a short neck, three strings and a soft, bright voice. It belongs to Kartli and Kakheti, where it accompanies men's table songs and the solo and choral polyphony of the region, the player strumming or plucking the strings to support the voice. Custom held that the panduri should hang on the wall of the house when not in use, ready for songs, and it was treated as a companion of family and village life rather than a mere concert instrument. With its larger four-string cousin the chonguri, the panduri is the most common plucked instrument of Georgian folk music and a familiar emblem of Georgian tradition, taught in music schools and played at every supra.

name: Pashmina Shawl
