description: The pashmina shawl is the fine, handwoven woollen shawl of Kashmir, made from the downy underfleece of the Changthangi goat that grazes the high plateaus of Ladakh and western Tibet. The word pashmina derives from pashm, Persian for the softest animal fibre, and the cleaned wool, only about fifteen microns thick, is spun by hand and woven on a handloom in Srinagar and the valley workshops, a craft that has produced some of the world's most expensive cloth. The shawl was already a luxury good at the courts of the Mughals, who wore and commissioned them, and Kashmiri weaving of fine wool was further stimulated from the 15th century by the arrival of craftsmen and by royal patronage. European taste for the shawl boomed in the 19th century, when Napoleon is said to have presented pashminas to Josephine, and European weavers tried for decades to imitate the Kashmir workmanship. Today genuine pashmina is protected by a Geographical Indication, and shawls are often embroidered with the fine needlework of the valley, though the name is widely copied in blended fabrics.

name: Perseus' Sickle
description: The curved sickle-sword, the harpe, with which Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa, given to him by Hermes on his quest. Ancient sources describe it as a sword or sickle that could shear through stone and serpent, and the severed head's gaze still petrified his foes. The deed closes the Medusa episode and arms Athena with the gorgoneion on her aegis. In vase painting Perseus is shown gripping the curved blade while the Gorgon's head falls, a scene that became a standard image of heroic triumph in the Greek world.

name: Phulkari
description: Phulkari is the traditional embroidery of the Punjab, in which coarse, hand-spun cotton cloth called khaddar is covered with silk stitches worked from the back in a simple darn stitch to form flowers, diamonds and glowing fields of colour. The name means 'flower work', and the craft is credited to the women of the Sikh and Hindu farming communities of the region, where it has been practiced since about the 15th century. A single piece is worked by hand and can take months; a shawl embroidered over its whole surface is called a bagh, a garden, and it is given as a wedding gift, with the deepest reds reserved for the bride and the most complex pieces started at a child's birth. The motifs show the world of the village, wheat stems, grain and the glitter of sun and mirrors, and each motif has a local name passed down from mother to daughter. Phulkari remains an emblem of Punjabi identity, worn at weddings and festivals and revived in contemporary fashion.

name: Phurba
description: The phurba is the three-sided ritual dagger of Tibetan Buddhism, whose pommel is carved with the head of a wrathful deity such as Vajrakilaya and whose triangular blade is meant to pin down demonic forces at the boundary between the worlds. Used by lamas in exorcism and meditation rituals, the phurba transfixes evil like a tent-peg, and in the rituals of the Nyingma school it is treated as the vehicle of the deity Vajrakilaya himself. The dagger is made of iron, brass, or wood, and inscribed and consecrated examples survive in temple collections; some are old weapons pressed into ritual service, while others were made purely for the rite. The practitioner drives the phurba into earth, sand, or the image of a demon, and its three edges symbolize the transformation of the three poisons of the mind. Beyond ritual use, the phurba has become one of the most collected and reproduced objects of Himalayan art, and it is displayed in museums worldwide as an emblem of Tibetan Buddhist power.

name: Pied Piper's Pipe
description: The pipe of the Pied Piper of Hamelin is the magic instrument that, according to the legend, lured the rats of the town of Hamelin to drown in the river Weser in 1284, and then, when the citizens refused to pay the promised reward, drew away a hundred and thirty of their children into a mountainside, never to return. No actual pipe survives, and the whole episode belongs to the semi-legendary medieval tradition of the town and its later retellings, including the Grimms' version and Robert Browning's poem. The date 26 June 1284 is recorded in the town's medieval chronicles, and a window in the church of Hamelin once showed the scene. Scholars have offered many theories for the children's disappearance, from emigration to a children's crusade, but the piper himself remains a figure of folklore. The pipe, whose music charms both beasts and children, has become the archetype of the irresistibly alluring tune.

name: Pirot Kilim
description: The Pirot kilim is a handwoven wool rug of the town of Pirot in southern Serbia, built on a vertical loom with a cotton warp and a dense woollen weft that produces a flat, reversible fabric. Weavers worked in the so-called vratilnice technique, knotting and braiding the weft in long strips so that the patterns interlock, and the classical designs pair a central medallion with borders of zigzags, hooks and stylised flowers in red, black, white and green. In the nineteenth century Pirot rugs hung on walls, covered floors and chests and formed part of the bride's dowry, and the town's weavers supplied households across the Balkans and the Ottoman court. Woven by women who guarded the pattern-books on the same looms, the Pirot kilim is counted a Serbian national symbol, and a small circle of masters still weaves it today.

name: Pishtaco Knife
description: The knife of the Pishtaco is the blade of the fat-stealer of the Andes, a figure who is said to creep upon sleeping travelers or the unwary on lonely roads and cut the fat from their bodies to sell it in secret, for candles, soap or, in the modern telling, to be shipped abroad for machines. The weapon is rarely seen; it is more feared than described, and a whistle or a shadow at the roadside is enough to raise the terror of the nakaq, as the same figure is called in Quechua. The belief is rooted in the real dread of the stranger and of the outsider, and historians note that it attached itself successively to Spanish priests, colonial officials, and later to police, missionaries and foreign aid workers, whichever authority the community distrusted. The knife is the visible edge of that fear, and stories of the Pishtaco circulate widely across Peru and Bolivia even today. It is one of the clearest cases in South American folklore of a weapon whose power lies not in its edge but in the story that hides behind it.

name: Polish Pisanki (Decorated Eggs)
description: Polish Easter eggs decorated by several regional techniques: batik wax-resist (pisanki), scratch-carving, and the solid raspberry-dyed eggs called byki. Patterns of rays, stars and plant sprigs vary by region, with Kraków, Łowicz and the Opoczno district known for distinct styles; eggs were exchanged at Easter as gifts and kept in the home as charms. The name comes from 'pisać', to write or paint, since the wax is drawn onto the shell with a pin dipped in a funnel of molten wax. The techniques include the kraszanki boiled in onion skins for a uniform red-brown, the skrobanki scratched through the dyed shell to reveal white, and the pisanki written with wax in several colours. In folk belief the decorated egg brought health and protection, and at Easter it was shared at the table and given to godchildren. The craft is still practised across Poland, and regions hold competitions in the days before Easter.

name: Pomlázka
description: The pomlázka is a braided whip of fresh willow twigs that Czech boys carry on Easter Monday, when they go from house to house lightly switching girls and women to wish them health, freshness and beauty, receiving painted eggs and coloured ribbons in return. The name comes from pomladit, 'to make young again', and the custom preserves an old spring-renewal rite of driving out winter and coaxing new life, in which the willow, one of the first trees to bud, was held to carry special power. Skilled makers plait eight, twelve or even more rods into a smooth handle, bind the tip with ribbon and often add a pair of dangling tassels, weaving the whip anew each spring. In Moravia the same whip is called the šibačka and in Slovakia the korbáč, and after the morning round the girls may pour water or perfume over the boys in the related Easter-Monday wetting custom.

name: Portuguese Guitar
description: The Portuguese guitar is the pear-shaped twelve-string cittern with a flat back and a sharp, ringing tone that is the defining instrument of fado, the song of Lisbon. It is played with a long plectrum, its six double courses of metal strings laid over a tear-shaped body, and it developed in Lisbon in the 18th and 19th centuries from the English cittern brought by British merchants, taking on its Portuguese character in the hands of local makers such as the Machado family. In fado the guitar answers and weeps with the singer, and the idiom is often said to voice saudade itself, the untranslatable longing at the heart of the song. From Lisbon the instrument spread to Coimbra, where a larger-bodied variant with its own tuning accompanies a separate tradition of sung poetry. Though a documented instrument rather than a mythic relic, it carries Portugal's musical folklore, and its sound is instantly recognised as the voice of fado.

name: Prayer Wheel
description: The prayer-wheel is the cylindrical device of Tibetan Buddhism that is spun to release the mantras printed on the paper scrolls inside, each revolution sending the prayer for compassion into the world. Rows of large wheels line the walls of temples and stupas, and smaller hand-held wheels are turned by pilgrims at shrines and along circumambulation paths, the turning of the wheel standing for the turning of the dharma. The practice descends from the Indian and Tibetan tradition of reading or rolling sacred verses, and the mantra most often printed inside is Om Mani Padme Hum, the invocation of the bodhisattva of compassion Avalokiteshvara. Devout practitioners regard the wheel as a powerful means of accumulating merit for all beings, and it is customarily turned clockwise with the right hand while walking a clockwise circuit. The prayer-wheel has become a universal emblem of Tibetan Buddhism, and it appears in art and objects made for pilgrims across the Himalayan world.

name: Primstav
description: A staff calendar of wood carved with notches, crosses, and figures marking the church feasts and farm year of Norway. Each primstav was tailored to its district and showed sowing, slaughter, the start of fishing, and the move up to the seter, runic signs mingling with Christian symbols. In use from the Middle Ages into the 19th century, it remained a symbol of Norwegian folk timekeeping. The staff was read along its edges, with each day marked by a notch and the great feasts by carved symbols, such as an anchor for the day of the fisherman's patron or a sheaf for harvest time; a farmer could tell the season and its work at a glance. The primstav lived on after the calendar reforms that made it obsolete, kept in the house as a piece of the old order and a link to the church year it once governed.

name: Prydwen
description: Prydwen, in Welsh tradition, is the name of King Arthur's ship, the vessel in which he sails on expeditions into the Otherworld. In Culhwch ac Olwen Arthur rides in Prydwen, and in the poem Preiddeu Annwn, the Spoils of Annwn, he sails in the ship with a chosen company to raid the cauldron of the Otherworld fortress of Annwn. The name, which some scholars connect with a word meaning 'beautiful form', is also given to Arthur's shield in some texts, so that a single word came to serve for both protection on land and passage by sea. The voyage to Annwn belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian legend, before the continental romances of the court and the Grail. Prydwen's journey places Arthur among the voyagers of Celtic tradition who cross the sea to the lands of the dead, a motif shared with the Irish immrama, or voyage-tales.

name: Puja Thali
description: The puja thali is the round metal tray on which the objects of Hindu home worship are arranged, so that the whole ritual can be performed from a single plate. Typical contents are a small diya (oil lamp), a container of kumkum (vermilion powder), incense sticks in a holder, a bowl of rice, a flower or marigold petals, and a camphor burner, and the plate is carried in the right hand while the flames are waved before the image in the arti. The thali is usually made of brass, bell metal, silver or stainless steel, and it doubles as the everyday plate of an offering: sweets are placed on it and then distributed as prasad. Because the tray is passed around the household, it is often kept on a low wooden stand in the prayer corner, and the pattern on its rim, floral or with a swastika, is itself chosen for auspiciousness. In many families the thali is a wedding gift and heirloom, and a well-kept thali signals both devotion and domestic order.

name: Pungastafur
description: Pungastafur, the 'purse stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn so that money would not run short and the bearer's purse would stay heavy. It is one of the most sought-after of the money-and-luck galdrastafir, a domestic charm against poverty in a subsistence economy, drawn on paper and carried about the person or carved on a coin-purse. The name itself speaks to its purpose: 'pungi' is the Icelandic word for purse or scrotum, so the stave works on the same idea as the money-magic of the necropants, keeping the bearer's wealth sealed in. It belongs to the same family as Kaupaloki and the other luck staves, and its earliest known source is the 19th-century Huld manuscript. The purse stave remains popular in modern reproductions of Icelandic staves as a symbol of financial protection.

name: Pyrgi Gold Plaques
description: The Pyrgi plaques, three thin sheets of gold found in 1964 at Santa Severa, the site of the Etruscan port of Pyrgi north of Rome, bear the earliest known bilingual text in Etruscan and Phoenician and are dated to about 500 BC. They record that Thefarie Velianas, ruler of the great Etruscan city of Caere, dedicated a temple, its sacred precinct, and a shrine to the Etruscan goddess Uni, identified in the Phoenician version with Astarte, in the third year of his rule, an offering that testifies to the close religious and commercial links between Etruscan Caere and the Phoenician world of the western Mediterranean. The long Etruscan text and the shorter Phoenician version together gave scholars a rare bilingual key to the Etruscan language, and the plaques are among the oldest historical documents from Italy. They are now in the Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia in Rome. The find reshaped understanding of Etruscan religion and of Caere's place in the Mediterranean network of the sixth century BC.

name: Pysanka (Ukrainian Decorated Egg)
description: Ukrainian Easter egg decorated by the wax-resist method: a stylus called pysachok draws lines of hot beeswax on the shell, which is then dyed in successive colours, ending with the wax melted away to reveal the pattern. Pysanky bear solar, plant and animal motifs linked to spring rebirth, and eggs were kept in the house as protective charms. The practice is ancient, and ornamented eggs from the region date back to pre-Christian times; the egg is sometimes said to carry the hope of the resurrection and the turning of the year. Each region keeps its own colours and motifs, from the black-red-white geometry of the Kyiv area to the floral wreaths of Podillia. Making pysanky is a seasonal craft concentrated in the days before Easter, and women guard their own family patterns. Today the craft is taught in schools and workshops and has spread around the world with the Ukrainian diaspora.

name: Põhjanael
description: The Põhjanael, the 'North Nail', the Estonian folk name for the North Star: in the old Baltic-Finnic worldview the sky was an upturned cauldron or great wheel turning on a nail driven through its centre, and that nail is Polaris. Farmers read the seasons from the stars turning around it, and folk sayings spoke of the sky-wheel's spokes and of the nail that holds the heavens fixed. The folklorist Matthias Johann Eisen recorded the motif in his 'Eesti Mütoloogia' and folk-astronomy notes, preserving a sky-picture in which the fixed North Star is the axle of the whole turning world.

name: Qobyz (Kazakh Horsehair Fiddle)
description: Bowed two-string fiddle of shamans and bakhsy among the Kazakhs, carved from a single piece of wood with horsehair strings and a leather-covered resonator. Legend names Korkyt Ata as its inventor; its sound was held to drive away evil spirits, sickness and death. The qobyz remains the emblematic instrument of Kazakh epic and ritual tradition. The two thick horsehair strings are bowed like a cello, the instrument held between the knees, and its deep, wavering tone was considered the very voice of the steppe. In earlier centuries it accompanied the bakhsy, the Kazakh shaman-healer, who used its sound to enter trance and to draw the spirits of the dead; the same instrument later served the singers of heroic tales. Korkyt, who is sometimes said to have strung his kobyz with his own sinews in pursuit of immortality, gives the instrument its sacred standing, and it remains a symbol of Kazakh national music.

name: Quipu
description: The quipu, or khipu, is the knotted-cord record-keeping system of the Andes, in which a main cord holds pendant cords whose colours, knot positions and spacings encode information, read by trained officials known as khipu-kamayuq. The Inca empire used quipus to keep accounts of tribute, census, harvests, armies, calendars and storerooms, and Spanish chroniclers called them the 'books' of the empire, records the colonial government could not match. Scholars have shown that the knots encode numbers in a decimal positional system, and a growing minority argues some quipus also carried narrative and genealogical meaning, though that reading remains debated. The cords were made of cotton or camelid fibre, and hundreds of examples survive, many unearthed from coastal tombs and highland caches. The Spanish destroyed thousands of quipus, yet some Andean communities continued to use them into the twentieth century, and the khipu has become a powerful symbol of Inca civilisation and of a knowledge system nearly lost.

name: Qulliq
description: The qulliq is the crescent-shaped soapstone lamp of the Inuit, burned with seal oil and a wick of moss or Arctic cotton, the only source of light and heat inside the snow house through the long polar night. It was tended by the women of the household, who trimmed the wick to keep the flame steady, melted snow for drinking water, dried clothes and boots over its warmth, and cooked simple meals beside it; a well-managed flame was a mark of a skilled housewife. The lamp gave the igloo its glow and its life, and the word qulliq itself is the everyday name for light in many Inuit languages. When the hunter returned, the lamp was also the signal of home. Today the qulliq survives as a powerful symbol, lit with ceremony at Inuit gatherings and cultural events, while modern homes keep it as a reminder of a past when a single small flame held a family warm against the polar night.

name: Qvevri (Georgian Wine Vessel)
description: The qvevri is the great egg-shaped earthenware vessel of Georgia in which wine is fermented and aged, buried up to its neck in the floor of the marani, the wine cellar, so that only the clay rim and lid rise above the ground. Grape must, skins and stems all go into the qvevri and rest there for months, the cool earth holding a steady temperature, which gives amber wines their tannic, textured character and the method its special place in winemaking. Potters coil the vessels by hand from local clay, line them with beeswax and fire them without glaze; archaeological finds from the Shulaveri-Shomutepe culture date the method some 8,000 years, making qvevri wine among the oldest in the world. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed the ancient Georgian traditional qvevri wine-making method on the Representative List, and the buried qvevri remains the heart of Kakhetian cellar life.

name: Raven Banner
description: A battle standard woven in the shape of a raven, carried by Viking commanders to signal the presence of a great leader. The Orkneyinga saga tells of Earl Sigurd's banner Landeyðan, said to predict victory by flapping its wings, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records a raven banner among Danish Vikings in 878. The raven was Odin's bird, making the banner a war-charm as much as a flag. The banner was carried before the army and was believed to share in the fate of the battle: when it stood stiff and full it promised victory, when it hung limp the men knew defeat was near, and a commander who lost his banner was held to have lost his luck. Because it was woven, not painted, the raven of the standard moved with the wind like a living bird, and the sight of it struck fear into those who faced the Viking host. No original banner survives, but the sagas and the chronicles keep its name alive.

name: Rewe
description: The rewe is the carved altar pole of the Mapuche, a notched wooden post raised in the ceremonial ground and in front of the machi's home, its steps climbed by the machi during rituals to draw close to the upper world of the spirits. The notches are a ladder, and the rewe is understood as the axis linking the worlds, planted at the point where the sacred and the human meet; it is often topped with carved figures of the beings or animals that guide the machi. Each machi's rewe is raised with ceremony, receives offerings and chants, and marks the ritual space where the community gathers for the ngillatun, the great ceremony of thanks and petition. The rewe is so emblematic of the machi's office that it is read as the symbol of Mapuche spirituality, and contemporary Mapuche communities still erect and tend their rewes. It stands as a living sign that the sacred is not far away but planted in the very ground of the ceremonial field.

name: Rilli Quilt
description: The rilli quilt is the patchwork bedding of Sindh, sewn by women from scraps and recycled cotton cloth cut into triangles, diamonds, squares and zigzag bands and joined in bright, ordered compositions. The craft is passed from mother to daughter, and the same word covers quilts made by applique, patchwork or embroidery, often combining several techniques in one cover. A rilli is laid over winter bedding or spread on the floor for guests, and quilts are made ahead of a wedding as part of the bride's trousseau, so a well-made rilli carries the reputation of the maker's skill and the household's fortunes. The patterns are traditional but not fixed, and women reuse older quilts and garment cloth so that each piece carries a history of the family's cloth and needlework across the generations of rural Sindh.

name: Robe of Medea
description: The poisoned robe and golden diadem Medea sent as bridal gifts to Glauce, Jason's new bride at Corinth; when the princess put them on, the dress burst into flames and consumed her, and her father Creon died as well when he tried to save her. Euripides makes the gifts the engine of his tragedy, delivered by Medea's own children, and the horror lies in how the objects of a wedding, the robe and crown meant to adorn a bride, become instruments of death. The motif recurs in Greek myth, most closely in the robe of Deianeira in Sophocles' Trachiniae, which destroys Heracles, and the poisoned garment became a stock 'deadly gift' of folklore, whose touch burns the wearer. Later sources expand Medea's revenge to the killing of her own sons, while the robe itself stands for the vengeance a scorned woman can take through the very language of gifts and kinship. The tale is the classic warning that a bride's finery can carry a bride's doom.

name: Robe of Nessus
description: The robe or tunic smeared with the centaur Nessus' blood that Deianeira gave Heracles, believing it a love charm; the poisoned blood burned Heracles so terribly that he begged to be burned on a pyre. Sophocles' Women of Trachis makes the robe the instrument of the hero's death, and the story became a byword for a gift that destroys its giver. The centaur's dying trick, meant to avenge himself on Heracles, turns a wife's love into a fatal weapon. The robe is among the most famous poisoned objects in Greek tragedy.

name: Rogatywka
description: The rogatywka is a four-pointed peaked cap of Poland, distinguished by a square crown whose corners fold out over the rim, evolved from the konfederatka worn by the Confederates of Bar in 1768-1772. Under the Second Polish Republic it became the standard headgear of the Polish Army, worn in khaki and grey by infantry and in crimson by the mounted uhlans, and variants served Polish units through the Second World War and into the modern armed forces. The four corners are traditionally said to mark the four quarters of the world or the soldier's virtues, and the cap also became a piece of civil national dress, still worn with folk costume, on ceremonial occasions and by marching bands. Because of its insurrection and wartime associations the rogatywka carries a heavy symbolic charge as a badge of Polish independence, and modern reproductions are made by military tailors for parades, re-enactments and formal dress.

name: Romanian Blouse (Ie)
description: Traditional Romanian blouse, the ie, a linen or cotton chemise whose sleeves and shoulders carry dense geometric embroidery; the shoulder ornament, altița, marks the wearer's region and status. Worn in village dress through the 20th century, the ie entered art and fashion through painters such as Matisse; in 2022 UNESCO inscribed 'the traditional blouse with altița' on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage. The embroidery is worked in cross-stitch on the sleeves, collar and hem, with colours and motifs varying by region, and the altița, a wide band of stitching running from shoulder to sleeve, is the most valued part. Young women prepared several blouses in their trousseau, and the finest were sewn with the thinnest linen and the most intricate patterns. A 'Day of the Romanian Blouse' is celebrated every year on 24 June, and the ie has been adopted as a modern symbol of Romanian identity in fashion and design.

name: Rooster of Barcelos
description: The Rooster of Barcelos comes from the Portuguese legend of a Galician pilgrim who, condemned to hang for a theft he did not commit, stood before the judge's table and swore his innocence by a roasted rooster, declaring that the bird would crow if he were innocent. As the noose was being fitted, the roast cock rose on the table and crowed; the pilgrim was freed, and he returned to Barcelos to raise a monument in thanks. The story, told in many collected versions in northern Portugal, is usually set at Barcelos on the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela, and some versions place it at the neighbouring parish of Barcelinhos. From the legend the painted ceramic rooster, the Galo de Barcelos, became the national symbol of Portugal and the country's most characteristic souvenir. The tale belongs to the wide family of miracle-of-the-roast-cock legends found across Europe, here fused with the cult of Saint James and the pilgrims' road.

name: Rostam's Spear
description: The heavy war-spear (nezeh) of the hero Rostam in the Shahnameh, carried alongside his bull-headed mace and his lasso (kamand) through the Haft Khan, the seven trials, and the wars against Turan, and used to strike down champions in single combat. In Ferdowsi's epic it is one of the enormous plain weapons that suit Rostam's strength, and it is with such arms that he takes the field in the duels against the Turanian heroes and in the fateful, unrecognised fight with his own son Sohrab. The epic seldom dwells on the spear's forging, so its particulars follow the conventions of Persian heroic poetry rather than any single description. In the later Iranian imagination, Rostam's whole war gear, spear, mace, and lasso alike, became part of the fixed image of the hero, shown across the centuries in miniature painting.

name: Rubab
description: The rubab is the short-necked plucked lute of Afghanistan, carved from a single block of mulberry wood with a belly of animal skin and three main melody strings played with a wooden plectrum. Two or three drone strings and up to a dozen sympathetic strings lie under the playing strings, giving the instrument its deep, ringing sound, and Afghan musicians call it the lion of instruments. It is the lead instrument of the classical music of Kabul and is also played in Pashto folk song and in the Sufi music of the region, and its repertoire runs from court compositions to the songs of the valleys. The rubab is made by instrument makers of Kabul who select the mulberry wood for its sound, and the instrument is taught within families of musicians, passed down through generations.

name: Rudraksha Mala
description: The rudraksha mala is a string of 108 prayer beads made from the seeds of the rudraksha tree, Elaeocarpus ganitrus, which grows in the Himalayas, the Indo-Malayan region and as far as Southeast Asia. The name means 'Rudra's eye', and the Shiva Purana relates that the rudraksha sprang from the tears that fell from the god Rudra-Shiva's eyes during his long penance, so that the beads are sacred to Shiva and are worn by Shaiva ascetics and householder devotees alike. Each bead is marked with vertical grooves called mukhi, from one to twenty-one, of which the five-faced type is the most common and most auspicious, and the Rudrakshajabala Upanishad gives rules for their wearing and the benefits of each count. The string is used for japa, the repetition of a mantra, and is also worn on the neck, wrist or arm as a guarantee of protection and spiritual merit. Because rudraksha is both a botanical product and a ritual object, it is traded widely, and its beads can be found strung with gold, silver or cotton thread in the markets of Nepal and Varanasi.

name: Rune Calendar
description: A rune calendar (runkalender or runstav), a perpetual almanac carved on a long wooden or horn staff, used in Sweden from the Middle Ages into the nineteenth century. Each year's structure was fixed with runes: one rune row marked the weekdays, another the golden numbers that place the movable feasts. The staff was read like a printed calendar and was long carried by Swedish farmers and seafarers. The weekday row used one rune for each day of the week, while a second row of nineteen runes showed the golden numbers, so that Easter and the other moveable feasts could be found for any year. Because the calendar was carved once and worked forever, the runstav was cheap and durable, and it travelled from the farmhouse to the boat, where it helped sailors keep the church feasts at sea. Such calendars were still in use in the nineteenth century, and they are prized today as some of the last living carriers of the old rune row.

name: Rushnyk (Ukrainian Ritual Cloth)
description: Embroidered ritual cloth of Ukraine woven from linen or hemp and decorated with geometric and floral embroidery at both ends. The rushnyk hangs on icons, frames doors and windows, joins the couple's hands at weddings and lines the coffin at funerals; its patterns carry protective meaning, and a woman's rushnyk collection testified to her skill. Made on the home loom and embroidered with cotton or silk thread in red, black and white, the cloths are kept for decades and passed down through families as heirlooms. The name shares its root with 'ruka', the hand, for the towel used to wipe the hands, yet the ceremonial rushnyk is never used for ordinary washing. In the wedding the bride presents rushnyky to the groom's family, and the cloth laid under the couple's feet is kept as a talisman for the marriage. Ethnographic museums treat the rushnyk as a central emblem of Ukrainian material culture.

name: Ruyi Jingu Bang
description: Ruyi Jingu Bang is the magic staff of Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of the great Chinese novel Journey to the West, and it is counted among the most famous weapons in all of Asian literature. The staff began as the great pillar of the Eastern Sea Dragon Palace, a golden-banded rod weighing thirteen thousand five hundred catties, which no one could lift until the Monkey King took it up and found it shrank and grew at his will, from a needle kept in his ear to a pillar that could reach the clouds. With it Sun Wukong defied the heavenly host, fought the armies of the Jade Emperor, and later escorted the monk Tripitaka to the West, the staff serving as both weapon and staff of office. The weapon's name is often translated as 'the complaisant golden cudgel' or 'wish-fulfilling staff,' and its image is inseparable from the character who wields it. Ruyi Jingu Bang appears throughout the sequel novel and in opera, film, and games, and remains the emblem of the irrepressible Monkey King.

name: Rósahjálmur
description: Rósahjálmur, the rose-helmet of the Huld manuscript, a protection stave said to make the bearer safe from any harm so long as it was worn. Its name suggests a floral or Christian-influenced design unlike the angular battle staves. It is one of the more intricate of the defensive galdrastafir recorded in the grimoires. The stave's effect was tied to the act of wearing: carried on the body, it was trusted to turn aside weapons, sickness, and hostile magic alike, and its round, blossom-like lines were sometimes read as an emblem of the Virgin's protection. Such helmet-staves belong to a wider family of defensive signs whose power lay in making the bearer untouchable rather than in striking back.

name: Sabar Drum
description: The sabar is the single-headed drum at the heart of Wolof and Serer music in Senegal, its goatskin head lashed to a carved wooden body with a signature system of lacing and seven pegs. Woodworkers of the lawbe caste carve the shell from baobab or dimb trunks, while griot percussionists of the gewel caste build, tune, and play the drum with one bare hand and a curved stick. Sabar rhythms are named, and older players say 'the sabar can speak': bakks, rhythmic phrases matched to spoken Wolof, were traditionally used to announce news, praise people, and summon the community. The drums anchor baptisms, weddings, and circumcisions, and every wrestler in the popular Lamb contests fields his own drumming group, whose rivalry is nearly as intense as the bout itself. Largely male through most of its history, sabar playing has opened to women and been carried worldwide by masters such as Doudou N'Diaye Rose, while its rhythms live on in the pop genre mbalax. Making a drum is itself touched by belief, for spirits (jinne) are said to dwell in certain trees, and watching a new head being fitted is held to bring good luck.

name: Saci's Red Cap
description: The red cap of the Saci is the knitted head covering of the most famous figure of Brazilian folklore, the one-legged spirit Saci-Pererê, who smokes a pipe, whistles through the dark, and raises whirlwinds along the roads. The cap is the seat of his power, and the tales hold that whoever can catch him and take the cap wins the Saci's obedience or his magic, a prize that always slips away, because the trickster escapes as soon as the cap is grabbed. In some versions the color changes, with the red-capped Saci of the paths joined by variants wearing green or other colored caps, each with its own mischief. Monteiro Lobato's stories of the early twentieth century fixed the image of the pipe-smoking, red-capped trickster in the national imagination, though the figure long predates him in Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous legend. The cap alone identifies the Saci in folk art, carnival costumes and children's books, making it one of the most recognizable objects of Brazilian folk culture.

name: Sacred Tooth Relic
description: The Sacred Tooth Relic is the most venerated object in Sri Lankan Buddhism, a tooth believed to be the left upper eye-tooth of the historical Buddha, brought to the island in the 4th century CE by Prince Danta and Princess Hemamala, who is said to have hidden it in her hair. The story of its journey from Dantapura in India is told in the Pali chronicle Dathavamsa, the Chronicle of the Tooth Relic, and the later chapters of the Mahavamsa trace its movement from the first capital, Anuradhapura, through the later capitals Polonnaruwa and Dambadeniya until it reached Kandy. In Kandy the relic is enshrined in the Temple of the Sacred Tooth (Sri Dalada Maligawa), and each summer it is honoured in the great Esala Perahera, a torchlit procession of elephants, dancers and drummers that is among the most spectacular festivals in Asia. The relic functioned politically as well as religiously, since the monarch who guarded it was held to legitimate his rule over the island, and a king who lost the tooth lost his claim to the country. Because the relic is regarded as the presence of the Buddha himself, it is displayed only rarely, and its inner shrine is kept under the most stringent guard.

name: Sakta Brooch
description: The sakta, the ancient Baltic breast brooch of bronze, silver or silver-gilt, fastened the folk costume — above all the bride's — at throat or chest, in one or several at once. Archaeological finds date the fibula type back roughly two millennia, and the later 'bubble' saktas, with hemispherical bosses set with glass studs, were trusted as a woman's savings, pinned to her dress as a portable store of value. A Latvian folk song says the goddess Laima makes fibulae for a girl, 'immersing them in silver', and the brooch was given at the coming-of-age ceremonies of girls and kept as an heirloom of the family.

name: Samoan Siapo (Tapa)
description: Barkcloth of Samoa, beaten by women from the inner bark of the paper mulberry into large sheets and decorated with geometric patterns in earth tones, either painted by hand or printed by rubbing colour over carved upeti stencil boards. Siapo is made for wrapping, dress and ceremony — it clothes chiefs, lines meeting houses and forms part of exchange gifts at weddings and funerals — and its designs are owned by families and districts, each pattern marking the cloth as coming from a particular place and lineage. Beating the bark, pasting the sheets together with starch and burnishing the finished cloth are skills passed from mother to daughter, and siapo remains central to Samoan ceremonial life today.

name: Samoan Tātau Tools
description: Set of combs and mallets used in the Samoan tatau, the hand-tapped tattoo applied by a tufuga ta tatau, the tattoo master. A comb of bone, turtle shell or later steel, set with teeth of graduated length, is dipped in soot pigment and struck with a wooden mallet to drive the ink into the skin, line by painful line. The tools and the art are traced by legend to the goddesses Taema and Tilafaiga, who brought the craft from Fiti to Samoa, and the full male pe'a and the female malu are still given with ceremony as marks of dignity and genealogy. A set of tools is the master's most guarded possession, used only within the ritual rules of the practice.

name: Samoan ʻIe Toga (Fine Mat)
description: Treasured fine mat of Samoa, woven from the thinnest strips of pandanus leaf by senior women and softened, oiled and polished until it gleams. The ʻie toga is the highest form of Samoan wealth, exchanged at weddings, funerals, title-bestowals and political occasions in the ceremonial economy of fa'alavelave, where it is always presented together with fine goods. The oldest mats are given names and genealogies, handed down through generations and counted among the most sacred possessions of the aiga, and a family's honour and standing are measured in the size and age of its store of fine mats.

name: Samovar (Russian Tea Urn)
description: Metal urn with a central fire-tube used to boil water for tea, a fixture of the Russian home from the early 18th century. The great workshops at Tula and in Moscow produced brass, nickel and silver samovars; around the samovar the family gathered for the evening tea, and it became a byword for hospitality in Russian daily life and literature. A charcoal fire burns in the inner tube, keeping the surrounding water at a rolling boil while the small teapot steeps on top, and the strong tea is poured from the spigot and diluted to taste in each cup. The form spread across Russia, Ukraine and the Caucasus and eastwards through Central Asia, and travellers carried samovars on long journeys. Tula became the centre of manufacture, and the city's museum of samovars preserves hundreds of examples, from the copper kettles of the 18th century to the mass-produced factory models of the 20th.

name: Sampo
description: The Sampo is the wonder-working mill of Finnish epic, forged by the great smith Ilmarinen as the bride-price demanded for the hand of the maiden of Pohjola. In the Kalevala the Sampo grinds out limitless grain, salt, and gold for its possessor, making it the engine of the northern world's wealth. The heroes of Väinölä and Louhi, the mistress of Pohjola, fight over it in the great raid that follows; during the sea-battle the Sampo is shattered and lost overboard, and the fragments that wash ashore are said to have given the sea and the land of Finland their richness. Its true shape and nature are never fully described — it is a mill, a chest, a pillar, or simply 'the Sampo' — and scholars still debate what it originally was. It stands as the central object of the Kalevala, and its name lives on in Finnish art, music, and the Finnish word for a lucky wonder.

name: Sankha Conch
description: The sankha is the conch shell blown as a trumpet in Hindu ritual, and the shell is one of the four emblems held by Vishnu, whose own conch, named Panchajanya, was taken by the god from a demon who lived in the sea. In temple worship the sankha is blown at the start of the ceremony, its long low note summoning the devotees and warding off evil, and a smaller shell is used in the daily arti to pour water over the deity. The conch is also one of the chief auspicious objects of the household, printed on calendars and carved above doors, and a shell that spirals to the right, the dakshinavarti type, is prized as a rarity with special protective power. In the stories of Vishnu the conch sounds together with the discus as the signature of the god, and the vishnu-story repeats the pairing of these attributes. Because the natural shell is the matured body of a sea animal, its use in India is now balanced by ritual injunctions about the taking of life, and artificial shells are common in the shops.

name: Sanni Yaksha Mask
description: The sanni yaksha mask is a carved and painted wooden face of a Sinhalese disease demon, worn in the exorcism rites that Sri Lankan tradition calls shanthi karma or tovil. There are eighteen principal sanni demons, each named for a particular affliction, such as fever, madness, dropsy or jaundice, and each has its own mask with a distinctive colour, expression and headdress. The finest carving comes from Ambalangoda on the south coast, where the mask carvers cut the traditional kaduru wood and finish it with vegetable and mineral pigments. In the ritual the masked dancer enacts the demon's story to coax it into speech, then frightens or bribes it into leaving the sick body, so the mask is both an artwork and a working instrument of healing. The ceremony is said to recall a plague once healed by a healer at Vaishali, and the sanni masks are still danced today in Sri Lanka.

name: Santo Caliz
description: The Holy Chalice of Valencia, an agate cup of the 2nd or 1st century BC set in medieval gold mounts with pearls and gems, is venerated in the Cathedral of Valencia as the cup of the Last Supper. The lower bowl is a genuine ancient stone vessel; the goldwork, stem, and handles are medieval, and the cup has been documented at Valencia since 1437, after being kept at Huesca and, by tradition, brought from Jerusalem to Rome and then to Spain. The identification rests on tradition rather than on any contemporary evidence, and scholars dispute the whole chain of custody, so it is more honest to call it a relic claimed as the Grail than the Grail itself. An archaeological study by Antonio Beltrán in 1960 dated the agate bowl to the late Roman Republic, confirming the antiquity of the stone but not the Christian legend. The chalice remains a focus of pilgrimage and the chief Spanish claimant among the many vessels said to be the Holy Grail.

name: Sao Bronze Bracelet
description: The bronze and copper ornaments of the Sao people come from the mound sites of the Lake Chad basin, where a succession of urbanised societies flourished from around the sixth century BC to the fifteenth century AD. Excavations at towns like Mdaga and the islands of the Chari and Logone rivers have yielded bracelets, anklets, pendants, and small anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figurines cast by the lost-wax method. The careful casting of rings and armlets shows a metalworking tradition of real technical skill, and the spread of finds hints at long-distance trade in metal along the Sahel. The modern populations of the region remember the Sao in legend as giants and founders of vanished cities, so the bracelets bind living folklore to the archaeological record. Major collections are preserved at the National Museum in N'Djamena, and the objects remain key evidence of early Central African metallurgy.

name: Saukele (Kazakh Bridal Headdress)
description: Tall conical wedding headdress of Kazakh brides, covered with silver plaques, coral, beads and gemstones, with a fur-trimmed brow and long veils. The most expensive item of a bride's dowry after the yurt, the saukele symbolised the beginning of married life; it was handed down from mother to daughter and worn until the birth of the first child. The cone is built over a stiffened cloth or felt base, wrapped in velvet or brocade, and studded with silver medallions and carnelian; a fringe of coral and pearls falls over the forehead, and long beaded tassels hang past the shoulders. The weight of a richly made saukele could reach several kilograms, and a bride might wear it only for the wedding and the following days. The name is sometimes said to come from 'sau', well-being, and 'kele', crown, for the headdress that brings fortune. Museums in Kazakhstan and Siberia hold 19th-century examples, some kept as family heirlooms for generations.

name: Scarab Amulet
description: The scarab amulet is the Egyptian image of the dung beetle, carved in glazed faience, stone, or hard materials and worn or placed on the body from the Old Kingdom onward, as the emblem of the god Khepri, who rolls the sun across the sky as the beetle rolls its ball of dung. The beetle's habit of appearing from the ground was read as self-creation, so the scarab became the sign of creation and of rebirth, and from the Middle Kingdom the heart scarab, inscribed with chapter 30 of the Book of the Dead, was laid over the mummy's heart to keep it from testifying against the deceased at the judgement of the dead. Hundreds of scarabs were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun, in rings, necklaces, and pectorals, and the commemorative scarabs of Amenhotep III were issued like royal bulletins. As an amulet of protection and renewal the scarab is among the most widespread objects of Egyptian material culture, and its form endured into Greek and Roman amulets.

name: Scepter of Ra
description: The was-sceptre, the long staff with a forked base and a stylised animal head, is the Egyptian emblem of power and dominion, and as the sceptre of the sun god Ra it stands for the authority of the creator who orders the world. Gods are shown holding the was-staff as the sign of their rule, and kings carry it in ritual scenes to declare that they exercise the dominion the gods have given; its name is written with its own hieroglyph, and the sceptre was a fixture of temple reliefs, royal ceremony, and funerary art from the Old Kingdom onward. Its forked foot and forked head are sometimes read as the form of the Set-animal or of an antelope, and the staff is often paired with the ankh and the djed pillar in the offering scenes that cover temple walls. As the staff of Ra it passes to the pharaoh as the earthly representative of the sun god. It survives as the standard visual shorthand for divine authority in Egyptian art.

name: Sefer Yetzirah
description: The earliest surviving Hebrew text of Jewish mysticism, the 'Book of Formation', which describes how the world was created through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet and the ten sefirot, and sets out paths by which the mystic may emulate that act. Its opening lines attribute it to the patriarch Abraham, though scholars date its present form to roughly the second to the sixth century CE, and it circulated in short and long recensions. The text maps the letters and the sefirot onto the cosmos, the year, and the human body, presenting creation as an act of speech and counting. It shaped the whole later development of Kabbalah, whose language of sefirot and letter-mysticism grows directly from it, and it remained a living book of contemplation, even of reported magical practice, for centuries.

name: Selkie's Seal-Skin
description: The seal-skin of the selkie is the central object of the seal-people tales of Scotland, Ireland and the northern isles, a pelt that lets its wearer take human form on land. A selkie who wishes to return to the sea must put the skin back on, so a human who steals and hides the skin can hold a selkie bride or husband captive, and the marriage lasts only until the skin is found and returned. The motif drives the classic selkie-bride stories, from the Faroese tale of Kópakonan to the Hebridean, Orcadian and Icelandic variants collected by folklorists, in which the wife grieves by the shore until a child or a neighbour reveals the hiding-place. The stolen skin gives the tale its haunting shape: love bought by captivity, and the sea always calling. The skin is sometimes said to be hidden in a chest or under a roof beam, and its discovery is always the turning point. In modern retellings the seal-skin has become a symbol of identity, longing and the cost of belonging to two worlds.

name: Serge (Yakut Carved Hitching Post)
description: Carved wooden hitching post of the Yakut (Sakha) people, set up at home and at the ysyakh summer festival, often topped with carved horse-heads. The sacred Aar Baah Serge of the festival stands on the eastern side as a symbolic world-tree, a ladder linking earth to the upper world where the aiyy deities dwell; horses are tied facing east during the celebration. The post is hewn from a single larch or birch, its foot buried deep and its upper part carved into a horse's head or into stacked, cup-shaped tiers. Around a family dwelling several serges stood, each with its use: the home post for daily tethering, the wedding post for the horse of the groom, and the sacrifice post for the white stallion offered to the sky spirits. Folklorists read the serge as the axis of the homestead, an image of the world-tree connecting the three levels of the Sakha cosmos. Carving a good serge was a mark of mastery, and old posts are preserved as ancestors' property.

name: Seto Folk Costume
description: The Seto women's folk costume of south-eastern Estonia's Setomaa: a striking white, black and red ensemble of striped or checked skirt, linen blouse, woven belt and heavy silver jewellery, above all the large seto silver brooch with its coin pendants. The costume is integral to leelo, the polyphonic singing tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, for the Seto choir sang in traditional dress, and it is worn for church feasts, weddings and Seto Kingdom Day, where it announces the wearer's village and lineage. The dress is made and passed down by Seto women, whose handicraft knowledge — of weaving, embroidery and silverwork — is as much a part of Setomaa's heritage as its songs.

name: Shahmaran Amulet
description: The Shahmaran amulet carries the image of the serpent queen of Caucasian and Anatolian legend, a being with the head of a beautiful woman and the body of a serpent, who is said to have taught healing and the secrets of nature to those who dwelt in her underground kingdom. Silver and brass amulets, pendants, bracelets and wall plaques bearing her figure are worn or hung to turn away the evil eye and to bring luck and health, and her serpent-woman form appears on carpets, on jewellery and throughout the traditional story cycle of Azerbaijan, Turkey and Iran. The British Museum holds amulets of the serpent queen, and the legend of Shahmaran survives strongly in folk belief, especially among women who seek her protection in childbirth and sickness. As a wearable image of a living folk deity, the Shahmaran amulet links ancient serpent worship to modern jewellery.

name: Shanyrak (Yurt Crown)
description: The crown of the Kazakh yurt: a circular wooden rim with radiating cross-beams (uyk) that supports the roof and lets smoke and daylight pass through the top opening. Beyond architecture, the shanyrak is the foremost Kazakh symbol of home, family continuity and the nation; it stands at the centre of Kazakhstan's state emblem, and custom passes the family shanyrak to the household heir. In yurt construction the shanyrak is the keystone: curved wooden ribs are lashed to its rim, felt and ropes are laid over the frame, and the whole dwelling can be dismantled and loaded on horses in under an hour. The crossing beams radiate from a central crown, and the shanyrak appears in the wedding, where newlyweds are blessed beneath it. The word itself carries the idea of the home as a circle of kin, and a Kazakh saying holds that the strength of a family is measured by the soundness of its shanyrak.

name: Shebeke (Sheki Stained-Glass Lattice)
description: Shebeke is the stained-glass lattice window of the Azerbaijani town of Sheki, built by fitting hundreds of small panes of coloured glass into a web of walnut strips that hold together by interlocking notches, without glue, nails or any backing frame. Each joint is cut and fitted by hand, and a single panel can take months of patient work, which is why the masters call the craft the art of patience. The finest surviving example is the Sheki Khan's Palace of 1762, whose roughly 190 windows hold up to five thousand glass fragments, throwing soft blue, red and green light across the painted walls of the palace. Since the palace was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019, the surviving shebeke workshops have revived the craft, training new masters in the old joinery.

name: Sherpa Pangden
description: The sherpa pangden is the striped front apron woven and worn by Sherpa married women over their chuba, the strip of red, white and black stripes marking the wearer's married status and adulthood. The aprons are woven on backstrap looms from sheep's and yak's wool, and the narrow stripes and their colours follow family and regional convention, so that the pangden is a badge of household and of womanhood as much as a piece of dress. The custom is hundreds of years old and is also found among related Himalayan peoples and in Tibetan regions, where similar striped aprons are made. A girl receives her pangden as she comes of age and is expected to wear it in daily life and at festivals, and the making of the aprons remains a home craft of Sherpa women weavers in the valleys below the Everest massif.

name: Shichishito
description: An iron sword with seven branch-like projections along its blade, dedicated at the Isonokami Shrine in Nara and recorded in the Nihon Shoki as a gift from the kingdom of Baekje to the Yamato court. Its long gold-inlaid inscription, which dates the sword to the mid-fourth century, describes offerings made to a sun deity and names the Baekje court that sent it, making it one of the oldest inscribed iron objects of Japan and a rare physical relic of early Korean-Japanese exchange. With its strange branched form it is not a practical weapon, and it is best understood as a ritual or ceremonial sword, kept for centuries as a shrine treasure. Today it is registered as a National Treasure of Japan and displayed only rarely, still guarded at the shrine that received it some sixteen hundred years ago.

name: Shield of Achilles
description: The great shield Hephaestus forged for Achilles in the Iliad, the poem's supreme example of the god-smith's craft and the model of the cosmic artifact in Greek epic. Five metal layers of bronze, tin, gold and silver carry scenes of the whole world: earth, sea and sky with sun, moon and stars, two cities, one at peace with weddings, lawsuits and dance, one besieged in war, fields ploughed by oxen, a ripe harvest, a vineyard, a cattle raid with lions, and a choir of dancers, all encircled by the stream of Ocean. Homer describes its making at length when Thetis visits Hephaestus, and the finished shield mirrors the mortal world Achilles is about to leave; the passage became the defining example of ekphrasis, a poem describing a work of art. The motif was imitated in the Shield of Heracles and in Virgil's Roman answer, and it remains the archetype of the hero's world-in-miniature, an object whose decoration, not its metal, gives it power.

name: Shield of Aeneas
description: The shield Vulcan, the Roman Hephaestus, forged for Aeneas at the request of his mother Venus, engraved with the future of Rome and described at length at the close of the eighth book of the Aeneid. Its bronze bears the city's destiny: the she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, the rape of the Sabine women, Rome's kings, the defence against the Gauls, the punishment of the conspirator Catiline, and the sea battle of Actium with Augustus triumphing over Antony and Cleopatra, all framed within scenes of the empire that was to come. The ekphrasis deliberately answers the Shield of Achilles in Homer: where Achilles' shield shows the whole cosmos and mortal life, Aeneas' shows a single people's ordained future. The shield is the emblem of Roman destiny made visible in metal, and the image of Aeneas lifting onto his shoulder a shield whose glory he does not understand closes the poem's first half. It remains the classic portrait of a nation reading itself in its own artifacts.

name: Shimenawa
description: The shimenawa is the sacred rope twisted from rice straw that marks off the dwelling-place of the kami in Shinto practice, hung across the entrance of shrines, over torii gates, and around sacred trees, rocks, and rice paddies. Its origin is tied to the founding myth of the sun goddess Amaterasu, who sealed herself in the Heavenly Rock Cave and left the world in darkness until the other gods lured her out and strung a rope across the mouth of the cave to keep her from retreating again. The shimenawa draws a boundary between the purified ground of the kami and the defiling world outside, and its presence warns humans not to cross unbidden. It is braided from freshly harvested straw, in some regions hemp or straw hung with the paper streamers called shide, and the rope is renewed each year as part of New Year preparations at shrines across Japan. Larger examples, some spanning several metres, hang over the great torii of shrines such as Izumo Taisha and Fushimi Inari, making the rope one of the most visible symbols of Shinto itself.

name: Ship of the Flying Dutchman
description: The ghost ship of the Flying Dutchman is a spectral East Indiaman of Dutch maritime legend, doomed to sail the waters off the Cape of Good Hope for ever after its captain, variously named Van der Decken, Falkenberg or the Vanderdecken, swore a blasphemous oath in the teeth of a storm. Mariners reported seeing the phantom vessel from the seventeenth century onward, often glowing with a supernatural light, and a sighting was taken as a warning of disaster or death at sea. The legend was spread by travellers' and sailors' tales in the 1830s, and Richard Wagner's opera Der fliegende Holländer of 1843 fixed the story of the captain condemned to sail until redeemed by a woman's love. No physical vessel survives or ever existed, and the tale is classed as maritime folklore rather than history. The ship has been retold in poems, novels and films, making the Flying Dutchman the archetype of the haunted ship.

name: Shiva Lingam
description: The lingam is the upright, pillar-like aniconic emblem of the Hindu god Shiva, found in temples, shrines and homes across India and the South Asian diaspora, and worshipped as the formless presence of the god. Its classic shape is a smooth column set in a circular base called the pitha, which represents the yoni of the goddess Shakti, so that the two pieces signify the union of the male and female principles. The foundational legend, the lingodbhava, tells that Shiva revealed himself as an infinite pillar of fire, so vast that neither Brahma nor Vishnu could find its top or bottom. In daily worship the lingam is bathed with water, milk and other offerings while the priest recites mantras, and to step over the lingam is considered a serious offence; certain lingams, the jyotirlingas, are among the most sacred pilgrimage sites of Shaivism. The form is also found as the mukhalinga, carved with Shiva's faces, and as the natural river-worn stones called banalingas, collected by devotees from the Narmada river.

name: Sibylline Books
description: The nine books of prophetic verses the Cumaean Sibyl offered to the Roman king Tarquin, of which she burned six when he refused her price and sold the last three for the full amount of the original nine; Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus record the story. The surviving books, written originally on palm leaves, were kept in the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitol and were consulted only by the state, through the priestly board of the quindecimviri, at moments of grave public danger, plague, or portent, when their verses prescribed the sacrifices and rites that might turn aside the disaster. The books were thus an oracle without a voice, opened only by decree of the Senate. They were destroyed in the burning of the Capitol in 83 BC and only partially reconstructed, and their loss is itself a legend. The tale of the Sibyl's burning books became the emblem of a state that haggles with prophecy and pays the price.

name: Sieidi Stone
description: A natural stone, boulder, or outcrop venerated by the Sámi as the dwelling of a spirit and a place of offering, the sieidi or seita. Hunters, fishers, and herders left antlers, bones, silver, or food at sieidis to secure luck and damaged the stone when crossed. Many stand at lakes, rivers, and passes across Norwegian Sápmi, and the custom survived in the far north into modern times. Each sieidi was home to a spirit of its own, and the people who used it knew which offering suited the place, whether a reindeer's antlers for the herd or a silver coin for the fishing luck. If the stone failed the one who prayed to it, it could be beaten or turned as a punishment, showing that the power was a bargain, not a blind faith. The sieidis are still respected today as the oldest sacred places of the Sámi landscape.

name: Sif's Golden Hair
description: Sif's golden hair is the treasure that the dwarven sons of Ivaldi made for Sif, the wife of Thor, after Loki maliciously shaved her head. To atone for his mischief Loki had the sons of Ivaldi forge hair of pure gold so fine that it grew from Sif's head like real hair, and the making of it opened the great contest of treasures in which the dwarves vied against each other — the same contest that produced Gungnir, Skíðblaðnir, Mjölnir, and Draupnir. In the Prose Edda the golden hair is listed among the gifts the sons of Ivaldi delivered, and the story explains why gold is called 'Sif's hair' in skaldic kennings. The tale shows the dwarves as the great craftsmen of the gods and Loki as the instigator of their finest work. Sif's hair remains a standard example of the dwarven gift-hoard and of gold-kennings in Old Norse poetry.

name: Signbook
description: A signbook (signeringsbok), a hand-copied Swedish book of signs used by folk healers and 'kloka gummor', the wise women and men of the parish. The volumes collected prayers, magical signs, and formulae for 'signing' wounds, bleeding, disease, and fire. Several Swedish signbooks from the 17th to 19th centuries survive in archives, mixing Christian prayers with folk-magical practice. The practice of 'signing' — speaking or drawing a fixed formula over the ailing part — was the ordinary work of the kloka, who might be consulted when the parish priest could not help. Some books were copied from one another for centuries, and a famous line of them descends from the so-called Lappman Jon Johansson, whose signerier, printed in 1917, collected the oldest Swedish formulas. The books were practical manuals: they list what to speak for a bleeding wound, a burn, snakebite, and a house on fire, always in a mixture of biblical words and older charms.

name: Silver Branch of Emain
description: The silver branch of Emain is the singing apple-branch carried by a woman of the Otherworld who visits the hero Bran mac Febail in the medieval Irish tale Immram Brain, the Voyage of Bran. The branch bears silver apples and sweet blossoms, and its music lulls those who hear it to sleep while the branch itself sings of the delights of the Land of Women across the sea. When Bran refuses to part with the branch and follows its bearer, he begins the famous voyage that carries him and his company from island to wonder-filled island. Messengers of the Irish Otherworld are traditionally shown bearing such singing branches of apple, a token of the supernatural world's beauty and its power to summon mortals away. The branch's music, which opens the mind to the otherworld, marks it as one of the most evocative of Irish wonder-objects. It later found its way into the poetry of W.B. Yeats, who drew on the image of the silver and golden bough.

name: Silver Buckles
description: Silver buckles and clasps worn with Swedish regional folk dress, on belts, shoes, and collars. Such silver, often inherited and re-used across generations, was engraved with initials and dates and served as both ornament and stored wealth. Wealthy folk wore heavy rectangular 'spännen'; poorer folk wore simpler clasps. The buckles are a documented part of the folk-costume tradition. The silver was a family's movable fortune: a bride might receive buckles, brooches, and chains that were passed down and re-fashioned by local silversmiths, with the owner's initials and the year engraved on the face. Great regional pieces, like the broad buckles of Dalarna or Skåne, marked a wearer's home district at markets and church, and the weight of silver on a person's belt was read as a sign of standing. When the folk costume fell out of daily use, the buckles were kept as heirlooms, and they are still worn today at festivals and on modern folk-dräkt celebrations.

name: Sindhi Topi
description: The sindhi topi is the embroidered cylindrical cap of Sindh, worn by men at daily work and at festivals, with a rounded crown and a characteristic arch-shaped cut-out above the forehead edged with stitched mirror work. The caps are made across the province, with centres such as Tharparkar known for fine needlework, and the shape and embroidery vary from town to town so that the topi can show where a wearer comes from. Sindhi tradition pairs the cap with the ajrak shawl, and the two together are treated as a badge of the province's culture; Sindhi Cultural Day is marked by wearing both. A widely repeated saying holds that the topi carries the honour and pride of the man who wears it, so that knocking it from his head is a grave insult, and the cap is a fixture of Sindhi weddings, political gatherings and everyday dress.

name: Singing Bowl
description: The singing bowl is a metal bowl of the Himalayan Buddhist world that produces a long, sustained tone when its rim is rubbed with a wooden striker or struck, and it is used in offerings, meditation and the opening and closing of ceremonies. The bowls are cast in bronze and brass bell-metal alloys, often in the workshops of the Kathmandu valley, and many carry embossed decoration or an incised invocation such as the six-syllable mantra Om Mani Padme Hum. Their use in ritual is old, though the precise history is uncertain, and the bowls became widely known outside the Himalayas only from the late twentieth century, when the trade through Patan and Thamel grew and the sound was adopted in meditation circles. Monks and lay people alike treat the ringing as an offering to the deities and a way of clearing and focusing the mind.

name: Skíðblaðnir
description: Skíðblaðnir is the best of all ships, built for the god Freyr by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi and listed among their marvels in the Prose Edda. It is large enough to carry all the gods and their weapons, yet it can be folded up like a cloth and carried in a pouch when not in use. The ship always finds a fair wind wherever it sails, so the gods never lack for a swift voyage, and it is sometimes said to be made of wood thin enough to fold without breaking. In Snorri's account the ship is counted as one of the greatest treasures of the gods, and it also sails the company of the gods at Ragnarök in some retellings. Though no physical counterpart survives, the name has lived on in Scandinavian shipping and fiction as a byword for a perfect, always-favorable vessel.

name: Slutsk Belt
description: Woven silk belt produced from the mid-18th century at the Slutsk manufactory of the Radziwiłł family in present-day Belarus, worn with the kontusz coat by Polish-Lithuanian nobility. Double-sided silk with gold and silver thread, floral and checkered borders and maker's marks woven into the ends; genuine Slutsk belts were prized across the Commonwealth and are now a national symbol of Belarus. The manufactory, founded around 1758, employed weavers from Persia and the Ottoman lands, and its belts imitated the prized sashes of the East so well that Polish nobles asked for 'Slutsk belts' in place of Persian ones. A belt was up to four metres long and folded several times around the waist, with one side in bright colours for daily wear and the other in sombre tones for mourning. Production ended in the 1840s, but the pattern entered heraldry and modern Belarusian imagery, and the belt is reproduced in museum workshops today.

name: Smjörstafur
description: Smjörstafur, the 'butter stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn or carved to bring success in making butter. In an agrarian world where dairy was wealth, a charm for a full churn was practical magic, and the stave sits among the agricultural signs recorded beside the luck, protection, and money staves of the grimoires. It was probably drawn on the churn itself or on a paper carried with the dairy work, though the sources give little detail of its use. Like all the galdrastafir, its earliest known source is a 19th-century manuscript that collected older folk-magic material, and it is now reproduced in books and on merchandise as part of the Icelandic stave revival. The butter stave is a good example of how the stave tradition reached into the humblest household work.

name: Soapstone Bird of Great Zimbabwe
description: The soapstone birds of Great Zimbabwe are carved birds about 40 centimetres tall, with human lips, folded wings, and feet that grip the columns on which they once stood within the ruined stone city. Eight are known, six large and two small, and they are believed to have been royal emblems of the Shona state that built the city between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, possibly representations of the bateleur eagle, the fish eagle, or a spirit bird of kingship. The birds probably crowned the walls and monoliths of the royal enclosure, marking the authority of the ruler, and the city itself gave its name to modern Zimbabwe. In the 1890s the carvings were hacked from their columns and carried to South Africa, where one passed into the hands of Cecil Rhodes; five birds were returned in 1981 and the last in 2026, ending more than a century of exile. The bird was adopted as Zimbabwe's national symbol in 1924 and appears on the flag, the coat of arms, and the country's coins.

name: Solomon Islands Shell Money
description: Traditional currency of the Solomon Islands, made from small discs ground from shell — the red money of Malaita being prized above all — drilled and strung on fibre into long strings and rolled coils. Shell money is still exchanged in bride-price, compensation, feasts and chiefly obligations, its value fixed by the species of shell, the fineness of the grinding and the length of the string. On the Reef Islands and Santa Cruz the most spectacular form is red feather-money: rolls of scarlet feathers from the cardinal honeyeater glued to a fibre base, so prized that only the greatest payments were made with it. The making and the value of these moneys remain part of living island economies.

name: Solomon's Flying Carpet
description: The carpet of Solomon, woven of silk and green stuff, said in Islamic tradition to be large enough to bear the king, his throne, and his whole court, carried through the air by the wind at his command and shaded from the sun by a flock of birds overhead. The Quran records the wind as made subject to Solomon, so that it carried his vessel at his bidding, and later commentators and storytellers, among them al-Tabari, al-Kisa'i, and the Thousand and One Nights, expanded this into the famous flying carpet. The details, its size, its crew of men and jinn, and the birds that formed its canopy, grow with each telling, and the carpet itself never appears as a physical relic. In the West it became, together with the genie's lamp, one of the two signature marvels of oriental legend, though its developed form belongs to Islamic exegesis rather than to any single book.

name: Somali Dabqaad Incense Burner
description: The dabqaad is the incense burner of Somali homes, a small clay or soapstone bowl raised on short legs and covered by a perforated lid from which the smoke of frankincense and myrrh rises. Somalia sits at the eastern end of the ancient incense lands, and the gums burned in the dabqaad were the same resins traded to Egypt, Rome, and the Gulf for thousands of years. In daily use the burner perfumes the house, and a lit dabqaad is placed near the door to welcome guests, to scent the rooms after cooking, and to sweeten the air at weddings and religious gatherings. The perforated lid lets the smoke rise in a fine plume, and the burner is carried from room to room by the women of the household. The dabqaad keeps the Horn of Africa's incense culture alive in domestic form, linking modern Somali life to one of the oldest trades in the world.

name: Stabbur
description: The Norwegian timber storehouse raised off the ground on wooden posts or flat stones to keep food, grain, wool, and heirlooms safe from damp and vermin. A flight of outside steps led to the door of the upper loft, and the space beneath was often roofed as a porch where tools and barrels were kept. Protective marks were sometimes carved or painted on the doorways, for folk belief guarded the larder as carefully as any lock, and the nisse of the farm was said to keep watch over the grain in the loft. The stabbur remained the standard farm building of Norway through the 19th century and is still raised on some farms today.

name: Stavkirke
description: A medieval Norwegian timber church built on a post-and-plank frame, with steep shingled roofs, carved portals, and dragon-head finials. Around thirty stave churches survive of the more than a thousand once built, among them Borgund, Urnes, and Heddal. In folklore the churches mark where the old faith met the new, and legends tell of trolls turned to stone at the sound of their bells. The post-and-beam construction, with the roof supported by tall staves inside the walls, lets the churches stand for centuries, and the carving that ornaments them, from the Urnes portal to the dragon gables, carries on the art of the pagan age under Christian roofs. The stave churches were built with tarred wood that blackened with age, and they remain the most distinctive monuments of Norwegian medieval building and the setting of countless tales of trolls, giants, and the church bells that held them at bay.

name: Sudanese Girba Water-Skin
description: The girba is the traditional water-skin of Sudan, made from the whole hide of a goat turned inside out so that the sealed legs hang as a bag while the neck serves as the opening for filling and pouring. The soft leather container is carried over the shoulder or slung on a donkey, and its porous surface slowly lets a thin film of water evaporate, which cools the contents even under the fierce heat of the northern Sudan. Tanning with acacia bark and vegetable juices, and rubbing with oils, keeps the skin supple and waterproof, and a well-kept girba can survive for years, being cleaned, dried and re-oiled between uses. In villages and camps the girba was the everyday vessel for carrying water from the Nile or the well, taking the place that clay jars hold elsewhere, and it shares its design with the Spanish bota bag and other leather flasks of the Mediterranean world. The girba is also a familiar prop in Sudanese folk memory, where hospitality is measured by the cold water poured from it for the weary guest.

name: Sudanese Kaskara Sword
description: The kaskara is the straight, double-edged broadsword of Sudan and the neighbouring regions of Chad and Eritrea, with a long blade, a cruciform quillon guard and a flattened disc pommel. Although most surviving examples date from the 19th century, the type is thought to have appeared around the 14th century and to preserve the straight-bladed style of the medieval Arab sword. The kaskara was an essential possession of most men across the central and eastern Sudan, from Chad through Darfur to the Red Sea coast, and it was worn horizontally across the back or between the upper arm and the chest. Some fine examples combine locally made Sudanese hilts with imported blades, as with a sword in the Met Museum whose Iranian watered-steel blade bears the name of Nasir al-Din Shah Qajar and which was taken as booty at the battle of Omdurman in 1898. Beyond its warrior use, the kaskara served in dances, oaths and ceremonies, and as a badge of manhood and honour among the peoples of the Nile and the Sahara.

name: Sudarshana Chakra
description: The Sudarshana chakra is the spinning, razor-edged discus of the Hindu god Vishnu, held in his upper right hand together with the conch, mace and lotus in the classic four-armed image. Its name means 'beautiful in form' or 'auspicious disc', and in myth it is the personal weapon that Vishnu casts at enemies, flying to its target and returning to his finger.
