In the churning of the ocean the chakra is sometimes said to have been the weapon that cut off the head of the demon Svarbhanu, the being who became the ascending and descending nodes Rahu and Ketu when the gods and demons churned for the nectar of immortality. The chakra also appears in the hands of Narasimha, Vishnu's man-lion avatar, who destroyed the demon king Hiranyakashipu and is worshipped together with the discus in temple images. Because the weapon is inseparable from Vishnu, it is a standard element of the temple icon, engraved on stones and invoked in protective prayer, and its recurring presence ties every one of the avatar stories to a single divine wielder.

name: Supay Figurine
description: Supay is the lord of the uku pacha, the world beneath the earth in Quechua cosmology, a realm of the dead and of the roots of the mountains; his images and masks, carved in stone or modeled in clay, stand for his power over that hidden country. In the colonial era his name was pressed into service as the Quechua word for the Christian devil, and the figure was forever blurred in two, ancient lord of the underworld on one side, Christian demon on the other. The ambiguity survives in the festivals of the Andes: at carnival and in the mining towns of Bolivia and Peru dancers wear elaborate Supay masks, and in the tin and silver mines he is courted with coca, cigarettes and chicha as the 'tío,' the uncle of the depths, who both gives the ore and may take the miner. Offerings and images of Supay were and are set out to keep his favor, especially by those who work beneath the earth. The figurine thus carries a double history, of the pre-Christian dead and of the devil the priests once taught.

name: Svalinn
description: Svalinn, 'the chill' or 'the cooling one', is the shield that stands before the sun in Norse mythology, named in the poem Grímnismál. According to the stanza, the shield protects the earth from the burning rays of the sun goddess Sól as she is dragged across the sky by the horses Árvakr and Alsviðr, and 'mountains and sea would be set in flames' if it ever fell from its place. The shield is also named in Sigrdrífumál and in Snorri's list of shield-names in Skáldskaparmál, and scholars have suggested it preserves a Bronze Age image of the sun as a round, shield-like disc. Unlike a warrior's shield, Svalinn is a world-sustaining object, and its role in keeping creation from burning up makes it one of the most purely cosmic objects in the Eddic corpus. It is sometimes cited in modern writing as an early image of solar protection.

name: Swedish Folk Costume
description: The Swedish folk costume (folkdräkt), the regional dress of parish and province, worn for work and festivals and gradually codified from the 18th century. Each district had its own colours, cut, embroidery, and accessories such as the flounced apron and the bodice. The national costume, the Sverigedräkt, was created in 1903 by Märta Jörgensen and has since been widely adopted. In the countryside the dress told every beholder where a person came from: the cut of the skirt, the shape of the bodice, and the colour of the stockings changed from parish to parish, and the right to wear certain garments was guarded with pride. Wool and linen were woven and dyed at home, while the silver buckles and brooches that fastened the clothes were the work of the village smith. When the folk costume died out in the later nineteenth century it was preserved by the museums, and in the twentieth it was revived for national holidays — most famously the blue-and-yellow Sverigedräkt, which remains Sweden's most worn ceremonial dress.

name: Sweetgrass Basket
description: The sweetgrass basket is the coiled basket of the Gullah people of the South Carolina Lowcountry, woven from sweetgrass with palmetto fronds and longleaf pine needles, a craft carried from West Africa to the American rice coast. The tight coil stitch descends directly from West African prototypes, and for centuries the baskets were practical tools, above all the broad fanners used to winnow rice on the coastal plantations. Weavers of Mount Pleasant and the Sea Islands passed the skill from generation to generation, and by the late 20th century the baskets were recognised internationally as fine art, collected by museums and buyers. Modern weavers still harvest sweetgrass by hand with respect for the plant, and the baskets remain a living emblem of African continuity in the Americas. The sale of the baskets along Highway 17 has made them a familiar sight and a powerful symbol of Gullah heritage.

name: Sword of Attila
description: The sword said to have belonged to Attila the Hun is known first from the Roman historian Jordanes, who writes in his Getica that a shepherd found a blade in the ground after cattle had trodden the place bare, and that Attila called it the Sword of Mars, a pledge of world dominion. By the eleventh century a richly decorated sabre was honoured in the Hungarian royal court as the Sword of Attila; the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld records that Queen Anastasia gave it to Otto, Duke of Bavaria, in 1063. The weapon that survives, kept in the imperial treasury of the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna and traditionally called the Sabre of Charlemagne, is in fact a Hungarian sabre of the early tenth century, long after Attila's death, with a gilded, gem-set hilt and curved blade of steppe form. The sword is sometimes said to have been recovered from Charlemagne's grave by Otto III in the year 1000, and to have been carried in the coronations of Holy Roman Emperors. No physical link to Attila can be proven, but the legend made the blade one of Europe's most famous royal relics.

name: Sword of Damocles
description: The sword of Damocles, suspended by a single horse-hair over the head of the courtier Damocles at the court of Dionysius II of Syracuse, is the object by which Cicero, in the Tusculan Disputations, taught that royal power is bought with anxiety. When Damocles envied the tyrant's happiness, Dionysius seated him at a banquet served in gold and silver and had him look up to find a gleaming sword hanging by a hair above his neck; the pleasure of the feast turned to dread, and Damocles understood that the ruler lives each moment under the threat of death. The image, which some ancient writers trace to still earlier tellings, became the universal emblem of the peril hidden in high place, of fortune's insecurity and the price of power. It survives in daily language wherever a 'sword of Damocles' is said to hang over an enterprise, a reputation, or a life. No such object ever existed; its whole force is in the image.

name: Sword of Theseus
description: The sword of the Athenian hero Theseus, left with a pair of sandals beneath a great rock at Troezen by his father Aegeus. When Theseus grew strong enough to lift the rock, the tokens proved his royal birth, and he carried the sword to Athens, where his father recognized him by it on the eve of his first trials in the city. Plutarch and Pausanias record the tokens of Troezen. He chose the harder road to Athens by land and cleared it of bandits with the very sword, so that he entered the city already a hero.

name: Szczerbiec
description: Szczerbiec, the jagged coronation sword of the kings of Poland, is the only surviving piece of the medieval Polish crown jewels and is kept in the treasure vault of Wawel Castle in Kraków. Its name comes from the Polish szczerba, 'gap' or 'notch', and legend attributes the damage to Bolesław the Brave, said to have struck the blade against the Golden Gate of Kiev in 1018, though the gate was not built until 1037 and the surviving sword dates to the thirteenth century. The hilt is decorated with Christian symbols, floral ornament and magical formulae, and a narrow slit in the blade holds a small shield bearing the Polish coat of arms. The earliest known use of the name is in the Chronicle of Greater Poland, which records an angel giving the sword to Bolesław so that he would triumph in battle. First used at a coronation in 1320, the sword was looted by Prussian troops in 1795, passed through nineteenth-century collections, and was returned to Poland only in the twentieth century after being evacuated during the Second World War. The legend of the notched blade remains a powerful emblem of Polish kingship and national memory.

name: Székely Kapu
description: The Székely kapu is the carved wooden gateway of the Hungarian Székely villages of Transylvania, an oak structure built in two parts: a large wagon gate for carts and hay and a smaller door beside it for people on foot. The finest examples, carved from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, are covered with tulips, the tree of life, suns, rosettes and heraldic devices, and often bear inscriptions such as 'Isten hozott' ('God brought you') or the name and year of the householders. Folk belief held that the large gate belonged to the living and the small gate to the dead, who were carried through it one last time on their way to the grave. Because each gate recorded the family, the land and the faith of its owners, the surviving Székely gates - the earliest dated remnant is from Mikháza in 1673 - are read as genealogies in wood.

name: Sámi Drum
description: The frame drum of the Sámi shaman, or noaidi, a shallow bowl of carved pine covered with reindeer skin painted in red alder juice with figures of gods, animals, and the sun. Struck with a reindeer-horn hammer while the noaidi sang, the drum revealed answers in the path of a jumping ring. Hundreds were burned by missionaries in the 18th century, and survivors are treasured museum objects. The drum was both an instrument and a sacred map, its painted surface showing the upper, middle, and lower worlds and the figures of the gods who governed the herd, the weather, and the sick. The noaidi used it to find lost reindeer, to answer the questions of the community, and to travel in spirit, and each drum's pictures were painted anew by its owner so that no two are alike. Only a small number survive, and they are among the most important evidence of the old Sámi religion.

name: Sølje
description: A Norwegian silver brooch worn at the throat, made of a central disc or crescent with dangling pendants, fine wirework, and sometimes small spoons or drops of silver. Soljer were the most important piece of a woman's festive dress, passed down through families, and often given as betrothal or christening gifts; a bride might wear several at once on her finest bunad. Regional workshops developed their own local shapes, and the brooch is still made today. It remains a standard part of the bunad worn at weddings, confirmations, and on Constitution Day, and old family soljer are counted among Norway's most treasured heirlooms.

name: Tabla
description: The tabla is the pair of hand drums that accompanies most North Indian (Hindustani) classical music, consisting of a small wooden drum on the right called the dayan, tuned to the tonic, and a larger metal or clay drum on the left called the bayan, which produces the deep bass. The heads of both drums are built in layers of skin with a black patch of iron and flour paste in the centre, the syahi, which lets the player produce the intricate spoken syllables of tabla language, such as dha, dhin and te te. The drums are struck with the fingers and palm, and a master tabla player can mimic speech, imitate the dance steps and end a composition with a ringing roll. The invention of the instrument is sometimes attributed to the 13th-century poet-musician Amir Khusrau, who is said to have split the older barrel drum, the pakhawaj, in two, and the story is still told in music schools, though scholars now treat it as legend. From court performance to kirtan, ghazal and film, the tabla has become the percussion voice of North Indian music worldwide.

name: Tabua (Whale Tooth)
description: Polished sperm whale tooth of Fiji, its base pierced and threaded with a cord of braided sennit, presented with a formal speech as the highest mark of respect and goodwill. The tabua is offered to seal covenants between chiefs, to atone for wrongdoing, to open negotiations or requests that are then rarely refused, and it is kept by the recipient as the living record of the promise. Originally only teeth of beached or stranded whales were available, and later whale-tooth or ivory substitutes were traded in; today the tabua is not sold but exchanged at weddings, birthdays, funerals and chiefly occasions, and its image appears on the Fijian 20-cent coin and in the name of Fiji Airways' Tabua Club.

name: Tagine Cooking Vessel
description: The tagine is the conical clay cooking vessel of Morocco and the wider Maghreb, which gives its name to the slow-braised stews that are cooked and served in it. Its tall, dome-shaped lid traps rising steam, which condenses and drips back onto the food, so the dish cooks in a small amount of liquid over embers or a low flame without much oil or added water. Traditional tagines are hand-thrown from terracotta and may be left unglazed or covered with a decorative glaze, and the glazed base of the pot is carried to the table with the conical lid still in place. The Arabic name tajin is used for both the pot and the food, and although the dish's precise history is debated, the Amazigh population of North Africa is generally credited with developing the slow-simmering vessel, while early cookery books from the medieval Islamic world already attest to similar stews. Because a well-made tagine can be cooked over a simple brazier of charcoal, it remains an everyday utensil in mountain villages and urban kitchens alike, served family-style with bread used for dipping.

name: Tahitian Vaʻa (Outrigger Canoe)
description: Ocean-going sailing canoe of the Tahitians, built as a dugout hull with a single outrigger float lashed on booms and a lateen sail of pandanus matting. The vaʻa was the vessel of the great Polynesian navigators, who read the stars, the swells and the flight of birds to cross the Pacific and settle island after island, and the hull was shaped by carvers working from inherited knowledge of timber and lines. Today the same outrigger canoe races on as a sport in the vaʻa of French Polynesia, where crews paddle long ocean-going canoes in competitions such as the Hawaiki Nui Vaʻa, keeping the voyaging canoe at the centre of Polynesian identity.

name: Talismanic Shirt
description: The tilsimli gömlek, the talismanic shirt of the Ottoman court, is a garment painted with Qur'anic verses, magic squares, the names of the four archangels, the Seal of Solomon, and the numbers of abjad calculation, worn next to the skin under armour by sultans and princes against wounds, illness, and ill luck. The making was governed by astrology: the court astronomer fixed the wearer's auspicious hour, and the shirt was begun and finished only when the sun stood in the required sign, so that each one is a document of its owner's horoscope as well as a talisman. The earliest dated example in the Topkapı collection is the shirt of Cem Sultan, begun on 30 March 1477 and finished on 29 March 1480, made for his bid for the throne and, as the story goes, never worn, its collar never opened. About eighty such shirts survive in the palace collection, most from the 16th century. They are among the most mysterious objects of Ottoman material culture, blending piety, magic, and the science of the stars.

name: Talos
description: Talos, the bronze automaton forged by Hephaestus and given to Minos to patrol the shores of Crete, a giant man of bronze with a single vein of ichor sealed by a nail at the ankle. In the Argonautica he hurls rocks at passing ships, turning the sea against the Argonauts, until Medea charms him and the plug is drawn, draining his life-fluid. The tale is one of the earliest machines in Greek myth, a guardian who cannot be wounded except at one secret point. Talos has been read both as an ancient robot and as a relic of Minoan bull imagery.

name: Tandoor
description: The tandoor is the large clay oven of the Indian subcontinent and of Central and Western Asia, a vase-shaped or bell-shaped pit of baked clay, either sunk into the earth or set above it in a brick surround. It is fired with wood or charcoal and reaches temperatures around 480 degrees Celsius, so the walls bake naan and roti flatbreads directly and roast marinated meat and vegetables hung from hooks, the dishes known collectively as tandoori. In the Punjab the oven was a communal institution, with one village tandoor serving many families of bakers, and the tradition remained largely regional until after the 1947 partition, when Punjabi migrants carried tandoori cooking to the restaurants of Delhi and beyond. Archaeological clay ovens of similar form are known from the Indus Valley civilization around the third millennium BCE, and the word tandoor travelled with the cooking technique across Iran and Central Asia into the Horn of Africa. Because the oven seals in moisture and reaches a dry, fierce heat, it gives the flatbreads and skewers cooked in it a distinctive flavour that cannot be reproduced in a normal domestic stove.

name: Tar (Azerbaijani Long-Necked Lute)
description: The Azerbaijani tar is a long-necked plucked lute with a deep figure-of-eight body, a lambskin soundboard and three courses of steel strings, played with a small plectrum held between the fingers. Master-builders hollow the body from mulberry wood, and the instrument's design was refined in the nineteenth century, when the tar became the leading solo and ensemble instrument of Azerbaijani music. It leads the mugham trio of tar, kamancha and frame drum that performs the classical modal suites of Azerbaijani tradition, and it accompanies ashiq narrative song as well. In 2012 UNESCO inscribed the craftsmanship and performance art of the tar on the Representative List, and Azerbaijani composers have written concert works for the instrument, making it a rare folk lute with a classical repertoire.

name: Tara Brooch
description: The Tara Brooch, a masterpiece of early medieval Irish metalwork, is a silver-gilt annular brooch decorated with gold filigree panels, amber studs and coloured glass, made in Ireland around the eighth century AD. It was found in 1850 on the beach near Bettystown, County Meath, and was given the name 'Tara' by its first owner to exploit the royal associations of the Hill of Tara for sale. The brooch is one of the finest surviving examples of Insular art, its interlacing animal and geometric patterns echoing the illuminated manuscripts of the same period, and it survives with its original chain and pin intact, a rarity for its age. Such brooches were status symbols worn at the shoulder to fasten a cloak, the standard dress-fastener of the early medieval Irish elite. It is now displayed in the National Museum of Ireland in Dublin, where it remains one of the most admired objects of Celtic jewellery in the world.

name: Tarnhelm
description: Tarnhelm, the magic cap of invisibility in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied, is taken by the hero Siegfried from the dwarf Alberich after he overpowers the dwarf and seizes the Nibelung hoard. Whoever wore the cap, the Tarnkappe, became invisible and could perform feats of strength as though unseen, and Siegfried uses it in the poem to fight in disguise. Richard Wagner transformed the object for his Ring cycle: in Das Rheingold the Tarnhelm is forged by Mime, gives its wearer the power to change shape or travel at speed, and is won by the god Wotan as part of the cursed treasure. The medieval poem's humble cloak thus became, in Wagner's hands, a helmet that enables the deceit and greed at the heart of the Ring. The name, from the German tarnen, 'to conceal', is the classic German equivalent of the cloak of invisibility found across European fairy tales.

name: Teke Kidumu Mask
description: The kidumu is a round, flat face mask of the Teke people of the Republic of the Congo, cut from wood and painted with bold geometric patterns in red, white, and black. Worn by the men of the kidumu society at initiations, funerals, and the dances that mark the transfer of authority from one generation to the next, the mask is held before the face horizontally or vertically depending on the region. The painted motifs are not mere decoration: they allude to the sacred knowledge of the group, and elders say the patterns echo the Teke account of creation, in which the world grew from the back of a great turtle. Different mask types correspond to different grades within the society, and the masks are stored in sacred places out of sight of women and the uninitiated. Teke mask-making survives in the republic today, and kidumu masks have become familiar worldwide through museum collections.

name: Temalacatl
description: The temalacatl was a great round stone disk set flat in an Aztec plaza as the stage for gladiatorial sacrifice, a rite tied to the festival of Xipe Totec in which a captive was bound, usually by a rope through the central hole, and made to fight successive armed warriors while holding only a feathered club. Bernal Diaz del Castillo, who watched the combat in Tenochtitlan, recorded the ordeal in vivid detail, describing how the exhausted captive was finally cut down and his body carried away. The best-known survivor, the Stone of Tizoc, is a basalt disk carved with the conquests of the emperor Tizoc and was dug up in 1791 during work on Mexico City's cathedral plaza. Because its shallow central depression could have held offerings, archaeologists have long debated whether such stones were true temalacatl or cuauhxicalli heart-vessels; Richard Townsend even suggests the depression may have been cut in the 16th century. Either way, the disk shows how Mexica sacrifice and imperial tribute were fused into public spectacle.

name: Teponaztli
description: The teponaztli is a horizontal slit drum made from a hollowed log whose H-shaped cut in the top produces two different pitches, struck with rubber-tipped sticks (olmaitl) rather than played by hand. Alongside the upright huehuetl it formed the core percussion of Aztec ritual music, and early accounts say its deep, carrying tone could be heard across Tenochtitlan during festivals, dances and war ceremonies. Fray Bernardino de Sahagun's Florentine Codex describes the instrument in detail, and colonial codices show pairs of players beating it before temple courtyards. Surviving examples, often carved from hardwoods, show that makers tuned the two tongues carefully and decorated the drum with religious carving. Similar twin-tongued slit drums were used across Mesoamerica, and the instrument survives in modified form in modern Mexican folk ensembles, its once-sacred festival role now largely secular.

name: Tewhatewha
description: The tewhatewha is the long-handled fighting staff of the Maori, a wooden weapon with a flat, axe-like blade at one end and a shaped base, often hung with a bunch of feathers or dog hair at the bottom of the handle. It was swung in sweeping strokes and could be thrust or thrown, and the feathers at the base were used in training and in challenge, flicking and flashing to distract the opponent or to call out a warrior before a duel. The weapon was also carried in war dances and chiefly display as a mark of martial skill, and its handling was taught within the whare-taua, the house of war. The tewhatewha is carved from hardwood or whalebone, and named examples are recorded in the accounts of early European observers of Maori warfare.

name: Thangka
description: The thangka is the painted or embroidered scroll image of Tibetan Buddhism, hung in monasteries, homes and shrines across the Himalayan world and framed in a silk brocade border. The painter first lays out a precise iconometric grid on cotton or silk, then works with mineral pigments and gold in the traditional palettes of the Newar and monastic painters, finishing with an outline in black and the consecration of the image. The subjects are buddhas, bodhisattvas, fierce protectors, mandalas and scenes of the lives of the saints, and each figure must follow strict proportions and attributes so the painting can serve as an aid to meditation and as a support for the deity's presence. A thangka is treated with respect, hung in a clean high place, and often blessed, and the form has been painted continuously for centuries from the monasteries of Nepal and Tibet.

name: The Ark of the Covenant
description: The gilded chest built at Sinai to hold the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, carried before the Israelites in the wilderness and kept in the Holy of Holies of the Jerusalem Temple, where it stood as the throne of God's presence. According to the biblical books it was made of acacia wood overlaid with gold, topped by a mercy seat between two cherubim, and it was borne on poles by the Levites; its presence was held to go before Israel in battle, as at the fall of Jericho. Legend holds that it was hidden away before the Babylonian destruction of the Temple, while Ethiopian tradition claims that it rests today in the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Aksum. No archaeological witness survives, so all descriptions depend on the biblical text, yet the Ark remains one of the most enduring images of sacred kingship and covenant in world culture.

name: The Arrow of Arash
description: The arrow shot by Arash the archer from the summit of Mount Damavand to fix the frontier between Iran and Turan, a flight said to have been blessed by the giving of his own strength, so that his body wasted as the arrow flew. Reaching the far bank of the Oxus at noon, the arrow ended the war between the two kingdoms and fixed the boundary for the people of Iran. The story is known from Avestan references and from Ferdowsi and other Persian sources, and the arrow's course, hundreds of miles from the Elburz peaks to the Amu Darya, has been endlessly debated and romanticised. The twentieth-century poem 'Arash the Bowmaker' by Siavash Kasrai revived the tale as a symbol of national sacrifice, and the ancient festival of Tirgan still honours the shot.

name: The Barrel Bung
description: A barrel bung, the wooden stopper of a cask, that works magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Barrel Bung', the small wooden plug proves able to conjure food, drink, or gold for its owner. It is one of the many humble objects that Swedish wonder-tales turn into providers of plenty. In the Swedish telling, famine has dried the parish of Bolinge while the rich Lady Skinflint's cows never fail; the boy Jerker discovers why — she keeps an enchanted barrel that gushes milk whenever the bung is drawn. When she hides the bung, the barrel is only wood and iron, and the king's men find nothing; Jerker must watch and wait until the bung is carried back, then seize it in a single dash. The magic bung, once stolen, feeds the whole starving village through the winter, and the boy is rewarded with wool and silver for his courage. The tale makes the smallest of farm objects the key to plenty and to justice.

name: The Bayon Smile
description: The Bayon smile is the serene, downcast smile of the great stone face-towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom, built in the twelfth century under the Buddhist king Jayavarman VII. Scores of colossal faces, each several metres high, gaze from the four sides of the towers, and scholars debate whether they portray the king himself, the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, or the fusion of the two in the king's consecrated image. Khmer legend and local tradition read the many faces as the king's presence watching over his kingdom from every direction, a gaze both compassionate and sovereign. The temple was the state temple of Jayavarman's capital, and its face-towers combine Mahayana Buddhist devotion with the Khmer tradition of the devaraja, the god-king. The Bayon smile has become the emblem of Angkor and of Cambodian identity, appearing on the national flag and in art worldwide as an image of serene royal power.

name: The Belt of Tahmineh
description: A belt said in some tellings of the story to have been woven by Tahmineh of Samangan, mother of Sohrab, and given to the hero Rostam on the night of their meeting, binding their union. The motif varies sharply across recensions of the Shahnameh and in modern retellings, and Ferdowsi's own text describes no single canonical belt, so the object's particulars rest on later tradition rather than on the epic's lines. In some versions Tahmineh also binds a token, a jewel or an armlet, on Sohrab so that the boy might one day know his father, and it is this token that drives the tragedy when father and son meet unknowing on the battlefield. The belt is therefore best read as a romantic elaboration of the episode, invented to give the doomed pair a visible bond, and any account of it must be marked as uncertain.

name: The Bewitched Knife
description: An iron knife that Swedish folk tradition used against harmful magic, one of the many protective uses of steel and iron in Nordic belief. A knife or other steel object laid across a newborn's cradle was believed to keep the bortbyting, the changeling, from swapping the child, and similar iron was set under the birthing bed and over the stable door to hold off trolls and the mare. A knife was also run through a bewitched churn, struck into the threshold, or thrown over the roof to break a spell that had soured the milk or the luck of a farm. The sign-carved knife served the healer in 'signing' rites, where a knowledgeable woman or man traced protective marks and spoke a formula over the sick. Iron's power to turn the hidden folk and their magic is one of the oldest and most widespread motifs of Scandinavian folk belief, surviving into the 20th century in rural custom.

name: The Black Book (Sortebog)
description: A handwritten book of prayers, charms, and remedies kept by Danish cunning folk, the 'black book' or Cyprianus, named after the apocryphal magician-bishop Cyprianus of Antioch. The books mixed church prayers with healing formulas against disease, worms, and bewitchment, and with charms for finding lost or stolen goods. Hundreds survive in Danish archives as evidence of a living folk magic that continued well into the 19th century, alongside the law's efforts to stamp it out. Reading from the black book was said to be a dangerous art, best left to the wise.

name: The Black Book of the Clergy
description: The black book (svartbok), a manual of black magic that Swedish tradition placed in the hands of a priest or 'klok' man who had studied 'the black art'. Actual svartkonstböcker, filled with conjurations, signs, and instructions, survive in Swedish archives from the 17th-19th centuries, and they mix prayers, biblical names, and runic-looking signs in the same hand that kept the parish register. Legend said the priest's black book could be passed on only on his deathbed, since the book had been given him by the powers of the dark and would burn or vanish if it fell to an unworthy hand. The book was used to find thieves, heal the bewitched, conjure answers, and bind spirits, and it made the clergy who owned it feared as much as respected. The black book stands at the meeting-point of church and folk magic, where the man of God was also the master of the dark art.

name: The Bottle of the Ifrit
description: The sealed copper bottle cast up in the fisherman's net in the Thousand and One Nights tale of the Fisherman and the Jinni, from which a vast ifrit escaped in a pillar of smoke and, furious at his long imprisonment, threatened to kill the man who had freed him. The fisherman saved himself by doubting that so great a being could fit into so small a vessel, tricking the spirit back through its narrow mouth and sealing the bottle once more. In the tale the jar carries the seal of Solomon, whose name had trapped the ifrit in the deep for hundreds of years, and it is the loss of that power that lets the spirit out. The vessel became the archetype of the bottled-jinn motif in world folklore, echoed in every story of a spirit, demon, or giant confined by a magician's seal and released by the unwary.

name: The Brazen Serpent
description: The bronze serpent made by Moses at God's command to heal the Israelites bitten by serpents in the wilderness, raised on a pole so that the stricken who looked upon it lived, as told in the Book of Numbers. Kept for centuries in the Jerusalem Temple, it was later destroyed by King Hezekiah as an idol under the name Nehushtan, when the people had come to burn incense to it. Its story is told in Numbers and in 2 Kings, and the object itself is known only from scripture, with no archaeological trace. In later tradition the brazen serpent became a type of healing lifted up for all to see, and Christian exegesis read it as a foreshadowing of the cross, a reading that has kept the image alive in religious art for two thousand years.

name: The Broom King
description: The broom king, the broom that rules all brooms, from the Swedish tale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'. In the tale a broom proves to be the king of its kind, sweeping away the story's dangers with a command that no other broom could match. The tale plays on the humble household object raised to kingship, a comic inversion in the spirit of the Scandinavian wonder-tales where the lowliest tool of the house shows the greatest power. The broom was in any case no ordinary thing in folk belief, being used to sweep out evil at the threshold, to sweep luck into the house at New Year, and as a mount in the lore of witches. Making the broom a king gathers all that magic into one homely hero, and the tale delights in seeing the farmyard champion reign.

name: The Cat of Norrhult
description: A bewitched cat in a folk tale from Norrhult in Småland. In the tale 'The Cat of Norrhult', a cat behaves in ways that betray a witch's or troll's power behind it, and the cat's strange actions reveal the magic at work in the village. Cats were the favourite disguise of witches and of the trolls' servants in Nordic belief, and a cat that walked on two legs, spoke, or wore something out of place was read as the true witch showing herself. The tale belongs to the wide Swedish family of stories about animals that are not what they seem, where the sharp eye of a neighbour or the luck of a household exposes the creature. In Norrhult the cat gives the village its name for the wonder, and the story still colours how the place remembers the event.

name: The Church Bell Against Storms
description: Swedish church bells were believed to protect the parish: they were rung to break up thunderclouds, drive away storms and pestilence, and even to help stop fires. The casting of a new bell was accompanied by rites, and the bells were thought to carry a blessing that evil powers could not withstand. Ringing against bad weather ('ringning mot oväder') is recorded in many Swedish parishes. The sound of the consecrated bell was held to drive off the trolls and evil spirits that raised the weather, and the clergy were asked to ring while a storm passed, sometimes with a formula of words recited as the bell swung. When a fire broke out, the same bell was rung to alarm the parish and, in folk belief, to check the flames themselves. The rite of casting — pouring the bronze with prayers and watching over the new bell — made each bell a sacred object, and church bells were consequently treated with the respect owed to relics.

name: The Church Keys
description: The church key used in the Swedish divination called nyckelprövning, the key test. A key was bound between the pages of a Bible, which was then hung or turned while names were read, and it was believed the key would point out or shake at the name of a thief. The key-and-Bible test is documented in Swedish folk tradition for finding stolen goods, and it was trusted because the church key and the holy book brought God's judgement into the search. The test belonged to the wider family of divination by the Bible, psalm, or sieve that country people used when the law could not find the guilty. Because the outcome could ruin a name, the practice was discouraged by the clergy, yet it lingered in villages into the 19th century as a feared and resorted-to last judgement.

name: The Cowbell of the Skogsrå
description: A cowbell heard in the forest in Swedish belief, and a mark of the skogsrå, the forest spirit who leads cattle astray. She is said to ring her bell or to ride a cow, and the tinkle of a bell where no cow is to be seen warns the woodsman or the herder of her presence. The cowbell ties the skogsrå to her trade of seducing cattle into the forest, where she keeps them in her care and returns them only on her own terms; a herd that wandered off was said to be 'with the skogsrå'. Her bell is a sound of both warning and temptation, for she appears as a beautiful woman from behind and a hollow or tailed thing when seen clearly. The cowbell is part of the skogsrå's folklore as a seductive and misleading spirit, whose call the wary were meant to resist.

name: The Crook and Flail
description: The crossed crook (heka) and flail (nekhakha) carried by Osiris as emblems of royal authority and of the shepherd's care for his flock, laid crossed over royal mummies in their coffins. Temple reliefs show the living pharaoh handing the pair to the god of the dead and receiving it back, and gilt and blue-faience examples were buried with kings such as Tutankhamun, whose tomb yielded several full sets. The crook descends from the shepherd's staff and the flail from the winnowing fan or cattle prod, and together they fix the enthroned image of Osiris that endured for three thousand years. In the Osiris myth the two signs, held by the dead god, tie the promise of the afterlife to the order of kingship that the pharaoh upheld on earth.

name: The Cup of Jamshid
description: The cup of the legendary shah Jamshid, in which, according to Persian tradition, the whole world could be seen as in a mirror, so that nothing on earth or in the seven climes was hidden from the king, who used it in divination. Despite a common modern assumption, the cup does not appear in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh; it belongs to later literature, where it is also given to the Kayanid king Kay Khosrow, and it became a byword for far-seeing wisdom in the verses of Hafez and Attar. In later elaborations the cup was said to hold an elixir of immortality and to carry the seven rings of the heavens, and some described it as the 'cup of the seven planets' used like an astrolabe. Sufi poets read it as the purified heart that perceives divine truth, and in the twentieth century Allama Iqbal made it an image of the self that cannot be known from outside. Its ties to the older idea of the king's divine glory, the xvaranah, are debated by scholars.

name: The Danevirke
description: A system of ramparts, walls, and moats running across the base of the Jutland peninsula at Schleswig, built from the 5th century onward to guard the southern border of the Danish realm. It was manned, extended, and rebuilt at many points in its history, most notably under King Gudfred in 808, and it is described in early royal chronicles. The surviving stretches, some still under the modern border, are a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Danevirke remained a working fortification into the 19th century, making it one of the longest-used defensive lines in northern Europe.

name: The Derafsh Kaviani
description: The leather apron of the blacksmith Kaveh, raised on a spear when he led the people of Iran against the tyrant Zahhak after the tyrant had devoured his children; the new king Faridun then adorned it with gold, silk, and jewels, and it became the royal standard of the Shahs under the name Derafsh Kaviani. In the Shahnameh, Kaveh refuses the tyrant's bribes and carries his apron to Faridun, and the banner, embellished with a four-pointed star and streamers, was said to have been borne before Iranian armies into the Islamic period. The story is retold each Newroz as a symbol of popular revolt and rightful rule. Scholars note that the apron-banner is a literary invention of the epic tradition, yet the name and the image of the blacksmith's standard remained so potent that later dynasties claimed to carry the true Derafsh.

name: The Djed Pillar
description: The columnar sign shaped like a stylised tree trunk or a stack of ribs, symbol of stability and of Osiris, whose backbone it was said to be. Set up as a temple emblem and ritually raised by the king in the sed festival to renew his reign, it was also worn as an amulet of gold or faience to give the wearer firmness of life. In the Osiris myth, Isis and Nephthys restore the god beside the pillar, and the raising of the djed in the festival of Sokar re-enacted his resurrection each year. Countless faience djed amulets survive from graves, often strung with the tjet of Isis and the ankh as a protective triad, so that the sign remained a living token of stability from the Pyramid Texts well into Roman Egypt.

name: The Emerald Buddha's Robes
description: The three robes of gold worn by the Emerald Buddha are the seasonal garments changed on the sacred image in the Wat Phra Kaew, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha in Bangkok, in a ceremony performed by the king. The image, carved from a single block of jade, sits above the golden pedestal in the royal chapel, and its vestments are swapped three times a year, at the start of the hot, rainy, and cool seasons, in a rite that binds the monarchy to the welfare of the realm. The robes themselves are made of gold cloth and jewelled ornaments, and their alternation is fixed by royal ritual. The image's long history, moving through Laos and Cambodia before being enshrined in Bangkok, is told as the palladium of the Thai state, the object whose possession legitimized the kingdom. The Emerald Buddha and its robes are the axis of Thai national and religious identity, and the ceremony draws crowds whenever the garments are changed.

name: The Feather of Ma'at
description: The ostrich feather worn on the head of the goddess Ma'at, goddess of truth, order, and justice, and placed on the scales of judgment as the counterweight to the heart of the dead. A heart lighter than the feather passed on to the afterlife; a heavier one was devoured by Ammit. The feather, also worn by the god Shu in his role of lifting the sky, became the emblem of a life measured by truth. Ma'at herself is rarely shown without it, and the hieroglyph for the feather stands for her name and for the idea of justice itself. In later and modern thought it has become a byword for fair judgment, and the phrase 'feather of truth' is now used far beyond Egyptology.

name: The Feather of the Simurgh
description: The feather given by the great bird Simurgh to the abandoned prince Zal and later to his son Rostam, to be burned whenever they needed the bird's aid, at whose smoke Simurgh came flying from Mount Alborz. In the Shahnameh the feather carries the infant Zal to safety when he is cast out for his white hair, and in Rostam's direst need, when the hero lies bound and helpless in a pit, the burning feather summons Simurgh, who teaches him how to escape. The gesture became so fixed that the burning of a simurgh feather is a standing motif of Persian heroic poetry. In later Sufi writing it became an emblem of the soul's reliance on divine help, the feather a sign that even the greatest hero must call on a power greater than himself.

name: The Flower of Happiness
description: The flower of happiness, the marvel of a tale told at Sunnymount Crest: a flower whose possession, or whose bloom, was said to bring happiness to whoever found it. In the tale the search for the flower tests the seeker, and the happiness it brings is measured in the finding rather than in any magic of the blossom itself. The tale belongs to the great European family of quests for a thing of pure good fortune, from the golden apple to the singing tree, where the journey works the change in the hero. At Sunnymount Crest the flower is tied to a real place, and the story shapes how the landscape is remembered. The flower is an object-lesson of the wonder-tale rather than a real plant, a reminder that happiness is found by those who seek it well.

name: The Flying Trunk
description: The enchanted wooden trunk of Andersen's tale, given to a spendthrift merchant's son by his father and used by its owner to fly through the air to the land of the Turks and court a princess in her tower. When he squanders his remaining coins on fireworks to amuse the court, a spark sets the trunk alight, and it burns to ash, leaving him wandering the world with a story no one believes. The tale plays the magic object as both luck and ruin, and the trunk itself is one of Andersen's most famous flying vehicles, built on older folk motifs of the magical vehicle.

name: The Four White Umbrellas
description: The four white umbrellas are the tiered white standards that the Burmese chronicles place among the regalia of the first kings of the Bagan and later dynasties, emblems of the right to rule granted from above. In the creation tale of kingship, the story of Thagya Min and the first king, the white umbrella is the mark of the king chosen by heaven, and the number of umbrellas carried over a ruler marked his rank, with the great white umbrella of the king symbolizing the highest authority. The image of the king as the bearer of the white umbrella survives in the Hmannan Yazawin chronicle and in the coronation imagery of the Burmese court, and the umbrella standard still crowns Burmese pagodas and throne halls as marks of sacred authority. The same iconography is shared with Thailand and Laos, where the tiered white parasol is the emblem of the Buddhist king. The four umbrellas bind earthly sovereignty to the blessing of the nats, the spirits who watch over the realm.

name: The Golden Cradle
description: A cradle of gold in a Swedish folk tale, in which a special child is laid and around which the tale's wonder unfolds. In 'The Golden Cradle', the precious cradle marks the child's destiny and the family's fortune, and its making or finding drives the story. The cradle, the most intimate of household objects, is here lifted out of the everyday into the realm of the marvellous, a sign that the child in it is no ordinary child. Tales of golden cradles and foundling princes appear across Europe, and in the Swedish version the treasure is bound up with the home it blesses. The golden cradle is an emblem of the wonder-tale's promise of wealth and favour, and of the belief that the household's luck rests on its children.

name: The Golden Falcon of Hierakonpolis
description: The great gold head of the falcon god Horus found in the Main Deposit of the temple at Hierakonpolis (ancient Nekhen), the cult centre of Horus and one of the oldest religious and political capitals of Egypt. Made of beaten gold and fixed to a copper statue of a falcon, it is set with polished obsidian eyes and crowned with a twin-plumed headdress and a royal uraeus cobra on the brow. Long dated to about 3100 BCE and linked to the era of the Narmer Palette, which was found in the same cache, it is now more commonly assigned by scholars to the Old Kingdom, around the Sixth Dynasty (c. 2345-2181 BCE). Standing as a rare surviving cult statue of a deity, it shows the falcon god as patron of kingship, and a royal statuette once placed beneath its breast made visible the bond between the living pharaoh and his divine protector.

name: The Golden Goose
description: Die goldene Gans, the golden goose of the Grimms' fairy tale of the same name (KHM 64), is found by the simpleton Dummling in the wood after he shares his food with a little grey man. The goose is made of gold, and it sticks fast to anyone who touches it, so that when the simpleton carries it home the innkeeper's daughters, the parson and the sexton all become stuck to it in a growing chain. The absurd procession makes the sad princess laugh for the first time in years, and by the tale's rules this wins Dummling her hand and half the kingdom. The goose is the classic fairy-tale marvel: absurd, adhesive and socially levelling, rewarding the kind-hearted simpleton over his clever brothers. The Grimms recorded the tale from German oral tradition in the early nineteenth century. The goose exists only in fiction, but its picture of a laughing kingdom remains one of the most cheerful images in the collection.

name: The Golden Keys
description: Golden keys that appear in a Swedish folk tale, unlocking a reward or a forbidden treasure for the hero who obtains them. The keys belong to the tale's wonder-logic: ordinary locks fall open before them, and possession of the keys brings the hero to fortune. The motif is told as part of the tale 'The Golden Keys'. In the Swedish version the humble meadow-maid Lena meets three fairies who give her a golden key to a magical dream garden, on the strict condition that she tell no one of it; when the young king falls into danger, she must break her word to save him, and her selfless choice earns her the king's hand. The key thus works as the fairy gift of the tale: a secret treasure that tests the holder's worth more than it rewards the greedy. The fairies belong to the älvor, the beautiful but otherworldly spirits of Swedish forests and meadows, who grant gifts only to those who keep faith with them.

name: The Golden Stool (Sika Dwa)
description: The Sika Dwa, the Golden Stool of the Asante, is a gold-covered wooden stool kept unseated upon as the soul, the sunsum, of the Asante nation, the supreme emblem of its sovereignty. Tradition holds that in the late seventeenth century the priest Okomfo Anokye called it down from the sky, and it settled onto the lap of the first king, Osei Tutu, proving his divine right; since then the stool has never been allowed to touch the ground, and a blackened stool commemorates each departed king. When a British governor demanded the stool in 1900, the Asante rose in the war led by the queen mother Yaa Asantewaa, choosing to fight rather than surrender their nation's soul. The stool sits on its own stool, sheltered in the palace at Kumasi, and is brought out only on the greatest occasions. Its history joins the spiritual, the political and the martial in a single object of wood and gold.

name: The Golden Whip of Genghis Khan
description: The golden whip of Genghis Khan is the legendary whip that the great conqueror is said to have carried and brandished to rally and reward his warriors, and in some tellings the source of his military genius. One of the most retold stories claims that Genghis Khan rode with a whip made of gold that he used to command his armies, and that its mere sight could turn a retreat into a charge. No such whip survives, and the Secret History of the Mongols does not name it; the golden whip appears instead in later heroic retellings and in the popular narrative that grew around the conqueror's rise. The object is thus best understood as a modern legend rather than a documented relic, and its currency reflects the way Genghis Khan has been reimagined as a national and pan-Asian hero. The golden whip nevertheless appears in monuments and museums, and it stands for the charismatic authority by which the steppe armies were held together.

name: The Grail of Peredur
description: The dish or salver carried in the mysterious procession at the castle in the medieval Welsh romance Peredur ab Efrawg is the Welsh cousin of the Holy Grail. In the romance, Peredur, staying at a strange castle, watches a procession in which a youth carries a spear with blood dripping from its tip, followed by a woman bearing a salver on which lies a severed head. Peredur does not ask about what he has seen, and for his silence he is cursed; only later does he learn that the head was that of his cousin, slain in vengeance, and that the vision was linked with the wounding of the Grail king. Unlike the French Grail romances of Chrétien de Troyes, the Welsh text centres on the bleeding head and the dish rather than a chalice, preserving a distinct Celtic strand of the legend. The tale survives in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest. The object is legendary and unattested, but Peredur's procession remains one of the most debated scenes in Arthurian literature.

name: The Great Cat of Dovrefjell
description: The monstrous cat of the Norwegian folktale collected by Asbjornsen and Moe, in which a traveller brings his cat to a Dovrefjell farm whose Christmas feast is ruined by trolls every year. When the trolls return, the cat seizes the troll wife in the dark and is taken for an enormous bear, and the trolls flee, calling home their warning that the great cat is still alive and the farm is lost to them. The tale is usually read as a story of a clever animal that turns the trolls' own fear against them. It is one of the best-known Norwegian troll tales and gave its name to the mountain farm setting of the story.

name: The Green Knight's Axe
description: The enormous green-steel axe carried by the Green Knight into King Arthur's hall at Camelot on New Year's Eve in the fourteenth-century alliterative poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. The weapon, described as an unwieldy blade of enormous size, is the instrument of the beheading game: Gawain strikes off the Knight's head with it, and the Knight calmly picks up the severed head, which reminds Gawain to meet him at the Green Chapel in a year and a day. The axe thus becomes the token of the exchange-of-blows bargain that drives the poem's testing of Gawain's honour. When Gawain flinches at the first swing of the return blow, the Knight taunts him with the very blade Gawain had used. The axe is sometimes read as a symbol of the winter god or the old year passing, its green steel binding the natural and chivalric worlds. It remains one of the most memorable props in medieval English literature.

name: The Gris-gris
description: A small leather pouch worn on the body, holding written Qur'anic verses, prayers, or magic squares, used across North Africa to protect, heal, or bring fortune, known in the Maghreb as a hirz. In Morocco the hirz was stitched shut by a fqih, a learned man, who wrote the contents in ink, and it was worn at the neck, arm, or belt, its power resting entirely on the writing sealed inside. The same pouch-and-writing custom appears from Senegal to the Sudan under other names, and the French term gris-gris, of uncertain origin, became the colonial-era label for the whole family of talismans. The practice is documented in ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk religion and survives today, adapted to modern materials but still stitched and worn as before.

name: The Heavenly Loom
description: The heavenly loom is the celestial weaving frame of Zhinü, the Weaver Girl, who in Chinese myth wove the patterned clouds of the sky beside the Heavenly River, the Milky Way. When she married the cowherd Niulang and neglected her weaving, the Jade Emperor or the Queen Mother of the West separated the pair across the river, allowing them to meet only once a year; on the seventh night of the seventh month, magpies form a bridge over the river and the lovers reunite. The tale, first recorded in Han-era poetry, became the origin of the Qixi festival, the Chinese Valentine's day, when girls pray to Zhinü for skill in needlework and for love. The loom is thus the engine of the sky's patterned beauty and the emblem of the craft that the festival celebrates. The same story is told in Korea as Chilseok and in Japan as Tanabata, where the weaving goddess Orihime is remembered with strips of paper hung on bamboo.

name: The Holy Spring
description: The holy spring (heliga källan), a spring or well that Swedish folk tradition credited with healing. Such springs, often named for a saint, were visited for cures on particular days, usually the saint's feast or a church holiday, and the water was drunk, bathed in, or carried home in flasks for the sick and the cattle. Pilgrims left offerings of coins, linen, or small crosses, often hanging them on a nearby tree, and some springs were said to swell, run warm, or glow before a miracle. When a cure failed, the spring might be slandered as having lost its power. Many Swedish holy springs became local pilgrimage sites that the church later absorbed by blessing them anew, or closed altogether, yet the custom of visiting them survived into the 19th and even the 20th century in parts of the countryside.

name: The Jade Emperor's Gong
description: The Jade Emperor's gong is the bronze instrument of a Vietnamese folk tale in which a frog leads a deputation of animals to heaven to complain that rain never falls. Because the frog croaks so loudly, the Jade Emperor hears it above the clouds and summons the delegation; the frog is granted the power to control rain, and to this day the croaking of frogs is said to warn of coming rain. In some tellings the frog beats the Jade Emperor's own bronze gong to announce the arrival of the animals, or to wake the sleepy god, and the tale survives chiefly through oral retellings across the Red River delta. The gong is a story element rather than a documented artifact, and it belongs to the large Vietnamese cycle of pourquoi tales about the order of the natural world. The story explains both the frog's croak and the dragon's water-taming work, and it is one of the most retold animal tales in the Vietnamese classroom.

name: The Jambiya
description: The short curved dagger with a broad double-edged blade worn at the belt by Yemeni men, a symbol of honor and manhood carried from youth and drawn in the bara', the ritual war dance of Yemen in which lines of dancers flourish their daggers to drumming and chant. Silver-sheathed jambiya hilts, some of rhino horn, are treasured heirlooms and marks of tribal and social standing, and a fine jambiya can be the most valuable thing a man owns. The wearing of the dagger, its angle at the belt, and the dance itself are all attested across Yemeni material culture and in the songs and poetry that surround them. Though the trade in rhino horn has been banned, the jambiya remains the national emblem of Yemen, worn in daily life and in the bara' as a living custom.

name: The Jelling Stones
description: The two great runestones of the royal monument at Jelling, Jutland, raised by kings Gorm and Harald Bluetooth in the 10th century. The smaller stone was raised by Gorm in memory of his queen Thyra, and the larger, carved with a figure of Christ and a great beast, was raised by Harald in memory of his parents. Harald's runes announce that he won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian, marking Denmark's conversion in the royal monument's own words. The stones stand in the churchyard of Jelling, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

name: The Kettle of the Underjordiska
description: A pot or kettle that the underjordiska, the hidden people beneath the earth, were said to borrow from farm households. In Swedish legend a woman lends a kettle to the hidden folk, often for a christening or a feast in their underground halls, and finds it returned filled with gold, a silver gift, or the sweet smell of their food — or learns that borrowing from them carries its own price. The motif of the borrowed vessel, known across Scandinavia, plays on the housewife's neighbourly duty to the hidden people and her reward or punishment for how she meets it. If she gave generously and asked no questions she was blessed; if she grudged the loan or told the world about it, the kettle came back fouled or the farm's luck turned. The borrowed kettle is one of the commonest objects in the story-world of the underjordiska.

name: The Khamsa
description: The open-hand amulet of the Maghreb and the wider Middle East, called the Hand of Fatima after the Prophet's daughter in Muslim usage and the Hand of Miriam in Jewish usage, hung in homes, worn as jewelry, and painted on doorways, cradles, and vehicles against the evil eye. The silver khamsa was the standard talisman of North African Jews and Muslims alike, made in every register from plain sheet silver to fine filigree set with coral and enamel. The open palm, shared with the wider Mediterranean hand-amulet tradition, reaches back to Punic and ancient Near Eastern hands of blessing, so the form carries an ancient root beneath its later name. Today the khamsa has crossed into global fashion as a pendant and charm, while its protective use continues undiminished in the societies that gave it its name.

name: The Knot of Isis
description: The looped red tjet amulet, the 'girdle of Isis', worn by the living and the dead for the goddess's protection and said to be her blood, her girdle, or the knot of her dress. Spell 156 of the Book of the Dead directs that it be made of red jasper and placed on the neck of the deceased so that the might of Isis would guard the throat and chest. Red carnelian and faience tjets are common in New Kingdom burials, where they sit with the djed and ankh in protective groupings, and the sign itself often accompanies the goddess in temple reliefs. As the girdle that Isis is said to have used to protect the infant Horus in the marshes, the amulet carried the mother-goddess's care into every grave where it was laid.

name: The Lapp Drum
description: The Lapp drum, the sacred drum of the Sami noaidi or shaman, made of a frame of pine with a reindeer-skin head painted with figures in alder-bark juice. The drum was beaten for divination, and the noaidi sought answers in the drumming while its figures of sun, gods, reindeer, and man mirrored the Sami cosmos; a pointer or ring moving across the painted skin gave the answer to the question asked. Many drums were confiscated by missionaries in the 17th-18th centuries and burned or sent to collections, so that only a few dozen survive in museums, each one an irreplaceable map of the old belief. The drum's power was believed to travel with its owner, and the noaidi used it to find lost reindeer, cure the sick, and travel between the worlds. The Lapp drum is the central object of the older Sami religion and a key witness to it.

name: The Ljungby Horn
description: The Ljungby horn, a great drinking horn with gilded silver mounts that is kept at Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania (Skåne), southern Sweden. Legend says the trolls who live beneath the great boulder Maglestenen once feasted on golden pillars at Christmas, and that a stable hand who rode out on their feast night came away with their horn and their pipe. As he rode, the drink he was offered burnt his horse's flank like acid, and the trolls pursued him to the castle gate; when he reached the plowed field and rode a cross shape over it, the trolls could not follow. They cursed the castle — the horse and the rider died, and the castle burned three times — and the horn and pipe were kept within the walls forever after. The objects survive to this day and are shown to visitors as proof of the trolls' feast, making the horn one of the best-known relics of Swedish legend.

name: The Ljungby Pipe
description: The Ljungby pipe, a whistle of carved bone or ivory kept together with the Ljungby horn at Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania, southern Sweden. In the legend the trolls beneath the boulder Maglestenen offered the pipe, together with their drinking horn, to a stable hand who came to their Christmas feast; it was playable from both ends and formed one half of the trolls' treasure. When the servant fled with the horn and the pipe, the trolls' pursuit broke against the cross-shaped furrows of the plowed field, and their curse fell on the castle instead. The pipe was long counted among the wonders of Trolle-Ljungby, kept beside the horn in a glass case that no one dared to open, for the trolls had warned that if the objects were ever removed the owner would meet great misfortune. Together the horn and pipe preserve the memory of a troll feast at a real Swedish castle.

name: The Luckstone
description: A luckstone (lyckosten), a stone with a natural hole, worn on a cord or kept in the pocket for luck and protection in Swedish folk tradition. Such pierced stones were also called 'hängesten', hanging stones, from the way they were strung and hung, and 'örngottsstenar'; they were hung in stables, on the neck, or by the bed to ward off the mare and misfortune, and the hole was the mark that gave the stone its power. In some districts the stone was hung over the stable door to keep the cattle safe, in others carried by sailors or travellers as a charm against storms and robbers. The lucky stone is known across the North Atlantic world as the 'witch stone' or 'hag stone', and the Swedish names record the same belief in the seeing and warding power of the pierced stone.

name: The Lur
description: A long S-shaped horn of hammered bronze from the Nordic Bronze Age, cast with an ornamental disc at the mouth and decorated in fine raised bosses and engraving. More than fifty lurs survive, most from Denmark, found in peat bogs and hoards, including the famous Brudevaelte lurs from Zealand. Their curved form and fine workmanship make them among the oldest surviving brass instruments in the world, and they were likely sounded in cult and sacrifice, perhaps in pairs, as Bronze Age rock carvings suggest. The lur also gave its name to the later wooden folk horns of the region, though the two are quite different instruments.

name: The Mace of Faridun
description: The bull-headed mace (gurz) forged to the measure of the young prince Faridun, which Ferdowsi describes being made before his campaign against the tyrant Zahhak, so that only his hand could wield it. With it Faridun struck Zahhak's crowned head and split the serpents that had grown on the tyrant's shoulders, ending a thousand years of unjust rule and binding the defeated Zahhak in a cavern of Mount Damavand, where he is said to be chained to this day. The mace, in its bull-headed form, links the hero to the cattle-rearing world of the old Iranian kings and stands in the epic as the plain, honest weapon that overcomes sorcery. It became the archetypal weapon of Persian hero-kings, echoed in the bull-headed mace that later poets give to Rostam.

name: The Madonna's Golden Shoe
description: The golden shoe of the Virgin Mary's statue, at the centre of the Swedish tale 'The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe'. In the tale a fiddler who plays for the church is rewarded when the Madonna herself bestows her golden shoe on him, a gift from the living statue that proves his music found favour in heaven's eyes. The tale is one of Sweden's many stories of a church statue that comes alive, a motif with deep roots in medieval legend where painted Marys nod, weep, or reach out to the faithful. The golden shoe turns the church's most precious ornament into a personal blessing, and the fiddler's reward shows how music and devotion were judged the same act. The tale survives as a favourite of Swedish folk storytelling, told of several churches across the land.

name: The Magic Book
description: A book endowed with supernatural power in the Danish tale of the same name, granting its owner knowledge, hidden secrets, or magical skill, and bringing both power and danger. The story tells of a boy who finds such a book in a magician's mountain dwelling and must read it with care, for the words come alive and threaten anyone who reads on. Magic books of this kind echo the real black books of Scandinavian folk magic, which were used to heal and to find lost things. The tale belongs to the Nordic cycle of grimoire legends, in which the book itself is a creature and a trap.

name: The Magic Carpet of the Nights
description: The flying carpet of the Thousand and One Nights cycle and of later oriental folklore, a woven rug that carried its riders through the air to far-off countries. Within the Nights corpus itself the carpet appears chiefly in the later tales, where Prince Husayn buys a magic carpet that bears its master wherever he wishes to go, and much of its modern fame comes from European retellings rather than from the medieval Arabic text. Its details vary widely from one telling to another, some giving it as a plain travelling rug, others as a king-sized carpet with a full retinue. The carpet's fame grew so far beyond its sources that the flying carpet, together with the lamp of Aladdin, became the signature prop of the Arabian Nights in world culture, endlessly redrawn and refilmed.

name: The Magic Churn
description: A butter churn that witches were believed to bewitch or to work from afar. In Swedish folk belief a witch (trollkona) could send a 'mjölkhare', a butter or cream hare, to steal milk from neighbours' cows and churns, or charm a churn so that butter would not come. Counter-magic included heating a knife in the fire and running it through the churn to break the spell. The milk hare — a small creature conjured by magic — was sent to suck the neighbours' cows dry or to draw the cream from their churns into the witch's own. When a churn refused to give butter, the household suspected such theft, and the remedy was to strike the churn with a red-hot iron so that the witch felt the blow wherever she sat. The belief belongs to the wider Scandinavian complex of milk magic, in which the daily dairy work was watched as closely as any field, and a neighbour could be quietly accused of prospering at the cost of others.

name: The Magic Mirror
description: The magic mirror of the queen in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Snow White' (KHM 53) is a speaking mirror that answers truly when its owner asks who is the fairest in the land. Each time the queen consults it, the mirror replies that she is fairest of all, until the day it names Snow White, and from that answer springs the queen's jealous persecution of the girl. The mirror thus acts as the story's engine and moral judge, an impartial voice that exposes the truth the queen cannot bear. In the Grimms' version the queen meets her end at Snow White's wedding feast, where she is forced to dance in red-hot shoes, and the mirror's last answer seals her fate. Mirrors that speak and tell the truth appear in folklore across Europe, and the motif was spread worldwide by the 1937 animated film, with its famous lines 'Magic mirror on the wall, who is the fairest of them all?'. The mirror exists only in fiction, but it has become one of the most recognisable objects in fairy tale.

name: The Magic Scythe
description: A scythe in Swedish folktales that cuts grain by itself, without a hand to swing it. In the tale of the magic scythe, the wonderful tool performs the harvest work of many men, sparing its owner the labour of mowing. The self-working scythe belongs to a family of Swedish wonder-tools in which ordinary farm implements act on their own. In the best-known telling the scythe is a loan from the hidden people: an elf of the huldufólk gives a poor farmer a blade that mows his grain by itself while he rests, on the single condition that it be returned to the elf's clearing each evening. When the farmer breaks his word and hides the scythe, it turns on him and mows down his fences and his house until he begs forgiveness, and the elf strips the magic away. The tale thus joins the wonder-tool motif to the strict bond between humans and the hidden people, who give generously and punish broken trust without mercy.

name: The Magic Table
description: A table that sets itself with food, a recurring wonder-object of Swedish folk tales. At a word the self-serving table covers itself with dishes and ale, so the hero never goes hungry; the motif usually appears in tales where a magic object is given as a reward and later stolen and replaced with a worthless copy. It belongs to the family of self-working marvels in Swedish wonder-tales. The tale is best known through the Grimm brothers' 'Tischlein deck dich', but Swedish versions circulated widely: a poor man serves a spirit or a mysterious helper, and in reward receives a little table that feeds him at a word. A dishonest innkeeper or a jealous brother steals the table and leaves a common one in its place, until the hero recovers the true treasure by showing its power. The self-setting table is one of a trio of wonder-gifts — the table, the money-dropping ass, and the stick that beats — and its promise of endless food made it a favourite of hungry listeners.

name: The Magician's Cape
description: A cape that gives its wearer magical power in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Magician's Cape', the cloak lets the hero fly, become invisible, or work spells, and is won, lost, and recovered through the story's tests. The cape is a classic object of wonder-tales: a garment of ordinary cut that carries extraordinary ability. In the Swedish telling the ancient magician of the mountain keeps a black flying cape sewn from the wings of a thousand bats and stitched with thread spun from midnight; with it he soars over the treeline and across seas, and no one can follow him. The captive girl Astrid watches his habits, steals the key from his belt, and takes the cape for herself, flying to the kingdom to bring soldiers against him. She keeps the cape and becomes the kingdom's messenger, flying from village to village — the stolen wonder-garment turned from the tyrant's weapon into the servant of the free.

name: The Mistletoe Spear
description: The mistletoe shaft with which the blind god Höðr, guided by Loki, slew Baldr the beloved. Only the mistletoe had not sworn to spare him, and Loki fetched it, fashioned it into a dart, and guided Höðr's hand. The killing of Baldr by the mistletoe spear set the doom of the gods in motion and stands at the centre of the Eddic tragedy. When Frigg had taken oaths from all things not to harm her son, she overlooked the young mistletoe as too small and weak to ask; Loki made the dart from that very plant and gave it to the blind god to throw in sport. Baldr fell dead, and the gods' attempts to restore him failed through Loki's malice, so that the death of the shining god became the first blow of Ragnarök. The mistletoe dart thus carries the whole weight of the myth: the small overlooked thing that brings down the beloved and unchains the end of the world.

name: The Naga's Jewel
description: The jewel of the naga is the luminous gem that the great serpent of the Mekong, the naga, is said to guard in its watery underworld palace, and that grants wealth, kingship, or the fulfilment of wishes to whoever obtains it. In Thai and Lao river lore the naga is the protector of the river and of the people who live along it, and the jewel is sometimes linked to the fireballs that rise from the water during the full-moon festival of the eleventh lunar month, when the naga is said to breathe fire in celebration. The motif echoes the wider South and Southeast Asian image of the naga as the keeper of the earth's hidden treasure, and the jewel recurs in tales of kings who win the naga's favour. Because the naga is both a guardian and a dangerous boundary-keeper, the jewel is a reward for courage or reverence and a fatal prize for greed. The legend is retold across the Mekong and its tributaries, binding the serpent to the geography of the river.

name: The Níðstöng
description: Níðstöng, the scorn pole of the sagas, most famously raised by Egil Skallagrímsson against King Eiríkr Bloodaxe and Queen Gunnhild. Egil set a hazel pole topped with a carved horse head, turned toward the mainland, and invoked the land-spirits to drive the royal pair from Norway. The pole was a curse made visible, meant to bring ruin and exile upon its target. The word níð carries the sense of insult and dishonour, and the pole formalised that insult as a public act of magic. By fixing a horse's skull on the stake and carving runes, the raiser handed the curse over to the land-spirits (landvættir), whose good will was thought necessary to those dwelling in the land, so that once driven out the cursed could not easily return. Later sagas record similar poles raised in feuds, making the níðstöng a recognised instrument of Norse legal-magical pressure.

name: The Offer Stone
description: The offer stone (offersten), a boulder with cup-shaped hollows where offerings were made. Hundreds of such stones survive across Sweden, often beside churches, springs, or old cult sites, and in places they are the only trace of a vanished place of worship. Small gifts of coins, food, butter, or tar were placed in the cups, sometimes on fixed holy days, and the stones were consulted for healing of people and livestock; in later Christian times they were avoided, or 'baptised' with a name to break their power. In some districts the cup-marks were called älvkvarnar, 'elf mills', from the belief that elves ground grain in them at night. The cup-marked stones, skålgropsstenar, are counted among Sweden's oldest cult objects, with the oldest hollows ground into the rock in the Bronze Age.

name: The Palette of Narmer
description: A ceremonial siltstone palette from Hierakonpolis carved around 3100 BCE, showing King Narmer on one face smiting a captured enemy with a mace and on the other reviewing decapitated captives, long read as an early record of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. The falcon-god Horus perches above a bound foe on the same face, holding a rope, and the king wears the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other. Found in 1898 in the Main Deposit of the temple along with the golden falcon and the Narmer macehead, it is one of the most analysed objects of Egyptian archaeology. While modern scholars caution that its scenes may record a single victory rather than a whole unification, its grammar of the smiting king, the divine falcon, and the ceremonial palette set the visual language of pharaonic royal power for three thousand years.

name: The Papyrus of Ani
description: The Papyrus of Ani is the finest surviving copy of the Egyptian Book of the Dead, a long illustrated roll commissioned for Ani, a scribe and accountant of divine offerings at Thebes, around 1250 BCE during the Nineteenth Dynasty. Its hieroglyphic spells, hymns and coloured vignettes were written by scribes and painted by artists so that Ani could pass the dangers of the underworld and reach the afterlife. The most famous scene is chapter 125, the weighing of the heart: Ani's heart is set on the scales against the feather of Ma'at, while Anubis tends the balance, Thoth records the result, and the devourer Ammit waits to consume the heart if it proves heavy with sin. Ani and his wife are shown worshipping the gods, including Osiris enthroned, and the accompanying hymns and spells invoke the goddesses Isis and Nephthys. The roll, some seventy-eight feet long, was purchased for the British Museum in 1888, where it is kept as EA 10470. It remains the classic witness to Egyptian funerary literature and the standard illustration of the judgment of the dead.

name: The Queen's Necklace
description: A necklace in a Swedish folk tale, worn by a queen and central to the story's test or reward. In the tale 'The Queen's Necklace', the necklace passes through the hands of the characters and its loss, theft, or recovery drives the plot. The jewel is a typical treasure of wonder-tales, standing for wealth, rank, and the queen's honour.
