In the Swedish telling the cruel king Hendrik gives his bride Blanzeflor a necklace of one hundred perfect pearls with the warning that her life hangs on it; the queen, finding her only joy in charity, gives the pearls away one by one to feed the poor. When the king discovers the empty string he condemns her to death, but the birds she has fed come to her cell, rescue her, and destroy the tyrant. The necklace is therefore the instrument of both the queen's imprisonment and her redemption — a chain of rank that a generous heart transforms into a ladder of rescue.

name: The Red Shoes
description: The enchanted red shoes of Andersen's tale of Karen, a proud village girl who wants shoes finer than her station. Once she puts them on they carry her dancing without rest, over fields and thorns and into the church, until she begs the executioner to cut off her feet, and only after years of humble repentance does she find peace. The tale, rooted in the strict dress codes of village life, made fine shoes a symbol of vanity punished, and it has been read ever since as a warning about pride and desire. It is one of Andersen's darkest tales.

name: The Relic of That Phanom
description: The relic of That Phanom is a sacred relic of the Buddha's breastbone enshrined in the great stupa of That Phanom on the Mekong, the most revered chedi of Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao legend holds that two monks carried the relic to the site and that a naga king, Phanya Sithan, invited the company and guarded the shrine, binding the sacred monument to the serpentine protectors of the river; the date of the enshrinement is given as the Year of the Goat and celebrated every year at the That Phanom festival. The stupa itself, a tall pyramidal chedi gilded in gold, was severely damaged by a storm in 1975 and rebuilt with a national campaign, and it remains a pilgrimage centre drawing people from both banks of the Mekong. The relic is venerated as a palladium of the region, and its festival in the twelfth lunar month, the Bun Pha That Phanom, is one of the great gatherings of Lao Buddhism. The connection of the shrine to the naga reflects the deep riverine religion of the Mekong valley.

name: The Roskilde Ships
description: Five Viking-age ships raised in 1962 from the mouth of Roskilde Fjord, where they had been scuttled in the 11th century to block the channel against raiders. The fleet holds a deep-sea cargo knarr, a Baltic trader, a small coastal boat, and two long warships, showing the whole range of Viking shipbuilding. They are displayed in the Viking Ship Museum at Roskilde, where the longship Skuldelev 2 has been rebuilt at full scale and sailed. The find is a key witness to how ships were built, sailed, and deliberately sunk in the late Viking age.

name: The Round Table
description: The Round Table of King Arthur is the great council table at which, in Arthurian romance, no knight could claim a higher seat than another, ending the quarrels over precedence that divided the court. In Geoffrey of Monmouth's twelfth-century History of the Kings of Britain the table is only mentioned among Arthur's household furniture, but later romance writers made it the heart of the court and the scene of the knights' vows. In some versions, notably the prose romances, the table is devised by Merlin, and the perilous seat at it is reserved for the knight who will win the Grail, with disaster striking any unworthy claimant. A great painted table said to be Arthur's hangs in the Great Hall of Winchester Castle, made in the thirteenth century and repainted in Tudor times. The table came to symbolise the ideal of equal fellowship among knights, an image that passed into modern politics and culture. It remains one of the defining symbols of the Arthurian world.

name: The Rök Runestone
description: The Rök stone (Rökstenen), the famous ninth-century runestone of Östergötland, raised beside Lake Vättern in memory of a dead son. Its inscription of more than 700 runes is the longest known runic text in the world, a riddling composition in verse that mentions Theodoric the Great, named heroes, and the runes themselves, and has been read as both a memorial and a locked challenge to be unravelled. Carved on every face of the stone in several scripts and cipher styles, the text was long studied by runologists, and modern readings have proposed everything from heroic legend to a reckoning of the dead. The Rök stone is one of the most studied objects of Swedish Viking-age runology, a landmark of the conversion period when the old script met new ideas.

name: The Scales of Ma'at
description: The great balance set up in the Hall of Two Truths (or Hall of Ma'at), where the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of truth before Osiris, with Thoth recording the verdict and the devourer Ammit waiting to swallow any heart found heavier than the feather. Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead describes the rite, in which the deceased recites the Negative Confession before the Forty-Two Judges. The scene, painted on tomb walls and funerary papyri from the New Kingdom onward, is among the most reproduced images of Egyptian religion. Because the heart (ib) was held to record the deeds of a life, its weighing decided the soul's fate: a heart in balance passed to the blessed afterlife, while one burdened by sin was consumed and ceased to exist. Modern exhibitions of Egyptian funerary art still make the weighing of the heart one of their centrepieces.

name: The Sea King's Ring
description: A golden ring given by the sea king in the Swedish ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King', a version of the old ballad about the maiden taken by the sea folk. The ring is the gift that binds the maiden to her underwater master, the token of a marriage that keeps her below the waves while her family mourns her above; in the ballad's ending the ring and its owner part in sorrow when the world above finally reclaims her. The ballad is documented in Swedish song collections from the 18th century and belongs to the international cycle of ballads about the seal-maiden and the water-man, in which a gift or a promise holds the human captive. The ring, like the sea king's crown, is the mark of the other world's power over the mortal who accepts it.

name: The Seal of Solomon
description: The signet ring of the prophet-king Solomon, engraved with the divine Name, by whose power he commanded the winds, the beasts, and the jinn in Jewish and Islamic tradition alike, told in the Quran, the midrash, and the Thousand and One Nights. The midrash adds the ordeal of its theft, when the jinn Sakhr stole the ring and ruled in Solomon's likeness for forty days until the king won it back and hurled the impostor into the sea. Its seal, often drawn as a six-pointed star or a pentagram, later became a widespread protective emblem across the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe, known in Islamic amulets as the khatam Sulayman. The name, transferred to the star pattern, still marks talismans and jewellery from Morocco to India, and the ring remains the archetype of the seal that gives its bearer command over spirits.

name: The Senet Board
description: The Egyptian board game of thirty squares in three rows of ten, played with five or seven counters and casting sticks or knucklebones, and the most common board game found in Egypt, in use from the Predynastic period to the Ptolemaic. The crossing of its hazardous squares mirrored the soul's journey through the afterlife, and vignettes in the Book of the Dead show the deceased playing senet against an unseen opponent to win passage into the next world. Boards ranged from simple scratched slabs to fine wooden boxes with drawers and playing pieces of faience and ivory; Tutankhamun's tomb alone held four complete sets. The game's funerary meaning grew so strong that senet scenes became a regular image of the tomb, yet it was also played for pleasure, with boards scratched into temple steps and pavements.

name: The Silver Spoon
description: A silver spoon said to be left by the vittra, the hidden folk of northern Sweden, for humans who helped them or as a sign of favour. In folk tradition such a spoon appeared where none had been, or a borrowed spoon returned with a gift of silver, and the finder knew the vittra had marked them out. The spoon was often a christening gift from the hidden folk to a human child they had blessed, a token of goodwill that the family kept and passed down. To lose the spoon, or to sell it, was to throw away the hidden people's protection and invite misfortune. The silver spoon belongs to the wider pattern of vittra gifts, where the hidden folk reward courtesy and punish greed, and it is a typical token of the goodwill that northern Swedish tradition set between the two worlds.

name: The Singing Harp
description: The singing harp of the giant in the English fairy tale Jack and the Beanstalk is one of the three treasures Jack steals on his second visit to the giant's castle in the clouds, beside the bag of gold and the hen that lays golden eggs. The harp plays by itself, and as Jack flees down the beanstalk it calls out 'Master! Master!', waking the giant and setting the pursuit in motion. When Jack reaches the ground he chops the beanstalk down and the giant falls to his death, so the harp's voice is the object that turns the theft into the tale's climax. The story, first printed in the eighteenth century and popularised in chapbooks and pantomime, makes the harp a magic object of the fairy-tale kind, able to sing and to act on its own will. The harp, the hen and the gold recall the classic triad of fairy-tale treasures. Its self-playing music marks it as one of the earliest and most famous talking objects in English folklore.

name: The Sistrum
description: A sacred rattle of looped bronze or copper rods strung across a frame, shaken in the cults of Hathor and Isis to please the goddess and to repel evil with its hissing, sibilant sound, called sesheshet in Egyptian after the noise it makes. Priestesses, queens, and kings bore it in temple ritual, and queens are depicted holding it in both hands; great ceremonial versions, often of gilt bronze, stood as temple furniture. Its naos-shaped variant carried the cow-eared head of Hathor between its handles and remained in use into Graeco-Roman Egypt, where it became an attribute of Isis in her universal form. The sistrum survives today as a liturgical instrument in Coptic Christianity and in Ethiopian Orthodox worship, making it one of the oldest sacred rattles still in continuous use.

name: The Six Swans' Shirts
description: The six shirts of the Grimms' fairy tale 'The Six Swans' (KHM 49) are woven by the princess from stinging nettles to break the enchantment that has turned her six brothers into swans. For years she must gather the nettles, spin and sew the shirts in complete silence, and her vow costs her dearly when her children are taken from her and she is condemned rather than speak. When the shirts are at last finished and thrown over the swans, her brothers become men again, though the youngest is left with a wing instead of an arm because one shirt was not finished. The tale belongs to the family of swan-brother stories, and the same task of weaving nettle shirts appears in Hans Christian Andersen's 'The Wild Swans'. The shirts are the tale's central ordeal, testing the sister's endurance, silence and faith. The story was told throughout Germany and is preserved in the Grimms' collection.

name: The Skin Satchel
description: A satchel made of animal skin that carries magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Skin Satchel', the humble leather bag turns out to hold an impossible store, or to have been sewn for a magical purpose, and its opening releases the story's marvels. The satchel is one of many everyday objects in Swedish wonder-tales that conceal power. In the Swedish version the poor Niklas sees a troll take six grains from a leather satchel and grow an entire field of wheat in minutes; to win the satchel he must keep hold of it through the long night while the trolls shake the ground, send ghostly apparitions, and howl like wolves, without letting go or speaking a single word. When dawn breaks the trolls retreat and the satchel is his, and its endless grain saves the starving village. The tale joins the wonder-bag motif to the classic ordeal of the trolls' night, where courage and silence win the treasure.

name: The Snow Queen's Mirror
description: The devil's magic mirror from the first chapter of Andersen's 'The Snow Queen'. It magnifies everything ugly and mean and shrinks all that is good and fair, and when the trolls drop it in their glee, it shatters into millions of splinters. Splinters blown into the eye and heart of the boy Kay make everything beautiful seem spoiled and let the Snow Queen carry him away, setting the whole story in motion. The mirror is thus the tale's opening image of a world seen through a corrupted glass, a figure Andersen would return to throughout his work.

name: The Solar Barque of Ra
description: The two celestial boats in which the sun god Ra sails: the day barque Mandjet crossing the sky and the night barque Mesektet crossing the Duat, the underworld, where the crew repel the serpent Apep with spears and enchantments so that dawn can return. The nightly battle myth inspired real solar barques buried beside temples and pyramids, most famously the dismantled cedar boat entombed beside the Great Pyramid at Giza, so that the king might make the same journey after death. The journey itself was written into the Pyramid Texts and the later Books of the Day and Night, which describe the gates and hours the barque must pass. Both the image of the sun sailing through the hours and the funeral barque that carries the dead echo through Egyptian art from the earliest dynasties to the Ptolemaic temples.

name: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
description: The one-legged toy soldier of Andersen's tale, cast last from the family's old tin spoon and brave out of all proportion. He falls from the windowsill, sails his paper boat down the gutter past rats and street boys, is swallowed whole by a fish, and at last is thrown into the stove with the paper dancer he loves; he never flinches once. The tale made the plain tin soldier a figure of quiet constancy and unspoken love, and it remains one of Andersen's most loved object stories. It was published in 1838 in his second collection of tales.

name: The Sun Chariot
description: The chariot of Sól, the sun goddess, drawn across the sky by the horses Arvakr and Alsvinn, with the shield Svalinn before them to temper the light. The wolves Sköll and Hati hunt the sun and moon, and at Ragnarök Sköll will at last swallow the sun. The chariot is described in Grímnismál and Gylfaginning. The horses are harnessed beneath the shield Svalinn, 'the cooling one', which keeps the earth from being burnt, and their manes are cooled by wind. Sól is sister to the moon-charioteer Máni, and both are doomed to be caught by the pursuing wolves; in the Eddic telling the sun grew pale as the end of the world neared, a sign of the long twilight to come. In retellings of Ragnarök the sun goes dark when Sköll finally seizes it, and the world plunges into the three winters without a summer.

name: The Sunken Church Bell
description: The sunken church bell is a recurring folk motif of Sweden and the wider Nordic region: a church bell that lies lost in a lake or river, usually because it sank while being ferried to a church or was dragged down by a troll or the water-folk who hated its ringing. The bell is sometimes said to toll faintly beneath the surface on Christmas night or other holy nights, and treasure-hunters who try to raise it are said to glimpse it and then watch it slip away again, unless a pure-hearted person can win it. The legend is told in many local variants across Sweden, Norway, and Finland, often tied to named lakes and parishes. It also echoes a real custom, since church bells were occasionally lost in transport. The motif survives in place-lore, folk music, and children's stories as one of the most beloved lake legends of the north.

name: The Sword of Antar
description: The sword Dhami, the chosen blade of Antarah ibn Shaddad, the pre-Islamic warrior-poet of the Arabian Peninsula whose exploits fill the medieval romance Sirah 'Antar. In the sira, Antar wins the sword in combat and carries it through the wars of the tribe of Abs and his long struggle to marry his cousin Abla, who appears in his poetry and in the romance as his lifelong beloved. The romance is literary, built up over centuries around the historical sixth-century poet, and the sword's named exploits grow with the telling, so that Dhami accrues its own mini-legend inside the larger epic. It stands alongside the legendary blades of Arabic tradition as the emblem of a hero who won his freedom and his name by the sword and the ode together.

name: The Sword of Goliath
description: The sword of the Philistine champion Goliath, taken as spoil after the shepherd David slew him and later kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at the sanctuary of Nob, where the fugitive David received it, saying there was none like it. The weapon is described in the First Book of Samuel, and David's possession of it anchors his kingship narrative in the biblical account, the champion's own blade becoming the king's trusted arm. The Philistine forging of iron in the early Iron Age made such swords prized and rare, which lends the story its realistic edge. Its fate after the reign of David is not recorded, so the sword survives only in the text, yet it remains one of the most famous spoils of war in biblical literature.

name: The Tallow Candle
description: The tallow candle of a poem credited to a young Hans Christian Andersen and found in the Danish national archive in 2012. In the poem a rough, unlit candle complains that it has never burned, until it finds its true use and gives light, a moral tale about purpose and self-worth. The discovery pushed the start of Andersen's literary career back to the early 1820s, and the poem is now treated as his earliest known work. The candle is remembered as the first of the everyday objects Andersen made speak.

name: The Temple Menorah
description: The seven-branched golden lampstand of the Tabernacle and later of the Jerusalem Temple, prescribed in the Book of Exodus as a beaten-gold work with almond-shaped cups, knobs, and blossoms, kept burning in the sanctuary before the veil. Carried by the Levites in the wilderness and set in the Temple built by Solomon, it was among the vessels plundered when the Temple fell; its image survives on the Arch of Titus in Rome, where Roman soldiers are shown bearing it off. The fate of the lampstand after 70 CE, whether lost at sea, hidden, or carried to Rome and later to Constantinople or Carthage, became a theme of Jewish legend and diaspora memory. The seven-branched form, the most enduring symbol of the Temple, was adopted in the modern era as the emblem of the State of Israel.

name: The Tinderbox
description: The magic flint and tinder of Hans Christian Andersen's tale, in which a soldier finds an old witch's tinderbox in a hollow tree guarded by three enormous dogs with eyes as large as saucers, wagon wheels, and round towers. Each strike of the flint summons one of the dogs, which bring him money, carry the princess to him at night, and finally rescue him from the gallows. The story, built on older folk motifs of the magic object and tamed or grateful animals, turned the homely tinderbox into the key to wealth and a kingdom. The three metal dogs of the tale are themselves remembered as folkloric creatures.

name: The Treasure in Säby Creek
description: A hidden treasure said to lie in a creek at Säby in Småland, at the centre of a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Treasure in Säby Creek', the buried hoard is guarded or hard-won, and the treasure-seekers' venture into the creek tests their courage and luck. It belongs to the large Swedish family of tales about treasure guarded in the landscape, where gold lies under stones, in mounds, or at the bottom of waters, and where the guardian is a troll, a draug, or a burning light that marks the spot. Such tales taught that the treasure could be won only by the right person at the right hour, often on a holy night, and that greed or a misread sign cost the seekers everything. The creek at Säby keeps the promise and the warning of all such hoards.

name: The Troll Shoes
description: Shoes worn by a troll in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Troll Shoes', the troll's footwear, or the wearing of it, lets a human stride over mountains or move faster than thought, and the shoes are won or put on during the tale's test. The wonder-shoes belong to a wider family of magic footwear in Nordic tales, where boots or shoes carry the wearer across any distance, the same gift that appears in tales of seven-league boots elsewhere in Europe. Winning them usually demands courage or a clever bargain with the troll, and wearing them well shows the hero's worth. The troll's shoes are a typical wonder-object of Swedish troll tales, where the hidden folk's tools are both a danger and a prize for the human who can take them.

name: The Troll's Mitten
description: A mitten that a troll or giant is said to have dropped and left behind, so large that a human could use it for shelter or sleep inside the thumb. The motif of the lost glove or mitten of the troll folk appears in Swedish tales as proof of the hidden people's size, and finding it is both marvellous and dangerous. In one telling a traveller lost in the woods finds shelter from the storm inside a huge abandoned mitten, only to learn at dawn that he has slept in the dropped glove of a jätte, one of the ancient giants of Swedish folklore. The giants and the trolls of Swedish tradition are close kin — both dwell in the mountains and the deep forest, and both are of impossible size — and the same lost-mitten story is told of each. The mitten is thus a story-teller's proof of the scale of the other world: a single dropped garment that shows how small the human world is beside the hidden one.

name: The Tunisian Fibula
description: The large silver pin or brooch, often triangular with a central coral or enamel stud and a long pointed pin, worn by Amazigh women across Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco to fasten the shawl, and passed down as a bridal heirloom and protective talisman. Known as a tazabt in Tamazight, it is among the most characteristic ornaments of Maghrebi dress, its shape echoing the Roman-era brooches that secured the cloaks of the same region. The fibula often held a chain linking a pair of brooches across the chest, and its pointed pin served as a weapon, a tool, and a token of married standing. Silver and coral remain the preferred materials, and museum collections of Maghrebi dress and jewellery display the fibula as a defining piece of Amazigh identity, still worn at weddings and festivals.

name: The Uraeus
description: The rearing cobra worn on the brow of the pharaoh and of deities such as Ra, embodying the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt and of the crown. The uraeus spat fire at the king's enemies and stood for the blazing eye that defended the sun god, and its image on the royal diadem made the king's anger divine. Golden examples survive on royal regalia, most famously the cobra and vulture that guard the brow of Tutankhamun's gold mask, the vulture being the goddess Nekhbet of Upper Egypt paired with Wadjet. In temple scenes the uraeus rises from the brows of gods and kings alike, and the 'uraeus serpent' became in Greek and Roman writers a byword for the power of the Egyptian crown.

name: The Vittra Gifts
description: Gifts of the vittra, the coins, bread, or small silver objects that the hidden folk of northern Sweden were believed to press upon helpful humans or to leave in their path. The gifts came as payment for a service, thanks for a kindness, or a promise of friendship, and accepting a vittra gift was held to bring luck to the farm and the family. The hidden people tested the receiver's character: gratitude and restraint were rewarded, while greed or disrespect brought misfortune, and the gifts sometimes turned to leaves or bark at dawn when taken in the wrong spirit. To refuse a vittra gift outright was also dangerous, as it insulted the givers. The giving of gifts is a core motif of Swedish vittra tradition, shaping the cautious courtesy that country people were expected to show the hidden folk.

name: The Votive Ship
description: The votive ship (votivskepp), a model ship hung from the vault of a Swedish church, given in thanks for rescue at sea. Sailors and fishermen commissioned the models after storms, and hundreds still hang in Swedish churches and chapels, some with their rigging and little flags intact, carrying painted names and dates of the storm or the voyage. The ship joins the church's prayers to the sea's dangers, a documented custom from the late Middle Ages onward, and the models were made with such care that they are prized as records of old shipbuilding. The gift placed the ship, her crew, and their families under the protection of the church and its saints, and the model kept the vow alive as long as it hung. The votive ship is one of the most moving objects of Nordic church folk-culture, the sailor's thanksgiving made visible.

name: The Völva's Staff
description: The staff of the seeress or völva, who in saga accounts carried a knobbed staff as the badge of her office. Eiríks saga rauða describes the seeress Þorbjörg with a staff topped with a brass knob as she worked her seidr. Iron rods found in Viking-age female graves may be such staffs, though the identification is debated by archaeologists. The staff was more than a tool: it was the visible sign of the woman who could chant the seidr, see the future, and speak with the dead. In Eiríks saga the staff of the visiting völva is described in detail, and its metal knob allowed it to be placed upright in the ground during the ritual. Tales of the völva's prophecy — as when a seeress was summoned to a chieftain's court to chant the fate of the land — keep the staff's image alive in later Icelandic story.

name: The War Shield of Neith
description: The emblem of the goddess Neith of Sais: a shield across which two crossed arrows are set, combining her natures as a war goddess and a weaver into a single sign. Attested as her writing from the earliest Egyptian hieroglyphs, the emblem was painted on her temple walls, carved on votive objects, and adopted as the badge of her cult city. The Greek and Roman writers Plutarch and Herodotus both describe the goddess and her warlike symbol, and Herodotus records the shrine of Neith at Sais with its festival of lamps. As one of the oldest goddess emblems of Egypt, the shield-and-arrows remained in use into the Graeco-Roman period, when Neith, identified with Athena, still bore the crossed arrows.

name: The Wesekh Collar
description: The broad beaded collar worn across the chest and shoulders by pharaohs, queens, nobles, and gods, built of rows of faience and semiprecious beads and capped with golden falcon-headed terminals, the name wesekh meaning 'broad'. Such collars were given as royal gifts, as the Amarna letters record the sending of broad collars of gold between courts, and they were buried with the dead, who are shown in tomb scenes receiving them from the gods. Tutankhamun's burial yielded dozens in gold, glass, carnelian, and turquoise-coloured faience, many laid directly on the mummy. The weight and splendour of the collar marked rank, and its spreading rays of beads lent the wearer the protection and favour of the sun god.

name: The Whistling Arrow
description: The whistling arrow is the signal arrow of the Mongol armies, tipped with a drilled bone or wooden head that shrieked in flight, and it was used by Genghis Khan's cavalry to direct charges, ambushes, and encirclements across the steppe. Described by Persian chroniclers such as Juvaini and by Chinese observers, the arrow worked by sound rather than by wounding: the drilled head, often globular with holes, screamed as it flew, and the direction and number of whistles could carry simple commands to units spread across the plain. The technology descended from the signal arrows of the earlier steppe peoples, and it allowed the tightly coordinated movements that made the Mongol armies so formidable. The whistle is also associated with hunting and with the signals of the ordo, the ruler's camp. The whistling arrow survives as a motif of the swift, coordinated warfare that built the empire, and reproductions are made for museums and festivals.

name: Three Sisters Garden
description: The Three Sisters garden is the Haudenosaunee method of planting corn, beans and squash together in a single mound, each crop supporting the others: the corn stalk gives the beans a pole to climb, the beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn, and the squash spreads its broad leaves to shade the roots and hold moisture. The three crops are called the sisters, or Deohako in Iroquoian tradition, inseparable companions given to the people by the Creator, and they are honoured in ceremonies through the growing season, especially at the Green Corn Festival. The system fed the Haudenosaunee confederacy for centuries and is today studied as a model of sustainable companion planting. Stories of the three sisters carry the moral of mutual support, and many modern gardeners and Indigenous food movements have revived the mounds. The garden remains the living foundation of Haudenosaunee agriculture and identity.

name: Thuan Thien Sword
description: Thuan Thien, the Sword of Heaven's Will, is the magic blade given to the farmer-king Le Loi during his revolt against the Ming occupation of Dai Viet in the fifteenth century, when the golden turtle god Kim Qui surfaced from the waters to present it. With the sword Le Loi's army defeated the Ming and he founded the Later Le dynasty, ruling as the national hero of Vietnamese independence. After the victory, when the king was boating on the lake in Hanoi, the great turtle rose again and seized the sword, returning it to its divine owner, and the lake was renamed Hoan Kiem, the Lake of the Returned Sword. The story is told in the fifteenth-century Lam Son thuc luc chronicle and is a centrepiece of Vietnamese national identity, and the island pagoda Ngoc Son on the lake commemorates the event. Thuan Thien is also celebrated in the legend of the turtle that bore the sword, and the blade remains the emblem of Vietnam's struggle for independence.

name: Thunderbird Club
description: The thunderbird club is a heavy carved club whose grip and head take the form of a great bird, most often the thunderbird, so that each blow falls with the power of the being whose wingbeats make thunder and whose flashing eyes cast lightning. Carried by chiefs and warriors of the Northwest Coast and some Plains nations, the club is both a weapon and an emblem, its carved beak, wings and tail binding the bearer to the great sky bird of the origin stories. Because the bird's image was itself charged with power, such a club was a personal and often hereditary treasure. The thunderbird appears across the continent in different guises, and its image on a weapon proclaimed that the bearer struck with the force of the storm. Surviving clubs are treasured in museum collections as masterworks of Native carving.

name: Tizerzai Brooch
description: The tizerzai is a large silver fibula brooch of the Amazigh (Berber) peoples of Morocco and Algeria, traditionally worn in pairs at the shoulders to fasten the tasseled woollen wraps and tunics of women. Triangular or delta-shaped, each brooch fastens with a long pin and is often richly worked with granulation, filigree, enamel and inset glass or coral, so that the clasp of a garment becomes a display of a family's wealth and craft. Ethnographic collections, including those documented by the French artist Jean Besancenot in his 1942 Costumes du Maroc, record pairs of tizerzai worn by dancers and brides in southern and Atlas communities, with some examples reaching more than a metre in length when the connecting chains are counted. In Amazigh tradition the ornaments protect the wearer from the evil eye and declare her social standing, and they are passed from mother to daughter along with the rules of how they should be worn. Because the fibula's shape is echoed in the triangular motifs of Amazigh weaving and tattooing, the tizerzai is today read as a marker of indigenous North African identity.

name: Tizona
description: Tizona is the sword the Cantar de Mio Cid names as El Cid's great blade, 'worth a thousand marks of gold', which the poem says he won from King Yucef of Valencia and later demanded back from the Infantes de Carrión after they had disgraced it. The sword kept at the Museo de Burgos has a straight double-edged blade of the 11th century, of high-carbon steel with a fuller, whose metal was studied by the Universidad Complutense de Madrid in the 1990s and confirmed as forged in the hero's era, from iron probably of Sierra Morena or northern Morocco; the Gothic hilt and the acid-etched inscriptions, 'Io soi Tizona fue fecha en la era de mille quarenta' and 'Ave Maria gratia plena Dominus mecum', are later additions of the 15th-16th century. The claim that it was El Cid's rests on legend and later provenance rather than on contemporary proof. Declared a national treasure in 2003 and bought by the Junta de Castilla y León in 2007, the blade remains the most iconic object connected with the Cid.

name: Tjurunga
description: The tjurunga is the sacred board or stone of the Arrernte and other central Australian peoples, engraved with the patterns of the Dreaming and treated as the physical body of an ancestral being. The boards are kept in secret storehouses and brought out for initiation and ceremony, and a tjurunga is handed down as a bond between the living, the land and the ancestral beings, its power bound to the pattern carved on its surface. The name is also spelled churinga, and the classic accounts were written by Spencer and Gillen from the Alice Springs region. Tjurunga are restricted objects of the men's law, and their designs and ceremonies are not shown to the uninitiated or to women, so the published records describe the boards only in general terms and with respect for the secrecy that still surrounds them.

name: Toki Poutangata
description: The toki poutangata is the ceremonial adze of the Maori, fitted with a blade of pounamu or basalt lashed to a carved wooden handle and hung with a plait of fibre and feathers. Unlike the working adze, the toki poutangata was not used for daily woodwork but was carried before a rangatira and raised in speeches as a badge of chiefly authority, and the finest blades were treasured heirlooms passed down through the great lineages. The name means the adze of the great chief, and the object appears in the ceremonial life of the marae, where the taking up of a toki could mark the acceptance of leadership or the settlement of a dispute. The greenstone blades were cut and ground over long months, so the finished toki carried the labour and skill of its maker as well as the mana of its owner.

name: Tongan Ngatu (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of Tonga, made by beating the inner bark of the hiapo (paper mulberry) into strips and pasting them together with starch into large sheets, which are then decorated in working parties called koka'anga. Women rub brown and black dyes over carved kupesi rubbing boards to print repeating geometric motifs — chevrons, zigzags and diagonal bands — that carry the patterns of their families and districts. Ngatu is given at weddings, funerals and royal ceremonies, used as floor mats, wall coverings and dance costumes, and the largest ceremonial pieces, some hundreds of metres long, are presented to the king on occasions of state, so that the cloth doubles as a record of the kingdom's ceremonies and its givers.

name: Topshur (Altai Two-String Lute)
description: Two-stringed plucked lute of the Altai people, carved with a shallow bowl body, hide soundboard and gut or horsehair strings. The topshur accompanies the kaychi storytellers, who perform the great Altai heroic epics such as the Tale of Maadai-Kara; its music is bound to Altai oral tradition and is often played before the fire and during ritual. The player holds the instrument against the body and plucks with a bare hand, and the music is thought to summon the presence of the epic's heroes as the singer speaks their deeds. The two strings are sometimes tuned a fourth apart, and the tone is soft and earthy, suited to the low, long-narrative voice of the kaychi. Because the epic is sacred, the topshur is treated with care, and a player is sometimes said to warm the hide soundboard by the fire before beginning, so that the instrument will sing. Kaychi performance of Maadai-Kara can last a whole night, the topshur's ostinato carrying the story through the darkness.

name: Totem Pole
description: Totem poles are tall carvings made from whole trunks of western red cedar, raised by the Haida, Tlingit, Tsimshian, Kwakwaka'wakw and other Northwest Coast peoples before houses, at graves and as welcome or memorial figures. The carved animals and beings are not idols but crests: they record a clan's lineage, its founding ancestors and the supernatural helpers who saved them, and a pole is read by those who know the family's history. House poles stood against the front of a big house, mortuary poles held an ancestor's remains, and the figures often include raven, eagle, bear, wolf, whale and thunderbird. Canadian law banned the potlatch in 1884, and carving declined sharply, but the art was revived in the twentieth century and has become a proud symbol of Indigenous identity across the region. New poles are still raised today with ceremony and feasting, continuing an unbroken tradition of sculptural storytelling.

name: Trident of Poseidon
description: The three-pronged trident of Poseidon, forged by the Cyclopes, that shakes the earth, splits cliffs, and raises or calms storms; with it he struck the rock of the Acropolis to produce a salt spring in his contest with Athena. It is the standard emblem of sea power and earthquakes in Greek myth, carried by the god in art from the archaic age onward. In later retellings the trident is the very tool by which horses and springs are drawn from the ground. Its three points became the sign of the sea in Mediterranean culture.

name: Trishula of Shiva
description: The trishula is the three-pronged spear or trident of the Hindu god Shiva, carried in his hand and planted before his shrines, so that the trident has become his most recognizable attribute. The three prongs are traditionally read as the three gunas of sattva, rajas and tamas, or as the triad of creation, preservation and destruction, and the weapon appears as an instrument of both justice and destruction in the myths. In the celebrated tale of the three demon cities, Shiva is said to have burned the demon Tripura and his aerial cities with a single arrow, while in other stories it is the trishula itself that he hurls to punish or to sever. In the two Ganesha legends the trident plays a decisive role, for it is Shiva's trishula that cuts off the head of the boy Ganesha at the door of Parvati's chamber, and the same blow is retold in different words in accounts of Ganesha's origin. The trishula is also carried by Shaiva ascetics, imprinted on offerings, and reproduced in metal as a protective emblem over homes and shrines.

name: Trobriand Yam House (Bwaima)
description: Ornate storehouse of the Trobriand Islands of Papua New Guinea, raised on posts with a steeply pitched roof and a decorative triangular gable, first described in the anthropological studies of Bronisław Malinowski. The facade is built of wooden slabs tied with coconut-husk fasteners, and yams — the central wealth and prestige crop — are displayed in tight rows through the slits so that the house announces its owner's abundance. Yams are still the symbolic currency of the islands: men cultivate them for their sisters' families under the urigubu obligation, and a man's status is read in the size and beauty of his yam house, which is built to display abundance as the symbolic face of his household.

name: Troiță
description: Troița is the wayside cross of Romania, a hand-carved wooden cross sheltered under a little roof, erected at crossroads, springs, bridges and village edges to protect travellers and to honour the dead. In the wood-carving country of Maramureș the crosses are true monuments, their beams covered with vine scrolls, geometric rosettes, suns and sometimes the image of the Crucified, with inscriptions naming the dead and the year, and the oldest surviving examples go back to the eighteenth century. The cross is set up by families for a departed relative, at the place of a sudden death, or as a vow, and passers-by cross themselves before it, so the troița stands at the meeting of Christian devotion and the old belief that crossroads and water were liminal, dangerous places. New troițe are still carved and raised every year, making the wayside cross a living school of Romanian folk woodcarving.

name: Troll Porridge Bowl
description: At Christmas, Swedish farm families set out a bowl of rice porridge with butter for the tomte, the farm's household spirit. The bowl was left in the attic, the barn, or by the hearth; if the butter was hidden or the porridge forgotten, the tomte was said to abandon the farm or work mischief. The custom, documented across Sweden into the twentieth century, is the subject of many tomte tales. The offering was made on Christmas Eve or Christmas night, and the family looked the next morning to see whether the porridge had been eaten; the tomte, a small bearded figure who watched over the farm, was easy to offend and quick to reward a well-kept household. Tales tell of the tomte thrashing the hired girl who hid the butter, or blessing the family that always remembered his bowl, so that the porridge became the heart of the farm's winter ritual. The custom survives today in the small bowl of rice porridge still set out in many Swedish homes.

name: Troll's Gift Ring
description: The troll's gift ring belongs to a widespread Nordic belief that the hidden folk — the huldra, the hill-folk, and the trolls — sometimes press gifts upon humans: rings, bracelets, belts, or coins that gleam like gold. In the folk tradition it is said that a person who accepted such a gift courteously and without greed could keep lasting luck, while one who snatched greedily at more, or refused rudely, would be cursed with misfortune; at dawn the fine gift might also be found to have turned to leaves, moss, or ashes, the standard fate of fairy gold. The motif is told across Norway, Sweden, and Denmark with many local variations, and it belongs to the wider Scandinavian lore of encounters with the underworld folk rather than to any single saga. The custom of the gift-ring illustrates the deep belief that luck in this world hung on how one treated the hidden neighbours.

name: Troll's Gold
description: In Norwegian legend, gold the trolls leave or press on humans, coins, rings, and bracelets that seem to be treasure. Such gold is often said to turn to leaves, shavings, or stone at dawn unless the finder keeps silence or is grateful. The tales warn that grasping after troll treasure brings misfortune, while freely given treasure could bless a whole household. The troll gold follows the same rule as every gift of the hidden folk: it is real only to the one who takes it without greed and keeps the secret, and it mocks the covetous by turning worthless in the hand. Farmers who found a ring or a coin on the mountain road knew better than to boast of it, and families that accepted a troll's gift in the right spirit kept their luck through generations. The motif runs through Norwegian sagn collections as a warning against the desire for easy wealth.

name: Trollkors
description: A protective cross carved, cut, or forged onto a building, door, or object to stop trolls and harmful powers from harming people or livestock. Documented chiefly in Uppland, Sweden, with similar marks on Norwegian medieval buildings, the crosses were set over doorways and windows and on cookware and loaves of bread. A looped-iron amulet from Dalarna in the 1990s became a tourist talisman. The carved cross worked by turning the object or the doorway into a sign of the blessed, which the hidden folk could not cross, and it was cut into the wood of new buildings, over the cattle-stall, and on tools that passed through dangerous places. The name trollkors records the enemy it was set against, and the mark survives in folk art and modern craft long after the belief that shaped it.

name: Trolls' Cast Stones
description: Large scattered boulders that Norwegian legend says trolls hurled in anger, or dropped while fleeing from the sound of church bells at dawn. Almost every valley names its stray blocks, and many show the supposed imprint of a giant hand, heel, or thumb; the same stones also mark the ends of the old paths the trolls were said to follow. Geologists read the boulders as glacial erratics carried by ice thousands of years ago, yet the trolls' version and the geologists' explanation long coexisted in popular speech. The names linger on maps, and the stones still anchor place-lore from Telemark to the far north.

name: Trundholm Sun Chariot
description: A Bronze Age cult figure found in the Trundholm bog on Zealand, Denmark, in 1902: a bronze horse pulling a large gilded bronze disc, all mounted on a six-wheeled stand. The disc is gilded on one side and plain bronze on the other, an image usually read as the sun drawn across the sky by day and returning beneath the earth by night. It is the oldest such sun-horse image in Nordic art and a central piece in the debate over Bronze Age sun worship. The chariot is now in the National Museum of Denmark and has become a national symbol, reproduced on coins and in popular culture.

name: Tsagaan Tug
description: The tsagaan tug, the white standard, is the ensign of Genghis Khan's lineage that Mongol tradition honours as the sacred symbol of the khagan's authority, kept at the mausoleum complex in Ordos and paraded at the Naadam festival together with the nine black banners. The standard is a spear shaft crowned with a horsehair tuft or a looped top, and its white colour links it to the heavenly realm, the midday sun, and peace, while the nine black standards of the great khan stood for war and the nine tribes of the Mongols. In Mongol belief the tug is an object of reverence in its own right, and the ceremony of raising and lowering it is attended by ritual and by the offering of airag, fermented mare's milk. The white standard is central to the cult of Genghis Khan that survives among the Ordos Mongols, who preserve his relics in the mausoleum. The tug remains the emblem of the steppe khans and of Mongolian sovereignty.

name: Tuareg Takuba Sword
description: The takuba is the straight-bladed sword of the Tuareg of the Sahara and Sahel, a double-edged blade of about a metre with a deep crossguard and a flat metal pommel. Because Tuareg custom regards iron as unclean, the guard and grip are covered with tooled leather, and the scabbard is worked with stamped and pierced designs that reflect the wealth and rank of its owner. Swords were made and mounted by the inadan (blacksmith) caste, who spoke their own secret language and were credited with magical power over metal. Given to a young man as he came of age, the takuba marked nobility and courage, and it was carried in raids, duels, and the caravan wars of the desert until firearms displaced it. Many blades came from European or Arab forges and were remounted in Sahelian style, evidence of a long trade across the Sahara. Today the takuba is worn at festivals and ceremonies as a badge of Tuareg identity and honour.

name: Tubeteika (Tatar Skullcap)
description: Hemispherical embroidered skullcap, the traditional headwear of Tatar men. Decorated with silk or velvet embroidery in floral and geometric patterns, the tubeteika was worn at home and in public, while the taller cone-shaped kelepush was worn outdoors. Embroidered tubeteikas were part of festive dress and remain a symbol of Tatar national identity. The cap is made of velvet or thick cotton sewn in four wedge-shaped panels, joined at the crown and embroidered by hand with gold thread, silk and beads; the ornament covers the crown and often spills over the band. In Tatar custom a man removed his tubeteika only indoors and in his own home, and a cap was sewn specially for weddings and festivals. Kazan Tatar embroidery is famous for its small, dense stitches, and 19th-century examples in museum collections show the deep red, green and gold palette typical of the region. The tubeteika is still worn by Tatar men on holidays and by performers of Tatar music.

name: Tulwar
description: The tulwar is the classic curved sabre of the Indian subcontinent, with a single cutting edge, a shallowly curved blade and a distinctive hilt capped by a disc pommel with a pierced tang button. The hilt, with its broad, flanged guard and long grip, gives the sword an unusually well-balanced feel, and tulwars were carried by Rajput, Maratha and Mughal horsemen for centuries, from the late medieval period through the wars of the 18th and 19th centuries. Blade steel was often made locally or imported from Persia, and many surviving tulwars preserve fine watered-steel blades with armourers' marks, while ornamental examples are damascened with gold lines. The sword also functioned as a social marker: a warrior's tulwar was honoured, taken on campaign, carried on his person at court and given as a reward for valour, and old tulwars frequently carry inscriptions naming their owners. Museums now catalogue these sabres as the standard sidearm of Indian cavalry, and the tulwar's design influenced the swords carried by British army units in India.

name: Tumi
description: The tumi is the crescent-bladed ceremonial knife of the Andes, a wide arched blade of gold, silver, copper or bronze on a rectangular handle, used for sacrifices and depicted in Moche art cutting the throat of victims. Later Sican and Lambayeque metalworkers made ornate gold tumis crowned with the figure of Naylamp, the mythic founder of the Lambayeque dynasty shown as a bird-man, and the knife passed into Chimu and Inca ritual. The most famous example, the Tumi of Illimo or of Lambayeque, is a gold blade about 41 centimetres tall weighing nearly a kilogram, recovered from Huaca Las Ventanas at Batan Grande in 1936. Because most known examples are of precious metal, scholars believe they were largely symbolic, displayed in ritual and buried with lords rather than used for daily work. In modern Peru the tumi has become the national symbol of the country, reproduced in folk art, tourism souvenirs and even the emblem of the Peruvian College of Physicians.

name: Tune Rune Stone
description: The oldest known Norwegian runestone, found in pieces at Tune in Østfold and dated to around 400 CE. Its short inscription in the early runic alphabet records how heirs divided a man's estate and is among the earliest attestations of a Germanic language. The archaic word forms make it a key document for scholars of early Norse language and runic writing. Cut from red granite in the shape of a rough pyramid about two meters high, the stone stood at a farm before being set into the floor of a church doorway, where it was rediscovered in the 19th century. Its inscription in Proto-Norse, 'ek wiwaz after woduride... worahto runor', 'I, Wiwaz, made the runes in memory of Woduridaz, my lord', names the carver and the dead, and scholars long debated the reading of the names before the text was settled. The stone now stands in the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo.

name: Tunisian Chechia Cap
description: The chechia is the traditional red felt cap of Tunisia, worn by men since the early modern period and regarded as a national emblem of the country. Its production was long a chain of specialized workshops: wool was combed, spun and knitted into a raw cap, then fulled with water and heat at sites such as El Battan on the Medjerda river, dyed crimson with madder or similar dyes, and finally stretched and finished over wooden moulds in Tunis. The craft flourished with the arrival of Andalusian Morisco artisans at the start of the 17th century, and their guild became so influential that a whole quarter of the medina of Tunis, the Souk Ech-Chaouachine, was built in 1691-92 for the trade of the so-called chaouachis. A single chechia could take about two months to pass through the hands of these workshops, and the finished caps were exported across North and West Africa and even to Europe. Worn for prayer, for feasts and weddings, and formerly as part of daily dress under the turban, the chechia is distinct from the Ottoman fez and remains a living symbol of Tunisian identity.

name: Tupilak
description: The tupilak is a spirit figure of the Greenlandic Inuit, assembled by an angakkuq, a shaman, from the parts of animals, bone, skin, hair and sinew, sometimes joined with the remains of a dead child, and given life through ritual chants so that it could be sent against an enemy. The tupilak was cast into the sea and swam to its victim, but the magic was dangerous in both directions: if the victim proved stronger, the spirit was said to turn back on its maker, and only a public confession could break its power. Because the figures were made from perishable matter, none of the true tupilak survive, and the ritual was feared more than seen. In the early twentieth century carvers began making grotesque figures from walrus ivory, whale tooth, wood and caribou antler, and the tupilak became a celebrated form of Greenlandic art, sold across the world. The carvings carry the old menace into the gallery, part talisman and part monster.

name: Tuvaluan Paopao (Fishing Canoe)
description: Small sailing canoe of the Tuvaluan islands, fitted with a single outrigger float and a triangular sail, used for fishing on the lagoon and the open reef and for the short voyages between the atolls. Built by hand from island timber, with the hull lashed with sennit to the outrigger booms, the paopao is light enough to be beached above the tide and sailed by one or two men. Its design, like that of the canoes of the wider Pacific, was carried by navigational knowledge passed down across the atolls, and the paopao remains both a working fishing craft and a symbol of Tuvaluan seamanship.

name: Tyrfing
description: Tyrfing is the cursed sword of the Hervarar saga, forged by the dwarves Dvalinn and Dulinn for King Svafrlami. When the king forced the dwarves to give him the finest blade they could make, they laid a curse upon it in return: the sword would never miss a stroke, never rust, would kill a man every time it was drawn, and would be the cause of three great evils. After killing the dwarves, Svafrlami was himself slain in a duel with the berserk Arngrímr, and the blade passed into the hands of Arngrímr's sons. The shield-maiden Hervör later raised the sword from the barrow of her dead father Angantýr by overcoming his ghost, and the curse drove the saga's later heroes, including Heiðrekr, to their deaths. Tyrfing is one of the archetypal cursed blades of Germanic legend and is often compared with Sigurðr's Gram.

name: Tzompantli
description: The tzompantli, from Nahuatl for 'skull rack', was a structure of wooden poles threaded with the skulls of sacrificial victims, erected beside Aztec temple platforms where daylight could display them to the sun. Spanish chroniclers were astonished by the great rack beside the Templo Mayor; Andres de Tapia counted the skulls in the tens of thousands, and Bernal Diaz described towers of them stacked in the ceremonial precinct. Excavations at the Templo Mayor uncovered the Huey Tzompantli, a carved stone platform of skull rows with hundreds of drilled skulls still mounted on wooden posts. The practice was not unique to the Aztecs: Maya centres such as Chichen Itza raised similar racks decorated with carved skulls. Beyond the macabre display, tzompantli were part of the Mesoamerican belief that sacrifice fed the sun and the earth, making the racks a public record of cosmic debt.

name: Ulfberht Sword
description: A class of high-quality Viking-age swords bearing the +ULFBERHT+ mark, found in large numbers in Norwegian graves and hoards. Their crucible-made high-carbon steel was far harder and stronger than the ordinary bloomery iron of the day, making them treasured war gear; some blades carry misspelled copies of the mark and were likely forgeries made on poorer steel. The name itself is Frankish, and metallurgical analysis points to origin in the Rhineland or Carolingian territory, showing that the finest Norse swords were trade goods brought north. About a hundred and seventy blades are known across Scandinavia and beyond, spanning the ninth to eleventh centuries, and the name has since passed into popular culture as a byword for the Viking sword.

name: Ulu
description: The ulu is the broad-bladed knife of the Inuit and other Arctic peoples, a semicircular blade of slate or iron fitted with a short handle, used by the women of the household for every cutting task of the camp. With its curved edge and its grip held in the whole hand, the ulu lets pressure be applied with the arm, slicing through thick hide, frozen meat and fish with a rocking motion, and it is used for skinning game, trimming skins, cutting food and scraping hides for sewing. The shape is ancient, blades of ground slate have been found in Arctic sites, and it was adapted to steel when trade made metal available; regional forms range from the small knife of fine work to larger blades for heavy hide. The ulu is primarily a woman's tool and a symbol of the household's life, and it remains in use across the North today, with modern steel versions sold and used alongside traditional ones. Its quiet usefulness made it, with the qulliq, one of the two essential tools of the Arctic home.

name: Urnes Stave Church
description: The oldest of Norway's surviving stave churches, standing at Urnes on the eastern shore of the Sognefjord and dated to around 1130. Its carved west portal, worked in the so-called Urnes style of interlaced beasts, serpents, and slender climbing vines, carries on Viking-age animal ornament even as the timber church above it was rebuilt in the mid-12th century. The stylized lion battling the serpent on the portal is often read as a Christian image of Christ overcoming evil. The building is a UNESCO World Heritage site and a key link between pagan Norse animal art and the architecture of the medieval church, and the portal's carvings are among the most studied images in Scandinavian medieval art.

name: Urðarbrunnr
description: Urðarbrunnr, the well of fate that lies beneath a root of the world tree Yggdrasil, beside which the three Norns dwell and shape the fates of men. The gods hold their council there, and swans swim in the well. Each day the Norns water the tree with its clay-white water and dew so that it never withers, making the well the source of all destiny in Norse myth. The well takes its name from Urðr, the eldest Norn, whose sisters Verðandi and Skuld spin and cut the threads of every life. Beneath other roots of the ash lie Mímir's well of wisdom and the spring Hvergelmir, so that the tree is nourished by the waters of fate, memory, and chaos at once. The daily watering — pouring the holy water and the clay over the ash — is the act that keeps the world tree alive, and the swans upon the well are the ancestors of all the swans in the world.

name: Ushabti Figurines
description: Small mummiform figurines placed in Egyptian tombs to perform field labour for the dead in the afterlife, inscribed with spell 6 of the Book of the Dead, in which the figure answers 'here I am' when summoned to work in the fields of the god of the dead. A single burial could hold several hundred, from a modest clay set to the 413 ushabtis buried with Tutankhamun in faience, wood, and stone, each furnished with the tiny hoe and basket of the peasant. The name derives from the Egyptian word meaning 'answerer', and the figures were made from the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period, their form and text changing little across two thousand years. Overseer ushabtis, distinguished by a kilt and whip, were added in the New Kingdom to supervise the labouring rows. Today they are among the most common and most recognisable artefacts of Egyptian museum collections.

name: Vajra of Indra
description: The vajra is the thunderbolt weapon of Indra, the storm god of the Rigveda, and the foremost weapon in early Indian mythography. In the Vedic hymns Indra wields the vajra to strike down the serpent-demon Vritra, who held back the world's waters, and by that blow releases rivers, rain and light; the word itself came to mean both the physical bolt and the diamond, as being unbreakable and irresistible. Later Puranic tradition gives a dramatic origin for the weapon, telling that the sage Dadhichi offered his own bones, from which the divine smiths forged the indestructible thunderbolt with which Indra defeated Vritra. In Hindu iconography the vajra appears as a short metal club with ribbed heads, carried by Indra and sometimes by other deities, while in Vajrayana Buddhism the same name and form were adopted for the ritual scepter held in the right hand during meditation and consecration, paired with a bell. Because of this double life, the vajra spans the worlds of Vedic warfare and Buddhist ritual as a symbol of indestructible truth.

name: Valaskjálf
description: Valaskjálf, the silver-roofed hall of Odin described in Grímnismál, one of the god's dwellings raised by the gods themselves. Within it stands Hliðskjálf, the far-seeing high seat from which Odin can watch all the worlds. The hall is thus the setting for the All-Father's watchfulness and a model for later accounts of his court. Snorri places the hall among Odin's greatest houses, roofed with silver and crowned by the seat that gave the god knowledge of everything that happens among gods, elves, men, and the dead. From Hliðskjálf Odin watched the journeys of his champions and the movements of his enemies, and it was from that seat that he could perceive all that was hidden. The name is sometimes glossed as the hall 'of the chosen', and it stands beside Valhöll as one of the two great royal halls of the one-eyed god.

name: Valaška
description: The valaška is the small axe of the Carpathian shepherds, a light iron head set on a long wooden haft that reaches the waist, serving at once as walking staff, digging tool and weapon. Slovak bača shepherds and hikers of the High Tatras carry the valaška through the mountains, and its handle is often ornamented with engraved patterns or metal mountings that mark the maker and the owner. Folk legend places the valaška in the hand of Juraj Jánošík, the eighteenth-century outlaw of the Tatra country who is said to have robbed the nobles and shared the booty with the poor, and the axe became an attribute of highland identity as much as the flute and the pipe. In the twentieth century the valaška was adopted as an emblem of Slovak mountaineering and folk life, and carved examples are kept as souvenirs and in ethnographic collections.

name: Valhöll
description: Valhöll, 'the hall of the slain', Odin's great hall where the Einherjar — warriors who died bravely in battle — fight each day and feast each night. Gylfaginning describes a hall of 540 doors, so vast that armies could pass through each. Its roof is said to be made of shields and spears, and Odin's wolves and ravens share the hall with the fallen. The warriors chosen by the valkyries from the battlefields were carried to the hall to train for the last battle at Ragnarök, when Odin would lead the Einherjar out against the wolf Fenrir and the hosts of chaos. At dawn they fought and at dusk they rose whole again to eat of the boar Sæhrímnir and drink mead, while the goddess Freyja took half the fallen to her own hall, Fólkvangr. In retellings of the end of the world, Valhalla is the gathering place where the dead heroes arm themselves for the doom of the gods.

name: Vanuatu Slit Drum (Tamtam)
description: Hollowed log drum of Vanuatu, carved from a single tree trunk with a narrow longitudinal slot and open ends, struck with wooden beaters to send a deep, carrying sound across the village and reef. In the northern islands, where the great carved tamtam stand upright before the village, the drums are monuments as much as instruments: many are carved with faces and stand several metres tall as records of chiefs and ancestors. The slit drum calls people to gatherings, announces deaths and ceremonies, keeps the rhythm of dances, and in grade-taking and other graded society rites the number and size of drums a village holds reflects its prestige.

name: Varnarstafur Valdemars
description: Varnarstafur Valdemars, 'Valdemar's protection stave', one of the most popular defensive signs of the Huld manuscript, drawn against enemies and ill-wishers. Its name is attached to a legendary king, and in the folk tradition it was carved on shields, doorways, and tools, carried wherever a person went armed or unarmed against harm. The Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Holmavík describes the stave as one that 'increases favour and happiness', and when evil was feared it could be laid out inside a hen-egg membrane with plaice gut and worn in the hat. The stave's work blended practical protection with the hope of a welcome reception, making it one of the most frequently reproduced of all the galdrastafir.

name: Vasilisa's Doll
description: Small wooden doll given to Vasilisa by her dying mother in the Russian fairy tale, which eats a morsel of the girl's food and helps her perform impossible tasks so that she survives her cruel stepmother and Baba Yaga. Recorded in Afanasyev's collection as 'Vasilisa the Beautiful', the doll is the helper-object of the tale, a folk counterpart to the magical helpers of later European fairy tales. The mother's blessing is essential: the doll works only for Vasilisa, must be fed a little food, and loses its power if others discover it. When Baba Yaga sets the impossible tasks of sorting grain, cleaning the hut and weaving cloth, the doll completes them overnight, and the witch herself wonders how the girl succeeds. The doll is sometimes said to carry the soul of the dead mother watching over her daughter; folklorists read it as motherly care transformed into a protective object.

name: Veena
description: The veena is the principal string instrument of South Indian (Carnatic) music and the emblem of Saraswati, the goddess of learning, who is always depicted holding a veena whose sound is said to be the voice of wisdom itself. The modern concert-instrument form, called the Saraswati veena, has a large resonator of jackwood with a second smaller gourd behind the neck, twenty-four fixed brass frets on the long fingerboard, and seven strings, four melody and three drone; it is plucked with a wire plectrum while the player sits cross-legged on the floor. Because it belongs to the goddess, the veena is also a ritual object, placed on a stand in the prayer room, and the celestial musicians of Hindu mythology, the gandharvas and the kinnaras, are traditionally pictured playing it together with lutes and cymbals. The word vina appears already in the Vedas, though the instrument has changed shape many times over three thousand years, and it gave its name to later instruments such as the sitar. Today the veena remains the classical instrument of the Carnatic stage, taught from childhood and associated with devotion as much as with concert performance.

name: Vegvísir
description: Vegvísir, the 'wayfinder', is an Icelandic magical stave drawn as a central point with radiating runic spokes, first attested in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860. The accompanying text promises that whoever carries the sign will never lose their way in storm or bad weather, even when the path is unknown, and the stave is drawn on paper, wood, or metal and carried as a talisman. Although it is often called a 'Viking compass', the earliest known source is a 19th-century grimoire, and the symbol has no confirmed Viking-Age counterpart — a point that popular culture frequently overlooks. Vegvísir has become the most widely reproduced of all the galdrastafir, appearing in tattoos, jewellery, and merchandise, and the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík displays it among the living folk-magic tradition.

name: Vejigante Mask
description: The vejigante mask of Ponce, Puerto Rico, is a carnival face of papier-mâché crowned with horns, given fangs, bulging eyes and brilliant colors, worn by the vejigante, the trickster of the Puerto Rican Carnival who whirls through the crowds chasing children and driving off evil spirits. The tradition fuses the Spanish festival, the word comes from vejiga, 'bladder,' after the dried bladders the first celebrants carried, with African and Taíno elements, and each town gave the figure its own face. Ponce's masks are the most elaborate, built up with wings and bristling horns; in Loíza the vejigante instead wears a horned mask of coconut or wire and a costume of layered, fluttering cloth. The craft passed from the great twentieth-century mask-makers of the Ponce families to a generation of folk artists, and the careta is now collected as serious Puerto Rican art. At carnival time the masks still roar, horned and laughing, at the heart of the island's most exuberant festival.

name: Veracruz Hacha
description: A hacha is a thin, wide stone carving shaped like an axe head but with a deliberately blunt edge, produced in huge numbers by the Classic Veracruz culture of the Gulf lowlands between about 300 and 900 CE. Hachas take the form of human heads, often in profile, and animal faces, carved in fine andesite or basalt with great realism, and the finest examples come from sites such as El Tajin and the Remojadas region. Scholars read them not as working tools but as ballgame emblems, displayed with the great stone yokes and palmas worn by players in the Mesoamerican ballgame; the head-shaped hachas are thought by some to commemorate the severed heads of sacrificed players. Their varied faces make them a key record of Classic Veracruz religious imagery, linking the ballgame to sun worship and sacrifice. Hundreds survive in museums, prized as one of the finest portrait traditions of ancient Mexico.

name: Verbos Easter Palms
description: Tall bouquets of dried and dyed grasses, flowers, mosses, juniper and willow, bound with leaves and seeds onto a rod of hazel or willow, carried to church on Palm Sunday for consecration and kept afterwards in an honoured place at home. The verba tradition has been practised for at least seven generations in villages northwest of Vilnius and is documented in paintings and ethnographies since the mid-1800s, and the palms are still made for Palm Sunday, for Easter and for the St. Casimir's Fair in Vilnius each March. The consecrated verba is kept by the household as a protection against storms and misfortune, hung behind the door or on the wall through the year.

name: Víðarr's Shoe
description: Víðarr's shoe is the enormous foot-covering of Víðarr, the silent son of Odin, made from the pieces of leather that people are said to have cut from their own shoes at heel and toe and set aside for the god. The Prose Edda explains that every man who wishes to help the god should donate such scraps, and the collected leather forms a shoe strong enough to hold against Fenrir's jaws. At Ragnarök the silent Víðarr sets the shoe against the wolf's lower jaw, grips the upper jaw with his hands, and tears the wolf's mouth apart, avenging the death of his father Odin. The detail of the shoe-scraps is one of the strangest and most memorable practical customs in the Eddas, and it connects the cosmic battle to the ordinary work of mending shoes. Víðarr's vengeance remains a fixed scene in every retelling of Ragnarök.

name: Waka Taua (Māori War Canoe)
description: The waka taua is the Maori war canoe, a long carved vessel that carried war parties on raids and conveyed chiefs in ceremony, often paddled by forty or more warriors. It was built from a single totara trunk, with the hull hollowed and shaped by adze, and fitted with carved prow and stern posts, a raised wash-strake and lashings of fibre; the prow commonly carried the carved figure of a taniwha, the guardian water spirit of Maori tradition. The launching and naming of a waka taua were accompanied by ritual and karakia, and the canoe itself was a symbol of tribal mana, so that a great waka bore the name of its tribe and its ancestors. When a war party paddled out, the crew performed haka and chanted in time with the strokes, and the waka was both a transport of war and a work of carved art.

name: Wampum Belt
description: Wampum belts are woven from cylindrical shell beads, the purple from quahog clam shells and the white from whelks, strung and woven into belts that served Eastern Woodlands peoples, above all the Haudenosaunee, as records of treaties, laws and history. Because the patterns carried meaning that had to be read aloud, wampum worked as memory in material form: the Hiawatha belt records the joining of the Five Nations, and the Great Law of Peace was both encoded in and recited over the belts. Colonial governments and missionaries also used wampum for diplomacy, while European traders turned the shell beads into a currency that flooded the market and reshaped their value. Strings and belts were exchanged to confirm a treaty or a condolence, and a belt given and accepted bound both sides to the words spoken over it. Haudenosaunee nations still hold and read ancient belts, and new belts are woven for modern agreements.

name: War Bonnet
description: The war bonnet, or eagle-feather headdress, is the grand plume of upright golden-eagle feathers worn by honoured leaders of the Plains nations such as the Lakota, Cheyenne, Blackfoot and Crow. Each feather had to be earned, given for an act of bravery, a coup counted in battle, or received through a vision, and the bonnet itself was assembled with ceremony. The straight-up bonnet with its long trailer familiar from photographs became prominent in the nineteenth century; earlier and regional forms varied widely, including buffalo-horn bonnets and feather roaches. Feathers could be awarded for peace and generosity as well as war, and the bonnet marks its wearer as a man or woman of proven standing, worn with the responsibility that leadership carries. The style has since been imitated widely in popular culture, but among Plains peoples the bonnet remains a serious, earned honour.

name: Wings of Daedalus
description: The feathered wings the craftsman Daedalus built with wax and thread to escape the labyrinth of Crete with his son Icarus, the most famous image of doomed invention in Greek myth. Ovid's Metamorphoses gives the fullest telling: Daedalus warns Icarus to fly neither too low, where the sea soaks the feathers, nor too high, where the sun melts the wax, but the boy exults in flight, rises, and falls into the sea that took his name, the Icarian. The wings were the answer to King Minos' prison of the labyrinth, and their construction, each feather set in order like a real bird's wing, shows Daedalus' art at its highest and most tragic. In later legend the flight is sometimes said to have ended in Sicily, where Daedalus found refuge with King Cocalus. The melting wing has become the standing warning against hubris and against exceeding the limits of human craft, and the tale endures in the proverb 'don't fly too close to the sun'.

name: Witch Bottle
description: The witch bottle is a stoneware or glass bottle packed with pins, needles, nails, broken glass, hair and often urine, sealed tightly and hidden in a wall, chimney, hearth or floor of a home to protect it from witchcraft. The practice, brought from England and Europe to colonial America, worked by drawing the witch's curse into the bottle and then returning the harm to its sender; the pins and sharp contents were meant to wound the witch who sent the spell. Scores of such bottles have been excavated from colonial American buildings and English houses, often dating from the 17th to the 19th centuries, and similar 'spirit bottles' were buried to trap demons and fairies. Folklore says the bottle should be kept in the dark and never opened or broken, or the trapped harm is released. The witch bottle is among the most archaeologically visible forms of folk magic in the Anglo-American world.

name: Witch Broom
description: The broom (kvast) that, in Swedish folk belief, carried witches to Blåkulla, the witches' sabbath mountain, especially on Maundy Thursday before Easter. The 'påskkärring', the Easter witch, was thought to ride a broom, or a cow, goat, or pitchfork, to Blåkulla. People blocked chimneys and hid brooms behind stoves to stop the flights, and the belief shaped Sweden's Easter-witch custom. The journey was said to take place on Maundy Thursday night, when the witches flew to the mountain, danced, and made their pact with the devil; families therefore stopped up their chimneys, barred their doors, and hid every broom, for a broom left within reach could carry off the household's own luck. Children were forbidden to go out, and the custom of dressing children as Easter witches — with broomsticks and painted cheeks — grew directly out of this old night of fear. The belief is recorded in the witchcraft trials of the seventeenth century, where the flight to Blåkulla was confessed again and again.

name: Woomera
description: The woomera is the spear-throwing lever of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, a wooden handle with a peg or socket at one end that lengthens the thrower's arm and hurls a spear with far greater force and distance than the arm alone. It is shaped from a flat or curved branch with stone tools, and the peg is fixed with resin, and in the central and western regions it was the standard hunting and fighting weapon, with the same tool doubling as a dish, a digging stick or a fire-maker. The woomera was used across most of the continent, though it was unknown in Tasmania, and in initiation it may be engraved with the designs of the clan and treated with respect. The name entered English from the Dharug language of the Sydney region, and the tool is also known by the name miru in some areas.

name: Wycinanka
description: Wycinanka is the Polish folk art of paper cutting, practised above all by village women from the nineteenth century, who folded and snipped dyed paper with heavy sheep shears to make flat wall decorations. Regional schools differ sharply: the celebrated cutouts of Łowicz build up layers of brightly coloured paper into leafy bouquets, rosettes and birds, while Kurpie makers favour single-colour, symmetrical designs such as the jedynak, cut from one folded sheet in black, red or gold.
