The cutouts were pasted on the whitewashed beams and walls of rural cottages, hung around holy pictures and given as wedding gifts, borrowing their motifs freely from embroidery, tile painting and woven bands. Though few farmhouses now display them in the old way, wycinanki survive as an emblem of Polish folk identity, taught in workshops and collected in ethnographic museums such as those at Łowicz and Warsaw.

name: Xalam Lute
description: The xalam is a plucked five-string lute of the Wolof of Senegal, with a calabash or carved wooden bowl body, a skin head, and strings grouped into two melody and three rhythm strings. Played by griots (gewel), it produces the interlocking lines that back praise-songs, genealogies, and narrative epics, and its twanging rhythms support both festive dance music and the serious recitation of lineage history. Across the Sahel the same instrument appears under other names, such as the hoddu of the Fulani and the khalam, with each people tuning and playing it in its own idiom. A griot's xalam was far more than entertainment: the words carried by the strings could flatter, mock, or counsel, making the instrument the audible badge of the praise-singer's craft. Older songs survive within griot families, while contemporary musicians have carried the xalam onto popular stages, keeping the sound of praise orature alive in Senegal and the diaspora.

name: Xhosa Beadwork
description: Xhosa beadwork of South Africa is made with imported glass beads sewn onto leather, cotton, or cloth supports to create necklaces, aprons, headdresses, and panels of dress worn at the great passages of life. At initiation, the beads speak: the colours and patterns worn by a young man in the circumcision school, and by the women who celebrate his return, carry coded messages of love, status, and clan that are meant to be read by the initiated. Married women wear beadwork that records their lineage and their husband's house, while older styles of white and blue bands gave way to the bright colour families of the modern era. Beadwork was a woman's art, taught by mothers and grandmothers, and its patterns changed with fashion while keeping their social grammar. Today Xhosa beadwork is worn at weddings, initiation feasts, and church festivals, and the beaded garments of the Red Xhosa communities of the Eastern Cape remain the most photographed tradition. Cooperatives and designers now sell Xhosa beadwork across South Africa and abroad.

name: Xiuhuitzolli
description: The xiuhuitzolli is the pointed diadem of turquoise mosaic worn by the Aztec tlatoque, the supreme rulers, as the emblem of sovereignty, its name meaning 'pointed thing of turquoise.' The right to wear it was held to come from the gods and to pass with the kingship, and colonial accounts record that the ruler Motecuhzoma was crowned with one at his accession. The Codex Mendoza and the Florentine Codex show the crown above a headband of the same mosaic, and the turquoise itself was a material charged with solar and divine significance, gathered through long-distance trade and set by master lapidaries. The xiuhuitzolli was one element of a full regalia that included the nose-piece, ear-plugs, and the royal cloak, and its loss at the conquest was read as the end of legitimate Aztec rule. Surviving turquoise mosaic crowns and their fragments are among the most treasured objects of the museums of Mexico and Europe, and the diadem remains the icon of Aztec sovereignty.

name: Yap Stone Money (Rai)
description: Large circular discs of quarried calcite used as currency on the island of Yap, some measuring several metres across and weighing many tonnes, each with a central hole for carrying on a pole. The rai were quarried on Palau and sailed back to Yap by raft and canoe, and their value was fixed not by size alone but by the difficulty of the voyage and the lives lost in obtaining them — a stone that sank on the way was still counted as wealth because ownership was remembered. Since the discs were too heavy to move, ownership was recorded in memory and passed on orally at marriages, land deals and debts, so that a family's wealth stood in the village's recollection as much as in the stone itself.

name: Yaranga (Chukchi Portable Dwelling)
description: Large hemispherical tent dwelling of the coastal Chukchi, built on a wooden frame of poles and whale ribs and covered with walrus skins, with reindeer hides laid inside against the cold. A family camp could stretch up to twenty metres; inside, fur-lined sleeping chambers formed separate rooms. The yaranga was central to Chukchi coastal life. Its frame is assembled from long poles set in a circle and tied at the top, with heavy walrus hides laid over the sides and secured against the wind with stones and lines; the interior is divided into a cold outer ring and a warm inner chamber, the polog, a tent of reindeer hides where the family sleeps. Reindeer-herding Chukchi carried lighter versions that could be packed on sleds and pitched in an hour, while the coastal people built the heavier skin yarangas of the sea-hunters. The yaranga is sometimes said to turn its entrance away from the wind, and travellers could enter it even without invitation. Skins and poles are still used in Chukotka today.

name: Yasakani no Magatama
description: The curved jade bead (magatama) dangled from the branch of the sacred sakaki tree beside the mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave, and counted among the Three Sacred Treasures of Japan it symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's mandate to rule. The comma-shaped bead is far older than the myth, appearing in Jomon ornament and by the hundreds in Kofun-period tomb jewellery, where the huge jasper magatama found in the great burial mounds shows how much the form was treasured. The name Yasakani is explained in the chronicles as 'the jewel of Yasaka', a place-name tied to the shrine of Yasaka in Kyoto, though the identification is disputed. Together with the mirror and the sword, the magatama stands for the gentleness of the sovereign, one of the three treasures that together legitimise the imperial throne.

name: Yata no Kagami
description: The Eight-Fold Mirror hung from a sacred sakaki tree outside the rock-cave in which the sun goddess Amaterasu had hidden, its brilliance luring her out to illuminate the world again, in the central myth of Japanese kingship. Revered at Ise Grand Shrine as the mirror of the Three Sacred Treasures, it is held to represent the sun goddess and, with the jewel and the sword, the imperial regalia; its polished face stands for truth and reflection in Shinto thought. The mirror, like the other treasures, is wrapped and kept from public view, so that all descriptions of it rest on the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki rather than on sight. Bronze mirrors from the Yayoi and Kofun periods, found in burials by the hundreds, show how old and how central the sacred mirror was to the culture that gave Amaterasu her tale.

name: Yeibichai Mask
description: The yeibichai masks of the Navajo are painted buckskin masks worn by dancers in the Nightway, the great nine-night healing ceremony, so that the wearer may embody a Holy Person, or ye'i, such as Talking God (Yeibichai) or Water Sprinkler. Made anew for each ceremony under strict rules and handled only by initiated singers and dancers, the masks carry the facial markings, colours and headgear that identify each Holy Person to the community. The Nightway chants invoke the blessing of the Holy People and call on Changing Woman, the great female deity of Navajo tradition, and the other powers of the Fourth World. Because the masks are so sacred, they are traditionally never sold, displayed publicly or photographed, and knowledge of their making is closely guarded. In the ceremony the masked dancers' final public dance is itself called the Yeibichai, the vivid climax of a rite meant to restore balance and health.

name: Yeouiju
description: The yeouiju is the wish-granting jewel of Korean lore, the glowing orb that a serpent, imugi, must grasp to climb into full dragonhood, and that grants any wish to its holder. In the tales the imugi, a hornless dragon, waits for the jewel to fall from the sky or to be revealed by a righteous person, and the story of the imugi that lost the jewel at the waterfall is among the most famous Korean dragon tales. The yeouiju is also described as the possession of the dragon kings of the sea and of the mountain spirits, and its power is sometimes linked to the moon, whose light it is said to drink. In Buddhist-influenced versions the jewel is identified with the cintamani, the wish-fulfilling gem, and in shamanic tradition it is a shaman's treasure. The yeouiju appears in the imagery of the dokkaebi goblin as well, and it remains one of the most evocative objects of Korean mythic symbolism, standing for the attainment of the unattainable.

name: Yule Goat
description: The Yule goat (julbock), a goat figure of straw bound with red ribbon, made in Sweden at Christmas. The straw goat descends from older beliefs around Thor's goats and the 'julbock' who once brought the Christmas gifts before the tree took the role. Today the most famous example is the giant Gävle goat, erected and burned each December. In older custom the julbock walked the house at Christmastime, demanding drink and carrying the Christmas presents, and a man dressed as the goat was one of the stock figures of the old rural Christmas. The straw goat, made of bound and tied straw with red ribbon at the horns, is the decorative descendant of that figure, and it is hung on the tree or set beneath it as a charm of the season. Since 1966 the town of Gävle has raised a huge straw goat in its square each December, and its repeated burning by pranksters has made the Gävle goat a world-famous piece of Christmas folklore.

name: Yumi Bow
description: The yumi, the tall Japanese longbow, is asymmetrical, with its grip placed below the centre, a design that lets an archer shoot from horseback and from the knee without the lower limb striking the saddle or the ground; the true yumi is a composite of bamboo slats glued and bound together, often with wood and hemp, in the long tradition of the master bowyers. From the Heian period the bow was the samurai's chief weapon, and the court archery contests of the era made the yumi an instrument of ceremony and status as well as of war. The chronicles of the long-shooting contests at Sanjūsangen-dō record archers who sent arrows astonishing distances along the temple porch. The yumi's great length gives it a long draw and a strong, clean release, and it remains in use in kyūdō, the modern martial art of the bow, little changed from its medieval form. It is both a status symbol of the warrior class and a living piece of Japanese ritual.

name: Zangbeto Masquerade Costume
description: The zangbeto is the towering masquerade of the Fon of Benin, a cone-shaped costume of plaited straw and raffia worn over the body so that only a skirt of fibers is seen, with the performer hidden inside making the figure spin, whirl and race through the streets of its own accord. The word means 'night watchman,' and the zangbeto is exactly that: the masked guardian of the town that patrols after dark, hunting witches and thieves, and every village has its zangbeto society with its initiates and its rules. The costume is never empty, the spirit is said to enter it, and the figure dances, chants and admonishes the crowd, keeping the peace through a mixture of awe and discipline. The zangbeto is rooted in the Vodun religion of southern Benin and Togo, where it protects the community and judges wrongdoers. When the straw figure spins in the dark, the line between costume and spirit is meant to be forgotten.

name: Zanzibar Dhow
description: The dhow (jahazi) of Zanzibar is a lateen-sailed wooden vessel built on the Swahili coast for fishing, cargo, and the trade that rode the monsoons across the Indian Ocean. Hulls were traditionally sewn with coconut-coir fibre and caulked, and the ships carried ivory, cloves, mangrove poles, and grain between East Africa, Arabia, and India. The pattern of the monsoons set the rhythm of the whole coast: dhows sailed out on the kusi winds and returned with the kaskazi, and captains timed their passages by the stars. Seafaring was wrapped in maritime belief, and sailors made offerings and prayers to win the favour of the pepo, the sea spirits who were believed to command wind and water. The same trade carried the brasswork, textiles, and coral-stone architecture that shaped the coastal towns. Today traditional dhows still fish the Zanzibar channel, and the wooden dhow industry survives alongside modern vessels.

name: Zemi (Taino Effigy)
description: The zemi is the carved effigy through which the Taíno of the Greater Antilles kept their spirits close: figures of wood, stone, bone or cotton, shaped by carvers to hold a spirit and kept in the household, in the fields, or in the house of the cacique. The behique, the ritual specialist, consulted them for health, harvests and answers, and Spanish accounts describe caciques who owned great numbers of them, receiving the first fruits and offering cures before them. Some zemis were consulted in the cohoba ceremony, when the behique inhaled the powder of the sacred seeds and spoke the spirit's words, and a few wooden examples survive from the islands, carved with crouching human forms and small cavities for offerings. The word zemi names both the spirit itself and the object that houses it, so the effigy is the spirit given a body. Today they are prized museum pieces and a central symbol of Taíno heritage in Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic.

name: Zulu Iwisa Knobkerrie
description: The iwisa, often called the knobkerrie, is a Zulu club made from a single piece of hardwood, with a heavy round knob at the top of a straight or slightly curved handle. It was a close-combat weapon of the Zulu army, carried beside the spear and thrown or swung in the close fights of the impi, and it remained a warrior's constant companion when herding and walking. In peacetime the iwisa became a staff of rank: chiefs, headmen, and later officials carried finely carved examples, and the club is still raised in the air at ceremonies, weddings, and political gatherings as a gesture of authority. Craftsmen shaped the knob and handle with an adze and burnished them smooth, and the best pieces are polished to a deep shine. The knobkerrie has spread beyond the Zulu, serving as the famous weapon and walking stick of southern African leadership.

name: Zulu Iziqu Necklace
description: The iziqu is the necklace of a Zulu warrior, made of carved wooden beads strung on a cord and worn across the chest as a mark of valour. After a king recognised a man for bravery in battle, the warrior was permitted to carve and string the necklace himself, usually from the wood of the thorn tree, and each row was said to record a heroic deed; Maclean, who saw the court of Shaka in 1825, described the necklaces as orders of merit conferred by the king's own hand. The iziqu was the second-highest decoration of the Zulu army after the brass armband (ingxotha), and the carved beads could be combined with bone, horn, and skin in protective war charms. The most famous string, the long wooden necklace of King Dinizulu, was taken by Robert Baden-Powell in 1888 and inspired the wooden beads of the Scout Wood Badge. A giant bronze iziqu crowns the Isandlwana monument honouring the Zulu army of 1879. Today the iziqu is remembered as one of the few personal honours a common warrior could win.

name: Zulu Ukhamba Beer Pot
description: The ukhamba is the clay beer pot of the Zulu, a round, low-necked vessel fired from local clay and used to brew and serve utshwala, the sorghum beer at the centre of Zulu hospitality. Beer is not everyday drink but the medium of ceremony: it is brewed by women, offered to the ancestors at the start of every gathering, and shared at marriages, funerals, and the community work-parties that bind homesteads together. The pot's shape is practical, the round belly holding the fermenting beer and the narrow mouth keeping it clean, and the clay keeps the beer cool. Well-made ukhamba are prized, and a woman's skill at brewing and presenting beer is a matter of family pride. Decorated pots, incised with patterns or fitted with beadwork covers, are made for important occasions, and Zulu pottery has been collected and exhibited as art. The ukhamba remains in daily use in KwaZulu-Natal alongside the woven beer-strainers and calabashes that complete the brewing set.

name: Ægishjálmr
description: Ægishjálmr, the 'helm of awe' or 'helm of terror', is a protective sign of Norse and Icelandic tradition, drawn as a wheel of radiating prongs or staves. In the poem Fáfnismál the dragon Fáfnir is said to have worn the helm of awe, and the hero Sigurðr takes it as part of the dragon's hoard, suggesting a literal helmet in the oldest layer of the story. From the early modern period the name came to be attached to an eight-armed magical stave of the Icelandic galdrabækur, drawn on the forehead between the brows or on the brow of a person to strike fear into enemies and give victory and protection; the 17th-century grimoire tradition is where the familiar branched symbol comes from. The two uses are sometimes confused, and it is likely the modern stave design and the Eddic helmet are different things that share a name. Ægishjálmr remains one of the most reproduced of all Icelandic staves, in tattoos, jewellery, and fantasy art.

name: Óttastafur
description: Óttastafur, the 'fear stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn to strike fear into others. As a weapon of psychological magic it was meant to cow rivals or enemies without a single blow, so that the bearer's will prevailed and opponents lost heart. It is one of the aggressive galdrastafir, sitting in the same grimoires as the protective and luck-giving staves and showing that the stave tradition served harm as readily as help. Its earliest known source is a 19th-century manuscript that collected older folk-magic material, and like the other fear signs it is now reproduced in modern books and on tattoos. The fear stave is a reminder that Icelandic folk magic was a two-edged craft, used as often to intimidate as to defend.

name: Óðrœrir
description: Óðrœrir is the kettle that holds the mead of poetry, brewed by the dwarves Fjalar and Galar from the blood of Kvasir, the wisest of beings, mixed with honey. Whoever drinks the mead gains the gift of poetry and wisdom, and the brew is stored in three vessels — the great kettle Óðrœrir and the two bowls Boðn and Són. The giant Suttungr seized the mead after the dwarves killed his parents, and Odin stole it back from Suttungr's daughter Gunnlöð, drinking all of Óðrœrir in three draughts and escaping in eagle form. A little of the mead is said to have been spilled from Odin's beak, and that spill became the portion that is given to poets on earth. The name is sometimes interpreted as 'stirrer of inspiration' or 'mind-rousing one', and the mead remains the central symbol of skaldic poetry and of the gift of verse.

name: Þjófastafur
description: Þjófastafur, the 'thief stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn to guard livestock and goods against theft. The name literally means 'thief-stave', and the sign was meant to make a thief unable to take what belonged to the bearer, or to bring him back to face the community. It answered a real fear on isolated farmsteads, where herds and household goods had no other defence against thieves and wanderers. It belongs to the protective family of galdrastafir, and like most of the staves it is known from a 19th-century manuscript that preserved older folk tradition rather than from any Viking-Age source. The thief stave is still reproduced in books and on jewellery, and the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík displays it among the protective signs of the grimoire tradition.

name: Šajkača
description: The šajkača is the traditional Serbian cap, a rounded woollen cap with a raised crown whose four points fold into a characteristic V shape, made from a single piece of cloth and worn without a visor. Its name honours the šajkaši, the eighteenth-century Serbian river troops who crewed the šajka boats of the Danube and Sava under Habsburg command and who first wore the shape. From the nineteenth century the šajkača spread beyond the river garrisons to Serbian soldiers, teachers, priests and peasants, becoming a badge of Serbian national identity, worn in the Balkan Wars and the First World War and banned by the occupiers during the Second. The V of the crown is sometimes read as the spread wings of the eagle, and today the cap is worn at ceremonies, in folk ensembles and by diaspora Serbs as a mark of origin and belonging.
